concepts/national-debt-and-public-credit.title: The National Debt and Public Credit
concepts/national-debt-and-public-credit.content:
The National Debt and Public Credit
The national debt of Great Britain, and the system of public credit upon which it rested, was the most remarkable and the most debated financial innovation of the 18th century. It was, at one and the same time, the engine of Britain’s military power, the foundation of the monied interest’s prosperity, and the subject of the darkest forebodings from some of the most acute minds of the age.
Origins: The 1690s and the Birth of the Funding System
The national debt, properly so called, was born with the Revolution Settlement of 1688–1689. The War of the Grand Alliance (1689–1697) required sums far beyond the ordinary revenues of the Crown. The expedient adopted was the funded debt — the practice of borrowing upon permanent taxes, the interest upon which was secured by Act of Parliament, thereby giving the lender a legal claim upon the revenues of the state that no future administration could repudiate without a breach of parliamentary faith.
The Bank of England, incorporated in 1694, was the institutional centrepiece of the new system. Its foundation, as every historian has observed, was the work of Mr. William Paterson, a Scottish projector who perceived that the government’s desperate need for money might be turned to the advantage of private subscribers. The Bank advanced £1.2 million to the government at eight per cent interest, and received in return a charter of incorporation, the right to issue notes, and the management of the Exchequer accounts. The success of this experiment encouraged a number of imitative projects — most notably the South Sea Company, founded in 1711, which undertook to manage a portion of the unfunded debt in exchange for a monopoly of the trade to the South Seas.
The South Sea Crisis
The South Sea Scheme, so fully narrated by Mr. Smollett (Smollett History Vol X), was the first great crisis of public credit. The Company’s proposals, accepted by the legislature in 1720, involved the conversion of the greater part of the unprovided debt into South Sea stock, on terms that gave the Company the expectation of enormous profits from the supposed riches of the South American trade. The frenzy of speculation that followed — the South Sea Bubble — raised the price of the stock to above one thousand per cent of its nominal value, and its collapse brought ruin to thousands.
The crisis was a revelation of the dangers inherent in the funding system. The monied interest, which had grown powerful upon the profits of government loans, was seen to be vulnerable to the same passions of avarice and credulity that affected the rest of mankind. The public credit of the nation was shaken. It required the resolute exertions of Sir Robert Walpole to restore confidence and to carry through the necessary measures of financial reconstruction.
Walpole’s Cure: The Sinking Fund and the Restoration of Credit
Walpole’s management of the aftermath of the South Sea crisis established the principles upon which British public credit was to rest for the remainder of the century. The Sinking Fund, first established in 1717, was revived and rendered more systematic. Certain branches of the revenue were appropriated to the gradual redemption of the principal of the debt, and the government pledged itself to the punctual payment of the interest upon all funded obligations.
The restoration of credit was not achieved by a single measure but by a combination of prudent administration, the cultivation of confidence among the monied men of the City, and the avoidance of any measure that might shake the faith of the public in the government’s good faith. Walpole’s peace policy, which kept Britain out of European war for two decades, allowed the debt to be reduced and the revenues to be augmented by the natural growth of trade.
War Finance, 1739–1763
The wars of the mid-century — the War of Jenkins’ Ear, the War of the Austrian Succession, and the Seven Years’ War — placed the funding system under strain. Each war required the negotiation of new loans upon terms that reflected the increased risk of default. The cost of borrowing, as Dr. Joseph Massie demonstrated in his computations of the natural rate of interest, rose markedly in time of war, as the competition for capital between the government and the private sector drove up the price of money.
Captain Campbell, in his Naval History (Campbell Naval History Vol III), records the prodigious sums expended upon the naval establishment alone. The building of a first-rate ship of the line might cost £60,000 or more; the annual expense of a fleet of thirty ships of the line, including wages, victuals, stores, and repairs, might amount to two or three millions. These sums were borrowed upon the credit of the nation, and their repayment was deferred to an indefinite futurity.
By the Peace of Paris 1763, the national debt stood at approximately £132 million — a figure that, as Mr. Smollett observes, would have been thought incredible fifty years earlier. The annual charge for interest alone amounted to nearly £5 million, a sum that consumed a large proportion of the ordinary revenues.
Pitt’s Sinking Fund, 1786
The conclusion of the American war left the national debt at an unprecedented height: approximately £250 million. Mr. William Pitt the Younger, upon his accession to the Treasury in 1783, made the reduction of the debt one of the principal objects of his administration.
The Sinking Fund of 1786, as described by Mr. Belsham (Belsham Memoirs Vol IV), was the most ambitious scheme of debt redemption ever attempted. One million pounds per annum was to be set aside from the surplus revenues, invested in the public funds under the management of a board of commissioners, and allowed to accumulate at compound interest. The fund was to be inviolable — no government might touch it for any purpose save the purchase or redemption of the public debt. The mathematical principle was that the fund, growing year by year, would eventually redeem the entire debt within a calculable period.
Mr. Pitt’s scheme was founded upon the writings of Dr. Richard Price, a dissenting minister of considerable learning, whose Observations on Reversionary Payments had argued for the extraordinary power of compound interest when applied to the reduction of the public debt. The scheme commanded the approbation of Parliament and of the monied interest, who saw in it a pledge of the government’s determination to maintain the public credit inviolate.
The Revolutionary War Debt: 1793–1801
The war with France, commencing in 1793, destroyed the Sinking Fund and produced an explosion of public borrowing beyond any previous example. The expenditures of the war were so vast that no surplus remained to feed the fund; the borrowed sums themselves exceeded anything in the previous history of the nation.
Mr. Belsham supplies the figures: the debt rose from approximately £240 million in 1793 to upwards of £450 million by 1801. The interest upon the debt consumed the greater part of the annual revenue. The expedients of Mr. Pitt — the income tax, the assessed taxes, the multiplication of duties — were insufficient to keep pace with the demand for money. The nation was living upon credit, and that credit was sustained only by the exertions of the Bank of England, whose gold reserves were diminished to a point that caused the greatest anxiety.
Contemporary Critiques: Hume, Price, and the Alarmists
The growth of the national debt was not contemplated with equanimity by the most thoughtful observers of the age. Mr. David Hume, in his celebrated essay Of Public Credit (in his Political Discourses), delivered a warning that resounded through the century. Either the nation must destroy public credit, Hume wrote, or public credit will destroy the nation. He argued that the accumulation of debt must eventually produce either national bankruptcy, or a ruinous increase of taxation, or the destruction of the liberty of the subject by the extension of executive power.
Dr. Price, though the architect of Mr. Pitt’s Sinking Fund, shared some of Hume’s apprehensions. He believed that the debt, if not reduced, would ultimately crush the nation under its weight. His calculations of the compound growth of the fund were intended to show a path to deliverance — but they assumed a peace and prosperity that the war with France was to deny.
The alarmists — for such they were called by the advocates of the funding system — pointed to the example of France, whose credit had collapsed under the burdens of the old monarchy, and to the spectacle of the assignats, whose depreciation had brought ruin to the French Revolution. They argued that the British system, for all its apparent solidity, was built upon sand.

concepts/naval-power.title: Naval Power and Maritime Strategy
concepts/naval-power.content:
Naval Power and Maritime Strategy
The Royal Navy was the foundation upon which the entire edifice of British power in the eighteenth century was built. It protected the trade that financed the Fiscal-Military State, blockaded the ports of France and Spain, transported and supplied the armies that fought in America and India, and secured the colonial possessions that were the material basis of British wealth. The Navy’s dockyards, its manning system, its tactical doctrines, and its administrative infrastructure were the largest and most complex industrial organisation in the British Isles — and the most expensive. The cost of the Navy dominated the budgets of every eighteenth-century administration.
The Dockyard System
The Royal Dockyards at Portsmouth, Plymouth, Chatham, Deptford, Woolwich, and Sheerness were among the largest industrial establishments in Europe. They employed thousands of artisans — shipwrights, caulkers, ropemakers, sailmakers, blacksmiths — who built, repaired, and fitted out the ships of the fleet. Campbell, in his Naval History of Great Britain, describes the scale of operations: a first-rate ship of the line required the timber of approximately 2,000 oaks, took three to four years to build, and cost £60,000–£80,000.
Portsmouth was the premier dockyard, the home of the Channel Fleet and the base for the close blockade of Brest. Plymouth (Plymouth Dock, renamed Devonport in 1824) was the western base, essential for the Western Squadron’s operations in the Bay of Biscay. Chatham, on the Medway, was the principal building yard for ships of the line. The Victualling Board supplied the fleet with provisions from its own bakeries, breweries, and slaughterhouses; the Navy Board managed the timber supply, the Ordnance Board the guns.
The greatest administrative challenge of the dockyard system was the supply of timber. The Navy consumed an estimated 100,000 oaks per year at the peak of the eighteenth-century wars. The forests of the Baltic — Poland, Prussia, and Russia — supplied the naval stores (hemp, flax, pitch, tar, masts) that British forests could not provide. The dependence on Baltic supplies was a strategic vulnerability of the first order, a major consideration in British policy toward the northern powers.
Manning the Fleet
The manning of the Navy was the most intractable problem of British naval administration. In peacetime, the Navy employed perhaps 15,000 men; in wartime, this number expanded to 80,000–120,000. The means by which these men were obtained was impressment — the legal power to compel men into naval service, exercised by press gangs operating in port towns and at sea, and by the interception of homeward-bound merchant vessels.
Impressment was hated and feared by the seafaring population. It was also inefficient: pressed men made unreliable sailors, prone to desertion and, in extremis, to mutiny. The Quota Acts of 1795, passed in response to the manning crisis of the French Revolutionary Wars, required each county to supply a specified number of men for the Navy — a system that transferred the burden of impressment from the maritime counties to the whole kingdom.
The bounty system offered an alternative: volunteers who joined the Navy received a cash bounty, typically £5 (rising to £30 during the French wars). But the bounty was never enough to supply the fleet’s needs, and impressment remained the foundation of naval manning throughout the century. Campbell, a former purser in the Navy, wrote with direct experience of the system’s injustices.
The Western Squadron
The most important strategic innovation of the mid-century Navy was the development of the Western Squadron — a permanent cruising force stationed off the coast of Brittany, whose purpose was to maintain a close blockade of the French Atlantic port of Brest. Edward Hawke, who perfected the system during the Seven Years’ War, kept his fleet at sea throughout the winter of 1758–59, a feat of seamanship and organisation that had no precedent in naval history.
The close blockade of Brest achieved two strategic objects. First, it prevented the French Brest fleet from putting to sea without being intercepted — the prelude to Hawke’s great victory at the Battle of Quiberon Bay in November 1759. Second, it protected British trade routes and colonial expeditions by denying the French the freedom of the seas. The Western Squadron system, refined by Richard Howe and John Jervis in the later wars, remained the central strategic doctrine of the Royal Navy until the age of steam.
The Line of Battle and Tactical Innovation
The standard tactical formation of the eighteenth-century Navy was the line of battle — ships arranged in a single line ahead, each ship engaging its opposite number in the enemy line. The line was a defensive and an offensive formation simultaneously: it maximised the firepower that could be brought to bear while minimising the risk of being broken by a superior force.
The line-of-battle tactic had been established by the Fighting Instructions of the Commonwealth and Stuart eras, and it was followed with religious fidelity by most admirals. The great tactical innovators of the century were those who, at decisive moments, departed from the line. George Rooke at Vigo Bay (1702) and George Byng at Cape Passaro (1718) demonstrated the rewards of aggressive pursuit. Edward Hawke at Quiberon Bay abandoned the line entirely, ordering a general chase into a rock-strewn bay in a winter gale. George Rodney at the Battle of the Saintes (1782) broke the French line by passing through it — a manoeuvre that became the signature of Horatio Nelson’s tactical genius.
Prize Money and the Naval Career
The economic incentive system of the Navy was prize money — the proceeds of enemy ships captured in war, distributed among the captors according to a fixed scale. The captain of a successful privateer or a lucky frigate commander could make a fortune from a single cruise. The “Prize Act” of 1708 established the principle that the proceeds of captured enemy property belonged to the captors, subject to the droits of the Admiralty.
Prize money was the engine of the naval career. Young officers of ambition and ability — Nelson, Collingwood, John Jervis — were driven by the desire for prize wealth as much as by professional honour. But the system had its dark side: it encouraged the pursuit of private gain over the public service, and it created bitter disputes over the division of spoil.
The Health of the Fleet
The health of the fleet was a constant preoccupation of naval administrators. Scurvy — the deficiency of vitamin C — destroyed more seamen than enemy action. The voyages of George Anson (1740–44) and John Byron (1764–66) had demonstrated the mortality that scurvy could inflict: Anson’s squadron lost 1,300 men out of 1,900, the great majority to disease. The experiments of Dr James Lind (1754), who demonstrated that citrus juice prevented scurvy, were slow to be adopted by the Admiralty, but by the end of the century lemon juice was a standard issue on long voyages.
The naval hospital system — Haslar at Gosport (1746) and Stonehouse at Plymouth (1762) — provided the first purpose-built military hospitals in Britain. The sick and wounded were treated, invalids pensioned, and the dead buried at government expense. The health reforms of the later century, particularly under the administration of John Jervis as First Lord of the Admiralty (1801–1804), significantly reduced the mortality rate of the fleet.
The Mutinies of 1797
The Spithead and Nore mutinies of 1797 were the greatest crisis of discipline in the history of the Royal Navy. In April 1797, the Channel Fleet at Spithead refused to put to sea, demanding higher pay, better provisions, and shore leave — the “Spithead demands.” The mutineers acted with remarkable discipline and moderation, maintaining the routine of the fleet while refusing to sail. The Admiralty, after a tense standoff, granted most of the demands.
The Nore mutiny, which followed in May, was more dangerous and more radical. Led by Richard Parker, a former naval officer turned mutineer, the mutineers blockaded the Thames and demanded political reforms that went beyond pay and conditions. The government, fearing that the mutiny was part of a revolutionary conspiracy (the Irish Rebellion of 1798 was brewing), refused to negotiate. Parker was hanged, the mutiny collapsed, and the authority of the Admiralty was restored. The mutinies demonstrated both the legitimate grievances of the common seaman and the fragility of discipline in a fleet that had been expanded rapidly to meet the demands of total war.
The Cost
The naval estimates were the largest single item in the British budget. In the decade after the Peace of Paris (1763), the Navy cost approximately £2 million per annum in peacetime; during the French Revolutionary Wars, the cost rose to £8–10 million per annum. The naval debt — the accumulated arrears of naval expenditure — was a major contributor to the growth of the national debt and a constant preoccupation of Chancellors of the Exchequer.

concepts/parliamentary-patronage.title: Parliamentary Patronage and Old Corruption
concepts/parliamentary-patronage.content:
Parliamentary Patronage and Old Corruption
Parliamentary patronage — the system by which the Crown, the ministers, and the great aristocratic families exercised influence over the composition and conduct of the House of Commons through the disposal of offices, pensions, contracts, and electoral interest — was the organising principle of 18th-century political life. To understand this system is to understand the actual workings of the constitution, as distinct from its theory.
The Structure of Patronage
The Crown was the greatest patron in the kingdom. The disposal of offices in the royal household, the civil administration, the army, the navy, the church, the judiciary, and the revenue departments — amounting to many hundreds of places — gave the Crown an immense influence over those who held them. Every placement, from the Lord Chamberlain to the humblest clerk in the Excise Office, was assumed to owe some degree of gratitude and deference to the government of the day.
The system of pensions was almost as extensive. Secret service pensions, payable from the Treasury and charged upon the Civil List, were distributed to Members of Parliament whose support was thought necessary to the administration. Mr. Edmund Burke, in his Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents, complained that the influence of the Crown had increased, was increasing, and ought to be diminished — a phrase that became the rallying-cry of the opposition. He described a system by which the Crown, by the lavish distribution of its favours, had created a corps of “king’s friends” in Parliament, whose attachment was to the executive rather than to the public interest.
Government contracts — for the supply of the army, the navy, and the ordnance — were another great engine of influence. The merchants, manufacturers, and ship-owners who enjoyed these contracts were expected to support the administration in Parliament and at elections. The system, as Mr. Smollett observes (Smollett History Vol X), was the subject of perpetual complaint, but no ministry could dispense with it, for without it the business of government could not be carried on.
The Management of Parliament
The management of the House of Commons was the supreme art of 18th-century politics. Sir Robert Walpole, who perfected this art, governed by a combination of argument, bribery, and intimidation that his enemies called corruption and his friends called prudence. The “Treasury boroughs” — those constituencies in which the Crown or its officers possessed a decisive electoral interest — secured the return of Members who could be relied upon to support the administration. The number of such boroughs has been variously estimated; a careful calculation suggests that between fifty and seventy Members owed their seats directly to Treasury influence.
The “paymaster of the forces” was a particularly important figure in this system. The paymaster held vast sums of public money in his hands, which he could employ for political purposes before they were paid over to the troops. The accumulation of these balances, and the interest they yielded, made the office one of the most profitable in the gift of the Crown. The Paymaster General, as Mr. Belsham notes (Belsham Memoirs Vol IV), was in a position to oblige contractors, bankers, and Members of Parliament by the timely distribution of these funds.
The Rotten Borough System
The unequal distribution of seats in Parliament was the foundation upon which the patronage system rested. The ancient boroughs, many of them decayed villages or deserted fields, retained the right of returning Members, while great manufacturing towns such as Manchester, Leeds, and Birmingham sent none.
Old Sarum, a hilltop with a single inhabitant, returned two Members to Parliament. Gatton, with seven houses, returned two. A map of the parliamentary representation of the kingdom would have shown a concentration of Members in the southern and eastern counties, where the Crown and the aristocracy were strongest, and a deficiency in the north and the midlands, where the new manufacturing population had grown up without political rights.
The purchase of boroughs was an open and recognised practice. The price of a pocket borough — one in which the proprietor controlled both seats — varied according to the length of the Parliament and the temper of the electors. The Septennial Act of 1716 (Septennial Act 1716), which extended the maximum duration of Parliament from three to seven years, increased the value of borough property by giving the purchaser a longer term of enjoyment.
The Reform Movement: Burke’s Economical Reform and Wyvill’s Associations
The abuses of the patronage system gave rise, in the last quarter of the century, to a powerful movement for reform. The American war, which many attributed to the corrupt influence of the Crown, gave the movement its first great impetus.
Mr. Burke’s Economical Reform Bill of 1780 was the most comprehensive attempt to reduce the influence of the Crown by abolishing useless offices and restricting the disposal of public money. Burke proposed to abolish the Board of Trade, the Board of Works, the Treasurer of the Chamber, the Cofferer of the Household, and many other offices whose principal function was to provide places for the friends of the administration. He also sought to restrict the pension list and to prevent the grant of pensions to Members of Parliament. The measure was only partially successful; the opposition of the court, and the defection of those who feared the loss of their places, prevented the full realisation of Burke’s design.
Mr. Wyvill’s county association movement, which flourished between 1779 and 1785, was a more radical challenge to the existing system. The county associations demanded a reform of Parliament — shorter Parliaments, the addition of county Members, the abolition of rotten boroughs — and the reduction of the influence of the Crown. The movement, which drew its support from the independent country gentlemen and the middling sort, was the most formidable extra-parliamentary agitation since the Wilkite disturbances.
Pitt’s Reforms
Mr. William Pitt the Younger, who entered office in 1783 as a declared friend of parliamentary reform, disappointed the hopes of the reformers. In 1785 he introduced a bill for the abolition of thirty-six rotten boroughs and the transfer of their seats to the counties and the metropolis, but the opposition of his own party, many of whom held borough property, compelled its withdrawal.
Pitt did, however, effect a moderate reduction of sinecures and useless places, particularly in the revenue departments. The India Act of 1784, which placed the government of British India under a Board of Control and restricted the patronage of the East India Company, was a more significant reform, for it transferred a vast body of appointments from the Company’s directors to the Crown, thereby increasing rather than diminishing the influence of the executive.
Contemporary Critiques
The system of patronage was not without its critics among contemporaries. The Country Party tradition, which extended from the early 18th century to the age of Wilkes, denounced the “monied interest” and the “court faction” as enemies of the ancient constitution. The freeholder, the independent country gentleman, and the honest citizen were called upon to resist the encroachments of executive power.
Mr. John Wilkes and the Middlesex electors made the corruption of Parliament the central issue of their agitation. The right of electors to choose their representatives freely, without the interference of the Crown or the aristocracy, was the constitutional principle upon which they insisted. The Society of Supporters of the Bill of Rights, founded in 1769, demanded annual Parliaments, the exclusion of placemen from the House of Commons, and the publication of the proceedings of Parliament.
The radical demands for reform, which grew louder after the outbreak of the French Revolution, went far beyond anything that the moderate reformers had contemplated. The abolition of the monarchy, the destruction of the House of Lords, and the establishment of universal suffrage were proclaimed by some as the necessary conditions of a free constitution.

concepts/party-government.title: Party Government and the Court-Country Divide
concepts/party-government.content:
Party Government and the Court-Country Divide
The 18th century witnessed a profound transformation in the character of British political life: the gradual shift from a politics of court and country, in which the central division was between the executive and its critics, to a politics of party, in which organised Whig and Tory connections contended for power. This transformation was neither simple nor linear, and its meaning was the subject of continuous debate among contemporaries.
The Country Tradition: Bolingbroke and the Patriot King
The early decades of the century were dominated by the ideological division between the Court and the Country parties. The Court party, which commanded the administration under the first two Georges, comprised those who accepted the Revolution Settlement, supported the Hanoverian succession, and looked to the Crown and the executive for leadership. The Country party, which formed the opposition in Parliament and in the press, drew upon a republican tradition of suspicion of executive power, denouncing the corruption of the court and the growth of the monied interest.
Lord Henry St John Bolingbroke, the most brilliant and dangerous of Walpole’s opponents, gave intellectual expression to the Country ideology in his Dissertation upon Parties and his posthumous Idea of a Patriot King. Bolingbroke denounced the system of Parliamentary corruption by which Walpole governed, and called for a “patriot” king who would free himself from party attachments and govern in the interest of the whole nation. The Patriot King, rising above faction, would restore the ancient constitution and reconcile the interests of Crown and people.
The Craftsman, the great Opposition journal of the 1720s and 1730s, disseminated Bolingbroke’s ideas to a wide audience. Every issue exposed the corruption of the Walpole administration, the venality of the Commons, and the danger to English liberty from the growth of executive power. The Country programme — shorter Parliaments, the exclusion of placemen, the reduction of the standing army, and the reform of the revenue — remained the staple of opposition politics for a generation.
The Whig Supremacy
The long ascendancy of Sir Robert Walpole (1721–1742) was the age of the so-called “Whig Supremacy.” The Whig party, which had been the party of the Revolution and the Protestant succession, was transformed under Walpole into an instrument of executive management. The great Whig families — the Pelhams, the Russells, the Cavendishes, the Lennoxes — were united by kinship, connection, and interest in the support of the administration.
The opposition Whigs, who followed William Pulteney and later William Pitt the Elder, accused Walpole of betraying the principles of the Revolution. The true Whig, they insisted, was a defender of liberty against executive encroachment, not a placeman who sold his independence for a Treasury place. The distinction between “Old Whigs” and “Court Whigs” — between the pure principles of 1688 and the corrupted practice of 1720 — became a staple of political argument.
The Tories, who had been proscribed from office since the accession of George I, survived as a parliamentary and electoral force, particularly in the counties and the smaller boroughs. The Tory party was identified with the Church of England, the landed interest, and suspicion of foreign entanglements. It was also, in some of its branches, implicated in the Jacobite Rising of 1715 and the Jacobite Rising of 1745, a stain that excluded it from power for half a century.
Burke’s Defence of Party
The legitimation of party as a legitimate instrument of political action was the work of Mr. Edmund Burke. In his Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770), Burke delivered the most celebrated defence of party in the English language. Party, he wrote, is “a body of men united, for promoting by their joint endeavours the national interest, upon some particular principle in which they are all agreed.” This was a direct challenge to the Country tradition, which had condemned party as faction, and to the Bolingbrokean ideal, which had looked to a patriot king to govern without party.
Burke argued that party was necessary to the working of a free constitution. Without party, the Crown would be able to govern by dividing the leading men and purchasing their support individually. Party provided the means by which men of principle could combine to resist the corrupt influence of the court, to hold the administration accountable, and to present the nation with a choice of men and measures.
The Rockingham Whigs, with whom Burke was associated, were the first party in the modern sense — a connection united by common principles, personal loyalty to the Marquis of Rockingham, and a commitment to the limitation of the Crown’s influence. They called themselves the “Old Whigs,” and they claimed to represent the true principles of the Revolution Settlement against the innovations of the court.
The Fox-North Coalition: A Crisis of Party Identity
The coalition of Mr. Charles James Fox with Lord Frederick North in 1783 exposed the ambiguities of party allegiance. Fox, the champion of the people and the critic of the Crown, had denounced Lord North throughout the American war as the minister who had lost the colonies. North, the author of the Coercive Acts and the defender of the royal prerogative, had been Fox’s bitterest enemy. Yet the two men, driven by a common hostility to the Shelburne administration and the rising influence of Mr. Pitt, formed a coalition that scandalised the political world.
The coalition, as Mr. Belsham observes (Belsham Memoirs Vol IV), was defended by its members on the ground that party attachments must yield to the necessity of forming a stable administration. The king, George III, regarded the coalition as a personal affront, and his determination to destroy it produced the constitutional crisis of 1783–1784.
Pitt’s “Tory” Revival
The election of 1784, which returned Mr. Pitt to power with a large majority, was represented by contemporaries as a victory for the Crown and the people against the aristocratic factions. Pitt called himself a Whig — the name “Tory” was still tainted by its association with Jacobitism — but his administration drew support from the old Tory interest in the counties and from those who had been alienated by the Fox-North coalition.
Mr. George III’s open support for Pitt, and his equally open hostility to Fox, gave the new administration a character distinct from the Whig oligarchy that had governed since the Revolution. The term “Tory” began to be used again, not as a term of abuse but as a description of a party that supported the Crown, the Church, and the established constitution against the innovations of reforming Whigs.
The Meaning of Party in the 18th Century
Party in the 18th century was not what it became in the 19th. It was not based upon mass membership, a national organisation, or a clearly defined programme. It was, rather, a connection of families, interests, and personal loyalties, held together by the distribution of patronage and the authority of a few great men.
Kinship was the cement of party. The great Whig families were connected by marriage and inheritance; the younger sons were provided for by the influence of the elders; the dead were remembered and the unborn provided for by the disposition of offices and livings. The party was the family in its political aspect, and the family was the party in its domestic aspect.
Interest was the motive of party. The pursuit of place, pension, and profit was not considered dishonourable; it was the natural end of political activity. The reform of abuses was the business of those who had nothing to hope from the existing system.
Ideology, though not absent, was subordinate to connection. Whig and Tory principles — the meaning of the Revolution, the rights of the Crown, the authority of Parliament — were invoked as occasions required, but they did not determine the conduct of parties with the force that modern experience would lead one to expect.

concepts/political-economy.title: Political Economy
concepts/political-economy.content:
Political Economy
The eighteenth century was the great age of British economic thought. In the hundred years between the publication of Sir William Petty’s Political Arithmetick and Adam Smith’s Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776), a series of British writers — Joseph Massie, David Hume, Malachy Postlethwayt, and Smith himself — transformed the understanding of how nations grow rich and how governments should conduct their economic affairs. The debates they initiated — over the nature of money, the determinants of interest, the balance of trade, the wisdom of colonial monopolies, and the role of the state in the economy — were not merely academic. They shaped the fiscal and commercial policies of the British state and the larger debate about the moral foundations of commercial society.
Mercantilism
The dominant economic doctrine of the early eighteenth century was mercantilism: the belief that national wealth consisted in the accumulation of precious metals, that exports should be encouraged and imports restricted, and that the state should actively regulate trade to secure a favourable balance. The Navigation Acts, the protection of domestic manufactures, and the colonial monopoly were the practical expressions of this doctrine.
Malachy Postlethwayt was the most able British mercantilist of the mid-century. His Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce and Britain’s Commercial Interest Explained and Improved provided a comprehensive exposition of the mercantile system — the regulation of trade, the enumerated commodities, the protection of domestic industry, the importance of a favourable balance. For Postlethwayt, trade and national power were inseparable: “Commerce,” he wrote, “is the source of naval strength, and naval strength is the guardian of commerce.”
Yet Postlethwayt was no dogmatist. He criticised the restrictions that prevented the American colonies from trading directly with Europe, argued that the slave trade was economically inefficient, and proposed the cultivation of waste lands as a remedy for the nation’s commercial decline. His mercantilism was pragmatic and reformist, not rigid.
Massie and the Theory of Interest
Joseph Massie’s Essay on the Natural Rate of Interest (1750) was the first systematic refutation of the prevailing Lockeian theory of interest. John Locke had argued that the rate of interest was governed by the quantity of money in circulation: more money meant lower interest, less money meant higher interest. Massie demolished this argument by demonstrating, with a table of wheat prices and interest rates covering five periods from 1444 to 1748, that there was no correlation between the two.
The true determinant of interest, Massie argued, was the profits of trade. Interest was the price paid for the use of money, and that price was governed by the returns that could be earned by employing money productively. When profits were high, interest rose; when profits fell, interest fell. The quantity of money was irrelevant. This argument — that the rate of profit, not the quantity of money, governed the rate of interest — anticipated the classical theory of interest that Adam Smith would later adopt.
Hume’s Revolution
David Hume’s Political Discourses (1752) were the foundational texts of classical economics. In a series of essays — Of Commerce, Of Money, Of Interest, Of the Balance of Trade, Of the Jealousy of Trade, Of Taxes, and Of Public Credit — Hume laid the foundations for a systematic critique of mercantilism and a new understanding of the nature of economic life.
His treatment of money was revolutionary. Money, Hume argued, was not wealth but merely “a medium of exchange” — “a representation of labour and commodities, and nothing but a method of rating and estimating them.” The quantity of money in a nation was irrelevant to its real wealth, which consisted entirely in the industry and ingenuity of its people. An increase in the quantity of money did not make a nation richer; it merely raised prices.
This argument led to Hume’s most famous contribution: the price-specie-flow mechanism. If one nation accumulated specie through a trade surplus, prices would rise in that nation, making its exports less competitive and its imports cheaper. The surplus would naturally correct itself through the operation of the price mechanism. The mercantilist obsession with the balance of trade was, therefore, fundamentally mistaken: the balance of trade was self-correcting, and no government intervention was required.
Of the Jealousy of Trade was a masterpiece of economic liberalism. Hume argued that the prosperity of one nation did not come at the expense of another. Trade was not a zero-sum game but a positive-sum activity from which all participants benefited. The jealousy of trade — the belief that a rival’s gain was one’s own loss — was “a principle which is perpetual and universal” but which was “altogether groundless.”
Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations
Adam Smith’s Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776) was the capstone of eighteenth-century economic thought — the work that transformed the scattered insights of Hume, Massie, and the French Physiocrats into a comprehensive system of political economy. The book appeared in the same year as the American Declaration of Independence, a coincidence that symbolised the connection between Smith’s economic liberalism and the political transformation of the Atlantic world.
The Wealth of Nations was built on three foundations. The first was the division of labour, which Smith argued was the primary cause of the increase in productivity that distinguished civilised from savage nations. His famous description of the pin factory — ten men specialising in different operations could produce 48,000 pins per day, whereas each working alone could produce at most twenty — made the case for the division of labour with unforgettable force.
The second foundation was the theory of value. Smith distinguished between “value in use” (the utility of a thing) and “value in exchange” (its purchasing power) and argued that the real measure of exchange value was the labour required to produce a commodity. This “labour theory of value” became the foundation of classical economics.
The third foundation was the concept of the “invisible hand” — the mechanism by which the pursuit of individual self-interest in a competitive market promotes the public good. The merchant who seeks only his own advantage is “led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention.” Smith did not advocate laissez-faire in the absolute sense — he recognised a significant role for the state in defence, justice, and public works — but he provided the intellectual foundation for the attack on mercantilist regulation.
The Policy Debates
The theoretical debates of the political economists had direct policy implications. The debate over the Corn Laws — the restrictions on the import of foreign grain — turned on the question of whether free trade in corn would benefit or injure the nation. Smith argued for free trade; the landed interest, which dominated Parliament, argued for protection. The corn trade remained regulated throughout the century.
The colonial monopoly — the system by which the colonies were required to trade exclusively with Britain — was another target of Smith’s critique. The monopoly, he argued, was a tax on British consumers for the benefit of colonial planters and the shipping interest. The loss of the American colonies, which Smith predicted would not be an economic disaster, did not refute his argument: trade with the United States grew after independence.
The debate over the National Debt and Public Credit was perhaps the most urgent. Hume had warned in his essay Of Public Credit that the growth of the national debt would eventually destroy the nation — “either the nation must destroy the public credit, or the public credit will destroy the nation.” Smith was more sanguine but still concerned. The debt had been the engine of the Fiscal-Military State, but its accumulation raised questions about intergenerational justice and national solvency that the political economists could not resolve.
Political Economy and State Finance
The relationship between political economy and the fiscal state was intimate. The growth of the excise and customs revenues, the development of the public credit, and the creation of the modern tax system were all informed by the analytical categories of the political economists. Patrick Colquhoun, who was both a magistrate and a statistician, applied the methods of political economy to the problems of poverty, crime, and public order. His social table, based on the earlier work of Gregory King, classified the population by occupation and income and enabled the first systematic calculation of the national income.
The political economists of the eighteenth century did not agree on many things. But they shared a conviction — which their century had taught them — that the wealth of nations was not a fixed quantity to be divided among rivals but a dynamic process to be understood and promoted. That conviction, more than any particular doctrine, was their legacy.

concepts/poverty-and-poor-laws.title: Poverty and the Poor Laws
concepts/poverty-and-poor-laws.content:
Poverty and the Poor Laws
The relief of the poor was, in the eighteenth century, a matter of local parish administration under the framework of the Elizabethan Poor Law of 1601 — the 43rd of Elizabeth. By the end of the century, this system was under immense strain. The population was growing, the economy was being transformed by the Industrial Transformation, and the wars with France were driving up the price of bread. The cost of poor relief had risen from an estimated £200,000 per annum in 1601 to £4.27 million in 1803, according to Patrick Colquhoun’s Treatise on Indigence (1806). The question of how to relieve the poor without encouraging idleness — how to distinguish between the deserving and the undeserving, between poverty and indigence — was the central social problem of the age.
The Old Poor Law
The Poor Law of 1601 established the parish as the unit of poor relief. Each parish was required to levy a rate on the property within its boundaries and to use the proceeds to support the impotent poor (the aged, the sick, and the orphaned), to provide work for the able-bodied poor, and to apprentice poor children. The administration was in the hands of the parish vestry and the overseers of the poor, who were unpaid local householders serving a compulsory annual term.
The system was not a national programme but a patchwork of local practice. Some parishes were generous, some were not. Some built workhouses, others preferred “outdoor relief” — payments in money or kind to the poor living in their own homes. The only uniformity was the legal obligation of each parish to support its own poor — an obligation that created the system of settlement laws that restricted the mobility of the labouring population.
The Laws of Settlement
The Laws of Settlement, codified in the Settlement Act of 1662, were the most controversial aspect of the old poor law. They provided that a person could gain a “settlement” — a legal right to poor relief — only in the parish of his birth, marriage, apprenticeship, or property holding. To move elsewhere was to risk being “removed” — physically returned to the parish of settlement — if there was any likelihood of becoming chargeable to the poor rates of the new parish.
The settlement laws were a powerful constraint on the mobility of labour in an age when the economy demanded mobility. They discouraged the poor from seeking work in the new manufacturing towns. They enabled the wealthy parishes to expel the poor to poorer parishes, shifting the burden of relief from those best able to bear it to those least able. The abuses of the removal system were a constant theme of social criticism throughout the century.
The Workhouse System
The workhouse was the institutional response to the problem of the able-bodied poor. The Workhouse Test Act (Knatchbull’s Act) of 1723 empowered parishes to refuse outdoor relief and to require the poor to enter a workhouse as a condition of receiving support. The principle was that the workhouse would “test” the genuineness of poverty: the truly destitute would submit to the discipline of the house, while the idle would prefer to find work rather than enter it.
The workhouse was intended to be a deterrent — “a place of aversion,” as the reformers put it. Conditions were deliberately made harsh, the diet meagre, the work monotonous (typically picking oakum, beating hemp, or grinding corn). But in practice, many workhouses became repositories for the aged, the sick, the orphaned, and the mentally ill — the impotent poor for whom there was no other provision.
The Growth of the Poor Rates
The relentless rise of the poor rates was the most alarming fact of eighteenth-century social administration. Colquhoun, in his Treatise on Indigence, provides the definitive contemporary analysis. From £200,000 in 1601, the poor rates had risen to:





























YearPoor Rate Expenditure1601£200,000 (estimated)1700£600,000 (estimated)1750£700,0001776£1.53 million1803£4.27 million
Colquhoun attributes the increase to three causes: the growth of population, the rise in the price of provisions, and the decline of the “spirit of independence” among the labouring poor. His analysis distinguishes carefully between poverty — “that state in which every man must labour to obtain subsistence” — and indigence — “that state in which a person is incapable of labour, or unable to procure the means of subsistence.” Poverty, in his view, was the necessary condition of the labouring classes and the foundation of national wealth. Indigence was the evil to be prevented.
Speenhamland 1795
The Speenhamland system, adopted by the Berkshire magistrates in May 1795, was the most significant innovation in poor relief during the century. Meeting at the Pelican Inn in Speenhamland (near Newbury), the magistrates devised a scale of relief linked to the price of bread and the size of the labourer’s family. When wages fell below the scale, the parish would make up the difference — an “allowance in aid of wages.”
Speenhamland was not a parliamentary enactment but a local expedient, adopted in response to the crisis of high bread prices (following the poor harvest of 1794) and the wartime disruption of trade. But the system spread rapidly across southern England, adopted by parish after parish as the simplest solution to the problem of agricultural poverty in a time of war. The consequences were hotly debated: critics argued that the allowance system depressed wages (since farmers knew the parish would make up the difference), encouraged large families, and destroyed the moral character of the labouring poor.
Friendly Societies
The Friendly Society movement was the labouring poor’s own response to the problem of indigence. Friendly societies — voluntary associations of working men who contributed weekly sums to a common fund that provided sickness, burial, and old-age benefits — multiplied rapidly in the second half of the century. By 1800, there were an estimated 7,000 friendly societies in England, with perhaps 600,000 members.
Colquhoun, a supporter of friendly societies, saw in them a model for the improvement of the labouring classes. They fostered habits of thrift, regularity, and mutual support. They reduced the burden on the poor rates. And they offered a form of self-respect that outdoor relief, with its associated stigma of paupersm, could not provide.
Colquhoun’s Proposals
Colquhoun’s own prescription for the reform of the poor laws was comprehensive and systematic. He proposed:

A national system of poor relief, administered by a central Board of Public Police under a Secretary of State
The establishment of “Houses of Industry” in every district, combining the functions of workhouse, training school, and employment agency
The creation of a professional police force to regulate the casual poor, suppress vagrancy, and prevent crime
The encouragement of friendly societies and savings banks to promote self-reliance
The moral improvement of the labouring classes through education, religious instruction, and the inculcation of habits of industry

Colquhoun’s proposals were too systematic for the age, and they were not adopted. But his analysis of the problem — his insistence on the distinction between poverty and indigence, his understanding of the relationship between population growth, food prices, and poor relief, his recognition that the old parish system was breaking down under the weight of demographic and economic change — was the most sophisticated before the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834.
The Relief of the Poor in a Time of War
The French Revolutionary Wars (1793–1801) placed the poor relief system under unprecedented strain. The interruption of trade, the rise in the price of bread (which doubled between 1792 and 1795), and the increase in unemployment created a crisis that the parish system was not designed to handle. The Speenhamland system, the Gilbert Act workhouses, and the extension of outdoor relief were all emergency responses to conditions that the ordinary machinery of the poor law could not contain.
The poor rates rose to their highest level in history. The burden fell heavily on the ratepayers of the agricultural parishes of southern England, where the population was most dense and the demand for relief most acute. The crisis of the 1790s was the seedbed of the debates that would produce the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 — but that reform belonged to the next century.

concepts/radicalism-and-popular-politics.title: Radicalism and Popular Politics
concepts/radicalism-and-popular-politics.content:
Radicalism and Popular Politics
The 18th century was not only the age of aristocratic management in politics, but also the age of an emergent popular radicalism — a series of movements that claimed the rights of the people against the corruption of Parliament, the influence of the Crown, and the exclusive domination of the propertied classes. These movements, though suppressed or contained, left a lasting mark upon the political consciousness of the nation.
The Wilkesite Movement, 1763–1774
The radicalism of the 1760s found its first great champion in Mr. John Wilkes, a Member of Parliament of dissolute character but undoubted courage, who made the liberty of the press and the rights of electors the cause of his life. The publication of the North Briton No. 45 in 1763, in which Wilkes attacked the King’s Speech as a tissue of falsehoods, led to his arrest under a general warrant. The question of the legality of general warrants — by which the Secretary of State might arrest unnamed persons and seize their papers — became a constitutional cause of the first magnitude.
The Middlesex election of 1768–1769 raised the stakes. Wilkes, having been expelled from the House of Commons and outlawed, was three times elected by the freeholders of Middlesex, and three times the House voted to disqualify him, seating his defeated opponent, Colonel Luttrell, in his place. The “Middlesex election” became a national scandal. The right of the electors to choose their representatives freely, without the interference of the House of Commons itself, was the constitutional principle at stake.
The Society of Supporters of the Bill of Rights, founded in 1769, was the first mass political association in British history. It demanded annual Parliaments, the exclusion of placemen from the House, the abolition of general warrants, and the publication of parliamentary debates. It collected subscriptions from every part of the kingdom, organised petitions, and maintained a press campaign. Mr. Belsham’s narrative (Belsham Memoirs Vol IV) gives a full account of these proceedings and of the government’s determination to suppress the movement.
The County Association Movement
The failure of the Wilkesite agitation to achieve parliamentary reform led to a new phase of the reform movement in the 1780s. The county associations, led by the Reverend Christopher Wyvill, a Yorkshire clergyman of independent fortune, sought to mobilise the independent country gentlemen and the freeholders of the counties in favour of economical reform and a more equal representation.
The Yorkshire Association, formed in 1779, was the model for similar associations in other counties. Its programme was moderate: it demanded the addition of county Members, the abolition of rotten boroughs, and the reduction of the influence of the Crown. The movement reached its height in 1780, when petitions from every part of the kingdom were presented to Parliament. The House of Commons rejected the reform proposals, and the movement declined.
The Revolution Controversy: Burke vs. Paine
The outbreak of the French Revolution in 1789 transformed the character of English radicalism. The controversy between Mr. Edmund Burke and Mr. Thomas Paine — Burke’s Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) and Paine’s Rights of Man (1791–1792) — was the most important political debate of the age, and it defined the terms of political argument for a generation.
Burke defended the British constitution as the inheritance of ages, the accumulated wisdom of the nation, not to be overthrown in obedience to abstract theories of the rights of man. He denounced the French Revolution as an experiment in destruction, based upon the false philosophy of Rousseau and the Encyclopedists, and warned that it would end in military despotism.
Paine answered with a direct appeal to natural rights. Every man, he argued, was born with rights that no government might violate. The British constitution, with its Crown, its House of Lords, and its rotten boroughs, was an offence against reason and justice. The people had the right to abolish it and to establish a republic upon the principles of liberty and equality. Rights of Man, published in a cheap edition, reached an enormous audience among the common people.
The London Corresponding Society
The London Corresponding Society, founded in 1792 by Thomas Hardy, a shoemaker, was the first mass political organisation of the working classes. Its membership, drawn from the mechanics, artisans, and shopkeepers of the metropolis, paid a penny a week in subscription. Its purpose was to correspond with similar societies throughout the kingdom, to spread the principles of parliamentary reform, and to demand universal suffrage and annual Parliaments.
The Society grew rapidly. By the end of 1792 it claimed thousands of members. Its publications, including the pamphlets of Paine and the writings of the English Jacobins, were distributed through the provincial societies. The government, alarmed by the spread of French revolutionary ideas, determined to destroy the movement.
The Government Reaction
The government’s response to the radical movement was swift and severe. In May 1792, a Royal Proclamation against seditious writings was issued, and prosecutions were commenced against Paine and other radical authors. Paine, having been tried in his absence and convicted of seditious libel, fled to France.
The Treason Trials of 1794 were the government’s most dramatic assault upon the radical movement. Hardy, John Horne Tooke, and John Thelwall were tried for high treason before a special commission. The Attorney General, Sir John Scott (later Lord Eldon), argued that the London Corresponding Society’s activities amounted to a conspiracy to depose the King and establish a republic. The jury, to the surprise of the government and the delight of the radicals, acquitted the prisoners.
The acquittals did not check the government’s determination. The suspension of Habeas Corpus in 1794 allowed the ministry to detain suspected persons without trial. The Two Acts of 1795 — the Treasonable Practices Act and the Seditious Meetings Act — made it a capital crime to incite hatred of the King or the constitution, and prohibited meetings of more than fifty persons without a magistrate’s licence.
Mr. Belsham, who wrote as a reforming Whig, condemned these measures as a violation of the ancient liberties of Englishmen. The government, he argued, had been driven by panic to adopt the very instruments of tyranny that it claimed to be resisting.
The Legacy: Radicalism Forced Underground
By the end of the century, the radical movement had been crushed. The London Corresponding Society was dissolved. The provincial societies were suppressed. The radical press was silenced by prosecution and intimidation. The United Irishmen, who had adopted the principles of the French Revolution and sought the separation of Ireland from Britain, were driven to conspiracy and armed rebellion (Irish Rebellion of 1798).
But the radical tradition was not extinguished. The demand for parliamentary reform, for universal suffrage, for the abolition of slavery, and for the liberty of the press survived in secret societies, in the correspondence of exiles, and in the hearts of those who had read the works of Paine and the writings of the English Jacobins. The reform movement of the 19th century was to build upon foundations laid in the age of Wilkes, Wyvill, and the London Corresponding Society.

concepts/slavery-and-abolition.title: Slavery and the Abolition Movement
concepts/slavery-and-abolition.content:
Slavery and the Abolition Movement
The British transatlantic slave trade was, by the middle of the eighteenth century, the largest in the world. British ships carried more enslaved Africans to the Americas than those of any other European nation — an estimated 40,000 per year at the peak of the trade, representing about half the total Atlantic traffic. The wealth generated by slave labour in the West Indian sugar plantations financed British commercial expansion, supported a powerful interest in Parliament, and was intimately connected to the Atlantic System and Colonial Trade that was the foundation of the first British empire. Against this immense structure of commercial interest, a small but determined movement of humanitarian reformers — fired by religious conviction and philosophical principle — waged a campaign that, by the end of the century, had brought the abolition of the slave trade to the verge of parliamentary enactment.
The British Slave Trade
The British slave trade was conducted under the monopoly of the Royal African Company until 1698, after which the trade was opened to independent merchants. The “triangular trade” — British manufactures to Africa, enslaved Africans to the West Indies, West Indian produce to Britain — was the organising pattern. Bristol was the leading slaving port in the early part of the century, but by 1750 Liverpool had overtaken it. The Liverpool slavers, according to Malachy Postlethwayt’s Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce, sent approximately 100 ships annually to the African coast, carrying goods valued at £300,000 to exchange for slaves.
The Middle Passage — the transport of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic — was the most terrible stage of the trade. Enslaved people were packed below decks in conditions of unspeakable squalor, shackled in rows on platforms built to maximise the number of captives per voyage. Mortality rates averaged 10–15 percent per voyage, though on some ships the death rate exceeded 50 percent. The Dolben Act of 1788, which regulated the number of slaves per ton of shipping, was the first parliamentary attempt to mitigate the worst horrors of the passage.
Slavery in the Plantations
On the West Indian plantations, the enslaved population worked under a regime of relentless brutality. The sugar harvest was the most demanding agricultural labour in the Americas: the cane had to be cut and milled within 24 hours, requiring round-the-clock work during the harvest season. The slave codes of the British West Indies, modelled on the Barbados Code of 1661, denied the enslaved virtually all legal rights. They could not own property, give evidence in court, or marry legally. Punishment was at the discretion of the planter or his overseer.
The demographic regime of West Indian slavery was one of continuous importation. The enslaved population did not reproduce itself: the mortality rate exceeded the birth rate, and the sex ratio was heavily male. Barbados was the exception, with a relatively stable creole (island-born) slave population; in Jamaica and the newer colonies, the enslaved population could be maintained only by constant importation from Africa. This fact — that the slave trade was essential to prevent the depopulation of the plantations — became a central argument of the pro-slavery interest.
The Early Critics
The first sustained critique of the British slave trade came not from the humanitarian movement of the late century but from the Quakers and from individual moralists. The Quakers of Pennsylvania and London were the earliest organised body to denounce slavery as incompatible with Christianity. In 1727, the London Yearly Meeting condemned the trade, and by 1761 the Pennsylvania Quakers had excluded slave traders from membership.
The Somerset case of 1772 was a landmark. James Somerset, an enslaved African brought to England by his master, Charles Stewart, absconded and was recaptured. Lord Mansfield, Lord Chief Justice of the King’s Bench, ruled that slavery was “so odious” that it could exist only by positive law, and that since no such law existed in England, Somerset must be freed. The judgment did not abolish slavery in England — its scope was narrower than is sometimes supposed — but it established that the status of an enslaved person did not survive on English soil.
Granville Sharp, the scholar and philanthropist who had championed Somerset’s case, was the leading English abolitionist of the pre-Wilberforce era. His Representation of the Injustice and Dangerous Tendency of Tolerating Slavery (1769) was the first systematic English argument for abolition.
The Abolition Campaign
The abolition movement as a political force dates from the foundation of the Committee for the Abolition of the Slave Trade in 1787. The Committee, dominated by Quakers, brought together the most effective campaigners of the age: William Wilberforce, the independent member of Parliament for Yorkshire, who became the parliamentary leader of the cause; Thomas Clarkson, who spent years travelling the country collecting evidence of the trade’s horrors; and the Quaker Granville Sharp, the veteran of the Somerset case.
Clarkson’s investigations — he collected the iron manacles, the thumbscrews, the branding irons used by the slave ships — supplied the evidence on which the parliamentary campaign was built. His published works, particularly his Essay on the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species (1786) and his later History of the Abolition of the Slave Trade, provided the factual basis for the abolitionists’ case. The Committee organised a nationwide petitioning campaign that, by 1792, had collected over 500,000 signatures — an extraordinary expression of public opinion in an age before mass democracy.
The Parliamentary Battles
The abolition question entered Parliament in earnest in 1788. The Dolben Act, regulating the conditions of the Middle Passage, passed both Houses with William Pitt the Younger’s support. In 1791, Wilberforce’s first motion for the abolition of the slave trade was defeated by 163 votes to 88. In 1792, a second motion passed the Commons in principle (230 to 85) but was delayed in the Lords, where the planter interest was entrenched.
Belsham, in his Memoirs of the Reign of George III, describes the parliamentary debates as among the most remarkable of the age. Edmund Burke, Charles James Fox, and Pitt himself all spoke in favour of abolition. Pitt’s speech of 2 April 1792 was one of the greatest of his career — a sustained argument that the slave trade was contrary to every principle of justice, humanity, and sound policy. But the Lords, led by the Lord Chancellor, Lord Thurlow, insisted on hearing evidence, and the measure was talked out.
The Economic Arguments
The pro-slavery case rested on the immense economic stakes involved. The West Indian planters, represented by their agents in London and by sympathetic members of Parliament, argued that the abolition of the slave trade would destroy the sugar islands, impoverish the merchants, ruin the shipping interest, and weaken the Royal Navy (which depended on the mercantile marine for its supply of seamen). The value of the West Indian trade was estimated at £4–5 million per annum; the capital invested in the sugar plantations at £30 million; the number of British subjects dependent on the trade at hundreds of thousands.
The abolitionists responded with a fourfold argument. First, the trade was morally indefensible — a crime against humanity that could not be justified by any calculation of commercial advantage. Second, the trade was economically self-defeating: the continual importation of enslaved Africans was less efficient than the creation of a stable, self-reproducing free-labour force. Third, British commerce could survive without the slave trade, as the growth of trade with Asia and with the United States demonstrated. Fourth, the danger of a slave revolt — of which the Haitian Revolution (1791–1804) was a terrible example — made the continuation of the slave trade a risk to the security of the colonies themselves.
The Wartime Pause
The outbreak of the War of the First Coalition against Revolutionary France in 1793 suspended the abolition campaign. The political atmosphere of the 1790s, dominated by fears of revolutionary conspiracy and the repressive legislation of the Pitt government, was inhospitable to abolition. Wilberforce continued to bring forward his motion year after year, but the tide of war and reaction prevented it from passing. The abolition of the slave trade would not be achieved until 1807, but the moral and political battle had been substantially won in the parliamentary contests of 1788–1792. The cause had been established as a permanent question of British politics.

entities/adam-duncan.title: Adam Duncan, 1st Viscount Duncan (1731–1804)
entities/adam-duncan.content:
Adam Duncan, 1st Viscount Duncan (1731–1804)
Adam Duncan, created Viscount Duncan of Camperdown (1 July 1731 – 4 August 1804), was the British admiral who, in the darkest year of the French Revolutionary Wars, held the North Sea squadron together through the Mutiny at the Nore and then crushed the Dutch fleet at the Battle of Camperdown (11 October 1797) — a victory so complete that it destroyed the Batavian Republic’s navy in a single afternoon. His courage in the face of mutiny and his resolution in battle place him alongside John Jervis and Richard Howe as one of the great fleet commanders of the era.
Early Career
Duncan was born at Lundie in Angus, Scotland, the son of a landed gentleman. He entered the navy at the age of fifteen as a midshipman aboard the Trial, serving in the West Indies during the War of Jenkins’ Ear and later in the Mediterranean during the War of the Austrian Succession. He was promoted to lieutenant in 1755 and to commander in 1759, seeing service under Edward Hawke at the Battle of Quiberon Bay (1759) — the victory that shattered the French invasion plans of that year. He served as post-captain from 1761, commanding successive ships in the Channel, the Mediterranean, and the East Indies through the long peace that followed the Seven Years’ War.
Duncan’s career until 1793 was solid but unspectacular. He was a competent, reliable officer of the old school — a man of immense physical strength and placid temperament, more comfortable in action than in the politics of the Admiralty. He was promoted to rear-admiral in 1787 and to vice-admiral in 1793, when the war with Revolutionary France began. In 1795, he was given command of the North Sea Fleet, with his flag in the Venerable.
The North Sea Command and the Dutch Threat
The North Sea station was, in 1795, a command of the first strategic importance. The Batavian Republic—as the Dutch republic was now styled under French domination—had joined the war on the side of France, its fleet of some twenty sail of the line concentrated at the Texel, threatening the east coast of England, the Baltic trade routes, and the approaches to London itself. Duncan’s task was the most thankless of all naval duties: blockade.
He established a station off the Texel, and for two years he kept the Dutch fleet bottled up in their harbours. The service was brutal: winter gales, fog, the constant danger of the Dogger Bank shoals, and the monotony of weeks without sight of the enemy. Duncan held the line, his ships maintaining the offshore patrol even when storms drove them as far as Yarmouth for shelter. But it was not the Dutch who nearly broke him — it was his own men.
The Mutiny at the Nore
In the spring of 1797, the Royal Navy was convulsed by the great mutinies. The Spithead mutiny (April–May) was settled by concession—an increase in pay, better provisions, and the pardon of the delegates. But the Nore mutiny (May–June) was of a different character. It began on the ships of the North Sea squadron, and under the leadership of the delegate Richard Parker, it quickly took on a quasi-revolutionary cast. The mutineers demanded not only better conditions but political concessions; they blockaded the Thames, prevented the sailing of the convoy for the Baltic, and threatened to hand the ships over to the French.
Duncan found himself in an impossible position. His flagship, the Venerable, remained loyal under the influence of his captain, William Fairfax, but most of his squadron had raised the red flag of mutiny. He was left with only the Adamant and a handful of smaller vessels to maintain the blockade of the Texel. It was, by any rational measure, a hopeless situation: the Dutch fleet could put to sea at any moment, and Duncan could not hope to oppose them.
He did not retreat.
Duncan anchored off the Texel with his two loyal ships, and then played the greatest bluff of his career. He sent signals to an imaginary fleet over the horizon — messages ordering his supposed reinforcements to close on the Dutch. He sailed through the night with his ships showing as many lanterns as possible, simulating the approach of a full squadron. The ruse worked. The cautious Dutch admiral, Jan Willem de Winter, remained at anchor, uncertain of the British strength, while Duncan’s mutinous ships were coaxed back to duty by a combination of negotiation, the collapse of Parker’s authority, and the threat of the court-martial that Parker would himself face when the mutiny collapsed in June.
When the Nore mutiny was finally suppressed, Duncan was the hero of the hour — the man who had kept the North Sea squadron on station in the face of the greatest crisis in the navy’s history. The King himself expressed his admiration. But the strain had been terrible; Duncan was not the same man afterwards, his constitution permanently damaged by the anxiety of the affair.
The Battle of Camperdown
On 11 October 1797, Duncan’s patience was finally rewarded.
The Dutch fleet under Admiral de Winter had put to sea from the Texel during a gale that had driven Duncan’s squadron off station to shelter at Yarmouth. As soon as the storm abated, Duncan raced back, the wind at north-west, and at nine o’clock on the morning of 11 October the two fleets came in sight of each other. The Dutch were drawn up in line of battle off the coast of Holland, between the villages of Camperdown and Egmont, within sight of the shore.
Duncan faced a dilemma. De Winter had formed his line close to the shoals; if Duncan waited to form a conventional line of battle, the Dutch would escape back into the Texel. But if he attacked immediately, without order, he risked the worst vice of the naval commander — confusion.
He chose confusion.
Duncan made the signal to “bear up, break the enemy’s line, and engage them to leeward, each ship her opponent.” It was, as the official historian recorded, “a bold manœuvre, regardless of the danger of a lee-shore,” and it was fatal to the Dutch. Duncan’s division crashed through the enemy van, while Vice-Admiral Onslow’s division broke through the rear. The battle dissolved into a ferocious mêlée.
Duncan’s own ship, the Venerable, was in the thickest of the action from the first. She engaged the Dutch flagship, the Vrijheid, at pistol-shot range. The Dutch admiral, a giant of a man, fought with a courage that the British acknowledged with respect — his ship became a mere wreck, her masts gone, her decks slippery with blood, but her colours still flying. Only when the Venerable was joined by the Ardent and the Triumph did de Winter strike. He was brought on board the British ship, where Duncan greeted him with the respect due to a gallant foe. “It has been my fate,” said de Winter with dignity, “to be defeated by a superior force.” Duncan, with characteristic generosity, replied that the Dutch had fought like lions, and that only the fortune of war had given him the victory.
The battle lasted less than three hours. Nine Dutch ships of the line and two frigates were captured. Vice-Admiral Reintjies had also surrendered to Onslow. The Dutch losses in killed and wounded ran to some 1,500 men, including 500 on the admiral and vice-admiral’s ships alone. The British lost fewer than 800. One Dutch ship, the Delft, sank within sight of the British coast.
The fighting was the most savage of the war. Belsham remarks that “a more bloody conflict has seldom been fought.” The fleets were so close to the Dutch shore that every manoeuvre was visible to the thousands of spectators who lined the coast “the melancholy witnesses of the great disaster which had befallen their country from a power which professed to enter into the present war chiefly with a view to their protection.”
Camperdown was, in its own way, as decisive as the Nile. It destroyed the Batavian navy as a fighting force and eliminated the threat of an invasion of the British Isles from the North Sea in the most critical year of the war. While Nelson’s victory at Cape St Vincent was celebrated by professional men as “a most brilliant and scientific display of nautical skill,” Belsham records that Camperdown excited a much greater popular sensation — it was more decisive, more bloody, and fought against an enemy whose courage bordered on desperation.
Later Career and Death
Duncan was created Viscount Duncan of Camperdown and Baron Duncan of Lundie in recognition of his victory. He was given a pension of £3,000 a year and the thanks of both Houses of Parliament. The victory completed the ruin of his health; the combination of the Nore mutiny and the terrible exertion of Camperdown had worn him out.
He continued in nominal command of the North Sea fleet until 1799, when failing health forced his retirement. He died at his home at Lundie in Angus on 4 August 1804, at the age of seventy-three. A monument was erected to him in St Paul’s Cathedral, near those of Howe and Nelson.
Legacy
Duncan’s reputation rests on a single battle — but what a battle. Camperdown was the most complete fleet action of the French Revolutionary War to that point, and it established the conviction in the British public that the navy could meet any adversary, in any circumstances, and prevail. His conduct during the Nore mutiny reveals a man of exceptional fortitude — the kind of calm, unshakeable resolution that the age prized above all other military virtues.
He was not a Nelson — he lacked the flash of genius, the unerring instinct for the decisive moment. But he was an admiral who, in the most trying circumstances imaginable, never lost his nerve, never abandoned his post, and delivered the knockout blow the moment the opportunity presented itself. For the North Sea squadron, in the year of the mutinies, that was more than enough.
