entities/george-iii.title: George III (1738–1820)
entities/george-iii.content:
George III
George William Frederick (4 June 1738 – 29 January 1820) was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 25 October 1760 until the union of the two kingdoms in 1801, and thereafter King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland until his death. His reign of fifty-nine years — the longest of any British monarch until that of his granddaughter Queen Victoria — encompassed the end of the Seven Years’ War, the loss of the American colonies, the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, and the Union with Ireland. He was the third Hanoverian monarch and the first to be born in Britain and to speak English as his first language.
Early Life and Accession
Born at Norfolk House in London, George was the eldest son of Frederick, Prince of Wales, and Princess Augusta of Saxe-Gotha. His father’s death in 1751 brought him to the front of the succession at the age of twelve. He was raised in a deeply protective household at Leicester House under the tutelage of his mother and Lord Bute, her confidant — a circle that instilled in him a strict moral code, a reverence for the established Church, and a suspicion of the Whig grandees who had dominated politics under his grandfather.
George succeeded the throne on 25 October 1760 upon the death of George II. He was twenty-two years old. His accession speech to Parliament declared that he “gloried in the name of Britain” — a pointed contrast to his German-speaking predecessor, and an immediate signal of his desire to govern as a patriot king.
Belsham records the auspicious opening of the reign: the new Monarch’s “manners were in the highest degree decorous, his morals unblemished, and his personal accomplishments corresponded with the elevation of his rank and station.” The nation, fresh from the triumphs of the Annus Mirabilis, greeted him with transports of joy.
The End of the Seven Years’ War and the Bute Ministry
The King’s first act was to appoint his former tutor, the Earl of Bute, as Secretary of State and later First Lord of the Treasury. Bute’s rapid rise — and his Scottish background — excited immediate opposition. The Treaty of Paris (1763), which ended the Seven Years’ War, was bitterly attacked by William Pitt the Elder as too generous to France, though it secured Canada, the Mississippi valley, and Florida for Britain.
Bute, temperamentally unsuited to parliamentary combat, resigned in April 1763 after less than a year as Prime Minister. His departure did not end his influence: the “Cabinet of Carlton House,” centred on the King’s mother and Bute, continued to exert a secret and malign influence over affairs — what Pitt would later call “something behind the throne greater than the throne itself.”
The Grenville Ministry and the Wilkes Affair
George Grenville succeeded Bute as First Lord of the Treasury in 1763. The King found Grenville personally difficult — stiff, lecturing, insistent — but the ministry was competent. Its great crisis came with the prosecution of John Wilkes, whose paper The North Briton No. 45 had attacked the King’s speech from the throne, charging His Majesty with uttering a direct falsehood. Grenville’s government issued a general warrant for the arrest of the authors, printers, and publishers, and Wilkes was committed to the Tower.
The general warrant controversy — a warrant that named no specific person — became a cause célèbre. Lord Chief Justice Pratt ruled the warrant illegal, and Wilkes was released. The affair made Wilkes a popular hero and dealt lasting damage to Grenville’s reputation.
The ministry fell in July 1765 after Grenville, learning of the King’s attempts to replace him, demanded the dismissal of Bute’s allies as the price of remaining. George, thoroughly exasperated, dismissed him.
The Rockingham Ministry and the Stamp Act Crisis
The Marquis of Rockingham formed a ministry in July 1765. Its great achievement was the repeal of the Stamp Act (1765) — Grenville’s tax on the American colonies — which had provoked an unprecedented wave of colonial resistance. Rockingham coupled repeal with the Declaratory Act, asserting Parliament’s authority to legislate for the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.”
George III assented to the repeal reluctantly. He had supported Grenville’s American policy and believed the colonies ought to contribute to the costs of empire. The repeal was carried by a narrow majority in the Commons, with Pitt delivering powerful speeches in favour of colonial rights.
The Chatham Ministry and the Townshend Acts
The King’s next experiment was a ministry formed around Pitt, now Earl of Chatham. It was a catastrophic failure. Chatham’s health collapsed — he suffered from severe gout and what contemporaries described as a nervous disorder — and he withdrew from active business for months at a time. Into the vacuum stepped Charles Townshend, the brilliant but erratic Chancellor of the Exchequer, who in 1767 pushed through the Townshend Acts — duties on glass, lead, paper, paint, and tea imported into the colonies. The Acts rekindled American resistance at the very moment reconciliation seemed possible.
The Years of Lord North (1770–1782)
After Chatham’s collapse and Townshend’s sudden death in 1767, the Duke of Grafton led a weak ministry until 1770, when Lord North — a man of mild temper, pleasant wit, and unmistakable loyalty to the Crown — became First Lord. North would remain in power for twelve years, the longest continuous ministry of the reign.
North’s ministry was dominated by the American crisis. The Boston Tea Party (1773), the Coercive Acts (1774), the battles of Lexington and Concord (1775), and the Declaration of Independence (1776) followed in grim succession. The King threw his full support behind the policy of coercion. He read despatches from America with obsessive attention, wrote personally to his ministers, and refused all compromise. “I am fighting the battle of the legislature,” he declared. “The colonies must either submit or triumph.”
The war went catastrophically wrong. Burgoyne’s surrender at Saratoga (1777) brought France into the war. The loss of the West Indies and Minorca followed. The final blow came with Cornwallis’s surrender at Yorktown in October 1781. North received the news “as he would have taken a ball in the breast.” The King drafted a letter of abdication before accepting the reality of defeat.
The Fall of North and the Ministry of Shelburne
North resigned in March 1782, ending twelve years at the helm. The King, humiliated and furious, was forced to accept first the Rockingham ministry — whose leader he distrusted — and then the Shelburne administration. The Peace of Paris (1783) recognised American independence. George III lamented the loss but accepted it as an accomplished fact.
The Fox-North Coalition and the India Bill Crisis
The King’s greatest domestic battle came in 1783, when the Fox-North coalition — an unnatural alliance of his two most hated opponents — brought forward Charles James Fox’s India Bill. The bill proposed to transfer control of the East India Company’s territorial possessions to commissioners appointed by Parliament. The King considered it an unconstitutional usurpation of the royal prerogative.
Using the private influence of Lord Temple, the King made it known — through a card written and circulated — that “whoever voted for the India Bill was not only not his friend, but would be considered by him as his enemy.” The message was carried to the House of Lords, where the bill was defeated. The coalition fell immediately.
This intervention — the most direct of his reign — was fiercely criticised by Fox and Burke as a violation of constitutional propriety. The King defended it as a necessary defence of the Crown’s legitimate authority.
Pitt the Younger
The King’s victory over the coalition brought William Pitt the Younger to power at the age of twenty-four. Pitt would dominate British politics for two decades. Unlike North, he was not a creature of the court; unlike Fox, he was not the King’s enemy. The relationship between monarch and minister was professional rather than warm — Pitt kept the King at a careful distance — but it was stable.
The great achievement of Pitt’s first ministry was the India Act (1784), which placed the Company’s affairs under a Board of Control answerable to the Crown — a more moderate version of the defeated Fox bill. The King, having destroyed the original, accepted the revision.
The Regency Crisis of 1788
In the autumn of 1788, George III suffered his first major attack of what contemporaries called “madness.” Modern historians believe he suffered from porphyria, a metabolic disorder that causes delirium, hallucinations, and violent physical symptoms. The King raved for hours, could not be restrained, and was placed in a straitwaistcoat.
The crisis threw the political world into chaos. If the King was permanently incapacitated, a regency would be necessary — and the heir apparent, the Prince of Wales, was a close ally of Charles James Fox and the opposition. Pitt and his ministers moved cautiously, introducing a Regency Bill that would strictly limit the Regent’s powers. Before the bill could pass, the King recovered in February 1789 — a recovery celebrated with nationwide rejoicing.
The Regency crisis revealed the fragility of the constitution in an age of monarchical incapacity, and it deepened the enmity between the King and his eldest son.
The French Revolution and War
The French Revolution erupted in 1789. At first, Pitt’s government remained neutral, but the execution of Louis XVI in January 1793, followed by French declarations of war, drew Britain into a conflict that would last — with a brief interlude — until 1815.
The King, as head of state and Supreme Governor of the Church of England, was a natural symbol of resistance to revolutionary atheism and regicide. His piety, his domestic virtue, and his very plainness — he was known as “Farmer George” for his enthusiastic interest in agriculture — became emblems of British stability. His annual messages to Parliament, his proclamations for fasts and thanksgivings, and his constant presence at Windsor gave the nation a sense of continuity.
Yet the war was a heavy burden. The national debt soared. Food prices rose. The Irish rebellion of 1798, inspired by French revolutionary principles, was suppressed with severity.
The Union with Ireland
The rebellion convinced Pitt that the only permanent solution to the Irish problem was a legislative union between Great Britain and Ireland, with Catholic emancipation as its accompaniment — the removal of the remaining penal laws that excluded Catholics from Parliament and public office.
The Act of Union passed in 1800, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland on 1 January 1801. Ireland was granted 100 seats in the House of Commons and 28 representative peers in the Lords. But when Pitt attempted to deliver Catholic emancipation as the corollary of union, the King refused point-blank. He considered Catholic emancipation a violation of his coronation oath to defend the Protestant establishment.
Pitt resigned rather than abandon the measure, and the King took personal charge of the negotiations to form Addington’s ministry. Catholic emancipation was shelved for a generation.
The King’s Final Years
George III’s health deteriorated after 1801. He suffered a relapse in 1804, recovered, and then — in 1810 — suffered a final, permanent breakdown after the death of his beloved youngest daughter, Princess Amelia. The Regency Act of 1811 placed the Prince of Wales in power as Regent for the remaining nine years of the King’s life.
The King spent his final years at Windsor Castle, blind, deaf, and intermittently lucid. He died on 29 January 1820, at the age of eighty-one.
Character and Assessment
George III was the most conscientious of monarchs. He rose early, worked methodically through despatches, presided at Cabinet meetings with careful attention, and maintained a household of exemplary domestic virtue — in stark contrast to his profligate sons. He was a devoted husband to Queen Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, whom he married in 1761, and fathered fifteen children.
His interest in agriculture — he wrote pamphlets on farming under the pseudonym “Ralph Robinson,” corresponded with Arthur Young, and transformed Windsor Great Park into a model farm — earned him the affectionate nickname “Farmer George.” He was a patron of the arts: he supported Handel’s memory, founded the Royal Academy in 1768, and assembled the library that became the foundation of the British Library.
His political record is more contested. He was stubborn and often inflexible — qualities that served him well in resisting the French Revolution but badly in American policy. His personal intervention in the India Bill crisis of 1783 remains controversial. Some historians see him as a constitutional monarch defending his prerogative; others as a meddling executive who corrupted the constitution.
On the central question of America, George III was intransigent. He believed from first to last that Parliament’s authority over the colonies was absolute. Belsham, writing in the 1790s, captured the tragic dimension: a King who came to the throne amid universal rejoicing, whose reign opened with the greatest victories in British history, and who lived to see his empire sundered by a war that his own policies had done so much to provoke.

“He is a noble and magnificent prince; but he has a most unhappy temper for a king.” — The Duke of Grafton

entities/george-rodney.title: George Brydges Rodney, 1st Baron Rodney
entities/george-rodney.content:
George Brydges Rodney, 1st Baron Rodney (1718–1792)
George Brydges Rodney was the most flamboyant and controversial British admiral of the American Revolutionary War — a commander of extraordinary dash whose victory at the Battle of the Saintes saved the British West Indies and introduced the tactic of breaking the line to fleet action, yet whose career was marred by accusations of greed, favouritism, and a fixation on prize money that distracted him from the greater strategic game.
Early Career and the Seven Years’ War
Rodney entered the navy as a boy and was commissioned lieutenant in 1739. By 1742 he had risen to post-captain, commanding the Sheerness and later the Eagle. His first great service came during the Seven Years’ War: in 1759 he bombarded Le Havre, destroying the flat-bottomed invasion boats the French had assembled for a descent on England. In 1762 he captured Martinique from the French, a conquest of the richest sugar island in the Caribbean, and was rewarded with the governorship of Greenwich Hospital.
Between wars, Rodney’s financial indiscipline caught up with him. He lived extravagantly, ran up debts, and fled England in 1774 to live in Paris to escape his creditors. He remained there until the outbreak of the American Revolutionary War, when his debt was compounded by his inability to pay and his absence from English politics had cost him his Greenwich post. Yet the Admiralty, desperate for experienced commanders, recalled him.
The Relief of Gibraltar and the Moonlight Battle
At the beginning of 1780, the two great objects of British naval strategy were the relief of Gibraltar (besieged by the Spanish since 1779) and the defence of the West Indies. Rodney was appointed to the chief command in the latter theatre, but his orders required him to relieve Gibraltar on the way. He sailed from Plymouth on the 29th of December, 1779, with twenty-two ships of the line.
On the 8th of January, 1780, he fell in with a Spanish convoy of twenty-two sail carrying naval stores from San Sebastián to Cadiz; he captured the greater part, including vast quantities of wheat and flour destined for the Spanish fleet. Then, on the night of the 16th of January, off Cape St. Vincent, Rodney encountered a Spanish squadron of eleven ships of the line under Don Juan Langara. In what became known as the Moonlight Battle — fought through the darkness of a winter night — he overwhelmed the Spaniards, capturing four ships including Langara’s own Phoenix of eighty guns. The engagement did not end until two in the morning, when the Monarca, the headmost of the enemy’s fleet, struck to Rodney’s Sandwich. Two more Spanish ships had struck but escaped in the darkness. The victory sent a shock through the courts of Europe: a night action at sea, fought in a winter gale, was almost unheard of.
Rodney then proceeded to Gibraltar, where he landed the captured provisions and stores, relieving the garrison after more than a year of siege. He left a detachment under Admiral Digby to escort the prizes home and continued on to the West Indies.
The West Indies and the Frustration with de Guichen
Rodney arrived at St. Lucia on the 27th of March, 1780, to find the situation less dire than he had feared. The French fleet under the Count de Guichen lay in Fort Royal Bay, Martinique. Rodney sailed on the 2nd of April to provoke an engagement; de Guichen declined. On the 15th, the French slipped out under cover of darkness with twenty-three sail of the line. Rodney pursued and brought them to action on the 17th off Martinique.
The battle was brilliantly conceived but poorly executed by his subordinates. Rodney, in the Sandwich, engaged the French centre alone for an hour and a half, but the van and rear of the British fleet were too far distant to support him. He had anticipated a decisive victory; he obtained only a partial success. De Guichen escaped to Guadeloupe, and Rodney, frustrated by the failure of his captains to support him, returned to St. Lucia. The campaign of 1780 yielded no decisive result.
The Capture of St. Eustatius
In February 1781, with the rupture with Holland, Rodney captured the Dutch island of St. Eustatius, the great entrepôt of the Caribbean — a depot through which the Americans, French, and Dutch had traded throughout the war. The prize was enormous: warehouses crammed with merchandise, a convoy of thirty merchant ships in the harbour, and vast sums of cash. The total was estimated at £3–4 million.
But the capture became a scandal. Rodney lingered on St. Eustatius for weeks, personally superintending the sale of the captured property and settling the claims of British merchants, while the strategic situation in the West Indies deteriorated. He detached Sir Samuel Hood with a squadron to watch the French at Martinique, but Hood was too weak to intercept the French fleet under de Grasse when it sailed for the Chesapeake in the summer of 1781 — a failure that contributed directly to the catastrophe at Yorktown. Rodney was accused of sacrificing the war for the sake of prize money. The island was recaptured by the French in November 1781.
The Battle of the Saintes
Rodney’s redemption came on the 12th of April, 1782. By this time, de Grasse had sailed from Martinique with thirty-four sail of the line, intending to join the Spanish fleet and capture Jamaica — the richest remaining British possession in the Caribbean. Rodney, with thirty-six sail, intercepted him off the Îles des Saintes, a cluster of rocks between Guadeloupe and Dominica.
The two fleets engaged at seven in the morning. For hours the battle hung in the balance. Then, at half-past eleven, with the wind shifting to the south-east, Rodney seized the moment. In the Formidable, he bore down and broke through the French line — a manoeuvre that scattered de Grasse’s fleet beyond hope of recovery. The French admiral’s flagship, the Ville de Paris of 110 guns, was surrounded and forced to strike. Four other French ships of the line were taken. De Grasse himself was brought aboard the Formidable, a prisoner.
The victory at the Battle of the Saintes saved Jamaica, restored British naval prestige, and secured for Rodney a barony — he was created Baron Rodney of Rodney Stoke, Somerset. Yet the battle also triggered a long controversy. Several years afterward, John Clerk of Eldin, a Scottish gentleman of scientific pursuits, published a work on naval tactics claiming that the manoeuvre of breaking the line was his own invention, and that he had communicated it to Rodney through a common friend before the battle. The Admiralty investigated and declined to reward Clerk, noting that the tactic had been employed in earlier engagements — but the debate over who deserved credit for the Saintes has never entirely subsided.
Later Life and Legacy
Rodney returned to England in 1783 to a hero’s welcome. He was voted a pension of £2,000 per year by Parliament. But his health was broken, and his financial affairs remained disordered. He withdrew from active service and lived quietly on his estate in Somerset until his death on the 24th of May, 1792.
Rodney was, by all accounts, a man of extraordinary personal courage and tactical genius — the first admiral to deliberately break an enemy’s line in a major fleet action. His victory at the Saintes ranks with Edward Hawke’s triumph at Quiberon Bay and George Anson’s at Finisterre as one of the decisive fleet actions of the 18th century. Yet his legacy is shadowed by the St. Eustatius affair, the lingering suspicion that he valued wealth over duty, and the sense that his greatest victory owed as much to a shift of wind as to design. He was buried in the family vault at Rodney Stoke.

entities/george-rooke.title: Sir George Rooke (1650–1709)
entities/george-rooke.content:
Sir George Rooke (1650–1709)
Sir George Rooke (1650–1709) was an English naval commander who served as Admiral of the Fleet under Queen Anne, achieving the two most celebrated naval victories of the early War of the Spanish Succession: the destruction of the Franco-Spanish treasure fleet at the Battle of Vigo Bay (1702) and the capture of Gibraltar (1704). He also fought the largest fleet action of the war at the Battle of Malaga (1704), a tactical draw that confirmed Anglo-Dutch naval supremacy in the Mediterranean. A decorated veteran of the Nine Years’ War and the Baltic expedition of 1700, Rooke was also a Tory figure who became a lightning rod for partisan controversy in his later career.
Early Career and the Nine Years’ War
Rooke was born in 1650, the son of Sir William Rooke, a Kentish baronet, and Anne (née L’Estrange) of Hunstanton, Norfolk. He entered the Royal Navy in his youth and saw active service in the Third Anglo-Dutch War. By 1692, during the Nine Years’ War, he had risen to the rank of rear-admiral and fought at the Battle of Barfleur and the subsequent action at La Hogue (May 1692), where the combined Anglo-Dutch fleet under Edward Russell, Earl of Orford shattered the French invasion threat against England. Rooke commanded a division in the battle and was knighted for his conduct.
Promoted to vice-admiral, Rooke served in the Mediterranean under Russell and later commanded a squadron in the Channel. In 1697, with Russell’s elevation to the peerage and appointment as First Lord of the Admiralty, Sir George Rooke was declared Admiral of the Fleet and took command of the main fleet at Portsmouth. He found the ships “not half manned, and worse victualled” but by the end of June 1697 had assembled forty-four sail of the line. He escorted the Russian Tsar Peter the Great across the Channel in January 1698, a service that left the Tsar with a lasting interest in British naval discipline.
The Baltic Expedition (1700)
In the spring of 1700, King William III dispatched Rooke with a powerful squadron to the Baltic, where he was joined by a Dutch squadron to enforce a peace mediated by England and Sweden between Denmark and the Duke of Holstein-Gottorp. Rooke pushed into the Sound, manoeuvring against the Danish fleet under the guns of Kronborg Castle, and linked up with the Swedish fleet of Count Wachtmeister. The combined Anglo-Swedish-Dutch fleet of fifty-two ships of the line blockaded Copenhagen and covered the landing of King Charles XII of Sweden’s troops near Elsinore, which forced the Danes to sign the preliminaries of the Treaty of Travendal in August 1700.
The War of the Spanish Succession: Cadiz and Vigo Bay
Upon Queen Anne’s accession in March 1702, Rooke was appointed Vice-Admiral of England and given command of a massive combined English and Dutch fleet: thirty English and twenty Dutch ships of the line, with 13,801 troops under the Duke of Ormond. The expedition’s primary objective was the capture of Cadiz, the great Spanish Atlantic port.
The Failure at Cadiz
The fleet appeared off Cadiz on 12 August 1702. The Duke of Ormond argued for an immediate assault on the Isle of Leon, believing the town was in panic and could be taken by a sudden attack. But the sea officers in the council of war overruled him, insisting first on reducing the Fort of St. Catharine and Port St. Mary. The delay proved fatal: the landing at the Bay of Bulls on 15 August met only brief resistance, and the troops took Port St. Mary without a fight, but the army then became distracted by plunder and the looting of churches and private houses. Spanish resistance stiffened, the governor of Cadiz refused to surrender, and the expedition was abandoned in September. The plunder of Port St. Mary caused a scandal in England.
The Victory at Vigo Bay
The disaster at Cadiz was redeemed by one of the most spectacular naval actions of the century. While the fleet was returning home, Rooke learned from Captain Thomas Hardy (who had brought an express from Lisbon) that the Spanish treasure galleons, under the convoy of a French squadron commanded by Monsieur Château-Renault, had put into Vigo harbour on 16 September 1702. Rooke called an immediate council of war on 6 October, and the assembled flag-officers resolved to attack.
The harbour entrance was barely three-quarters of a mile wide, defended by a battery of eight brass and twelve iron guns on the north side, a platform of forty guns on the south, and a stone fort with a breastwork and trench mounting ten guns with 500 men. Across the harbour stretched a formidable boom of ships’ yards and topmasts, fastened with three-inch rope and hawsers, moored at each end to seventy-gun ships. Inside were five French men-of-war of sixty to seventy guns moored broadside to the entrance.
Rooke and his flag-officers removed their flags from the great first- and second-rates to smaller third-rates that could enter the harbour — Rooke moving from the Royal Sovereign to the Somerset. A detachment of fifteen English and ten Dutch men-of-war was ordered in, supported by fireships, frigates, and bomb-vessels. On 23 October 1702, the Duke of Ormond landed 2,500 men six miles south of Vigo, Lord Shannon stormed the stone fort with 500 grenadiers, and the British flag flew from the batteries. Vice-Admiral Hopson in the Torbay then rammed the boom and broke through, the Kent and the rest of the squadron pouring into the harbour. Despite a French fireship that grappled the Torbay (and was extinguished only because it carried a cargo of snuff), the English ships battered the French into submission. Fifteen French men-of-war and seventeen Spanish galleons were burnt, sunk, or taken. The treasure seized — or destroyed in the fighting — dealt a severe blow to the finances of France and Spain. Rooke was hailed a hero, though the plunder scandal from Cadiz dogged the campaign.
The Capture of Gibraltar (1704)
After Vigo, Rooke commanded the Mediterranean fleet in 1703 and early 1704. In the spring of 1704, with a fleet augmented by Sir Cloudesley Shovel’s squadron, Rooke considered several schemes — including a second attack on Cadiz — but found himself constrained by contradictory instructions from the Court of the Archduke Charles (the Austrian claimant to the Spanish throne) and the King of Portugal. Determined not to spend the summer “doing nothing of importance,” Rooke called a council of war in the roadstead of Tetuan on 17 July 1704. After a long debate, it was resolved to make “a sudden and vigorous attempt upon Gibraltar,” for three reasons: the place was poorly garrisoned and might be taken; its possession was of infinite strategic importance; and the capture would give lustre to Queen Anne’s arms.
The fleet arrived in the Bay of Gibraltar on 21 July 1704. The Prince of Hesse-Darmstadt landed 1,800 marines on the isthmus to cut off communications. The governor, summoned, declared he would defend the place to the last. At daybreak on 22 July, Rooke gave the signal for bombardment. The fleet poured fifteen thousand shot into the town in five hours, driving the defenders from their fortifications at the South Mole Head. Captain Hicks and Captain Jumper pushed ashore with their pinnaces and seized the fortifications. A Spanish mine killed two lieutenants and forty men, but Captain Whitaker and his seamen took a redoubt between the mole and the town. Rooke sent in terms, and on 24 July the governor capitulated. The garrison, the Prince of Hesse, and the seamen of the fleet — not a single soldier had been landed for the assault — had taken the Rock. The Spanish later claimed the place had neither garrison nor guns, but Campbell’s account records over one hundred brass pieces mounted on the defences.
The Battle of Malaga (1704)
After garrisoning Gibraltar, the fleet sailed to Tetuan for wood and water. On 9 August they sailed again, sighting the French fleet. For three days the French avoided combat, but on Sunday, 13 August 1704, Rooke brought them to action off Malaga. The French line consisted of fifty-two ships and twenty-four galleys under Count Toulouse, High Admiral of France. The Anglo-Dutch fleet numbered fifty-three ships, but the French had significant advantages: seventeen three-deck ships against just seven, six hundred more guns overall, cleaner hulls fresh from port, the assistance of galleys that could tow disabled ships out of the line and replenish their complements, and abundant ammunition.
Nevertheless, at ten in the morning, the English bore down in order of battle. Rooke opened the engagement with a chase-gun at the French admiral and threw out the signal for battle. The fighting fell heaviest on the Royal Catherine, the St George, and the Shrewsbury. The battle raged for the entire day. Several English ships were towed out of the line having exhausted their powder; the Monk of sixty guns was boarded three times by a seventy-gun French ship and beat her off each time. But by afternoon the French van gave way, and the battle ended with daylight. The French slipped away overnight using their galleys as tugs.
The Dutch — whose ships had formed the rear — declared Malaga “the best fought action recorded in history.” French claims of victory (Louis XIV ordered a Te Deum and struck a medal) were propaganda: the French fleet avoided battle for the remainder of the war, never again contesting the empire of the sea. Malaga, in Campbell’s judgment, was the battle that “decided the empire of the sea,” confirming Britain and the Netherlands as the undisputed maritime powers. Parliament voted its thanks, and Rooke’s name was bracketed with the Duke of Marlborough’s — the two great captains of the annus mirabilis of 1704.
Later Career and Controversy
Despite his triumphs, Rooke came under sustained attack from Whig historians and politicians, notably Gilbert Burnet, Bishop of Salisbury, who in his History of His Own Times accused Rooke of lukewarmness at Cadiz and downplayed the victory at Malaga. The partisan atmosphere in Parliament — Lord Haversham’s blistering speeches, the inquiries into Admiralty mismanagement, the attacks on the Prince of Denmark’s council — gave Rooke such disgust that after 1704 he declined further command. Campbell records that Rooke “desired that the Queen might be easy, and the nation well served, rather than that any opportunities might be given him of adding either to his reputation or estate.”
The Duke of Argyle defended Rooke’s memory in the House of Lords in 1740, calling Burnet “a very credulous weak man” and insisting that “the greatest part of [his account] is a downright lie.” The Tory pamphleteer Mr. Hornby, in his Caveat against the Whigs, wrote: “In 1704, Sir George Rooke, with a crew of cabin-boys, took the almost impregnable fortress of Gibraltar.”
Sir George Rooke died on 24 January 1709, at the age of fifty-eight.
Legacy
Rooke’s legacy rests on three achievements: the destruction of the treasure fleet at Vigo Bay, which damaged Franco-Spanish finances at a critical moment; the capture of Gibraltar, which gave Britain the strategic gateway to the Mediterranean for over three centuries; and the Battle of Malaga, which — though tactically inconclusive — broke French naval morale and left the allies unchallenged at sea for the remainder of the war. His Gibraltar prize, taken without a single soldier setting foot ashore, stands as one of the most astonishing feats of arms in the age of sail.
He is sometimes overshadowed by his contemporaries Cloudesley Shovel, who commanded under him at Malaga and later perished in the Scilly naval disaster of 1707, and Edward Russell, Earl of Orford, the victor of Barfleur. Among his subordinates at Gibraltar and Malaga were Sir John Leake, who would go on to capture Minorca and command in the Mediterranean, and George Byng, Viscount Torrington, the future victor of Cape Passaro.
