events/act-of-union-1707.title: Act of Union (1707)
events/act-of-union-1707.content:
Act of Union (1707)
The Act of Union (1707) — formally the Union with England Act (Scottish) and the Union with Scotland Act (English) — created the Kingdom of Great Britain, uniting the previously separate Kingdoms of England (including Wales) and Scotland into a single sovereign state with a single parliament. The Union took effect on 1 May 1707. It was the culmination of a century of on-again-off-again negotiations, driven into being by the disastrous Darien Scheme, English fears of a Jacobite Scotland allied with France, and the hard-headed calculations of Lord Godolphin’s ministry.
Background: The Road to Union
The Failed Darien Scheme (1698–1700)
The single most important proximate cause of the Union was the catastrophic failure of the Darien Scheme (1698–1700), Scotland’s attempt to establish a colony on the Isthmus of Panama under the auspices of the Company of Scotland Trading to Africa and the Indies. The scheme had been promoted by the Scottish financier William Paterson, co-founder of the bank-of-england, who envisioned Darien as a global trading entrepôt connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
The project captured the Scottish imagination: between one-quarter and one-half of Scotland’s liquid capital was invested in the Company. Four expeditions were sent, but the colony — called New Caledonia — was doomed from the start. The Spanish Crown claimed the territory as its own, the English Crown (under William III), eager to preserve peace with Spain during the Nine Years’ War, refused to supply or support the settlement, and the climate and disease devastated the colonists. By 1700, the settlement was abandoned with the loss of some 2,000 lives and a ruinous financial loss.
Burnet records that the loss was so universal and so operative in Scottish sentiment that “the Design on Darien, which the Jacobites had set on foot and prosecuted with so much fury, and with bad Intentions, did now engage many to promote the Union, who, without that Consideration, would have been at least neutral, if not backward in it.” Burnet, Vol. II
The Economic Consequence: The Darien disaster left Scotland’s mercantile class convinced that Scotland could not succeed as an independent colonial power. Without access to English markets and English naval protection, the Scottish economy could not compete. The investing classes who had lost heavily in Darien saw in the Union’s Equivalent a means of recovering their losses, and many threw their weight behind the project.
The Act of Security (1704) and English Alarm
If the Darien Scheme pushed Scots toward Union, English fears about Scottish independence pulled them. In 1703–1704, the Scottish Parliament, frustrated by English intransigence on trade and the succession, passed the Act of Security, which provided that upon the death of Queen Anne (who had no surviving children), Scotland would be free to choose a different successor to the Crown than the Hanoverian heir designated by the English Act of Settlement. The Act further provided for Scotland to be armed and prepared for war if the succession were not settled to its satisfaction.
This was a direct challenge to English strategic interests. If Scotland chose a Jacobite claimant — James Francis Edward Stuart, the “Old Pretender” — after Anne’s death, England would face a hostile, French-allied state on its northern border. As Burnet notes, the Act of Security “was imputed chiefly to the Lord Treasurer” (Godolphin), and threats of impeaching him for advising it were “often let fall” by his political enemies. Burnet, Vol. II
The English Parliament responded with the Alien Act (1705) , which threatened to treat Scots as aliens and cut off trade in cattle, coal, and linen unless Scotland either accepted the Hanoverian succession or entered into negotiations for a full incorporating union. The economic coercion was deliberate: Scotland’s primary export trade ran through England, and the threat of exclusion was devastating.
English Fears of Jacobite Scotland
Beneath the tactical posturing lay a deeper English strategic fear: the prospect of a Jacobite Scotland allied with Louis XIV’s France. Throughout the War of the Spanish Succession (1702–1714), the Jacobite court-in-exile at Saint-Germain maintained close contacts with dissident Scottish nobles. A French-backed Jacobite rising in Scotland, co-ordinated with the war on the Continent, could open a deadly second front. The Union would extinguish this possibility permanently by absorbing Scotland’s Parliament and foreign policy into a single British state.
As Campbell notes in his Naval History, the Union had profound naval implications: a unified British navy, Scottish access to English trade routes, and the birth of a truly British naval dominance. Campbell, Vol. III
The Negotiations
The Commissioners
In 1705, the English Parliament passed an Act authorising the Queen to name Commissioners to treat of a union. The Scottish Parliament reciprocated. Each side appointed 31 Commissioners, who met in London from 16 April to 22 July 1706 at the Cockpit in Whitehall.
English Commissioners included:

Sidney Godolphin, 1st Earl of Godolphin — Lord High Treasurer and chief minister
John Churchill, Duke of Marlborough — Captain-General, commanding the war on the Continent
Charles Montagu, 1st Earl of Halifax — Whig statesman
John Somers, 1st Baron Somers — former Lord Chancellor, leading Whig intellectual
Robert Harley — Speaker of the House of Commons
William Cowper — Lord Keeper of the Great Seal
Sir Thomas Trevor — Chief Justice of the Common Pleas

Scottish Commissioners included:

James Douglas, 2nd Duke of Queensberry — Lord High Commissioner to the Scottish Parliament, the dominant figure on the Scottish side. Created Duke of Dover in the Peerage of Great Britain as a reward.
John Erskine, 6th Earl of Mar — Secretary of State for Scotland
James Ogilvy, 1st Earl of Seafield — Lord Chancellor of Scotland
John Dalrymple, 2nd Earl of Stair — leading unionist, who “maintained the Debate on the last Day” and died suddenly the following night, his spirits “quite exhausted by the Length and Vehemence of the Debate” Burnet, Vol. II
David Boyle, 1st Earl of Glasgow — Lord Treasurer of Scotland
Sir James Ogilvy — Lord Advocate
Adam Cockburn, Lord Ormiston — Lord Justice Clerk
William Morrison — Lord President of the Court of Session

The Squadrone Volante
A pivotal role in the negotiations was played by an informal parliamentary group known as the Squadrone Volante (“Flying Squadron”), a group of some twenty to thirty Scottish nobles and gentlemen who were “in no Engagements with the Court” and who had “been disobliged, and turned out of great Posts.” They included the Marquess of Tweedale, the Earls of Rothes, Roxburgh, Hadington, and Marchmont. Burnet writes that they “kept themselves very close and united, and seemed to have no other Interest, but that of their Country” and that if they “had set themselves against the Union, the Design must have miscarried.” Burnet, Vol. II
The Opposition
The Union faced formidable opposition in Scotland. The leading opponents were:

James Hamilton, 4th Duke of Hamilton — the premier peer of Scotland, who led the parliamentary opposition with great vehemence but was “against all desperate Motions,” having “much to lose” Burnet, Vol. II
John Murray, 1st Duke of Atholl — believed by Burnet to be “in a foreign Correspondence” with the Jacobite court
John Johnstone, 1st Marquess of Annandale
Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun — the most intellectually formidable opponent, a Scottish patriot and political theorist who argued passionately for a federal rather than incorporating union, warning that Scotland would be “sunk into a Dependence on England”

Fletcher’s arguments were the most sophisticated articulated against the Union. He had earlier proposed a scheme of limitations on the Crown and a federal arrangement. His concern was that Scotland’s 45 MPs and 16 representative peers would be so outnumbered in the British Parliament — “above an hundred Peers and five hundred and thirteen Commoners” on the English side — that they could never hold the balance. Burnet, Vol. II
Popular Opposition
The debates in Edinburgh were accompanied by intense popular agitation. Mobs gathered in the streets; there were riots in Edinburgh, Glasgow, and Dumfries. The Presbyterian clergy and their flocks feared that the Union would submerge their Church in the English episcopal establishment. As Burnet records: “if the Presbyterians had not been possessed with a Jealousy, that the consequence of this Union would be, the Change of Church-Government among them, and that they would be swallowed up by the Church of England” — a fear that “took such root in many, that no Assurances, that were offered, could remove their Fears.” Burnet, Vol. II
The old Duchess of Hamilton (Anne Hamilton, 3rd Duchess) was said to have great credit with the Presbyterians and it was suggested that she and her son “had particular Views, as hoping, that if Scotland should continue a separated Kingdom, the Crown might come into their Family, they being the next in Blood, after King James’s Posterity.” Burnet, Vol. II
At one point, the situation appeared so dangerous that Queensberry despaired of succeeding and feared for his personal safety. He wrote to Godolphin suggesting an adjournment. Godolphin’s answer was blunt: “a delay was, upon the Matter, laying the whole Design aside.” He ordered troops in England and Ireland to be ready, and more forces from Flanders if necessary, with the observation that “the French were in no condition to send any Assistance” to potential rebels. Burnet, Vol. II
The Treaty: Twenty-Five Articles
The Commissioners produced 25 Articles of Union, which were laid before the Scottish Parliament in October 1706 and debated clause by clause over three months. The main provisions were:




























































ArticleProvisionSignificanceIThe two Kingdoms of Scotland and England shall be united into one Kingdom named Great BritainThe fundamental constitutional changeIIThe succession to the Crown of Great Britain shall be according to the Act of Settlement (i.e., the Hanoverian line)Settled the Protestant succession, extinguishing Jacobite hopesIIIThe United Kingdom shall have one Parliament, styled the Parliament of Great BritainThe most controversial provision — Scotland gave up its independent legislatureIVFull freedom of trade and navigation between Scotland and England, and with the colonies and plantationsThe great economic prize for ScotlandVIScotland to pay a share of the Customs and Excise duties on the same footing as EnglandScotland’s contribution was set at approximately one-fortieth of the wholeXVAn Equivalent sum of £398,085 10s to be paid to ScotlandCompensation for assuming a share of England’s national debt and for losses in the Darien SchemeXVI–XXIIUniformity of coins, weights, measures, and the salt and malt taxesEconomic integrationXXIIScotland to be represented by 16 Peers in the House of Lords and 45 Members in the House of CommonsDisproportionate to Scotland’s tax contribution but generous relative to populationXXIVThe Courts of Law and the legal system of Scotland to remain in forceGuaranteed the independent Scots law traditionXXVAll heritable offices, jurisdictions, and private rights to remain as before the UnionPreserved the feudal character of Scottish landholding
The Equivalent
Article XV provided for the Equivalent, a lump sum of £398,085 10s to be raised in England and sent to Scotland. Its purposes were threefold:

To compensate Scotland for assuming a share of the English national debt accumulated during the War of the Spanish Succession
To discharge the public debts of Scotland
To reimburse the Company of Scotland (the Darien investors) for their losses, with interest — upon which the Company was to be dissolved, with any overplus applied to the encouragement of manufactures

As Burnet notes, “the Equivalent was to be applied, to the Encouragement of Manufactures” and that in its disposition “great Partialities appeared, which were much complained of.” The ministry and those who depended on them “moved for very extravagant Allowances to those, who had been employed in this last, and in the former Treaty.” Burnet, Vol. II
Free Trade and Economic Integration
Article IV, guaranteeing free trade, was the single most potent argument for the Union in Scotland. As Burnet writes, “The opening a free Trade, not only with England, but with the Plantations, and the Protection of the Fleet of England, drew in those who understood these Matters, and saw there was no other way in view, to make the Nation rich and considerable.” Burnet, Vol. II
For Scotland’s trading classes, already burned by the Darien disaster, access to England’s protected colonial markets — the West Indian sugar islands, the North American tobacco colonies, and soon the East — was transformative. For England, the extension of its Navigation Acts to Scotland closed a loophole through which Scottish merchants had traded with the colonies as de facto aliens and secured a unified imperial trade system.
Scottish Representation
Scotland’s representation in the new Parliament of Great Britain — 16 representative peers in the Lords and 45 MPs in the Commons — reflected a careful balancing act. Scotland bore approximately one-fortieth of the tax burden, yet received “near the eleventh part of the Legislature” (16 of ~190 Lords, 45 of ~558 Commons). Burnet observes that “it is held a Maxim, that in the framing of a Government, a Proportion ought to be observed, between the Share in the Legislature, and the Burden to be born.” Burnet, Vol. II
The representative peer system was particularly controversial. Scottish peers lost their individual right to sit in the House of Lords — “the greatest of them all, which was the Voting in the House of Lords, was restrained to Sixteen, to be elected by the rest at every new Parliament.” Despite this, a greater majority of the Scottish nobility concurred in voting for the Union than in the other estates. As Smollett later records, the system proved contentious: when the Duke of Hamilton was created Duke of Brandon in the Peerage of Great Britain, the House of Lords ruled that Scottish peers created peers of Great Britain after the Union had no right to sit, a decision that “infringement of the union” inflamed Scottish opinion. Smollett, Vol. X
Preservation of Scottish Institutions
The Treaty guaranteed the preservation of two of Scotland’s most cherished institutions:
The Legal System (Article XXIV): The separate legal system of Scotland, based on Roman-Dutch civil law rather than English common law, was preserved in perpetuity. This guaranteed the continued existence of the Court of Session (the supreme civil court), the High Court of Justiciary (criminal), and the distinctive Scottish sheriff courts. Scots law continued to develop independently, and the Act of Union has been a foundational constitutional document in Scottish legal reasoning ever since.
The Presbyterian Church: Religious matters were explicitly excluded from the Commissioners’ remit — the Acts authorising the negotiations “expressly limited” that the Commissioners “should not treat of those Matters.” Instead, separate Acts of Parliament in both kingdoms were passed to secure the respective church establishments. The Act for Securing the Protestant Religion and Presbyterian Church Government (1706) — passed by the Scottish Parliament alongside the Union — guaranteed the permanent establishment of the Presbyterian Church (the Kirk). Smollett records that the Presbyterian clergy and General Assembly regarded this as “an essential and fundamental condition of the treaty of union” and remonstrated vigorously when the British Parliament later passed legislation affecting Scottish religious matters, such as the toleration granted to Episcopalian clergy. Smollett, Vol. X
The Legislative Process
In the Scottish Parliament
The Articles were debated in the Scottish Parliament from October 1706 to January 1707. Each Article was voted on separately, and the government’s majority held firm through every division. As Burnet describes it:
“The Commissioners from the Shires and Boroughs, were almost equally divided, tho’ it was evident they were to be the chief Gainers by it; among these the Union was agreed to, by a very small Majority: It was the Nobility, that in every Vote turned the Scale for the Union.” Burnet, Vol. II
The Squadrone Volante ultimately declared for the Union, and “not only joined in it, but promoted it effectually, and with Zeal.” The great debates were managed for the Union by the Earls of Seafield and Stair (for the Ministry) and the Earls of Roxburgh and Marchmont (for the Squadrone); against it by Hamilton, Atholl, and Annandale.
The Act passed the Scottish Parliament on 16 January 1707 and was sent up to London “in the beginning of February.”
In the English Parliament
The English legislative process was deliberately engineered to minimise opposition. Burnet records that the Bill was prepared by Sir Simon Harcourt with “so particular a Contrivance, that it cut off all Debates.” The Preamble was a mere recital of the Articles as passed in Scotland, together with the Acts for church security, and then “in conclusion, there came one Enacting Clause, ratifying all.” This drafting “put those, upon great Difficulties, who had resolved to object to several Articles… for they could not come at any Debate about them.”
The matter “was carried on with such Zeal, that it passed through the House of Commons, before those, who intended to oppose it, had recovered themselves out of the Surprize.” In the Lords, where the Articles “had been copiously debated there for several Days, before the Bill was sent up to them,” it passed with the support of Lord Treasurer Godolphin, the Earls of Sunderland and Wharton, Lords Townshend and Halifax, and above all Lord Somers. The bishops of Oxford, Norwich, and Burnet himself argued for it. Burnet, Vol. II
The royal assent was given on 6 March 1707.
The Union Takes Effect: 1 May 1707
The Treaty provided that the Union “was to commence on the First of May” and that “till that time, the two Kingdoms were still distinct, and their two Parliaments continued still to sit.” On 1 May 1707, the Parliaments of England and Scotland were dissolved, and the first Parliament of Great Britain met.
Burnet captures the significance with a note of providential reflection: “Thus this great Design, so long wished and laboured for in vain, was begun, and happily ended, within the Compass of Nine Months.” Burnet, Vol. II
Key Figures

































































FigureRolePerspectiveQueen Anne (1665–1714)Monarch of both kingdomsStrongly supported the Union as a means of securing the Protestant succession and ending Anglo-Scottish frictionSidney Godolphin, 1st Earl of Godolphin (1645–1712)Lord High Treasurer of England, chief ministerThe driving force on the English side; faced impeachment threats over the Act of Security; deployed bribes and patronage to secure votes in the Scottish Parliament; “bestirred himself with an Activity and Zeal, that seemed not to be in his nature” (Burnet)James Douglas, 2nd Duke of Queensberry (1662–1711)Lord High Commissioner to the Scottish ParliamentQueen Anne’s manager in Scotland; steered the Articles through the Scottish Parliament; created Duke of Dover as a reward; nearly despaired during the Edinburgh riotsAndrew Fletcher of Saltoun (1653–1716)Scottish Commissioner and MPThe leading intellectual opponent of incorporating union; argued for federal union and limitations on the Crown; his warnings about Scotland being overwhelmed by English numbers proved prescientJames Hamilton, 4th Duke of Hamilton (1658–1712)Leader of the parliamentary oppositionLed the anti-Union cause in the Scottish Parliament; a cautious oppositionist who “was against all desperate Motions”John Dalrymple, 2nd Earl of Stair (1673–1707)Scottish CommissionerLeading unionist debater; died suddenly the night after the final debate, his spirits exhaustedJames Ogilvy, 1st Earl of Seafield (1663–1730)Lord Chancellor of ScotlandManaged the Union through the Scottish Parliament for the MinistryJohn Somers, 1st Baron Somers (1651–1716)Whig statesman, English CommissionerArgued powerfully for the Union in the English House of LordsJohn Churchill, Duke of Marlborough (1650–1722)Captain-General, English CommissionerSupported the Union; his military victories improved English bargaining positionRobert Harley (1661–1724)Speaker of the Commons, English CommissionerPlayed a supporting role in the English legislative processThe Squadrone VolanteCross-party Scottish parliamentary groupThe swing votes: Tweedale, Rothes, Roxburgh, Hadington, Marchmont — their support made the Union possible
Chronology

























































DateEvent1698First Darien expedition sails for Panama1700Final abandonment of the Darien colony; financial ruin in Scotland1701English Act of Settlement settles the Crown on the House of Hanover1704Scottish Act of Security passes, threatening a separate succession1705English Alien Act threatens trade sanctions; both Parliaments authorise treaty negotiations16 Apr – 22 Jul 1706Commissioners meet at the Cockpit, Whitehall; 25 Articles agreed3 Oct 1706Articles laid before the Scottish Parliament; debate beginsOct–Dec 1706Popular rioting in Edinburgh, Glasgow, Dumfries; Queensberry despairs; Godolphin holds firm16 Jan 1707Scottish Parliament passes the Union ActFeb 1707Act sent to London6 Mar 1707Royal assent given in England1 May 1707The Union takes effect; the Kingdom of Great Britain is born
Economic Consequences
The Union transformed the Scottish economy over the following decades:

Colonial Trade: Scottish merchants gained immediate access to English colonial markets, and the tobacco trade in particular boomed. Glasgow became the leading tobacco-importing port in Britain by the 1720s.
Agricultural Improvement: Exposure to English markets and English agricultural techniques spurred the beginnings of the Scottish Agricultural Revolution.
The Equivalent: The £398,085 Equivalent compensated Darien investors and discharged Scottish public debt, but the actual disbursement was delayed — Burnet records that “Three Months passed, before the Equivalent was sent to Scotland” — and was attended by charges of partiality.
Naval and Imperial: As Campbell emphasises, the Union created a unified British navy and freed the English state from the strategic nightmare of a hostile Scotland allied to France. Campbell, Vol. III

Historiographical Notes
Burnet, writing within a decade of the Union, provides the most detailed contemporary account of the parliamentary politics. His narrative emphasises the providential hand of God in the affair, the decisive role of the Squadrone Volante, and Godolphin’s steely nerve during the Edinburgh riots. He also acknowledges the widespread use of bribery — “those of Scotland had learned from England, to set a Price on their Votes, and they expected to be well paid for them” — but treats this as a necessary means to a desirable end.
Smollett, writing half a century later, focuses more on the post-Union disputes — the Hamilton peerage case, the toleration controversy, the patronage bill — suggesting that the fruits of Union were contested from the start.
For subsequent historians, the Union of 1707 remains one of the most debated events in British history: was it a voluntary partnership of equals, or an English takeover lubricated by bribes? The truth lies somewhere between, as it was all of these things at once — a salvage operation for a bankrupt Scottish elite, a strategic necessity for an English state at war, and the foundation of the British imperial state.
Key Events Table













































DateEventSignificance1698–1700Darien SchemeFailed Scottish colonial venture that bankrupted the Scottish investing class and demonstrated Scotland’s inability to compete independently1704Act of SecurityScottish Parliament asserts right to choose a different successor; alarms English ministry1705Alien ActEnglish trade coercion against Scotland; forces the issue of unionApr–Jul 1706Treaty negotiations (Whitehall)31 Commissioners from each kingdom agree 25 ArticlesOct 1706 – Jan 1707Scottish parliamentary debatesThree months of fierce debate and popular agitation; Articles passed clause by clause6 Mar 1707Royal assent (England)Queen Anne gives assent to Union with Scotland Act1 May 1707Union takes effectKingdom of Great Britain established; Parliaments of England and Scotland dissolved
Cross-References

events/act-of-union-1800.title: Acts of Union (1800)
events/act-of-union-1800.content:
Acts of Union (1800)
The Acts of Union 1800 — passed by the Parliament of Ireland in Dublin and the Parliament of Great Britain at Westminster — united the Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Ireland into a single state: the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The Acts took effect on 1 January 1801. It was the most significant constitutional rearrangement of the British Isles since the Act of Union 1707 between England and Scotland, and it lasted until the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921 established the Irish Free State in 1922.
Background: The Irish Rebellion of 1798
The proximate cause of the Union was the Irish Rebellion of 1798, a catastrophe that convinced William Pitt the Younger and his ministry that a separate Irish parliament, sitting in Dublin with its own executive, was an unacceptable danger to the security of the British state.
The Rising
The Rebellion of 1798 was the most violent insurrection in modern Irish history. It was organised by the Society of United Irishmen, a revolutionary body founded in Belfast in 1791 by Wolfe Tone and Samuel Neilson. The United Irishmen were initially a reforming movement — inspired by the French Revolution, the American Revolution, and the principles of Edmund Burke’s constitutionalism — seeking parliamentary reform and Catholic emancipation within the framework of Grattan’s Parliament. But when the War of the First Coalition brought Britain into conflict with Revolutionary France in 1793, the government’s campaign of repression drove the movement underground and into armed conspiracy.
By 1796, the United Irishmen had transformed into a secret, oath-bound revolutionary organisation, organised along military lines, and actively seeking French military assistance. The French attempt of December 1796 — a substantial expeditionary force under General Lazare Hoche that arrived off Bantry Bay but was scattered by storms — demonstrated how real the threat was. Had the French landed, with the United Irishmen rising in support, Ireland might have been lost to the Crown.
The rebellion itself, when it finally erupted in May 1798, was savage on both sides. The insurgents achieved significant early successes — the battle of Vinegar Hill in County Wexford, the capture of Enniscorthy and Wexford Town — but the rising was crushed by government forces under General Gerard Lake and Sir John Moore, supplemented by locally raised yeomanry. The repression was ferocious: perhaps 30,000 people died in the space of three months, the vast majority of them Catholic insurgents butchered in the field or executed after summary courts-martial. The Battle of Ballinamuck in September ended the last French-assisted phase of the rebellion, and Wolfe Tone was captured, sentenced to death, and died by his own hand (or was killed) in November 1798.
The Political Fallout
The rebellion had two consequences that made Union irresistible. The first was security: a reconstituted and resentful Irish Parliament under Protestant Ascendancy control could not be trusted to manage so volatile a situation. Only the full incorporation of Ireland into the British state would ensure that the executive in Dublin was directly responsible to the Crown’s ministers in London, with the resources and authority of the imperial Parliament behind it.
The second was finance. The cost of suppressing the rebellion was enormous; Ireland’s national debt had risen from virtually nothing in the mid-century to nearly £30 million by 1800. The Irish Parliament had shown itself incapable of managing the kingdom’s finances, and the British Exchequer was effectively underwriting Irish solvency. Union offered fiscal consolidation: the absorption of Ireland’s debt into a larger British whole.
The Irish Parliament: Grattan’s Parliament (1782–1800)
The Parliament that voted itself out of existence in 1800 was a relatively recent creation. From 1494, Ireland had been subject to Poynings’ Law, which required all Irish legislation to be approved by the English Privy Council. In 1720, the Declaratory Act (6 Geo. I, c. 5) had asserted the right of the British Parliament to legislate for Ireland directly — a provision that Hamilton in the Federalist Papers called “one of the most flagrant usurpations of the rights of a free people.”
During the American Revolutionary War, with Britain militarily overstretched and vulnerable, the Irish Volunteers — a Protestant militia raised for defence — had forced the British government’s hand. In 1782, led by the Whig statesman Henry Grattan (who gave his name to the era), the Irish Parliament won what was effectively legislative independence. The Declaratory Act was repealed, Poynings’ Law was amended to require only the transmission of bills (not their approval in advance), and the Irish judiciary became independent of the English courts. Ireland and Great Britain were now separate kingdoms under the same Crown, with separate parliaments and legal systems, bound only by the person of the monarch.
Grattan’s Parliament (1782–1800) was a remarkable institution: a parliament of the Protestant Ascendancy — only Anglicans could sit — but one that governed an overwhelmingly Catholic country of some five million people. It represented a tight oligarchy of landed families, the borough-mongers, and the Church of Ireland establishment. It had genuine talents — Grattan himself was one of the greatest orators of the age — but it was built on an impossible contradiction: it was an independent legislature that represented only a fraction of the population of the island it governed.
The contradiction deepened during the 1790s. The Catholic Relief Act 1793 gave the Catholic forty-shilling freeholders the vote (but not the right to sit in Parliament), and the liberal Lord Lieutenant, Earl Fitzwilliam, was recalled in 1795 after briefly flirting with Catholic emancipation — a recall that convinced many Irish Catholics that only separation from Britain would ever deliver justice. When the rebellion came in 1798, the Protestant Parliament proved incapable of containing or settling the crisis.
The Negotiations: ‘The Union Was Bought’
The campaign to pass the Union through the Irish Parliament is one of the most sordid episodes in the constitutional history of the British Isles. It was driven through by a combination of official pressure, massive bribery, and systematic patronage — so extensive that contemporaries and historians alike concluded that the Union was not so much voted as purchased. The phrase “the Union was bought” became proverbial.
The Machinery of Bribery
The manager of the Union campaign in Ireland was Lord Castlereagh — Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh — then serving as Chief Secretary for Ireland under the Lord Lieutenant, Lord Cornwallis. Cornwallis and Castlereagh had a strategy: to make the Union irresistible by buying off the borough-owners and placement who controlled the Irish House of Commons.
The mechanism was straightforward. Under the terms of the Union, the Irish Parliament was to be abolished. This meant that the approximately 300 members of the Irish House of Commons — many of them representing pocket boroughs, serving as government placement, or holding their seats at the pleasure of patrons — would lose their seats and their political influence. The government offered them compensation. The price of a borough seat in the Irish Parliament was fixed at £7,500 per seat; the patron who controlled it was bought out. Sinecures, pensions, peerages, and promotions were distributed with breathtaking generosity. The total cost of the compensation and patronage has been estimated at over £1.2 million — a vast sum at a time when the entire Irish government budget was a few million pounds.
As William Belsham records, the methods employed to secure a majority were described as “corrupt and disgraceful” even by contemporaries who supported the Union in principle. The ministry was accused of “a profligate waste of the public treasure” and of “trafficking in the rights of the people with as little ceremony as the meanest pedlar in a fair.” Belsham, Memoirs of George III, Vol. VIII
The Opposition: Grattan and the Patriots
The opposition in the Irish Parliament was led by Henry Grattan, the great orator of Irish independence, and by John Philpot Curran, the Advocate-General. Grattan, who had won Ireland’s legislative independence in 1782, now argued that the Union would betray that independence — that it was a surrender of Irish sovereignty, not a merger of equals. His speeches against the Union are among the masterpieces of Irish political oratory.
In the Irish House of Commons on 27 January 1800, Grattan, who had been carried from his sickbed to speak, delivered a peroration that was long remembered:

“Let no man write my epitaph. While I have eyes to see, while I have ears to hear, while I have an understanding to conceive, I will never give my consent to the destruction of that constitution which the virtue of my ancestors has erected, and which my own efforts have assisted to secure. And I will pronounce my condemnation as the sentence of my country. The constitution may be destroyed by your vote — but the monument of my existence shall never be inscribed with the record of my country’s ruin.”

Despite Grattan’s eloquence, the result was never in doubt. The government’s majority, assembled through the systematic distribution of patronage, was unshakeable. The Union resolutions were carried in the Irish Commons on 7 February 1800 by 158 votes to 115 — a majority of 43 that subsequent research has shown was entirely the product of the seats that the government had bought.
In the Irish House of Lords, the opposition, led by the Earl of Charlemont and Lord Ventry, was even feebler. The Lords passed the Union resolutions with little effective resistance, the bench of bishops of the Church of Ireland voting solidly with the government after being assured that the Church’s establishment was secure.
The British Parliament
At Westminster, the Union passed with less drama. The British House of Commons was overwhelmingly in favour: Pitt’s majority was secure, and the Union was seen across the political spectrum as a necessary security measure in the wake of the 1798 Rebellion. Charles James Fox, the leader of the Whig opposition, spoke passionately against the measure — he had defended Irish legislative independence in 1782 and saw the Union as a betrayal of Whig principles — but he commanded only a minority. Fox denounced the means by which the measure was carried through the Irish Parliament as “a scene of corruption and profligacy almost unparalleled in the history of any country.” Belsham, History of Great Britain, Vol. XI
The British Union Bill passed the Commons on 23 May 1800 and the Lords on 2 July. The Irish Parliament gave its final assent on 1 August 1800. The royal assent was given by George III on the same day, and the Union was fixed to take effect on 1 January 1801.
The Terms of the Union
The Articles of Union between Great Britain and Ireland provided for a legislative, constitutional, and economic merger of the two kingdoms.























































ArticleProvisionSignificanceIThe Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Ireland shall be united into one kingdom, called the United Kingdom of Great Britain and IrelandThe fundamental constitutional change; the British flag added the cross of St Patrick to create the Union Flag still in use todayIIThe succession to the Crown of the United Kingdom shall be the same as the succession to the Crown of Great Britain (i.e., the Hanoverian line under the Act of Settlement 1701)No change to the succession; the Crown of Ireland had always been held by the British monarchIIIThe United Kingdom shall have one Parliament, styled the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and IrelandThe Irish Parliament was abolished; Ireland ceased to have a separate legislatureIVIreland to be represented at Westminster by 100 Members in the House of Commons and 28 representative peers (plus 4 bishops of the Church of Ireland, sitting by rotation of sessions) in the House of LordsApproximately proportional to Ireland’s tax contribution and population, but heavily skewed toward the Protestant AscendancyVThe Church of England and the Church of Ireland shall be united into one Protestant Episcopal Church, to be called the United Church of England and IrelandA crucial concession to the Protestant Ascendancy; the Established Church of Ireland remained Anglican, not CatholicVIFree trade between Great Britain and Ireland; both islands to be subject to the same customs duties and exciseThe great economic provision: Irish goods entered the British market freely, and vice versa; Ireland’s woollen, linen, and agricultural industries gained unrestricted accessVIIIreland to contribute two-seventeenths of the expenditure of the United KingdomIreland’s share of the joint costs; a figure that proved burdensome and was later revisedVIIIThe laws and courts of Ireland to remain as before, subject only to such alterations as the Parliament of the United Kingdom might makePreserved the separate Irish legal system and the Four Courts in DublinIXThe Irish national debt (approximately £28 million at Union) to be consolidated with the British debtIreland’s debts were absorbed into the larger British national debt
The 100 Irish MPs and 32 Peers
The representation of Ireland at Westminster was a carefully calculated compromise. Ireland, with a population of roughly five million (compared to England’s nine million and Scotland’s one and a half million), received 100 seats in the House of Commons — a ratio that under-represented it relative to population but over-represented it given its tax contribution. The 100 seats were largely drawn from the existing pocket boroughs of the Irish Parliament; many of them remained under the control of the same patrons who had been bribed to carry the Union, ensuring that the Irish representation at Westminster was for decades a conservative and landlord-dominated bloc.
In the House of Lords, Ireland sent 28 representative peers (elected for life by the entire Irish peerage) and 4 ecclesiastical lords (bishops of the Church of Ireland, sitting by rotation). The remaining Irish peers — there were over 200 of them at the time of the Union — retained their titles but lost their right to sit in the Lords unless they were also peers of Great Britain. This system mirrored (but improved upon) the Scottish representative peer system established by the Act of Union 1707.
Free Trade and Economic Integration
Article VI provided for full free trade between Great Britain and Ireland — a provision that was economically transformative. Ireland’s textile industries (especially linen and woollens) gained unrestricted access to British markets, and agricultural produce — grain, beef, butter, and provisions for the navy — flowed freely across the Irish Sea. For the British commercial classes, the Union secured the Irish market as an exclusive preserve, preventing it from falling under French commercial influence.
But free trade came at a cost. Ireland’s infant industries were exposed to full British competition, and the removal of tariff protection hurt Irish manufacturing — especially the woollen industry. The economic integration of the two islands was a one-sided bargain: Ireland became a supplier of raw materials and agricultural produce to the more industrialised British economy, a pattern of dependency that lasted well into the nineteenth century.
The United Church of England and Ireland
Article V united the Church of England and the Church of Ireland into a single established Protestant Episcopal Church. This was a critical provision for the Protestant Ascendancy: it guaranteed that the established religion of the new United Kingdom would remain Anglican, not Catholic, and that the tithe system by which the Church of Ireland was supported would continue. The provision meant that the vast majority of Irish people — Catholics and Presbyterians alike — would continue to pay tithes and taxes to support a church to which they did not belong.
Catholic Emancipation: The Broken Promise
The most consequential and tragic aspect of the Union was the promise of Catholic Emancipation — the right of Roman Catholics to sit in Parliament and hold high civil and military offices — that was understood by Pitt and his ministers to be the necessary complement to the Union, and that was then refused by the King, triggering a political crisis and Pitt’s resignation.
Pitt’s Understanding
William Pitt the Younger had long understood that the Union could not be a stable settlement unless the Catholic majority in Ireland were given civil equality. A Union that united Catholic Ireland with Protestant Great Britain while maintaining the legal disabilities of Catholics — the Test Act, the requirement of oaths and declarations against transubstantiation, the exclusion from Parliament, from the bench, from the higher ranks of the army and navy — would institutionalise the very grievance that had driven the Rebellion of 1798.
Pitt therefore intended to introduce a bill for Catholic Emancipation as part of the Union settlement. By granting Catholics the right to sit in Parliament, to hold civil and military offices, and to practise their religion without legal penalty, he hoped to reconcile the Catholic population to the loss of their separate Parliament and to create a genuine imperial identity that could embrace both faiths.
The King was not consulted during the negotiations. Pitt appears to have calculated that George III would accept Emancipation once the Union was carried, as a necessary consequence of the constitutional rearrangement. He was disastrously wrong.
The King’s Veto
George III had spent his entire reign defending the Protestant constitution as established by the Glorious Revolution of 1688. The Protestant succession, the supremacy of the Crown over the Church, the exclusion of Catholics from political power — these were not merely political positions but articles of faith. The King believed that his Coronation Oath — in which he swore to maintain the Protestant Reformed Religion — bound him personally and inviolably to oppose any measure that would admit Catholics to civil equality.
When Pitt formally proposed Catholic Emancipation in January 1801, the King reacted with the violence of a man whose deepest convictions had been violated. He declared that to consent to Catholic Emancipation would be a violation of his Coronation Oath — that no consideration of political expediency could release him from an obligation taken before God. His language was characteristically direct and emotional: “I shall consider any man my personal enemy who proposes any such measure.”
The King’s response was not merely political but had a pathological quality. His physicians feared a return of the mental illness that had incapacitated him during the Regency Crisis of 1788–1789. The interview with Pitt on 28 January 1801 was described as a scene of extreme agitation on the King’s part. When Pitt insisted that the measure was necessary, the King broke down: “What! What! Is it possible that a man like Mr. Pitt, upon whom I have heaped so many favours — on whom I have placed so entire a confidence — can be the person to propose such a measure? Then I have no comfort but in my closet, and there I shall remain!”
Pitt’s Resignation (February 1801)
Pitt was faced with an impossible choice: abandon Catholic Emancipation and remain in office, or resign rather than abandon a measure he believed essential to the stability of the Union he had just created. He chose to resign.
On 5 February 1801, Pitt informed the King that he could not continue in office if Catholic Emancipation were to be withheld. The King accepted his resignation with a mixture of relief and anger — relief that his conscience was safe, anger at what he regarded as Pitt’s betrayal of trust. Pitt formally resigned on 14 March 1801, though the actual transfer of power took place over several weeks.
Pitt’s resignation is one of the most significant acts of political self-sacrifice in British history. He had been Prime Minister for seventeen years, had carried Britain through the most dangerous years of the French Revolutionary Wars, and had just presided over the greatest constitutional rearrangement since 1707. He gave up the highest office in the state rather than abandon a principle.
Addington’s Ministry and the Delay of Emancipation
Pitt was succeeded by Henry Addington, the Speaker of the House of Commons, a trusted but uninspiring figure whom Pitt himself had recommended as his successor. Addington formed a ministry in March 1801 — a caretaker government designed to hold the Tory interest together while Pitt waited in the wings to return.
Addington’s ministry conspicuously abandoned Catholic Emancipation. The King had made his position unmistakable, and Addington had neither the inclination nor the political capital to press the issue. The question of Catholic Emancipation — which Pitt had seen as the necessary fulfilment of the Union — was postponed indefinitely.
It would take twenty-eight years before Catholic Emancipation was finally enacted in 1829, under the ministry of the Duke of Wellington and Sir Robert Peel, in the face of the threat of civil war in Ireland. The delay poisoned Anglo-Irish relations for a generation, ensured that the United Kingdom began its existence with a broken promise at its heart, and nourished the Irish nationalism that would eventually destroy the Union in 1922.
The End of Grattan’s Parliament
The final session of the Irish Parliament was a melancholy affair. On 2 August 1800, the Irish House of Lords and House of Commons assembled for the last time. The Lord Lieutenant gave the royal assent to the Act of Union in the presence of both houses, and the Lord Chancellor of Ireland, Earl of Clare, delivered the formal declaration. The Irish mace — the symbol of parliamentary authority — was removed from the chamber. The Irish Parliament had ceased to exist.
Henry Grattan was not present. He had made his final speech in the House of Commons on 26 May 1800, was told that his seat would be lost, and withdrew from public life. He returned to the Imperial Parliament at Westminster as one of the 100 Irish MPs in 1805, continuing his campaign for Catholic Emancipation, but the Parliament he had created in 1782 was no more.
The New United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland came into existence on 1 January 1801. The royal style was changed: George III was now “King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland” rather than “King of Great Britain and King of Ireland.” The Union Flag was modified to incorporate the cross of St Patrick (a red saltire on a white field), creating the flag that is still the national flag of the United Kingdom today.
The first Parliament of the United Kingdom met at Westminster in January 1801. The 100 Irish MPs took their seats — many of them the very borough-mongers who had been bribed to carry the Union — and the constitutional life of the new state began. But the absence of Catholic Emancipation, the broken promise at the foundation of the United Kingdom, was from the first a source of weakness. As Charles James Fox observed, a Union that excluded the majority of the Irish people from political participation was not a Union at all, but a conquest dressed in the language of consent.
Significance: The Union That Lasted 121 Years
The Act of Union 1800 created the political framework within which British and Irish history unfolded for the next 121 years. Its consequences were profound and contested:


Constitutional: Ireland ceased to have a separate legislature, and Irish affairs were governed from Westminster. Irish MPs became a permanent feature of British politics — sometimes a conservative bloc, sometimes a radical force (the Irish Parliamentary Party under Charles Stewart Parnell in the 1880s), and eventually the vehicle of Irish nationalism.


Religious: The failure to deliver Catholic Emancipation ensured that Irish Catholics experienced the Union as a Protestant ascendancy imposed from London. The Catholic Church became the unofficial national church of Irish nationalism, and Catholic Emancipation (1829), church disestablishment (1869), and land reform (the Land Acts) became the central axes of nineteenth-century Irish politics within the Union.


Economic: The Union integrated Ireland into the British economy as a supplier of agricultural produce and a market for British manufactures. The economic consequences were mixed: some sectors (linen, livestock, provisions) flourished; others (woollen textiles, manufacturing) declined under British competition. The Great Famine (1845–1852), in which a million Irish died and a million emigrated, demonstrated the catastrophic vulnerability of a dependent agricultural economy.


Nationalist: The Union created the conditions for modern Irish nationalism. Daniel O’Connell, the “Liberator,” built the first mass democratic political movement in Irish history around the demand for Repeal of the Union. When Repeal failed, the younger nationalists of the Young Ireland movement and later Fenian Brotherhood turned to physical force. Each generation produced a more radical nationalism: the Home Rule League, the Irish National Land League, Sinn Féin, the Irish Republican Army. The Union that was “bought” in 1800 was eventually destroyed by the force of arms in 1919–1921.


The Union ended on 6 December 1922, when the Irish Free State came into existence following the Anglo-Irish Treaty and the Irish War of Independence. The six counties of Northern Ireland remained within the United Kingdom, which was renamed the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland — a partition that was itself a direct consequence of the failure of the 1800 Union to reconcile the Catholic population of Ireland to British rule.
Key Figures

later served under Pitt again and held various cabinet postsCharles James Fox (1749–1806)Whig leaderOpposed the Union as a betrayal of parliamentary independence; denounced the bribery used to carry it; Historiographical Notes
The Acts of Union 1800 have been the subject of fierce historiographical debate. The nationalist tradition in Irish historiography regards the Union as an act of bad faith — a conquest disguised as a compact, bought by bribery and sustained by coercion, whose only lasting achievement was to provoke the national resistance that eventually destroyed it. The Union was indeed “bought”: the bribery and patronage deployed by Castlereagh and Cornwallis were on a scale that makes the methods used for the Act of Union 1707 look almost innocent by comparison.
The revisionist tradition — associated with historians such as R. F. Foster, J. C. Beckett, and W. E. H. Lecky — has emphasised the mixed motives behind the Union and the genuine difficulties of the Pitt ministry. The Rebellion of 1798 was a real security threat; the Irish Parliament was a corrupt and unrepresentative body; Catholic Emancipation was promised and might have been delivered had the King not intervened. The Union failed not because it was an inherently bad settlement but because its central promise — Catholic Emancipation — was broken.
What both traditions agree on is the centrality of the Union to the subsequent history of Ireland and Britain. The Union of 1800 created the United Kingdom that fought the Napoleonic Wars, governed the largest empire in human history, and struggled through the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with the Irish Question that ultimately broke it apart.
