events/gordon-riots-1780.title: Gordon Riots (June 1780)
events/gordon-riots-1780.content:
The Gordon Riots (2–9 June 1780)
The Gordon Riots were the most destructive civil disorder in the history of London — six days of arson, looting, prison-breaking, and mob violence that brought the capital of the British Empire to the brink of anarchy in the summer of 1780. What began as a mass Protestant petition against Catholic relief quickly escalated into a conflagration that destroyed Catholic chapels, private homes, the great prison of Newgate, the King’s Bench, the Bank of England, and dozens of other buildings, before the army — deployed on the personal order of George III — suppressed the rising with indiscriminate volleys that left an estimated 500 rioters dead in the streets.
The riots erupted at one of the most vulnerable moments in the American War of Independence, when Britain was fighting a global war against the American rebels, France, and Spain, and the ministry of Lord North was already reeling from the parliamentary censure of Dunning’s resolution. The Gordon Riots exposed the fragility of civil order in the unreformed metropolis and the depth of anti-Catholic sentiment that still animated the Protestant common people of England — a sentiment that the ruling classes had fatally underestimated.
Background: The Catholic Relief Act (1778)
The proximate cause of the riots was the Catholic Relief Act of 1778 (18 Geo. III, c. 60), a modest measure that removed some of the most oppressive penal laws against Roman Catholics in England and Wales. The Act was sponsored by Sir George Savile, a Yorkshire MP of liberal Whig principles, and supported by Edmund Burke, who had long argued that the penal laws against Catholics were not only cruel but counterproductive — they drove Catholic subjects into disaffection and deprived the state of the services of loyal men.
The penal laws had been enacted in the aftermath of the Gunpowder Plot and the alleged Popish Plot of the late seventeenth century, and they subjected Catholics to a regime of civil disabilities: they could not inherit or purchase land, could not practise law, could not bear arms, could not hold public office, and were subject to double taxation. The 1778 Act gave Catholics a limited relief: it allowed them to inherit and purchase land, and it removed the penalty of life imprisonment for Catholic priests who celebrated Mass. It did not grant Catholics the right to vote, sit in Parliament, or hold public office — it was, by any measure, a cautious and conservative reform.
The motive for the Act was not humanitarian sentiment but military necessity. Britain was fighting the American War of Independence and needed men. The ancient enemy — France — had entered the war on the American side in 1778, and Spain followed in 1779. The government calculated that the Catholic population of Britain and Ireland, if conciliated, could provide a valuable source of recruits for the army and navy. The Act was partly inspired by the Quebec Act of 1774, which had granted religious freedom to Canadian Catholics — a measure that had itself provoked furious Protestant opposition in Britain and America.
A separate Catholic Relief Act was passed for Ireland in 1778, and together the two Acts set in motion the slow, halting process of Catholic Emancipation that would occupy British politics for the next half-century. But in the short term, they provoked a violent Protestant backlash — and the most charismatic and reckless of its leaders was Lord George Gordon.
Lord George Gordon and the Protestant Association
Lord George Gordon (1751–1793) was the third and youngest son of the 3rd Duke of Gordon, a Scottish nobleman. He had entered Parliament in 1774 as MP for Ludgershall, a pocket borough in Wiltshire, but his political career had been restive and erratic. He was a man of intense, almost fanatical, religious conviction — a convert to a severe Calvinist Protestantism that saw the Catholic Church as the Whore of Babylon and the Pope as Antichrist. He combined this religious fervour with a genuine, if disordered, sympathy for the poor and a talent for popular agitation that made him a dangerous figure in the volatile politics of London.
In 1779, Gordon founded the Protestant Association, an organisation dedicated to securing the repeal of the Catholic Relief Act. The Association was modelled on the extra-parliamentary associations that had sprung up during the Wilkes affair and the county reform movement — it organised public meetings, distributed pamphlets, and collected signatures for a mass petition to Parliament. Its appeal was not limited to the lunatic fringe; many respectable Protestant clergymen, merchants, and gentlemen joined or supported it, alarmed by what they saw as the first step toward the legalisation of popery in England.
The Association’s campaign drew on the deep well of anti-Catholic sentiment that had been a constant of English popular culture since the Reformation. The memory of the Gunpowder Plot, the fires of Smithfield under Mary I, the Popish Plot of 1678, and the Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745 — in which Catholic Highlanders had marched on London — were still vivid in the Protestant imagination. The Catholic Relief Act seemed to many ordinary Protestants a betrayal of the Revolution Settlement of 1688, which had established the Protestant succession and excluded Catholics from power. The Quebec Act, which had granted toleration to Canadian Catholics, was already a grievance; the 1778 Act brought the danger home.
By the spring of 1780, the Protestant Association claimed to have gathered 120,000 signatures on its petition for the repeal of the Act — an enormous number in a population of perhaps six million in England and Wales. Gordon, by now the darling of the Protestant mob, resolved to present the petition to Parliament in person, accompanied by a mass demonstration of his supporters. The date was set for Friday, 2 June 1780.
The March on Parliament (2 June 1780)
On the morning of 2 June 1780, Lord George Gordon presided over a rally of the Protestant Association in St. George’s Fields, Southwark — the same ground where eleven years earlier the Massacre of St. George’s Fields had marked the escalation of the Wilkes affair. The crowd that assembled was immense. Estimates vary, but Gordon’s supporters numbered between 40,000 and 60,000 — a vast, disciplined, and ostensibly peaceful gathering of men and women wearing blue cockades, the badge of the Protestant Association, and marching under banners that read “No Popery” and “God Save the King.”
The march to Westminster was, in its first phase, orderly. Gordon, wearing a blue cockade in his hat, led the procession across London Bridge and through the streets of the City toward the Houses of Parliament. The crowd filled the approaches to Westminster Hall, the Palace of Westminster, and the streets around. Members of Parliament attempting to enter the House were jostled, threatened, and in some cases physically assaulted by the crowd. Bishops — whose support for Catholic relief was presumed — were singled out for special abuse. The Bishop of Lichfield was dragged from his coach and forced to take refuge in a nearby house; the Bishop of Lincoln was roughly handled; the Bishop of London was assailed with cries of “No Popery!” and pelted with mud.
Inside the House of Commons, Gordon presented the petition. The House was full, the atmosphere electric with tension. The debate that followed was one of the most extraordinary in parliamentary history, conducted to the sound of the mob’s cries through the windows and the crash of breaking glass. Edmund Burke — who had supported the Catholic Relief Act and who spoke powerfully against the repeal — was recognised and marked by the crowd for vengeance.
The House adjourned — but the crowd did not disperse. As evening fell, the discipline that had marked the day’s march collapsed. The mob, swollen by apprentices, labourers, thieves, and the volatile poor of London’s slums, turned from demonstration to destruction.
The Six Days of Riot
Friday 2 June — The First Outbreak
The violence began late on the afternoon of Friday 2 June. The first targets were the Catholic chapels attached to the embassies of Sardinia and Bavaria in Lincoln’s Inn Fields and Warwick Street. These were protected by diplomatic privilege — technically foreign soil — but the mob gave no heed to the niceties of international law. Both chapels were sacked, gutted by fire, and reduced to shells. The furnishings — altars, statues, vestments, and sacred vessels — were dragged into the street and burned in great bonfires. The spectacle of the burning Catholic images, watched by tens of thousands, was a deliberate echo of the fires of the Reformation.
From the chapels, the mob turned to the houses of known Catholics and of those who had supported the Relief Act. The home of the Catholic bookseller Thomas Parker was ransacked. The house of Sir George Savile — the author of the Act — was attacked but successfully defended by the sheriff and a party of constables. The mob, however, was not yet at full strength. The worst was to come.
Saturday 3 June — The Fires Spread
Saturday saw the violence spread across the city. The mob, now organised into bands that moved through the streets with terrifying efficiency, systematically attacked Catholic homes and businesses. The rich Catholic merchants of the West End, the Irish labourers of St. Giles, the French and Italian craftsmen of Soho — all were targets. The cry “No Popery!” was the signal; a blue cockade pinned to a door or a chalk mark on a lintel was sometimes enough to save a house from destruction — but those without the mark were looted and burned.
The Lord Mayor of London, Brackley Kennett, was conspicuously inactive. When called upon to read the Riot Act and call out the militia, he refused, or was too terrified to act. The City magistrates, intimidated by the mob, did nothing. The civil power in London had effectively collapsed.
Sunday 4 June — The King’s Birthday and the Prisons
Sunday 4 June was the King’s birthday. George III was at the Queen’s House (later Buckingham House) with his family, and the day passed quietly at court — but across London the riots were entering a new phase. The mob, which had so far confined itself to Catholic property, now turned on the prisons.
The first and most spectacular target was Newgate Prison, the great gaol at the western edge of the City, a symbol of arbitrary power and the brutality of the old criminal law. The mob attacked the prison with sledgehammers, crowbars, and fire. The gaolers, hopelessly outnumbered, fled. The gates were forced, the cells were opened, and the prisoners — some 300 men and women, felons and debtors, the innocent and the guilty — were released into the streets. Newgate was then set alight, and the great gothic edifice, with its famous iron gates, burned through the night.
The example set by Newgate was followed at every prison in London. The King’s Bench Prison in Southwark — where John Wilkes had once been confined — was stormed and burned, its prisoners released. The Fleet Prison, the Bridewell, and the Clerkenwell House of Correction were all attacked and opened. By the end of Sunday, every major prison in London except the Tower was either destroyed or evacuated. At least 1,000 prisoners were at large in the capital.
The destruction of the prisons was a turning point. The character of the riot changed. What had begun as a Protestant demonstration against Catholic relief became a general assault on property and authority. Thieves, desperadoes, and the desperate poor joined the mob, and the motives shifted from religious zeal to criminal opportunism. The Gordon Riots were now a proto-insurrection.
Monday 5 June — The Distillery Fire and the Looting of London
Monday 5 June saw some of the most horrifying scenes of the riots. A distillery in Holborn, belonging to a Mr. Langdale — a Catholic — was broken into by the mob. The rioters, instead of burning the place, tapped the vats of gin and spirits. The alcohol flowed into the streets — a river of gin. Men, women, and children drank from the gutters, scooped the liquor in their hats and hands, and fought over the flow. Dozens died of alcohol poisoning that night — estimates range from twenty to fifty — and others drank themselves into a stupor and drowned in the flood of spirits. The distillery was then set alight, and the flames spread to the surrounding houses. The whole of Holborn seemed to be on fire.
Across London, the looting continued unabated. Shops were broken into, houses stripped, and the goods carried off for sale in the markets of the East End. The mob had grown to a size that overwhelmed any possibility of civil resistance. The magistrates had fled. The constables had been beaten back. The military had not yet been deployed in force.
Tuesday 6 June — The Bank of England Attacked
By Tuesday 6 June, the mob had turned its attention to the great institutions of the state. The most audacious attack of the whole six days was attempted against the Bank of England — the financial heart of the British Empire, the repository of the government’s credit and the savings of the mercantile class. A large body of rioters advanced on the Bank in Threadneedle Street, intending to burn it to the ground.
The Bank was defended by a scratch force: the clerks, the armed servants of the Bank, and a detachment of soldiers hastily assembled by the authorities. The mob attempted to force the gates, but they were met with a volley of musket fire. The soldiers, commanded by Alderman John Wilkes — now the City Chamberlain — held their ground. Wilkes, the former radical who had once been the darling of the London mob, had now become the defender of property against popular violence. He gave the order to fire, and the crowd was driven back. The Bank was saved.
The paradox was not lost on contemporaries. Wilkes, who had made his political career by riding the wave of popular agitation, now stood with musket in hand against the same social forces. The cry of “Wilkes and Liberty!” had given way to the defence of property against the mob.
Wednesday 7 June — The Surrender of Gordon
On Wednesday 7 June, Lord George Gordon surrendered himself to the authorities. He had spent the preceding days at the head of the Protestant Association, issuing proclamations calling for order — but his influence over the mob was by now exhausted. The rioters no longer listened to him; the violence had acquired its own momentum. Gordon was arrested and committed to the Tower of London, charged with high treason.
His arrest did nothing to stop the rioting. The worst night was yet to come.
Wednesday night / Thursday morning 7–8 June — The Military Suppression
The government had been slow to act. For four days, the ministry of Lord North had hesitated, uncertain whether the civil power could restore order without the army, reluctant to call in the troops for fear of inflaming the situation further. The military commanders in London — Lord Amherst, the Commander-in-Chief — were constrained by the legal niceties that required a magistrate to read the Riot Act before troops could fire.
It was George III who broke the paralysis. The King, who had been kept informed of events throughout the riots, insisted on the deployment of the army. His response to the hesitations of his ministers was characteristically blunt: he declared that if the magistrates would not act, the military must act without them. There would be no negotiation with the mob.
On the night of Wednesday 7 June and into the early hours of Thursday, the army moved decisively. Troops of the Household Cavalry, foot guards, and militia patrolled the streets in force. They were given orders to shoot anyone engaged in rioting, arson, or looting. The King himself reviewed the troops, a dramatic gesture that became legendary.
The results were devastating. The soldiers fired volleys into the crowds. The streets of London were cleared by the bayonet. Bodies lay in heaps in the gutters — men, women, and children, many of them innocent onlookers caught in the indiscriminate fire. The exact death toll is unknown, but the best estimate is approximately 500 killed, with many hundreds more wounded. Some were shot by the troops; others died in the fires; others were trampled in the panics and stampedes of the suppression.
By dawn on Thursday 8 June, the riots were effectively over. The streets were quiet, littered with rubble, broken glass, and the dead. The great bonfires had burned down. London was a city of smouldering ruins.
Aftermath
The Destruction
The physical damage to London was enormous. The following had been destroyed or severely damaged:

Newgate Prison — burned to the ground
The King’s Bench Prison — burned
The Fleet Prison — burned
The Clerkenwell House of Correction — burned
The Bridewell — damaged
The Sardinian Embassy Chapel — gutted
The Bavarian Embassy Chapel — gutted
Langdale’s Distillery — destroyed by fire (the most destructive single fire, consuming several neighbouring houses)
Over 100 private houses — burned, including many belonging to Catholics and to supporters of the Relief Act
The Bank of England — attacked but saved
The Temple Bar — attacked but not destroyed

The total cost of the damage was estimated at £100,000 — an enormous sum in 1780, equivalent to many millions in modern currency.
The Trial of Lord George Gordon
Lord George Gordon was committed to the Tower on charges of high treason. He remained in confinement for eight months while the government prepared its case. His trial — presided over by Lord Mansfield, the Lord Chief Justice — was one of the great state trials of the eighteenth century.
Gordon’s defence was conducted by the brilliant lawyer Thomas Erskine (later Lord Chancellor Erskine), who argued that Gordon had not intended the riots and had in fact attempted to restrain them once the violence began. The Crown’s case was that by assembling the mob and presenting the petition in a manner calculated to intimidate Parliament, Gordon had incited the riot and was therefore guilty of treason.
The jury acquitted him. The verdict was a shock to the government and a vindication of the right of popular petition — but it was also, in retrospect, a recognition that Gordon, for all his recklessness, had not intended the catastrophe that followed. He was released, though his political career was effectively over. He later converted to Judaism — a bizarre coda to the career of the man who had led the most destructive anti-Catholic riot in English history — and died in Newgate Prison in 1793, having been convicted of libel for attacking the French Revolution.
The Political Consequences
The Gordon Riots had profound political consequences. They demonstrated, first and most obviously, the volatility of anti-Catholic sentiment in eighteenth-century England. The Protestant majority had shown, in the most violent terms, that the penal laws against Catholics were not merely dead letters — they were garrisoned in the hearts of the people. Any attempt to relieve the disabilities of Catholics would have to contend with the visceral hostility of the Protestant mob.
The riots also exposed the weakness of civil order in London. The magistrates had failed; the Lord Mayor had been useless; the police — such as they were — had been overwhelmed. The only force that could restore order was the army, and the use of the army against civilians raised uncomfortable questions about the nature of the British state. The Gordon Riots were the first time that the army had been deployed in force against a London crowd since the days of the Stuarts, and the precedent was troubling.
Politically, the riots weakened the North ministry, which was already struggling with the American war. The government’s slowness in responding to the crisis — four days of hesitation — was widely criticised. The King’s decisive intervention, by contrast, enhanced his popularity among the propertied classes, who saw him as the defender of order against the mob. The cry of “God Save the King!” replaced “No Popery!” in the streets of London.
The riots also had a chilling effect on reform. The county reform movement and the Economic Reform campaign, which had been gaining momentum in 1779 and early 1780, were set back by the riots. The association of popular agitation with mob violence made reform suspect in the eyes of the propertied classes. Edmund Burke’s plans for economical reform — the reduction of the influence of the Crown — had to contend with the argument that any weakening of the executive would leave the state defenceless against popular violence.
Catholic Relief in the Longer Term
The Gordon Riots delayed but did not halt the progress of Catholic relief. The cause was set back for a generation: any politician who proposed further concessions to Catholics knew that he risked provoking a repeat of 1780. It was not until 1829, after the heroic campaign of Daniel O’Connell and the threat of civil war in Ireland, that the Catholic Emancipation Act was finally passed — and even then, it was passed over the bitter opposition of the Protestant mob and the Tory party.
Key Figures
Lord George Gordon (1751–1793)
The central figure of the crisis — a Scottish lord, MP, and religious enthusiast who combined Protestant zealotry with a genuine sympathy for the poor. Gordon was not a cynical demagogue; he genuinely believed that the Catholic Relief Act was a betrayal of the Protestant constitution and that the Pope was Antichrist. His fatal flaw was that he did not understand — or did not care — that the forces he unleashed could not be controlled. He was acquitted of treason but lived the rest of his life in political obscurity, dying in the same prison he had helped to empty.
George III (1738–1820)
The King whose decisive intervention broke the riots. George III was the first member of the royal family to insist on military force — when the civil authorities faltered, the King gave the order to shoot. His conduct during the crisis enhanced his popularity among the propertied classes, who saw him as the defender of order. The Gordon Riots marked a turning point in the King’s relationship with his people: he was no longer the target of Wilkesite agitation but the symbol of resistance to anarchy.
Lord North (Frederick North, 2nd Earl of Guilford, 1732–1792)
The Prime Minister during the crisis. North’s government was already reeling from the disasters of the American War of Independence and the parliamentary censure of Dunning’s resolution (April 1780). His handling of the Gordon Riots was cautious to the point of paralysis: he hesitated for four days before authorising the military suppression, and he was overtaken by the King’s more decisive intervention. The riots further weakened his ministry, which survived only until March 1782.
John Wilkes (1725–1797)
The City Chamberlain of London during the riots — a remarkable reversal of roles for the man who had once been the most famous radical in Britain. Wilkes commanded the defence of the Bank of England, organising the clerks and soldiers who repelled the mob. He had completed the journey from popular tribune to defender of property. His conduct during the riots earned him the gratitude of the government and the establishment, though it cost him some of his popular following. He is remembered for giving the order to fire on the crowd he had once led.
Edmund Burke (1729–1797)
The great Whig philosopher-politician, who had supported the Catholic Relief Act of 1778 and spoke powerfully against the Protestant Association’s petition during the debate of 2 June. Burke was one of the few politicians of the first rank to defend Catholic relief against the popular tide, and his house was attacked by the mob. His support for Catholic emancipation was consistent throughout his career: he argued that religious persecution was incompatible with the principles of the Glorious Revolution and that the penal laws against Catholics were a relic of a darker age. He later supported the Catholic Relief Act of 1793 and the Irish Catholic cause.
The Riots in Historical Perspective
The Gordon Riots were the worst urban disorder in eighteenth-century Britain — far surpassing the Sacheverell riots of 1710, the excise riots of 1733, or the Wilkesite disturbances of the 1760s in scale, destructiveness, and loss of life. They were, in the words of one historian, “the nearest Britain ever came to a revolution from below” — a spontaneous rising of the London poor against property and authority, cloaked in the respectable language of Protestantism.
The riots also occupy a peculiar place in British historical memory. They are not, like the Wilkes affair or the Popish Plot, part of the Whig narrative of the advance of liberty: they were a reactionary movement, a defence of the old order of Protestant supremacy against the new spirit of toleration. They have no heroes — Lord George Gordon was a fanatic, the mob was destructive, the military response was brutal — and they left no positive legacy. But they mattered profoundly: they showed the limits of religious toleration in eighteenth-century Britain, the fragility of the civil order in the unreformed metropolis, and the enduring power of anti-Catholic sentiment in the English popular imagination.

“Never was such a consternation, such an alarm, in the city of London. The whole capital seemed to be in a flame.” — William Belsham, Memoirs of the Reign of George III


“The mob is the people — a terrible compound of ignorance, passion, and prejudice.” — Attributed to Edmund Burke

events/hastings-impeachment-1788.title: Impeachment of Warren Hastings (1788–1795)
events/hastings-impeachment-1788.content:
Impeachment of Warren Hastings (1788–1795)
The Impeachment of Warren Hastings (1788–1795) was the longest, most spectacular, and most consequential political trial of eighteenth-century Britain. For 145 days spread over seven years, the former Governor-General of Bengal stood before the House of Lords in Westminster Hall, charged with high crimes and misdemeanours committed during his thirteen-year administration of the East India Company’s Indian possessions. The prosecution, led by Edmund Burke, was the first sustained parliamentary attempt to hold an imperial administrator accountable for the conduct of colonial government. Though Hastings was ultimately acquitted in 1795, the trial established the principle that the agents of the British Empire were answerable to Parliament for their actions, and it raised a generation of public consciousness about the nature and morality of British rule in India.
Background: Hastings’s Governorship of Bengal (1772–1785)
Warren Hastings arrived in India in 1750 as a junior clerk in the service of the East India Company and rose, through a combination of talent, ambition, and survival instinct, to become the first Governor-General of Bengal in 1773. The Company he served had been transformed by Robert Clive from a trading corporation into a territorial power; Hastings inherited an empire in crisis. The Company’s treasury was empty, its servants were corrupt, and its Indian neighbours — the Maratha Confederacy, the Sultanate of Mysore under Hyder Ali, and the Nizam of Hyderabad — were pressing at its borders.
Hastings’s administration was characterised by aggressive expansion, administrative reform, and financial improvisation. He reorganised the revenue collection of Bengal, established a system of civil and criminal courts, patronised Oriental scholarship (founding the Asiatic Society of Bengal with Sir William Jones in 1784), and fought a series of expensive and controversial wars. His defenders called him the “Saviour of India”; his critics saw him as a despot who had corrupted every principle of justice and humanity.
The Rohilla War (1774)
The first great controversy of Hastings’s administration was the Rohilla War of 1774. The Rohillas were Afghan settlers who had established an independent state in the territory between Oudh and the Maratha dominions. The Nawab of Oudh, Shuja-ud-Daula, coveted their country. Hastings agreed to lend him Company troops in exchange for a payment of forty lakhs of rupees. The Rohillas were defeated and their territory annexed to Oudh; the Company collected its fee. Burke later denounced this as a mercenary war of aggression — a cynical transaction in which the Company had sold its military power to a native prince for the destruction of a defenceless people.
The Benares Affair (1781)
In 1781, Hastings faced rebellion in Benares, the holy city of the Ganges. The Raja, Chait Singh, a vassal of the Company under the Vizier of Oudh, had fallen behind in his tribute. Hastings travelled to Benares to demand payment and, when Chait Singh resisted, ordered his arrest. The arrest provoked an insurrection: Chait Singh’s troops attacked the British party, Hastings barely escaped with his life, and a punitive military campaign was required to restore order. Hastings confiscated the Raja’s estates and imposed a heavy fine. Burke’s prosecution would treat the Benares affair as a case of extortion by a rapacious governor who had provoked a rebellion to justify plunder.
The Begums of Oudh (1782)
The most sensational charge concerned the treatment of the Begums of Oudh — the mother and grandmother of the Nawab of Oudh, Asaf-ud-Daula. The Begums possessed vast treasure, inherited from the late Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula. Hastings, needing funds for the war against Mysore and suspicious of the Begums’s loyalty, demanded that Asaf-ud-Daula compel them to surrender their wealth. When the Begums resisted, their eunuch servants were imprisoned and starved until the treasure was yielded. The sum extracted was enormous — perhaps £1 million. Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s speech on the Begums charge at the trial was described by contemporaries as the finest oration ever delivered in the English Parliament.
The Campaign Against Hastings
Edmund Burke’s Crusade
The driving force behind the impeachment was Edmund Burke. Burke had been interested in Indian affairs since the early 1770s, when he served on a select committee investigating the Company’s abuses. He studied the evidence with extraordinary thoroughness — reading reports, examining witnesses, and mastering the details of Indian revenue systems, treaty obligations, and dynastic politics. The more he learned, the more he became convinced that Hastings was not merely a corrupt administrator but a tyrant who had “destroyed the whole framework of the Indian constitution” and ground the people of India under a “system of despotism and depredation.”
Burke’s campaign gathered momentum in the early 1780s. In 1781, he secured the appointment of a secret committee to investigate Indian affairs. In 1783, he introduced Charles James Fox’s East India Bill, which would have transferred the Company’s political authority to parliamentary commissioners — a bill that was defeated in the Lords after the King’s personal intervention, bringing down the Fox-North Coalition. But the evidence of misgovernment continued to accumulate, and Burke pressed relentlessly for action against Hastings personally.
The ‘Unjust Judge’ Accusation
A key element in Burke’s indictment was the case of Nandakumar (Nuncomar), a wealthy Bengali Brahmin who had accused Hastings of accepting bribes in 1775. Hastings’s enemy on the Supreme Council, Philip Francis, had taken up the accusation — but before it could be pursued, Nandakumar was himself arrested, tried for forgery before the Supreme Court under Sir Elijah Impey, convicted, and hanged on 5 August 1775. Burke charged that this was a judicial murder — that Hastings had suborned the Chief Justice to destroy his accuser, and that the “pure ermine of justice was stained and soiled with the basest contamination.” The Nandakumar case became the foundation of the most serious articles of impeachment.
The Parliamentary Campaign (1784–1787)
In the session of 1784, Burke moved for an inquiry into the affairs of India, but was blocked by William Pitt the Younger’s ministry. Henry Dundas, Pitt’s Indian minister, who had been Burke’s collaborator on the earlier select committees, had by now drawn back. Burke, speaking in July 1784, described the sufferings of the Indian people in terms that moved even his opponents: “The miserable objects it exhibited — nations extirpated, provinces desolated, cities and countries overwhelmed in one mass of destruction — constantly dwelt on his imagination. The cries of the native Indians were never out of his ears; an impression of horror had seized on his mind, which deprived him of sleep, and night and day preyed upon his peace.”
In 1786, Burke at last succeeded. On 4 April 1786, he laid before the House of Commons twenty-two charges against Hastings, drawn from the massive evidence accumulated over five years. The charges covered the Rohilla War, the Benares confiscations, the plunder of the Begums of Oudh, the Nandakumar execution, corrupt contracts, oppressive revenue settlements, and the general abuse of power. On 10 May 1787, after a year of committee work and debate, the Commons voted to impeach Hastings, and Burke, in the name of the House of Commons and of all the commons of Great Britain, repaired to the bar of the House of Lords to present the impeachment.
The Trial (1788–1795)
The Opening in Westminster Hall
The trial opened on 13 February 1788 in Westminster Hall. The ancient hall, the largest secular building in the kingdom, had witnessed the coronation banquets of the Hanoverian kings and the trial of Charles I. For the Hastings impeachment, it was fitted up with great magnificence — galleries for the peeresses and the public, a throne for the Lord Chancellor, a bar for the managers of the Commons, and a special enclosure for the prisoner.
The spectacle was unprecedented. The King, the Queen, the Prince of Wales, and the entire peerage attended. The court was the House of Lords itself, sitting in full judicial capacity. The prosecution was conducted by the greatest orators of the age: Burke, Fox, Sheridan, and the rising young Charles Grey. The defendant was the former Governor-General of Bengal, a man of fifty-five, composed and dignified, who conducted his own defence.
Burke’s Opening Speech
Burke’s opening speech lasted four days — 15, 16, 18, and 19 February 1788. It was the most sustained rhetorical performance of his career, a moral indictment of imperialism that still resounds across two centuries. He described Hastings as a “captain-general of iniquity” who had “exercised power without law, and dominion without principle.” He painted a picture of India before Hastings’s arrival — a land of ancient civilisation, settled government, and contented people — and of India after — desolated by war, plundered by extortion, and degraded by oppression.
Belsham, who was no admirer of Burke, describes the speech as “filled with vehement invective, with much rhetorical exaggeration, and with matter wholly extraneous to the subject of the impeachment.” But the effect on the audience was immense. The speech was extolled by Burke’s admirers as “a more than Ciceronian effort of eloquence.” The diarists of the age recorded that women wept, that peers sat transfixed, and that the accumulated weight of moral outrage was like a physical presence in the hall.
The Charges in Detail
The trial proceeded through the successive articles of impeachment, each opened by a different manager of the Commons:








































ChargeDatesOpening ManagerBenares charge22–25 February 1788Charles James Fox, concluded by Charles GreyBegums of Oudh charge13 April – 3 June 1788Mr. Adam (opening), Richard Brinsley Sheridan (summation)Ferruckabad charge2 March (in Commons stage)Mr. PelhamContracts charge16 March (in Commons stage)Sir James ErskinePresents charge2 April (in Commons stage)Richard Brinsley SheridanRevenues charge(Commons stage, 1787)Philip Francis
Sheridan’s speech on the Begums of Oudh — which lasted five days — was the dramatic highlight of the trial. He described the imprisonment of the Begums’ eunuch servants, the confiscation of the treasure, and the cruelty of Hastings’s methods with such emotional power that half the House was in tears. Pitt himself, who had been sceptical of the impeachment, is said to have moved for an adjournment so that the house could recover from the impact of Sheridan’s oratory.
The Famous ‘Dagger’ Scene
One of the most famous moments of the trial — though it belongs to the House of Commons debates rather than the Lords trial — was the “dagger scene.” During the 1793 debates on the war with revolutionary France, Burke, who had by then broken with Fox over the French Revolution, dramatised his point by dramatically drawing a dagger and hurling it across the floor of the House. The gesture was so violent and unexpected that it caused a sensation. While this scene is conventionally associated with Burke’s later political passions rather than the Hastings trial itself, it illustrates the same rhetorical intensity that characterised his prosecution of Hastings — a willingness to shock, to gesture, to perform the outrage that his words described.
More directly relevant to the trial was Burke’s penchant for physical props and vivid imagery: he described the sword of government being “converted to an assassin’s dagger” and the “pure ermine of justice stained and soiled” in Hastings’s India. The language of the dagger ran throughout the prosecution’s case.
The Length of the Trial
The trial dragged on for seven years — from February 1788 to April 1795. There were 145 days of actual proceedings, stretched over 18 sessions of Parliament. The delays were caused by the complexity of the evidence, the political distractions of the French Revolution (which from 1789 absorbed the energies of everyone involved), the illnesses of the principals (Burke was often too ill to attend), and the tactical procrastination of Hastings’s defence.
The length itself became a political issue. In 1794, during the debates on the Habeas Corpus suspension and the treason trials, opponents of the government remarked ironically that while the House was voting impeachments, the advanced guard of the enemy might meet them in the lobby. The trial’s protraction gradually drained the public’s interest and the prosecution’s momentum.
The Verdict: Acquittal (1795)
On 23 April 1795, the House of Lords delivered its verdict. The Lords voted on each of the articles separately. On every count, the verdict was not guilty. The most important votes were:









































ArticleForAgainstResultBenares charge——AcquittedBegums of Oudh charge——AcquittedPresents charge——AcquittedContracts charge——AcquittedRevenue charge——Acquitted
The precise numbers were not recorded, but it was known that a substantial majority of the Lords voted for acquittal on every charge. The Lord Chancellor, Lord Thurlow, who had opposed the impeachment from the start, pronounced the judgment with evident satisfaction.
Hastings was free. But the cost of his freedom was immense. He claimed to have spent £70,000 on his defence — a sum that left him in what he called “genteel poverty” for the rest of his life. He was not merely acquitted; he was ruined.
Significance
Accountability for Imperial Officials
The impeachment of Warren Hastings established a principle of incalculable importance: that the servants of the British Empire could be called to account before Parliament for their conduct in office. No previous colonial administrator had ever been subjected to such scrutiny. The trial created a precedent that imperial governance was answerable to the same standards of justice that governed the constitution at home. That Hastings was acquitted mattered less, in the long run, than the fact that the trial had taken place at all.
The Public Debate on Empire
The trial brought the realities of British rule in India into the public consciousness of Britain for the first time. The detailed evidence of Indian civilisation, Indian legal traditions, and Indian suffering that was presented at the trial — much of it gathered by Burke himself — educated a generation of Britons about the subcontinent they were conquering. The trial gave rise to a literature of imperial criticism, including Burke’s own published speeches, which remain among the most powerful indictments of colonial exploitation ever written.
The Constitutional Meaning
The impeachment was also a constitutional event of the first order. It was an assertion of the authority of Parliament — and particularly of the House of Commons — over the executive government and over the chartered corporations that exercised sovereignty abroad. It demonstrated that the Commons could impeach a servant of the Crown even against the wishes of the ministry (for Pitt’s government, though it eventually supported parts of the prosecution, had never been enthusiastic). It revived the ancient procedure of impeachment — dormant since the trial of Henry Sacheverell in 1710 — and demonstrated its continuing relevance as a check on executive power.
The Critique of Burke’s Methods
The acquittal owed much to the political context and to flaws in the prosecution. The French Revolution, which began in 1789, transformed the political landscape. Burke’s denunciation of the Revolution (in his Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790) made him a hero to conservative opinion but destroyed his political standing with the Whig party, splitting it irrevocably. Fox, Sheridan, and the majority of the Whigs supported the Revolution; Burke opposed it. The alliance that had brought Hastings to trial disintegrated in rancour. By 1794, Burke was politically isolated, and the trial had become a partisan embarrassment.
Moreover, many observers — including William Belsham, who recorded the events with a Whig sensibility — believed that Burke’s conduct of the prosecution had been injudicious. His opening speech, though magnificent, was filled with “rhetorical exaggeration” and “matter wholly extraneous to the subject.” The evidence, when it finally came, was less damning than the rhetoric had promised. Hastings, by contrast, was a calm, methodical, and effective witness in his own defence, patiently explaining the complexities of Indian administration to a British audience that had wearied of the whole affair.
Hastings’s Later Life
After his acquittal, Hastings retired to Daylesford in Gloucestershire — an estate he had purchased in 1788 with the intention of re-establishing the family seat that his ancestors had lost two centuries before. He spent his remaining years in obscurity, managing his estate, writing occasional memoranda on Indian affairs, and reading the classical authors who had been his lifelong companions.
The East India Company granted him an annuity of £4,000 per year, and in 1814, at the age of eighty-one, he was summoned to give evidence before the House of Commons on Indian affairs — a moment of belated recognition from the institution he had served. He was also given a loan of £50,000 by the Company to pay his debts, though the generosity was as much about protecting the Company’s reputation as about honouring Hastings’s service.
He died on 22 August 1818, at the age of eighty-five, and was buried in the church at Daylesford. His monument — designed by his admirers in the East India Company — stands in Westminster Abbey, opposite that of Robert Clive.
Timeline of the Trial

















































































































DateEvent1772Hastings appointed Governor of Bengal1773Regulating Act creates the Governor-Generalship; Hastings appointed first Governor-General1774Rohilla War1775Execution of Nandakumar for forgery1778Duel between Hastings and Philip Francis; Francis leaves the Council1780–1784War with Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore1781Benares insurrection — Chait Singh affair1782Confiscation of the Begums of Oudh’s treasure1784Pitt’s India Act establishes the Board of Control; Hastings founds the Asiatic Society of Bengal1785Hastings resigns the Governor-Generalship and returns to England17864 April: Burke lays twenty-two charges against Hastings before the Commons178710 May: The Commons votes to impeach Hastings at the bar of the Lords1788, 13 FebruaryTrial opens in Westminster Hall15–19 FebruaryBurke’s opening speech (four days)22–25 FebruaryFox and Grey open the Benares charge13 April – 3 JuneBegums of Oudh charge: Adam opens, Sheridan sums up (five days)1788–1789Continuation of prosecution evidence1789Outbreak of the French Revolution — political attention shifts1790Publication of Burke’s Reflections on the Revolution in France; Whig party splits1791Trial languishes; Hastings’s defence begins1792–1794Defence evidence and summation1793Outbreak of war with France; the trial becomes a secondary concern1795, 30 MarchFinal arguments concluded1795, 23 AprilLords acquit Hastings on all charges1814Hastings gives evidence to the Commons on Indian affairs1818Death of Hastings at Daylesford
Key Figures


Warren Hastings (1732–1818) — The defendant. First Governor-General of Bengal, architect of British rule in India, patron of Oriental scholarship. Acquitted but financially ruined. See Warren Hastings.


Edmund Burke (1729–1797) — The prosecutor. The greatest orator of the age, who made the Hastings impeachment the cause of his political life. His speeches remain foundational texts in the critique of imperialism. See Edmund Burke.


Charles James Fox (1749–1806) — Burke’s principal ally in the impeachment, who opened the Benares charge. A leader of the Whig opposition, Fox broke with Burke over the French Revolution, fatally weakening the prosecution’s political base. See Charles James Fox.


Philip Francis (1740–1818) — Hastings’s sworn enemy on the Supreme Council (1774–1778), who returned to England and became the prosecution’s most knowledgeable witness. Francis had fought a duel with Hastings in 1778 and pursued him with undying animosity. Possibly the author of the Letters of Junius.


Richard Brinsley Sheridan (1751–1816) — The playwright-politician whose speech on the Begums of Oudh was the trial’s greatest rhetorical moment. His oratory reduced the House to tears and was said by contemporaries to have been the finest ever delivered in Parliament.


William Pitt the Younger (1759–1806) — The Prime Minister. Pitt’s government was ambivalent about the impeachment: he supported some charges (voting for the Begums article) but his ministry never threw its full weight behind the prosecution. His Pitt’s India Act (1784) had already reformed Indian governance. See Pitt’s India Act.


Henry Dundas (1742–1811) — Pitt’s minister for Indian affairs. Originally a collaborator with Burke on the Indian committees, Dundas drew back as the impeachment progressed and became a target of Burke’s wrath for his “callous insensibility.”


Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809) — Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Calcutta, who presided over the trial and execution of Nandakumar. Hastings’s enemies charged that Impey was Hastings’s tool; his recall to England was demanded by the Commons in 1784.


Lord Thurlow (1731–1806) — Lord Chancellor, who opposed the impeachment from the outset and pronounced the verdict of acquittal. Famously dismissed the parliamentary reports on Indian abuses as “the romance of Robinson Crusoe.”


Cross-References

Edmund Burke — The prosecutor’s life and thought, including his writings on India and the French Revolution
East India Company — The corporation Hastings served; the object of the trial’s implicit critique
Pitt’s India Act (1784) — The reform that created the Board of Control, passed while the impeachment was being prepared
Robert Clive — Hastings’s predecessor; the conqueror of Bengal at Plassey
Charles James Fox — Burke’s Whig ally in the impeachment
Charles Grey — The young Whig who opened the Benares charge; later Prime Minister and author of the Reform Act of 1832
Philip Francis — Hastings’s enemy on the Supreme Council, chief prosecution witness
Richard Brinsley Sheridan — The orator of the Begums charge
William Pitt the Younger — The minister whose government was tested by the impeachment
Henry Dundas — Pitt’s Indian minister, Burke’s collaborator turned target
Sir Elijah Impey — The Chief Justice whose conduct under Hastings was a subsidiary charge
Regulating Act (1773) — The law that created the Governor-Generalship
William Jones — The Orientalist who founded the Asiatic Society with Hastings’s patronage
Lord Cornwallis — Hastings’s successor as Governor-General, who introduced the Permanent Settlement
Nandakumar — The Brahmin whose execution for forgery became a central charge against Hastings
Bengal — The province Hastings governed
Battle of Plassey — The foundation of British power in Bengal, which Hastings consolidated
Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan — The Mysore rulers who fought Hastings’s wars
French Revolution — The event that transformed Burke’s politics and drained the impeachment of momentum
Westminster Hall — The venue of the trial

Sources

events/irish-rebellion-1798.title: Irish Rebellion of 1798
events/irish-rebellion-1798.content:
Irish Rebellion of 1798
The Irish Rebellion of 1798 (May–September 1798) was the most violent and extensive uprising in Ireland since the Jacobite wars of the previous century. A fusion of Catholic and Presbyterian opposition to the Anglican Ascendancy — organised under the banner of the Society of United Irishmen — it exploded into open insurrection across the counties of Wexford, Antrim, Down, and Kildare, drawing in French revolutionary assistance and threatening the entire British position in Ireland. The rebellion was crushed with exceptional brutality; Belsham records that “upon a moderate computation, more than twenty thousand lives were lost, and a great part of the kingdom exhibited a horrid spectacle of misery and desolation.”
The rebellion was the immediate cause of the Pitt government’s determination to pass the Act of Union 1800, which extinguished the independent Irish Parliament and brought Ireland under direct rule from Westminster — a constitutional revolution that would shape Irish and British politics for the next 120 years.
Background
The Anglican Ascendancy and the Penal Laws
Eighteenth-century Ireland was governed by a narrow Protestant elite — the “Anglican Ascendancy” — who owned the vast majority of the land and monopolised political power through the Irish Parliament in Dublin. The native Catholic majority, comprising perhaps three-quarters of the population, was subjected to the Penal Laws: barred from voting, from sitting in Parliament, from holding public office, from practising law, from bearing arms, and from purchasing land from Protestants. A substantial Presbyterian population in Ulster, descendants of Scottish settlers, was also excluded from full civil rights, though they suffered nothing like the disabilities imposed on Catholics.
By the 1790s, the penal code had been somewhat relaxed — Catholic relief acts in 1778, 1782, and 1792 had removed the worst restrictions on property ownership and worship — but the fundamental structure of Ascendancy rule remained intact. Catholics could neither vote nor sit in Parliament, and the Irish Parliament itself was a corrupt and unrepresentative body, packed with placement and controlled from London through the patronage of the Lord Lieutenant.
The United Irishmen
The Society of United Irishmen was founded in Belfast in October 1791 by Theobald Wolfe Tone, a Dublin-born Protestant barrister of radical sympathies. Tone’s great insight — and it was a revolutionary one in the Irish context — was that the grievances of Catholics and Presbyterians were essentially the same: both were excluded from power by a corrupt Anglican oligarchy that maintained itself through division. As Tone wrote in his pamphlet An Argument on Behalf of the Catholics of Ireland (1791): “To subvert the tyranny of our execrable government, to break the connection with England, the never-failing source of all our political evils, and to assert the independence of my country — these were my objects.”
The United Irishmen drew inspiration from the French Revolution and the writings of Thomas Paine (whose Rights of Man was widely circulated in Ireland). Their early programme was parliamentary reform — the abolition of rotten boroughs, the extension of the franchise, and Catholic emancipation — but as the British government’s response to the Revolution became increasingly repressive, and as the war with France radicalised Irish politics, the movement turned towards armed insurrection and separation from Britain.
By 1795, the United Irishmen had been driven underground. The organisation was restructured along revolutionary lines — a secret oath-bound society, organised in cells on the model of the French Jacobins, with an executive directory at its head. Its membership included both Catholics and Presbyterians (the “Protestant, Catholic, and Dissenter” trinity of Tone’s founding vision), though in practice the Presbyterian element was strongest in Ulster, while the Catholic mass-movement dominated the south.
The French Connection
From the outbreak of war between Britain and Revolutionary France in 1793, the United Irishmen looked to Paris for deliverance. Tone went into exile in the United States in 1795, and from there made his way to France, where he presented himself to the French Directory as the agent of a nation ripe for revolution. His arguments were compelling: Ireland was Britain’s “soft underbelly,” a Catholic nation groaning under Protestant tyranny, whose 4.5 million people would rise en masse at the sight of French bayonets. A French invasion of Ireland, Tone argued, would do more to defeat Britain than a dozen campaigns in Germany or Italy.
The French Directory, eager to strike at Britain after the collapse of the War of the First Coalition, authorised a major expedition under General Lazare Hoche. In December 1796, a fleet of 43 ships carrying some 14,000 troops sailed from Brest. Tone himself sailed with the expedition, as a chef de brigade in the French army.
Hoche’s Expedition and the Bantry Bay Fiasco
The expedition was a disaster — but only because of the weather. The fleet arrived off the south-west coast of Ireland in late December 1796 and entered Bantry Bay, where, Belsham records, one of the frigates “came to anchor, in a very shattered state.” The wind, however, shifted violently to the east, making a landing impossible. For several days the French squadron struggled against the gales; the ships were scattered, the Séduisant was wrecked with the loss of 700 men, and the remnants of the fleet were forced to limp back to Brest. Tone, writing in his journal, recorded his despair: “England has not had such an escape since the Spanish Armada.”
The Bantry Bay failure was a turning point. The British government — and the Irish administration under Lord Camden — now knew that France was serious about Ireland. The response was a campaign of counter-insurgency that, far from pacifying the country, drove it headlong into rebellion. The countryside was flooded with troops, martial law was declared, the militia was quartered on the population, and a campaign of terror — flogging, pitchcapping, half-hanging, the burning of farms — was unleashed against suspected United Irishmen. The most notorious instrument of this repression was the Welsh-born magistrate and yeomanry commander, but the general direction came from Dublin Castle under Camden and the Chief Secretary, Thomas Pelham.
The Road to Rebellion
The Northern Star and the Arrests
Through 1796 and 1797, the United Irishmen grew rapidly in strength. The movement’s newspaper, the Northern Star (published in Belfast), spread radical ideas throughout Ulster. The government struck back: the paper was suppressed in May 1797, the militia and yeomanry were used to disarm the population of Ulster, and suspected leaders were rounded up.
In March 1798, the government’s intelligence network — which had thoroughly penetrated the United Irish organisation — delivered its masterstroke. Acting on information from informers, the Dublin Castle authorities raided the house of Oliver Bond in Dublin and arrested the entire Leinster provincial committee of the United Irishmen, including the revolutionary “Directory” that was supposed to coordinate the rising. Among those taken were Arthur O’Connor, Thomas Addis Emmet, and William James MacNevin. Lord Edward Fitzgerald — the most charismatic and dangerous of the rebel leaders, a younger son of the Duke of Leinster — escaped the initial round-up but was soon hunted down. On 19 May, after a violent struggle in which he killed one of his captors, Fitzgerald was captured; his wounds proved fatal, and he died in Newgate Prison on 4 June.
The arrest of the Directory threw the United Irish leadership into chaos. The rising, originally planned for May, was precipitated in confusion — orders and counter-orders flew across the country, and in many districts the rebellion began not as a coordinated insurrection but as a desperate, leaderless explosion.
The Government’s Position
The British and Irish governments were acutely aware of the danger. In the parliamentary session of 1797–1798, the Opposition had largely seceded from the House of Commons — Belsham notes that “the benches of opposition being in a manner deserted” — leaving Pitt and his ministers with an unopposed majority. The Habeas Corpus Act had been suspended in both Britain and Ireland; the Bank of England had been forced to suspend cash payments; the financial strain of the war was immense. In Ireland, Lord Camden — though personally moderate — presided over an administration that had effectively ceded control to the military, and the brutality of the counter-insurgency was creating a reservoir of bitterness that made rebellion almost inevitable.
The Rebellion
May 1798: The Outbreak
On 23–24 May 1798, the long-anticipated rising finally began. The original plan called for the simultaneous seizure of Dublin and the surrounding counties, but the arrest of the Directory and the death of Fitzgerald had fatally compromised the leadership. In Dublin itself, the rising fizzled; the government had packed the city with troops, and the intended signal — the stopping of the mail coaches — was only partially effected.
In the provinces, however, the rebellion burst forth with terrifying violence. The counties of Kildare, Carlow, Wicklow, and Meath rose in arms. But it was in County Wexford that the rebellion achieved its greatest — and most terrible — success.
Wexford: The Rebellion’s Heart
The rising in Wexford was different in character from the rest. Here, the leadership was predominantly Catholic — priests and farmers, not the Presbyterian radicals of Belfast — and the rebellion took on the character of a religious war. Belsham, drawing on contemporary accounts, paints a lurid picture: “The generality of the priests who appeared openly in this rebellion took the utmost pains to diffuse, as widely as possible, the malignant spirit of religious bigotry and inveterate animosity against the Protestants.”
On 28 May, the rebels carried the town of Enniscorthy “sword in hand.” Two days later, Wexford town surrendered and was occupied. The Protestant inhabitants were imprisoned; three gentlemen of large property, members of the United Irishmen who had been in custody awaiting trial, were liberated, and one of them — Beauchamp Bagenal Harvey — was nominated to the command of the rebel army, “though in no respect qualified for so arduous an office.”
The Battle of New Ross (5 June)
Flushed with success, the rebels marched under Harvey’s nominal command to attack New Ross, where General Johnson commanded with fewer than 3,000 regular troops. The rebels drove a vast herd of horses and oxen before them to disorder the king’s line and attacked with a weight of numbers that forced the troops back into the town. The fighting raged through the streets for eight hours — “a dreadful carnage” — before the rebels were at length compelled to retreat with heavy losses. Lord Mountjoy was killed early in the action, fighting at the head of his regiment.
The defeat at New Ross triggered the worst atrocity of the rebellion.
The Scullabogue Barn Massacre
Enraged by their repulse at New Ross, and by the knowledge that the military had been executing suspected rebels under martial law, the rebel leadership in Wexford resolved on a terrible revenge. Belsham records that “the rebel chiefs condemned a great number of the loyalists of Wexford and Enniscorthy to death — and this sentence was carried into effect a few days after, with circumstances of excessive barbarity.”
The most notorious incident occurred at Scullabogue (or Scollobogue), a barn near the foot of Carrickburn mountain, some miles distant from the battlefield. Here, upwards of two hundred Protestant prisoners — men, women, and children — had been confined under guard. On the orders of Father John Murphy, one of the rebel commanders, the barn was set alight, and all perished “amidst surrounding shouts of savage exultation.”
The atrocity at Scullabogue — and the mass executions that followed — permanently blackened the reputation of the Wexford rising. Belsham, who is generally critical of government policy in Ireland, writes of these events with undisguised horror, describing Murphy as “the bloody bigot” and recording that after the defeat of Vinegar Hill, he was “soon after taken in his flight, and most deservedly hanged.”
The Wexford Bridge Executions
After the recapture of Wexford, the government exacted a terrible retribution. General Lake recorded in his dispatch of 22 June that General Moore had entered the place “so opportunely as to prevent it from being laid in ashes; and, which was still more interesting, to render impracticable the premeditated massacre of the remaining prisoners — eighty-six persons having been murdered by them the preceding day, military music attending and playing a dead march, and their bodies, pierced with pikes, thrown over the bridge.”
Harvey, the rebel general who had “expressed some disapprobation of these enormities,” was stripped of his command after the battle of Ross. He attempted to conceal himself in a cave on one of the rocky islands in Wexford harbour, but was discovered, tried by court-martial, and executed on 26 June on Wexford Bridge, along with several other rebel leaders.
Vinegar Hill (21 June)
By mid-June, General Lake — the most aggressive of the British commanders — had assembled a large force to crush the Wexford insurrection. The main rebel army, numbering 18,000 to 20,000 men, had taken up an extraordinarily strong position on Vinegar Hill, a mile from Enniscorthy. From this eminence, Belsham observes, “had they possessed any share of military skill, it would have been difficult, if not impracticable, to dislodge them.”
On 21 June, Lake launched his attack. Four columns — under Generals Johnson, Dundas, Duff, and Needham — converged on the hill from different directions. The rebels maintained their ground obstinately for an hour and a half, but when they perceived the danger of being surrounded, they “fled with great precipitation” — some to the mountains of Wicklow, others to the chain of hills separating Carlow and Wexford. The pursuit was merciless: “no quarter given,” Belsham records, “they sustained immense loss; while of the king’s troops the whole number of killed, wounded, and prisoners, was something less than a hundred — a surprising proof of the superiority of skill and discipline over mere unenlightened courage.”
The Rebellion in the North (Antrim and Down)
While Wexford burned, the northern Presbyterians rose in arms. On 7 June, the town of Antrim was briefly seized by the rebels under Henry Joy McCracken, but they were driven out after a sharp engagement in which Lord O’Neill received a wound of which he later died. On 12 June, the main northern force — no more than 6,000 or 7,000 men — was “attacked and totally defeated at Ballynahinch” by General Nugent. A party of rebels was also repulsed at Carrickfergus. Within a short time, the general body of insurgents in the north laid down their arms, and “the tranquillity of the province of Ulster was restored.”
The Suppression
Lord Cornwallis Appointed
The rebellion had been largely crushed by the time the government’s response changed character, but the change was decisive. In Dublin, it was judged that Lord Camden had lost control of the situation; what was needed was a military commander of the highest rank who could at once pacify the country and restrain the orgy of execution and reprisal that the local authorities were conducting. The man chosen was Charles Cornwallis, 1st Marquess Cornwallis — the same Cornwallis who had surrendered at Yorktown in 1781, but whose subsequent career as Governor-General of India had restored his reputation for ability and moderation.
Cornwallis arrived in Dublin on 20 June. Under his auspices, Belsham records, “the general system of government immediately changed to that of moderation and lenity.” A general amnesty was proclaimed; the state prisoners — including O’Connor, Emmet, and MacNevin — were allowed to transport themselves to any country not at war with Britain; and the systematic executions that had followed the suppression of the Wexford rising were brought under control.
Nevertheless, some severe examples were deemed necessary. A special commission was opened in Dublin for the trial of the principal conspirators. The brothers John and Henry Sheares were tried and executed; William Michael McCann, secretary to the provincial meeting, and O’Byrne, a noted member of the United Association, suffered the same fate. Oliver Bond was convicted on 23 July and condemned, though he died in prison before the sentence could be carried out — or, as some accounts have it, the government offered to commute his sentence to banishment if he would betray his associates, a proposition he “nobly rejected.”
March of the Rebels to Wicklow
After Vinegar Hill, most of the rebel corps that had retreated to the mountainous parts of Wexford and Wicklow took the benefit of the amnesty and laid down their arms. Those who still resisted, Belsham notes, “were rather banditti, who confined themselves to nocturnal depredations, than troops in arms against the government.”
The French Landings
Humbert at Killala (August 1798)
The rebellion had been suppressed before any French assistance arrived — but the French came anyway, too little and far too late. On 22 August, three weeks after the Wexford rising had been crushed, a small French squadron appeared off the coast of Connaught and cast anchor in Killala Bay. The force — a mere 1,100 men under General Jean Joseph Amable Humbert — was part of a much larger expedition that had been scattered or delayed.
Humbert’s men landed unopposed and occupied the bishop’s palace at Killala. A green flag was raised over the gate with the inscription “ERIN GO BRAGH!” — “Ireland for ever!” The French troops, according to the bishop of Killala (Dr. Stock), whose published Narrative Belsham cites, “conducted themselves with the most exemplary moderation.” They were soon joined by several thousand of the Irish peasantry, all Catholics. Humbert and his officers expressed “the utmost chagrin and surprize” that the Protestants “continued, to a man, firm in their attachment to the government.”
The “Races of Castlebar”
Humbert marched on Castlebar, the chief town of County Mayo. General Lake — the same who had crushed the Wexford rising — was posted there with a force far superior to the French. But on 27 August, the French attacked by surprise, and the British troops, after a resistance that Belsham diplomatically describes as “not very vigorous,” were compelled to retreat with the loss of 800 men and ten pieces of cannon. The engagement became known, with bitter Irish irony, as the “Races of Castlebar” — a reference to the speed of the British flight.
Castlebar surrendered, and the French were joined by deserters from the Irish militia regiments. For a few days, it seemed possible that the west of Ireland might become a second Wexford.
Ballinamuck (8 September)
But Cornwallis was now in command, and he acted with decisive energy. Collecting a great army, he moved to enclose the French on all sides. Humbert, who had from the first entertained no hope of ultimate success, began a circuitous retreat, allowing the Irish recruits to escape — an opportunity “the far greater number embraced.”
On the morning of 8 September 1798, the British van came up with the French rearguard at Ballinamuck in County Longford. After a short but gallant resistance, the French were summoned to surrender and laid down their arms. The Irish who remained with them — perhaps a few hundred — fled in all directions and “suffered very severely.” When the return of French prisoners was made, the public was astonished to find that “this formidable host amounted to no more, officers included, than the insignificant number of 844.”
The garrison left at Killala — French troops under Colonel Charost — defended the place with great bravery but was overwhelmed. Charost’s conduct was “marked throughout by valor, tempered with honor and humanity.” When the bishop’s palace was recaptured, “not a single article of private property was found missing.”
Sir John Borlase Warren’s Victory (October 1798)
A second French expedition, sailing from Brest in October, met an even worse fate. The squadron — consisting of the Hoche (80 guns) and eight frigates — was intercepted off the coast of Ulster by a superior British force under Sir John Borlase Warren. On the morning of 12 October, the action commenced; by eleven o’clock, the Hoche had struck her flag, and six of the frigates were captured. Among the prisoners taken in the Hoche was Theobald Wolfe Tone.
The Trial and Death of Wolfe Tone
Tone was brought to Dublin and tried by court-martial. He did not attempt to deny or extenuate his offence. Belsham records his speech — one of the most famous in Irish history — in full:

“Into the service of the French republic I originally entered with the view of serving my country. From that motive I have encountered the toils and terrors of the field of battle; I have braved the dangers of the sea, covered with the triumphant fleets of the power I opposed; I have sacrificed my prospects in life; I have courted poverty; I have left my wife unprotected, and my children fatherless. After doing this, for what I thought a good cause, it is but little that I die for it. In such a cause as this success is every thing. I have attempted that in which Washington succeeded and Kosciusko failed. What awaits me I am aware of, but I scorn to supplicate or to complain.”

Belsham adds: “After a long pause, no doubt of involuntary admiration and regret, he was informed that his request would be submitted to his excellency.” Tone, who had been promised a soldier’s death — death by firing squad, rather than the degradation of hanging — found that the government was unlikely to grant his request. On 19 November 1798, he died in prison; according to the accepted account, he cut his own throat with a razor. “As this extraordinary man was the original author,” Belsham concludes, “his trial might be considered also as the last concluding scene of this short but bloody rebellion.”
Atrocities and the Character of the Rebellion
The Irish Rebellion of 1798 was marked by atrocities on both sides. The rebels massacred Protestant prisoners at Scullabogue and at Wexford Bridge; they tortured and killed in the name of religion, urged on by priests like Murphy. The government, for its part, conducted a campaign of counter-insurgency terror before the rebellion — burning, flogging, pitchcapping — and, after the suppression, executed thousands of suspected rebels under martial law, often without anything resembling a fair trial.
Belsham, writing within a few years of the events, offers a Whig — and morally complex — judgement. He condemns the atrocities of the rebels in the strongest terms, but he also condemns the government that drove them to rebellion: “Thus was the kingdom of Ireland once more reduced to peaceable subjection to the crown of Great Britain, and a dangerous rebellion crushed, which, had the government of the country been previously actuated by the beneficent spirit of the nobleman who now filled the highest office in it, would never have existed.”
He quotes Samuel Johnson’s Journey to the Western Islands: “To hinder insurrection by driving away the people, and to govern peaceably by having no subjects, is an expedient that argues no great profundity in politics: to soften the obdurate, to convince the mistaken, to mollify the resentful, are worthy of a statesman; but it affords a legislator little self-applause to consider that where there was formerly an insurrection there is now a wilderness.”
The Political Consequences: The Act of Union
The rebellion convinced William Pitt the Younger that the existing constitutional relationship between Britain and Ireland was unsustainable. The Irish Parliament — the corrupt and exclusively Protestant Parliament in Dublin — had manifestly failed to govern Ireland; the Ascendancy had proved itself incapable of either conciliating the Catholic population or defending itself without British military assistance. Pitt’s solution was the complete legislative union of the two kingdoms: the abolition of the Irish Parliament and the representation of Ireland at Westminster.
The Union was Pitt’s own measure, driven through against fierce opposition in both countries. In Ireland, the brilliant orator Henry Grattan — who had won legislative independence for Ireland in 1782 — led the opposition, denouncing the Union as the betrayal of Irish nationhood. But Pitt offered irresistible inducements: peerages, pensions, and cash payments to the Irish borough-owners whose seats would be abolished, and the promise of Catholic emancipation (the removal of the remaining civil disabilities on Catholics) once the Union was accomplished.
The Act of Union received the royal assent in July 1800 and came into effect on 1 January 1801, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The promise of Catholic emancipation — which had been the bait that reconciled many Irish Catholics to the Union — was betrayed when George III refused his consent, believing that his coronation oath forbade it. Pitt resigned in consequence, though he returned to power in 1804. The failure to deliver emancipation poisoned the Union from its birth and ensured that the “Irish Question” would remain the most persistent problem in British politics for the next 120 years.
Key Figures

Theobald Wolfe Tone (1763–1798) — Founder of the United Irishmen, architect of the French-Irish alliance, captured on the Hoche and died by suicide in prison. The founding father of Irish republican nationalism.
William Pitt the Younger (1759–1806) — British Prime Minister, who drove the Act of Union through Parliament in response to the rebellion.
Charles Cornwallis, 1st Marquess Cornwallis (1738–1805) — Lord Lieutenant of Ireland from June 1798, whose policy of “moderation and lenity” after the initial suppression prevented further bloodshed.
General Gerard Lake (1744–1808) — Commander of the forces that crushed the Wexford rising at Vinegar Hill; notorious for the brutality of his counter-insurgency tactics before the rebellion.
Lord Edward Fitzgerald (1763–1798) — United Irish leader, captured and mortally wounded in May 1798, died in Newgate Prison.
General Jean Joseph Amable Humbert (1767–1823) — Commander of the French expedition that landed at Killala; defeated at Ballinamuck.
Father John Murphy (c. 1753–1798) — Rebel priest, commander at the Scullabogue massacre, hanged after Vinegar Hill.
Henry Joy McCracken (1767–1798) — Presbyterian leader of the rebellion in Antrim; executed after the defeat at Ballynahinch.
Beauchamp Bagenal Harvey (1762–1798) — United Irishman and nominal commander of the Wexford rebels; executed on Wexford Bridge.
Sir John Borlase Warren (1753–1822) — British admiral who intercepted the second French expedition and captured Tone.
