events/jacobite-rising-1715.title: Jacobite Rising of 1715
events/jacobite-rising-1715.content:
Jacobite Rising of 1715
The Jacobite Rising of 1715 (also known as the Fifteen Rebellion) was an armed attempt by James Francis Edward Stuart (the Old Pretender) to recover the British throne for the Stuart dynasty. It broke out in September 1715, barely a year after the Hanoverian succession placed George I on the throne, and was the first major Jacobite rising of the eighteenth century. The rebellion was characterised by the Earl of Mar’s rapid raising of a large Highland army, the indecisive Battle of Sheriffmuir, the collapse of an English rising at Preston, and the Pretender’s belated and futile arrival in Scotland before fleeing to France in February 1716.
Background
Hanoverian Succession and Whig Ascendancy
The accession of George I upon the death of Queen Anne on 1 August 1714 was deeply unwelcome to the Jacobite party. The new king was a German Lutheran who spoke no English, had little interest in British affairs, and arrived determined to break the power of the Tory Party, which had dominated the last years of Anne’s reign. The Whigs, led by Robert Walpole, James Stanhope, and Charles Townshend, seized the opportunity to cement their ascendancy, impeaching the former Tory ministers Oxford and Bolingbroke for their role in the Treaty of Utrecht negotiations. Bolingbroke, fearing impeachment and execution, fled to France in March 1715 and entered the service of the Pretender, an act that both encouraged and embarrassed the Jacobite cause (Smollett, vol. X, lines 6773–6827).
The Jacobites had placed great hopes in Oxford and Bolingbroke, expecting that a Tory ministry would favour a Stuart restoration. Instead, George I’s first government was an exclusively Whig administration, and the Septennial Act was eventually passed to secure Whig dominance. The Pretender’s manifesto, issued from Lorraine, appealed to the disaffected and was circulated covertly in England, though it provoked a diplomatic incident with the Duke of Lorraine (Smollett, vol. X, lines 6780–6810).
The Earl of Mar’s ‘Hunting Party’
John Erskine, the 22nd Earl of Mar, had been a leading Scottish politician under Queen Anne and had initially paid court to George I after the succession. Snubbed by the new king and excluded from office, he turned to the Jacobite cause. Under the pretext of a hunting party, Mar assembled a large gathering of Highland chiefs at Braemar on 6 September 1715 (O.S. 27 August). There he proclaimed James Francis Edward Stuart as King James III and VIII, raised the Stuart standard at Castletown, and began recruiting an army (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1588–1619; Smollett, vol. X, lines 8380–8410).
The standard itself bore the ill-omened inscription “No Union,” a reference to Mar’s own role in negotiating the Union of 1707, which many Highlanders resented. Within weeks, Mar had assembled an army of some 10,000 men from the Highland clans — Camerons, MacDonalds, MacLeans, Frasers, and others — making the rising the most formidable Jacobite force ever gathered in Scotland.
Military Campaign
Operations in Scotland (September–October 1715)
Mar’s initial strategy was to secure the Scottish Lowlands and open a route into England. He occupied Perth without opposition and established his headquarters there. The government response was led by John Campbell, 2nd Duke of Argyll, the commander-in-chief in Scotland. Argyll, a veteran soldier and a Campbell — traditional enemy of many Jacobite clans — had only a small regular force of some 3,500–4,000 men, mostly raw recruits and a few regiments of dragoons recently arrived from Ireland. He established his base at Stirling, the key to controlling the Forth crossings.
In October, Mar made an abortive attempt to cross the Forth and was checked by Argyll’s forces. Meanwhile, Simon Fraser, Lord Lovat, who had professed Jacobite sympathies, opportunistically seized Inverness for the government in October, driving out Sir John Mackenzie and securing the northern communications for the Crown (Smollett, vol. X, lines 8574–8580; Belsham, vol. II, lines 1728–1732).
The English Rising and the Surrender at Preston
In England, the Jacobite rising was led by Thomas Forster (a Northumbrian MP and Protestant Jacobite) and James Radclyffe, 3rd Earl of Derwentwater. With a force of English Jacobites, they appeared at the head of a considerable armed force in Northumberland in October 1715, hoping to surprise Newcastle upon Tyne where they expected ample supplies of arms and stores. However, both churchmen and dissenters in Newcastle formed a town guard of 700 men and a corps of 700 keelmen (mostly dissenters) who embodied for the town’s defence, rendering the attack abortive (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1640–1655).
Foiled at Newcastle, Forster and Derwentwater altered their route northward to Kelso, where they were joined by a body of Highlanders under Viscount Kenmure. Reinforced, they re-entered England by the western border, proclaiming the Pretender at Warkworth, Penrith, Lancaster, and other towns as they marched south. On their arrival at Preston on 12 November 1715 (O.S. 1 November), they were attacked by government forces under generals Charles Wills and George Carpenter, who invested the town on all sides and compelled the rebels to surrender at discretion (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1656–1666; Smollett, vol. X, lines 8490–8510).
Battle of Sheriffmuir (13 November 1715)
On the very same day as the Preston surrender, the main Scottish armies clashed at Sheriffmuir, near Dunblane in Stirlingshire. Mar, learning of Argyll’s position, decided to force a crossing of the Forth to join his southern friends. He marched to Auchterarder and reviewed his army before advancing. Argyll, apprised of Mar’s intention, crossed the Forth at Stirling on 12 November and took position on the heights of Sheriffmuir, his left anchored at the village of Dunblane and his right stretching towards the muir (Smollett, vol. X, lines 8520–8532).
The Highland army, numbering about 9,000 effective men (horse and foot), greatly outnumbered Argyll’s force of 3,500. The clans that formed part of the centre and right wing of the Jacobite army, with Clanranald and Glengarry at their head, charged the left wing of the king’s army sword in hand with such impetuosity that in seven minutes both horse and foot were totally routed with great slaughter. General Whetham, who commanded the government left, fled at full gallop to Stirling declaring the royal army totally defeated (Smollett, vol. X, lines 8534–8541; Belsham, vol. II, lines 1676–1698).
However, on the other wing, the Duke of Argyll personally led the right, charging the enemy’s left with Stair’s Dragoons and Evans’s Dragoons, and drove them two miles before him as far as the Water of Allan. Though the Jacobite left attempted to rally ten times, Argyll pressed them hard. Meanwhile, the victorious right wing of the rebels, having pursued Whetham, returned to the field and formed in the rear of Brigadier Wightman’s three supporting battalions, now numbering some 5,000 men. Argyll, returning from his pursuit, joined Wightman who had faced about and taken possession of enclosures and mud-walls (Smollett, vol. X, lines 8542–8559; Belsham, vol. II, lines 1699–1709).
In this posture both armies fronted each other till evening, when Argyll drew off towards Dunblane and the rebels retired to Ardoch without mutual molestation. Next day, Argyll marched back to the field of battle, carried off his wounded with four pieces of cannon left by the enemy, and retreated to Stirling. Casualties were about 500 men on each side. Though tactically indecisive — each general claimed the victory — the battle was a strategic success for the government: Argyll, with an inferior force, had entirely disconcerted Mar’s plans and prevented him from crossing the Forth to link up with the English Jacobites. As Belsham records, “all the honour as well as the advantage of the fight rested with the duke of Argyle” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1715–1727; Campbell, vol. IV, lines 13960–13963).
Arrival of the Old Pretender
Despite the reverses at Sheriffmuir and Preston, the Pretender resolved to land in Scotland, arriving at Peterhead on 26 December 1715 (O.S. 15 December). He immediately issued proclamations summoning a convention of the estates, ordering all fencible men to repair to his standard, and fixing a day for his coronation. His reception was lukewarm: even his own supporters were dismayed by his lack of martial spirit and his rigid Catholic piety. In council, when presented with the draft of a declaration to be circulated in England, he objected to passages promising to secure the established churches of England and Scotland, declaring he could not in conscience make such promises (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1775–1787). Lord Bolingbroke, who had joined the Pretender’s service, was so alarmed by the king’s religious obstinacy that he refused to countersign the declaration.
When intelligence arrived of Argyll’s advancing army, the Pretender’s resolution collapsed. “For me,” he told his council, “it will be no new thing if I am unfortunate: my whole life, even from my cradle, has shown a constant series of misfortunes” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1740–1746).
Suppression by the Duke of Argyll and Flight to France
Argyll, now heavily reinforced, advanced towards Perth. The Pretender, accompanied by the Earl of Mar and the Earl of Melfort, embarked on board a French snow lying in the harbour of Montrose on 4 February 1716 (O.S. 23 January 1716). The vessel stretched over to Norway to avoid pursuit, then coasted along the shores of Germany and Holland, arriving in five days at Gravelines in France. This escape was narrowly managed — English men-of-war were in the vicinity but the French snow kept so close alongshore that pursuit proved impossible (Campbell, vol. IV, lines 13965–13971; Belsham, vol. II, lines 1749–1760).
The rebel army, left without leadership, retreated northward and quietly dispersed without making any further effort or receiving molestation from the government forces (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1760–1762).
Aftermath
Trials and Executions
The government’s response to the rebellion combined swift military suppression with a campaign of exemplary punishment. The lords Derwentwater, Nithsdale, and Nairne, with divers other noblemen, were tried in Westminster Hall for high treason, with Earl Cowper presiding as Lord High Steward. Despite earnest intercession from their families — the Countesses of Derwentwater and Nithsdale and Lady Nairne threw themselves at the king’s feet, pleading for mercy — George I remained implacable (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1865–1878).
A motion in the House of Lords, supported by the Earl of Nottingham, to address the throne requesting a reprieve for such of the condemned lords as should deserve mercy, was carried by a majority of only five voices. But George I replied haughtily that “on this and all other occasions he would do what he thought most consistent with the dignity of the crown and the safety of his people.” Nottingham was so far incurring the displeasure of the court that he was within a few days removed from his office as President of the Council (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1880–1898).
Earl of Derwentwater was executed on Tower Hill on 24 February 1716. A young nobleman of considerable virtue and accomplishment, he had been persuaded, though with difficulty, to plead guilty in the hope of obtaining a pardon. In his last declaration, he acknowledged the disingenuousness of this expedient but professed that, had he been granted life, he would never have taken up arms again against the king (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1899–1911).
Viscount Kenmure was also executed.
Earl of Nithsdale famously escaped from the Tower of London on the eve of his scheduled execution, aided by his wife. Lady Nithsdale, with the assistance of a female servant and another woman, smuggled him out of his cell disguised in women’s clothing — a feat that became one of the most celebrated prison breaks of the century.
Many of the lower classes also suffered execution. One Paul, a clergyman and vicar of Orton-upon-the-Hill in Leicestershire, who had joined the rebels at Preston, was tried and convicted of high treason and suffered the utmost rigour of the law with undaunted resolution. On the Sunday before his departure he preached a sermon at his own parish church from Ezekiel xxi. 26–27: “Thus saith the Lord God: Remove the diadem, and take off the crown. Exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1916–1925).
Political Fallout
Lord Bolingbroke, reflecting on the rebellion’s failure, observed that “if milder measures had been pursued, the tories would never have universally embraced Jacobitism; the violence of the whigs forced them into the arms of the Pretender, and dyed the royal ermines in blood” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1931–1936).
The Disarming Act (1716)
In the wake of the rising, Parliament passed the Disarming Act 1716 (1 Geo. I, st. 2, c. 54), which sought to pacify the Scottish Highlands by prohibiting the possession of weapons by unauthorised persons and by disarming the clans that had participated in the rebellion. The Act authorised government forces to search for and seize arms and punished non-compliance with severe penalties. Though unevenly enforced — many Highland clans hid their weapons or were protected by sympathetic local officials — it marked the beginning of a sustained government campaign to break the military power of the clan system.
Legacy
The failure of the Fifteen demonstrated that a Jacobite restoration would require substantial foreign assistance. The rising’s deficiencies were laid bare: Mar’s cautious generalship, the Pretender’s personal inadequacy, the lack of coordination between northern and southern forces, and the impossibility of defeating regular troops with Highland charges alone. Bolingbroke’s damning verdict on the Pretender — “his religion is not founded on the love of virtue… the spring of his whole conduct is fear; he has all the superstition of a capuchin” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 1800–1811) — underscored the fatal incompatibility between Stuart Catholicism and British Protestant sensibility.
Yet the rebellion also revealed the stability of the new Hanoverian regime: the rising was suppressed within five months despite widespread disaffection, and the institutions of the state — Parliament, the army, the navy under Sir George Byng, and the financial system — held firm under Robert Walpole’s steady management. The Fifteen was a prelude to the more serious Forty-Five, but its failure confirmed that the Stuarts could not reclaim their throne without a fundamental shift in British politics or a major European war.
Chronology









































































DateEvent1 Aug 1714George I succeeds Queen Anne under the Hanoverian successionMar–Apr 1715Bolingbroke flees to France; Whig ascendancy solidifies6 Sep 1715Earl of Mar’s ‘hunting party’ at Braemar; Stuart standard raised at CastletownSep–Oct 1715Mar occupies Perth; Duke of Argyll establishes base at StirlingOct 1715Lord Lovat seizes Inverness for the governmentOct 1715Forster and Derwentwater campaign in Northumberland, fail at NewcastleNov 1715English Jacobites march from Kelso through western border12 Nov 1715English rising surrenders at Preston13 Nov 1715Battle of Sheriffmuir — indecisive engagement near Dunblane26 Dec 1715Old Pretender lands at PeterheadJan–Feb 1716Government reinforcements reach Argyll; Pretender’s position deteriorates4 Feb 1716Pretender, Mar, and Melfort flee from Montrose to FranceFeb 1716Rebel army disperses; rebellion effectively ended24 Feb 1716Earl of Derwentwater executed on Tower HillFeb 1716Earl of Nithsdale escapes the Tower disguised as a woman1716Disarming Act passed to pacify the Highlands
Key Figures
Jacobite Command

John Erskine, Earl of Mar — The ‘Bobbing John’ of Scottish politics, a former secretary of state for Scotland who turned Jacobite after being spurned by George I. Raised the largest Highland army of any Jacobite rising but proved a hesitant and ineffective general. After the rising, he fled to France with the Pretender and died in exile.
James Francis Edward Stuart (the Old Pretender) — Son of James II, recognised by Louis XIV as James III. Landed in Scotland too late and too half-heartedly to revive the rebellion; his rigid Catholicism and personal indecisiveness fatally undermined the cause. Bolingbroke described him as having “all the superstition of a capuchin” and “the native narrowness of his understanding.”
Thomas Forster — Northumbrian MP and Protestant Jacobite who led the English rising. Captured at Preston.
James Radclyffe, 3rd Earl of Derwentwater — Young, personable, and wealthy English Catholic nobleman who raised men in Northumberland and was executed for high treason. His execution provoked widespread sympathy.
William Gordon, Viscount Kenmure — Scottish Jacobite peer who joined Forster at Kelso and was captured at Preston. Executed.

Government Command

John Campbell, 2nd Duke of Argyll — Commander-in-chief in Scotland. With a greatly inferior force, he fought the indecisive Battle of Sheriffmuir but strategically prevented Mar from crossing the Forth. His leadership, local influence, and the loyalty of the Campbell interest were decisive in suppressing the rising.
General Henry Whetham — Commanded the left wing at Sheriffmuir; his wing was routed in seven minutes by the Highland charge, and he fled to Stirling declaring the army destroyed.
General William Cadogan — Served as Argyll’s second-in-command; later commanded the pursuit of the retreating Jacobites.
General George Wade — A rising military figure during the Fifteen; Wade’s later road-building programme in the Highlands (the Wade roads) was a direct consequence of the 1715 rebellion’s demonstration that the government lacked the means to move troops rapidly into the interior of Scotland.
General George Carpenter — Commanded at Preston, investing the town and compelling the surrender of the English Jacobites.
Simon Fraser, Lord Lovat — Former Jacobite who opportunistically seized Inverness for the government in October 1715, securing northern communications. His later Jacobite career in the Forty-Five ended on the block.
Sir John Norris — Admiral who commanded naval forces in Scottish waters during the rising; kept watch for French intervention.

Cross-References

George I — The Hanoverian king whose accession provoked the rising
George Byng Torrington — Naval commander whose squadron safeguarded the Channel and prevented French reinforcement
Robert Walpole — Whig leader whose financial and parliamentary management stabilised the government during the crisis
James Stanhope — Whig minister and soldier who helped secure the regime
Charles Townshend — Whig statesman, Secretary of State during the rising
Bolingbroke — Tory minister who fled to the Pretender’s service
Earl of Oxford — Impeached Tory minister, imprisoned during the rising
Sir John Norris — Admiral commanding the North Sea squadron
Acts of Union 1707 — The Union that feature of Jacobite grievance
Disarming Act 1716 — Legislation passed to suppress Highland military capability
Jacobite Rising of 1745 — The second, more famous Jacobite rising
Battle of Sheriffmuir — The decisive indecisive engagement
Preston — Site of the English Jacobite surrender
Montrose — Port from which the Pretender escaped
Peterhead — Where the Pretender landed in Scotland

Sources

Belsham, History of Great Britain, vol. II — lines 1588–1619 (standard raised), 1640–1666 (English rising), 1666–1727 (Sheriffmuir), 1728–1762 (Pretender’s arrival and flight), 1763–1811 (character of Pretender, Bolingbroke’s verdict), 1865–1936 (trials and executions)
Smollett, History of England, vol. X — lines 6773–6827 (political background, Pretender’s manifesto), 8380–8410 (Braemar), 8490–8580 (Sheriffmuir, Lovat at Inverness)
Campbell, Lives of the Admirals, vol. IV — lines 13940–13977 (overview of rising, Pretender’s escape from Montrose, naval dispositions under Sir John Jennings)

events/jacobite-rising-1745.title: Jacobite Rising of 1745
events/jacobite-rising-1745.content:
Jacobite Rising of 1745
The Jacobite Rising of 1745 (also known as the Forty-Five Rebellion) was the last major armed attempt by the Stuart dynasty to reclaim the British throne. Led by Charles Edward Stuart — the Young Pretender, popularly known as Bonnie Prince Charlie — the rising erupted in the summer of 1745 and, within four months, carried a Highland army from the remote western islands of Scotland to within a few days’ march of London. The enterprise collapsed in the spring of 1746 at the Battle of Culloden, after which the British government under George II and his son William Augustus, Duke of Cumberland enacted a systematic destruction of the Highland clan system. The ‘45 was the last pitched battle fought on British soil and the final chapter of the Jacobite military challenge to the Hanoverian succession.
Timeline





























































































DateEvent23 July 1745Charles Edward Stuart lands on Eriskay in the Outer Hebrides19 August 1745Standard raised at Glenfinnan; the gathering of the clans begins4 September 1745Jacobite army crosses the Forth and advances on Edinburgh17 September 1745Edinburgh surrenders without resistance; Charles takes up residence at Holyrood Palace21 September 1745Battle of Prestonpans — Sir John Cope’s government army routed in under ten minutes31 October 1745Jacobite army departs Edinburgh for England8 November 1745Jacobites cross the River Esk into England15 November 1745Carlisle surrenders to the Jacobite army26 November 1745Jacobite army enters Manchester4 December 1745Jacobite army reaches Derby — the high-water mark of the rising5 December 1745The Council of War at Derby decides to retreat to Scotland6 December 1745Jacobite army abandons Derby and begins retreat northward20 December 1745Jacobite army recrosses the Esk into Scotland30 December 1745Carlisle surrenders to the Duke of Cumberland3 January 1746Jacobite army arrives in Glasgow; heavy contributions exacted17 January 1746Battle of Falkirk — Jacobites defeat General Henry Hawley1 February 1746Jacobites abandon the siege of Stirling Castle and retreat northMarch–April 1746Cumberland advances from Aberdeen; Jacobite army dwindles16 April 1746Battle of Culloden — decisive defeat of the Jacobite armyMay–September 1746Charles Edward Stuart’s five-month flight as a fugitive in the Highlands20 September 1746Charles escapes to France on a French privateer
Background
The Jacobite Hope after 1715
The failure of the Jacobite Rising of 1715 had not extinguished the Stuart cause. James Francis Edward Stuart, the Old Pretender, continued to reside at Rome, recognised by the papacy and the French court as the rightful king of Great Britain. His exile had become a fixture of European diplomacy. Throughout the 1720s and 1730s, successive French ministries toyed with the idea of a Stuart restoration as a means of weakening Britain, though the pragmatism of Robert Walpole’s long ministry kept the peace. The Jacobite party within Britain — a shifting coalition of disaffected Tories, Catholic recusants, Episcopalians in Scotland, and Highland clansmen bound by feudal loyalty to the Stuarts — nursed their hopes in private, awaiting a conjuncture of events favourable to a new attempt.
The War of the Austrian Succession
The death of Emperor Charles VI in 1740 and the ensuing War of the Austrian Succession provided that conjuncture. Britain, allied with Austria, committed substantial forces to the continent in support of Maria Theresa. A British army under the personal command of George II fought at Dettingen in 1743 — the last time a British monarch led troops in the field — while the Duke of Cumberland commanded in Flanders, fighting the disastrous Battle of Fontenoy in May 1745. By the summer of 1745, the best British regiments were on the continent, leaving the home islands dangerously denuded of regular troops. Only a skeleton force remained in Scotland under Sir John Cope, consisting of raw recruits and a few veteran companies. The French court, seeing an opportunity, encouraged the Young Pretender to make a descent on Britain, promising arms, money, and a diversionary invasion of southern England (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4368–4377).
The Landing
Eriskay and the Gathering
Charles Edward Stuart, aged twenty-four, handsome, charismatic, and utterly determined, resolved to stake everything on a bold venture. He had no permission from the French king for an expeditionary force; his father, the Old Pretender, counselled caution. Charles ignored them both. On 23 July 1745, he landed on the island of Eriskay in the Outer Hebrides, accompanied by only the ‘Seven Men of Moidart’ — a small party of Irish and Scottish exiles, including the elderly Sir Thomas Sheridan and the marquis of Tullibardine. The landing party carried a modest store of arms and a few thousand louis d’or, but no army, no artillery, and no assured support (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4380–4383).
The initial reception was discouraging. Alexander Macdonald of Sleat and Norman Macleod, the most powerful chiefs in the region, both refused to join him, deeming the enterprise hopeless. But Charles’s personal charm, his fluency in Gaelic, and his passionate conviction persuaded the younger generation. Donald Cameron of Lochiel, the most influential of the Jacobite chiefs, reluctantly committed his clan after much agonising — reportedly telling Charles that he would join the rising rather than see the prince’s cause perish for want of a single clan. With Lochiel’s adhesion, others followed.
Glenfinnan
On 19 August 1745, Charles raised his father’s standard — a banner of crimson silk bearing the white cockade — at Glenfinnan at the head of Loch Shiel. Around 800 Camerons and MacDonalds had assembled. Within days, the numbers swelled as clansmen from the Camerons, MacDonalds of Clanranald, MacDonalds of Glengarry, MacDonells of Keppoch, MacGregors, and Grants of Glenmoriston poured in. The army, initially around 3,000 strong, began its march south-eastward through the Great Glen (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4383–4392).
The March to Edinburgh and Prestonpans
The Capture of Edinburgh
Sir John Cope, the commander-in-chief in Scotland, collected what troops he could at Stirling. The Jacobite army descended through the passes of the Highlands, moving more rapidly than Cope anticipated. While Cope marched to Inverness, hoping to block the rebel advance in the north, the Jacobites swept past him through the Corrieyairack Pass and descended on the Lowlands. By 4 September 1745, they had crossed the Forth. Panic spread among the Protestant population. The capital, Edinburgh, was protected only by a city guard and an untrained citizen militia.
On 17 September, a detachment of Highlanders under the command of James Drummond, Duke of Perth (a title in the Jacobite peerage) entered the city through the Netherbow Port under cover of night, seizing the gates without firing a shot. The garrison — the town guard and a few dragoons — offered no resistance. On the morning of 18 September, Charles Edward Stuart entered Edinburgh in triumph, walking in procession to the Palace of Holyroodhouse, the ancestral residence of the Stuart kings, where he took up quarters. His father was proclaimed King James VIII of Scotland and III of England at the Mercat Cross (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4422–4431). A reward of £30,000 was offered by the Regency in London for Charles’s apprehension (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4393–4396).
The Battle of Prestonpans
Cope, hearing of Edinburgh’s fall, hurried back south from Inverness. On 20 September, he encamped with an army of about 3,000 regular troops — infantry, dragoons, and artillery — near the village of Prestonpans, east of Edinburgh, on a flat coastal plain intersected by drainage ditches and enclosures. The Jacobite army, roughly equal in number, approached under cover of a mist on the morning of 21 September.
The battle was over in under ten minutes. The Highlanders charged with broadswords and Lochaber axes, their terrifying war-cries and ferocious momentum overwhelming the government soldiers, who were unaccustomed to the Highland manner of fighting. The government line disintegrated; the dragoons fled. Cope’s regulars were routed with heavy losses. Belsham records that Colonel James Gardiner, a veteran officer of distinction and a native of Scotland, had warned Cope that his dispositions were unsound and predicted defeat. Gardiner, refusing to survive the disaster, fell covered with wounds in sight of his own mansion (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4437–4456).
Cope was heavily censured for his conduct of the engagement. The Jacobite victory at Prestonpans left Charles in effective control of Scotland, with only a few fortresses (Edinburgh Castle, Stirling Castle, Fort William) still in government hands. The victory brought in new adherents: the lords Kilmarnock, Cromarty, and Balmerino, along with many other men of rank, now joined the prince. French ships landed supplies and money at Montrose and Stonehaven. For the first time, the rising, which had seemed a romantic gamble, wore a serious aspect (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4457–4464).
The March into England
The Decision to Invade
After Prestonpans, the Jacobite court at Holyrood debated the next move. The cautious counsel of Lord George Murray — the ablest Jacobite general, a seasoned soldier who had fought in the British army before joining the Stuart cause — was to consolidate control of Scotland, await the promised French invasion of southern England, and advance only with adequate support. Charles, impatient and headstrong, overruled him. The prince believed that a rapid march into England would trigger a popular Jacobite uprising among the English Tories and country gentry, who he imagined were secretly yearning for a Stuart restoration.
On 31 October 1745, the Jacobite army — now approximately 5,000–6,000 strong, though some sources put the figure lower — marched south from Edinburgh. They advanced in two columns, one under Murray and one under the Duke of Perth, maintaining tight discipline and forgoing the plunder that might have alienated the English population (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4469–4484).
Carlisle and Manchester
The first significant obstacle was Carlisle, a walled city on the English border held by a weak garrison of militia and invalided soldiers. Surrender was demanded; the garrison capitulated on 15 November after a token resistance, giving the Jacobites their first English foothold and a store of arms and supplies.
The army marched south through Lancashire, passing through Penrith, Kendal, and Lancaster. At Manchester on 26 November, they met their warmest reception in England. A regiment of Jacobite volunteers, the Manchester Regiment, was formed under the command of a young Catholic merchant, Francis Towneley. Elsewhere, the expected English rising did not materialise. The towns they passed through were sullenly loyal or openly hostile; the mass of the population showed no enthusiasm for the Stuart cause. The Jacobite general John O’Sullivan later complained that the English Jacobites were content to drink to the prince’s health in private but would not risk their necks in public (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4488–4489).
The Crisis at Derby
By the end of November, the Jacobite army had reached the heart of the Midlands. Crossing the Mersey at Stockport on 29 November, they marched through Macclesfield and Congleton, reaching Derby on 4 December 1745. London was in a state of near-panic. King George II prepared to take the field in person, with the royal standard ordered to be erected on Finchley Common. The shops were shut; there was a run on the Bank of England. Marshal Saxe’s promised French invasion — a force of some 15,000 men assembled at Dunkirk — had been frustrated by contrary winds and the vigilance of the Royal Navy, which kept a blockading squadron off the Channel coast.
On 5 December 1745, the Jacobite commanders assembled at a council of war at the house of the Earl of Exeter in Derby. The situation was bleak. The army had been marching and fighting for three months; many Highlanders were barefoot, their supplies exhausted, their pay in arrears. Three government armies were converging on them: the Duke of Cumberland, recalled from Flanders, was approaching with a well-equipped army of veteran troops; General Wade’s army at Newcastle was marching south-west; and a third force under Sir John Ligonier was assembling in Staffordshire. The French invasion had not materialised. The English Jacobites had not risen. Lord George Murray argued forcefully that it would be madness to advance further: they were outnumbered, outmanoeuvred, and dangerously extended. The only rational course was to retreat to Scotland, regroup, and await the promised French reinforcements.
Charles argued passionately for continuing the advance. He insisted that the government’s forces were scattered, that London was defenceless, and that a bold stroke would yet turn the tide. For hours the debate raged. Murray carried the council, and the decision was made: the army would retreat.
This was the decisive moment of the rising. As Belsham records, the retreat from Derby was “a virtual relinquishment of his object, which indeed could only be accomplished by a series of desperate efforts crowned with continual and decisive success” (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4492–4507). Charles never forgave Murray for what he regarded as a cowardly betrayal. On the Jacobite side, the belief took root that they had been only a few days from taking London and that the retreat had cost them the throne.
The Retreat to Scotland
The Harried March North
No sooner was the retreat resolved upon than it was executed with astonishing speed. On 6 December 1745 — the Feast of St Nicholas — the Jacobite army abandoned Derby and marched north. The vanguard entered Manchester on the 9th; by the 19th, they were at Carlisle. The retreat was a remarkable feat of military discipline: the Highlanders covered the distance in just thirteen days, outpacing the pursuing armies of Cumberland and Wade. Belsham notes that no violence was offered, no outrage or rapine committed, despite passing through “a country abounding with plunder, and presenting every temptation to the unrestrained indulgence of military rapacity” (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4518–4528).
Cumberland, now in command of the pursuit, invested Carlisle on 21 December. The garrison of 400 men — mostly the Manchester Regiment — held out for nine days but surrendered at discretion on 30 December. Cumberland showed no mercy: the captured officers were marked for execution as traitors, and the common soldiers were imprisoned, many to be transported to the colonies.
Falkirk and the Last Jacobite Victory
The Jacobite army crossed the Esk back into Scotland by 20 December, reaching Glasgow on 3 January 1746. Charles exacted heavy contributions from the city in punishment for its loyalty to the Hanoverian cause, then marched on Stirling and invested Stirling Castle. General Henry Hawley, who had assumed command of the government forces in Scotland, marched from Edinburgh to relieve the fortress. The two armies met at Falkirk Mur on 17 January 1746.
The battle began in a driving rainstorm. Hawley’s dragoons attempted to charge the Highland line but bogged down in the sodden ground. The Jacobite clans, led by Lord George Murray and supported by the Duke of Perth, delivered one more devastating Highland charge, routing the government left wing. Hawley’s army was driven from the field, though the pursuit was checked by the superior discipline of the regular infantry, which retired in good order. The Jacobite victory was real but incomplete — Hawley escaped with most of his army intact, having lost “more disgrace than loss,” as Belsham puts it, noting Hawley’s empty boast that with two regiments of dragoons he would drive the rebel army from one end of the kingdom to the other (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4539–4550).
Culloden
Cumberland Takes Command
Falkirk proved to be the last Jacobite victory. The Duke of Cumberland himself arrived at Edinburgh with substantial reinforcements and assumed personal command of the government army, moving towards Linlithgow. The Jacobites, their supplies dwindling and their Highland troops drifting away to their homes, abandoned the siege of Stirling Castle on 1 February and retreated northward. Cumberland secured the passes of Stirling and Perth and pushed on to Aberdeen, which he reached in late February.
For six weeks, the armies rested and prepared. Cumberland drilled his army at Aberdeen, training them specifically in bayonet drill designed to counter the Highland charge — the tactic that had swept away Cope and Hawley. The Jacobite army, meanwhile, dwindled as clansmen returned home. Charles, against the advice of his best officers, resolved to fight a pitched battle on open ground.
The Battle
On 8 April 1746, Cumberland began his advance from Aberdeen. On 12 April, he crossed the River Spey without opposition. On 14 April, the Jacobite army, now reduced to around 5,000 exhausted, hungry, and poorly supplied men, was drawn up on Culloden Moor, a flat, boggy expanse to the east of Inverness. Charles Edward Stuart, against the advice of Lord George Murray, insisted on fighting on this unfavourable ground, which was ill-suited to the Highland charge.
The morning of 16 April 1746 was cold, wet, and windy. Cumberland’s army, approximately 9,000 strong — well-fed, well-rested, and drilled to perfection — formed up in three lines, their infantry equipped with plug bayonets and loaded muskets. The Jacobite army was drawn up in thirteen divisions; many of the clansmen had had nothing to eat for two days and had spent the night huddled on the moor in the rain.
The battle began around 1 p.m. with an artillery duel. Cumberland’s guns, served by the Royal Artillery, were far more effective than the Jacobite cannon, whose ammunition was defective and poorly aimed. The Highland line was torn by roundshot for twenty minutes before the order to charge was finally given. The charge — the famous Highland onslaught with broadsword and Lochaber axe — had been the Jacobites’ great weapon at Prestonpans and Falkirk. But at Culloden, the ground was soft and broken, impeding the Highlanders’ momentum. Cumberland’s troops, trained to meet this attack, did not flinch. The front rank fired a volley and the second rank fired through the gaps; then they fixed bayonets and met the Highlanders hand-to-hand, executing the new bayonet drill in which each soldier attacked not the man directly in front of him but the man to his right, where the Highlander’s targe offered no protection.
In less than thirty minutes, the Jacobite army was utterly destroyed. The clans were broken, the survivors fleeing in all directions. Cumberland’s orders — whether explicit or implicit — were to give no quarter. The cavalry pursued the fleeing Highlanders across the moor, cutting down men who had thrown down their arms. Belsham, though generally restrained in his criticism of the government cause, records that “unnecessary and wanton barbarities were committed on the persons and families of the rebels long after the cessation of resistance,” adding that the duke “sullied the glory of his victory by displaying a savage thirst of revenge.” He qualifies this by noting either that Cumberland was “transported into these temporary excesses by that rage which is so frequent and horrid a concomitant of civil discord” or that he genuinely believed such severity necessary to prevent further resistance (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4591–4615).
Aftermath
The Pacification of the Highlands
Culloden was followed by a campaign of systematic brutality that earned the Duke of Cumberland the lasting sobriquet “Butcher Cumberland.” For several months, government troops scoured the Highlands, burning villages, slaughtering livestock, destroying crops, and executing anyone suspected of Jacobite sympathies — often without trial. The policy was deliberate: to make the Highlands incapable of sustaining another rising. The wholesale destruction of the clan lands was an act of state terror that succeeded in its immediate strategic objective but left a legacy of bitterness that persists in Scottish folk memory to this day.
The Disarming and Heritable Jurisdictions Acts
Parliament moved swiftly to dismantle the social and military structure of the Highlands. The Disarming Act of 1746 made it illegal to carry broadswords, dirks, or firearms in the Highlands, and banned the wearing of Highland dress — kilts, tartans, and the belted plaid — which were symbols of clan identity and martial culture. (This ban remained in force until 1782.) The Heritable Jurisdictions Act of 1747 abolished the judicial powers of the clan chiefs — the right to hold courts, administer justice, and call out their tenants for military service — which had been the legal foundation of the clan system. Together, these acts destroyed the hereditary authority of the chiefs and transformed the Gaeltacht from a semi-independent martial society into an integrated — if impoverished — part of the British state.
The abolition of the clan system was swift and total. Clan chiefs, who had once been lords over men, became landlords overseeing sheep. The Highland clearances of the next century would not have been possible without the destruction of the chiefs’ traditional obligations to their people that followed Culloden. Over 1,000 Jacobite prisoners were transported to the colonies; 120 were executed, often after brutal show trials. Among those executed on Tower Hill were the Jacobite peers Lords Kilmarnock, Balmerino, and the aged Simon Fraser, Lord Lovat — the last man in England to be beheaded. Lord Lovat, an inveterate intriguer of notoriously profligate character who had played both sides during the rising, faced the scaffold at the age of eighty with unexpected dignity. Belsham, quoting Sir Dudley Carleton on a similar occasion, observes: “So much easier is it for a man to die well than to live well” (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4635–4654). The Earl of Derwentwater, who had been condemned in 1716, was executed on the same sentence without a new trial; only the Earl of Cromarty received a pardon.
The Escape of Charles Edward Stuart
Charles Edward Stuart escaped from the field of Culloden and spent the next five months as a hunted fugitive in the Highlands and Western Isles, with a price of £30,000 on his head. He moved from hiding place to hiding place, sheltering in caves and bothies, protected by a network of loyal supporters who risked their own lives to keep him safe. The most famous episode of this odyssey involved Flora Macdonald, a young Hebridean woman who accompanied Charles in disguise as her Irish maidservant, “Betty Burke,” on a hazardous crossing from North Uist to the Isle of Skye. After reaching Skye, Charles was passed from safe house to safe house, eluding the systematic searches of government troops.
On 20 September 1746 — five months after Culloden — Charles boarded a French privateer at Moidart and sailed for Morlaix in Brittany. He never returned to Scotland (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4615–4631). The rest of his life was a long, sad Anti-climax: the romantic prince who had captivated the Highlands degenerated into an alcoholic exile, estranged from his family, abandoned by his mistress, and ultimately a pathetic figure in the courts of Europe.
The Fate of the Manchester Rebels
Of the English Jacobites, none suffered more harshly than Francis Towneley and the officers of the Manchester Regiment who had been captured at Carlisle. They were tried for high treason, convicted, and executed at Kennington Common in London. Towneley’s head was displayed on Temple Bar, a grim warning to any Englishman who might contemplate serving the Stuart cause.
Key Figures
Charles Edward Stuart (1720–1788)
The Young Pretender, grandson of James II, was a charismatic but flawed leader. His courage and personal magnetism raised a formidable army from almost nothing, but his strategic judgment was poor, his temperament impatient, and his willingness to listen to his more experienced commanders (notably Lord George Murray) increasingly diminished as the campaign progressed. After the failed rising, he became a tragic figure — the ‘Bonnie Prince Charlie’ of romantic legend bore little resemblance to the sullen, embittered exile he became.
William Augustus, Duke of Cumberland (1721–1765)
The third and favourite son of George II, Cumberland had been the leading British commander in Flanders before the ‘45, where his defeat at Fontenoy in May 1745 had damaged his reputation. His victory at Culloden and the ruthless pacification that followed earned him the lasting title of “Butcher” in Highland memory. He was conspicuously honoured by Parliament, which added £25,000 per annum to his revenue and lauded him as the saviour of the Protestant succession (Belsham, vol. IV, lines 4645–4650).
Lord George Murray (1694–1760)
The military genius of the Jacobite cause. A younger son of the Duke of Atholl and a veteran of the British army, Murray had fought in the Jacobite Rising of 1719 and had been pardoned. He joined Charles in August 1745 and served as lieutenant-general. He planned the manoeuvres that captured Edinburgh, the devastating charge at Prestonpans, and the brilliant retreat from Derby. His disagreements with Charles after the decision to retreat were sharp and permanent; Murray left the army after Falkirk and was not present at Culloden. He later went into exile, dying in Holland in 1760.
Flora Macdonald (1722–1790)
A young woman of Clan Macdonald of Sleat, Flora Macdonald became the most celebrated figure of the Jacobite escape. Her courageous decision to guide the prince in disguise across the Minch to Skye, and her subsequent (brief) imprisonment in the Tower of London, made her a romantic heroine both in Scotland and in England. She eventually married and emigrated to North Carolina, returning to Scotland before her death in 1790.
Cross-References

Jacobite Rising of 1715 — The first major Jacobite rising, which established the pattern of Highland armies, dashed hopes, and punishment
James Francis Edward Stuart — The Old Pretender, Charles’s father, and the Stuart claimant during the 1715 rising
George II — The Hanoverian king against whom the rising was directed
Duke of Cumberland — The king’s son who crushed the rising at Culloden
Charles Edward Stuart — The Young Pretender who led the rising
Battle of Prestonpans — The Jacobites’ greatest victory in the field
Battle of Culloden — The final, decisive battle of the rising
Battle of Dettingen — The last battle commanded in person by a British monarch
Battle of Fontenoy — Cumberland’s defeat in Flanders that preceded the ‘45
War of the Austrian Succession — The continental war that opened the strategic window for the rising
Hanoverian succession — The constitutional settlement the rising sought to overturn
Acts of Union 1707 — The union that the Jacobites, particularly Scottish Jacobites, opposed
Septennial Act — One of the pillars of Whig dominance that the Jacobites sought to overturn

References

Belsham, William. History of Great Britain, from the Revolution, 1688, to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Amiens, 1802. Volume IV (1805). Book X. Lines 4368–4659. [Belsham’s narrative provides the principal source for this account, covering the landing at Eriskay through the aftermath of Culloden, including the executions of the Jacobite lords.]
Smollett, Tobias. A Complete History of England. Volume X (1759). Book IX. [Smollett’s volume ends before the ‘45; the work is referenced for background on the War of the Austrian Succession and earlier Jacobite context.]

events/loss-of-minorca-1756.title: Loss of Minorca and Execution of Admiral Byng (1756–1757)
events/loss-of-minorca-1756.content:
Loss of Minorca and Execution of Admiral Byng (1756–1757)
The Loss of Minorca in 1756 and the subsequent execution of Admiral John Byng in 1757 form one of the most controversial and consequential episodes in the history of the Royal Navy. The failure of a British relief expedition to save the Mediterranean island of Minorca — a British possession since the Treaty of Utrecht — from a French invasion ignited a political firestorm in Britain that cost the Newcastle ministry its majority, and culminated in the judicial execution of a British admiral by firing squad on the quarterdeck of his own flagship. The affair became proverbial for harsh military justice when Voltaire wrote that the British “shoot an admiral from time to time to encourage the others.”
Background
The Diplomatic Revolution
The Seven Years’ War (1756–1763) was preceded by a sweeping realignment of European alliances known as the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756. The traditional enmity between Bourbon France and Habsburg Austria — which had structured European diplomacy for nearly two centuries — gave way to a startling new configuration: France and Austria became allies, while Great Britain formed a defensive pact with Prussia (the Treaty of Westminster, January 1756). The rapprochement between France and Austria, sealed by the First Treaty of Versailles (May 1756), freed France to concentrate her military resources against Britain and Prussia on a global scale (Belsham, Vol. IV, lines 4877–4900).
In the Mediterranean, this meant that Minorca, which Britain had held since its capture in 1708 and formal cession at Utrecht in 1713, became a prime French target. Minorca’s superb natural harbour at Port Mahon was Britain’s principal naval base in the Mediterranean — the key to controlling the western basin, commanding the sea lanes between Gibraltar, the Italian states, and the Levant. Its loss would sever Britain’s Mediterranean communications and gravely weaken her strategic position.
The French Expedition
In the winter of 1755–1756, the French court resolved to strike at Minorca before Britain could reinforce it. A powerful expeditionary force, assembled at Toulon, was placed under the command of Marshal the Duke of Richelieu, one of the most celebrated soldiers of his age and a grand-nephew of Cardinal Richelieu. The naval escort was entrusted to Lieutenant-General Roland-Michel Barrin de la Galissonière, a seasoned naval commander who had served with distinction in Canada.
On 10 April 1756, Richelieu’s transports, escorted by twelve ships of the line under de la Galissonière, landed some 15,000 French troops on the coast of Minorca. The island’s small British garrison, commanded by the aged General William Blakeney, fell back before the overwhelming French force and concentrated in the fortress of Fort St. Philip at the mouth of Port Mahon harbour. Richelieu immediately laid siege to the fort, establishing batteries that began a systematic bombardment (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 148–153).
Byng’s Expedition
The Decision to Sail
The British Admiralty had been slow to appreciate the danger. Although intelligence of French preparations in Toulon had reached London as early as January 1756, the administration of the Duke of Newcastle — notoriously indecisive — dithered over the response. Only in March did the Admiralty order a squadron to the Mediterranean, and the command was given to Admiral John Byng, a man whose courage and abilities were as yet untried in independent command (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 137–140).
Byng was the son of George Byng, 1st Viscount Torrington, the victor of the Battle of Cape Passaro (1718) and one of the most celebrated admirals of the previous generation. The younger Byng had risen through the Navy on the strength of his family name and respectable prior service, but he had never commanded a fleet in action. His appointment reflected the peacetime habit of giving important commands to well-connected officers rather than to those proven in war.
Byng was ordered to sail with ten ships of the line and a small transport carrying a battalion of the English fuzileers (the 60th Regiment of Foot), together with a number of officers and recruits destined for the Minorca garrison. His instructions from the Admiralty were emphatic: he was to relieve Minorca “at all events,” using every possible exertion to throw succour into Fort St. Philip and, if necessary, to engage the French fleet (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 206–210).
Gibraltar
Byng reached Gibraltar on 2 May 1756. There he received alarming intelligence from Captain Edgecombe of the Louisa, who had been driven from Minorca by de la Galissonière’s squadron: the French had already landed fifteen thousand men, the siege of Fort St. Philip was well advanced, and the French fleet of thirteen ships of the line commanded the waters around the island (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 148–153).
At Gibraltar, Byng encountered a bureaucratic tangle that fatally delayed his operations. General Thomas Fowke, the governor of Gibraltar, had received three contradictory letters from the War Office concerning the battalion destined for Minorca. The first ordered the fuzileers to remain at Gibraltar; the second — contradicting the first — ordered a battalion to be embarked for Minorca; the third concerned only the embarkation of women and children. At a council of war held at Gibraltar, Byng and Fowke attempted to reconcile these conflicting orders. The council resolved to embark only a small detachment — one captain, six subalterns, five drums, and two hundred and thirty-five privates — far short of the full battalion originally intended. The engineers at Gibraltar also expressed the opinion that throwing succours into Fort St. Philip would be “extremely difficult, if not impossible” (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 156–210).
Campbell’s narrative is unequivocal on this point: “This resolution of the council of war was certainly wrong.” The council had been overcautious, and Byng had acquiesced in a decision that fatally reduced his capacity to reinforce the garrison (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 181–186).
Byng sailed from Gibraltar on 8 May with his squadron still not fully manned and with insufficient troops to make a decisive difference.
The Battle of Minorca (20 May 1756)
The Fleets Sight Each Other
Byng made the coast of Minorca on the morning of 19 May. To his relief, the British flag still flew over the castle of Fort St. Philip, though he could see several French bomb-batteries playing upon it from the enemy’s works. He despatched Captain Hervey in the Phoenix, together with the Chesterfield and Dolphin, to reconnoitre the entrance to the harbour and, if possible, to convey a letter to General Blakeney. Hervey got round the harbour before nine o’clock and made signals for a boat, but none came off — the garrison, apparently, could not spare a boat under the intensity of the bombardment. Shortly afterward, Byng’s lookouts sighted the French fleet to the south-east, and he recalled Hervey (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 215–247).
Byng stood toward the enemy. About two in the afternoon, he made the signal for the line of battle ahead, distributed seamen from the frigates to the ships most in want of hands, and converted the Phoenix into a fire-ship. At seven in the evening, the French squadron — about two leagues distant — tacked to gain the weather-gage. Byng, unwilling to surrender that advantage, put his ships about as well. The two fleets manoeuvred through the night.
The Engagement
The morning of 20 May was hazy, and the French fleet could not be seen until nearly noon. At two o’clock, Byng made the signal to bear away two points from the wind and engage. What followed was one of the most baffling and controversial actions in British naval history.
Rear-Admiral Temple West, commanding the van division, was at too great a distance to comply with both of Byng’s signals — the signal to bear away and the signal for the line of battle — and chose to interpret his orders aggressively. He bore away seven points from the wind and attacked the French van with such impetuosity that several of the enemy’s ships were soon obliged to quit the line. West’s division fought magnificently (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 258–296).
But Byng’s own division did not advance. The admiral’s flagship, the 90-gun Ramillies, hung back. The Intrepid, the sternmost ship of the van, lost her fore-topmast, and Byng later claimed that this obliged his whole division to back their sails to avoid falling foul of each other. The court-martial that subsequently examined the action found otherwise: immediately after the signal for engaging, while West’s van bore down upon the enemy, Byng in the Ramillies had edged away some points, causing the Trident and Louisa to get to windward of him. To bring them back into station, he backed his mizen-topsail and attempted to back his main-topsail — a manoeuvre that “necessarily retarded all the ships in his division, and gave the enemy time to escape” (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 298–311).
De la Galissonière seized the opportunity. His ships, being cleaner and more weatherly than the British, made sail and withdrew. Byng did not pursue.
The engagement had been indecisive. British casualties were forty-two killed and one hundred and sixty-eight wounded — remarkably light for a fleet action. No ship was lost on either side. But the strategic result was a French victory. The French fleet had been engaged and had retired in good order, while the British had failed to cripple it or to establish command of the sea around Minorca.

Byng’s Retreat
Instead of renewing the action the following day, Byng called a council of war. The council, noting the damage to the Intrepid and the battered state of several other vessels, the superiority of the French fleet in numbers (twelve ships of the line against Byng’s ten), and the impossibility of throwing reinforcements into Fort St. Philip while the French fleet remained in being, resolved that it was “not expedient to make any further attempt” to relieve the garrison. Byng ordered the squadron to return to Gibraltar.
He reached Gibraltar on 19 June 1756. Minorca was left to its fate.
Fort St. Philip held out under General Blakeney against Richelieu’s siege for seventy days, surrendering on 28 June 1756. The garrison, which had suffered terribly from the bombardment and from disease, was granted the honours of war. Blakeney himself returned to England to a hero’s welcome, becoming a folk-hero precisely because the disaster was so universally blamed on Byng.
The Outcry
When news of the loss of Minorca reached London in July 1756, the public reaction was volcanic. The British people had endured several years of mounting humiliation at French hands — the loss of the Ohio Valley, Braddock’s defeat on the Monongahela, the French seizure of the Mediterranean settlements — and the collapse of Minorca was the culminating blow. The mob burned Byng in effigy; the London press vilified him in terms as savage as any ever directed at a British officer.
The Newcastle ministry was itself in crisis. The Duke of Newcastle had been First Lord of the Treasury since 1754, but his administration had proven lamentably unequal to the challenges of war. The public, searching for a scapegoat for a catastrophe that was at least partially the result of ministerial incompetence — the unpreparedness of the fleet, the contradictory orders that had paralysed the council at Gibraltar, the failure to reinforce Minorca before the French struck — fastened on Byng with ferocious intensity. The government, desperately seeking to deflect blame from itself, did nothing to discourage the clamour.
Byng, Admiral West, and General Fowke arrived at Portsmouth on 3 July 1756. West was ordered to London and graciously received by the King; his conduct in the action was universally praised. Fowke was court-martialled for disobedience of orders in failing to send the battalion from Gibraltar and was sentenced to be suspended for a year — a sentence the King later aggravated by dismissing him from the service. Byng was placed under arrest and confined, first at Portsmouth and then at Greenwich Hospital, where he remained a close prisoner until December (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 643–659).
The Court-Martial
Proceedings
Byng’s court-martial opened on 28 December 1756, on board HMS St. George in Portsmouth harbour. The court consisted of four admirals and nine captains of the navy — a panel of Byng’s peers, many of whom had served alongside him. They sat for a month, examining evidence daily for and against the prisoner (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 660–663).
The case against Byng was damning. Admiral West testified that he saw no reason why the whole squadron could not have been brought into action. The evidence showed that the British fleet had held the weather-gage, that Byng had not brought his own division into effective range, that he had ordered the Deptford out of the line of battle (reducing his line to the same number of ships as the French — a decision for which the court censured him), and that he had failed to pursue the retiring French fleet. The signal books and logs demonstrated that Byng’s manoeuvring of the Ramillies had retarded the whole centre division.
But the court also found mitigating circumstances. Byng had warned the Admiralty before sailing that his squadron was undermanned. The contradictory orders at Gibraltar had been beyond his control. His personal courage — though put in question by the finding — was not equivalent to the cowardice that the popular fury alleged. The court explicitly found that Byng’s misconduct “did not proceed from want of courage, or from disaffection” (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 703–707).
The 12th Article of War
The charge against Byng was under the 12th Article of War, which provided:

“Every person in the fleet, who through cowardice, negligence or disaffection, shall not use his utmost exertions to take or destroy every ship which it shall be his duty to engage; and to assist and relieve all and every of his majesty’s ships which it shall be his duty to assist and relieve.”

The penalty prescribed for breach of this article was death. The court-martial, by the narrowest possible construction of the law, found Byng guilty of “negligence” — though they had acquitted him of cowardice and disaffection — and sentenced him to be shot. But the same court, in a powerful expression of their own unease, unanimously recommended him to his majesty’s clemency (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 695–707).
The Legal Wrangle
The Admiralty was troubled. The court had found Byng guilty of “negligence” under the 12th Article, yet the article itself named cowardice, negligence, or disaffection as the culpable states of mind. Since the court had explicitly acquitted Byng of cowardice and disaffection, the Lords of the Admiralty were uncertain whether the sentence was legally sound. They presented a memorial to George II requesting that the opinion of the twelve judges of the realm be taken (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 709–719).
The judges pronounced the sentence legal.
Some members of the court-martial then petitioned Parliament to be released from their oath of secrecy, hoping to reveal information that might incline the King to pardon Byng. A bill to this effect passed the House of Commons, but when it reached the House of Lords, each member of the court-martial was separately asked whether he had anything to reveal that might warrant a pardon. “Strange as it may seem,” Campbell records, “they all answered in the negative!” (Campbell, Vol. V, lines 721–728).
It has been whispered ever since — Campbell records the rumour explicitly — that Lord Anson’s private remonstrances deprived Byng “of that last ray of hope which some scruples of conscience gave him reason to expect.” Anson, as First Lord of the Admiralty, had been instrumental in the conduct of the war. A pardon for Byng would have been, by implication, a reflection on the Admiralty that had sent him out with an inadequate force.
The Execution
On 14 March 1757, Admiral John Byng was brought on board the 74-gun [[HMS Monarch|HMS Monarch]] in Portsmouth harbour for execution. Byng himself had requested death by shooting rather than hanging, a privilege accorded to his rank.
The scene was solemn and theatrical. Byng walked to the quarterdeck, where a cushion had been placed for him to kneel on. He refused a blindfold, saying that he would look his executioners in the eye. He was persuaded to permit a handkerchief to be bound over his eyes. He dropped a handkerchief as the signal — his own command — and the marines, six in number, fired. Byng was killed instantly.
The shot left a crowd of thousands watching from the shore and from small boats in the harbour, many of whom had come expecting a last-minute reprieve that never came. Campbell notes that Byng faced his death with perfect composure, accepting the sentence as the due of any officer who accepted a commission with the articles of war in his hand.
He was buried at his family estate in Southill, Bedfordshire.
Significance
Voltaire’s Epigram
The most enduring epitaph for the Byng affair was written not by an Englishman but by Voltaire, who watched the affair with sardonic detachment from his exile in Geneva. In his novel Candide (February 1759), Voltaire has the hero arrive in Portsmouth and witness the execution of an admiral. When he asks why the officer is being shot, he is told that “it is the custom here to shoot an admiral from time to time, to encourage the others” (pour encourager les autres). The phrase has passed into every European language as a byword for harsh, arbitrary, or politically motivated punishment.
The Legacy of Injustice
The Byng affair left a profound and lasting scar on the Royal Navy. The message sent to every officer was unmistakable: failure — even failure born of inadequate forces, contradictory orders, or honest misjudgement — could cost a man his life. The effect on naval decision-making was paradoxical. Some later historians have argued that the Byng execution made British admirals more cautious, more prone to call councils of war, and less willing to take the bold risks that had characterised the navy under Sir John Leake or Sir George Rooke. Others have contended that it had the opposite effect — that the threat of execution drove later commanders like Sir Edward Hawke to ever more aggressive tactics, culminating in the daring pursuit into the reefs of Quiberon Bay in 1759.
What is certain is that the execution was a political act. The Newcastle ministry fell within months of Byng’s conviction, and William Pitt the Elder came to power in December 1756, inaugurating the extraordinary run of global victories that would secure Britain’s imperial supremacy. Byng was the sacrifice offered to a public that demanded blood, and the political establishment — including the Admiralty, the Crown, and the judiciary — had co-operated in the sacrifice.
The Byng Family
The tragedy was rendered more poignant by the family history. Sir George Byng, John’s father, had been the victor of Cape Passaro (1718), the greatest British naval victory of the previous generation — a smashing, decisive triumph in which Byng’s father had destroyed the Spanish fleet without losing a single ship of his own. The father had been rewarded with a peerage (Viscount Torrington), the thanks of Parliament, and a place in the nation’s pantheon of naval heroes. The son’s fate — to be shot on the quarterdeck as a warning to his fellow officers — could not have been more cruelly different.
John Byng’s brother, Edward Byng, served as a commissioner of the Navy, and the Byng family’s naval tradition continued through the 18th century. But the shadow of the execution never lifted.
Constitutional Reflections
The case raised profound questions about military justice that continued to reverberate. The 12th Article of War, under which Byng was convicted, had been deliberately framed in the broadest possible terms to ensure that officers could not evade responsibility by legalistic quibbling. But its application in Byng’s case revealed the dangers of such breadth. A man who was not cowardly and not disaffected — a man found to have acted from negligence, but negligence in a context where his ships were undermanned, his instructions contradictory, and the enemy superior — was nonetheless executed.
The Earl of Hardwicke, Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain and one of the most eminent legal minds of the age, was deeply involved in the deliberations over Byng’s sentence. Hardwicke advised that the sentence was legal under the articles of war as they stood, and he opposed the parliamentary bill that would have released the court from its oath of secrecy. The Byng affair thus stands as a landmark in the history of military law, a case study in the tension between discipline and justice that has never been fully resolved.
In 1779, the 12th Article of War was amended to give courts-martial greater discretion in sentencing — the direct result of the Byng case — so that no future officer could be condemned to death for negligence alone. But the amendment came twenty-two years too late for John Byng.
