Key Figures


George III (1738–1820) — The King. Afflicted by what modern historians believe was porphyria, his first serious episode of mental illness created the constitutional crisis. His unexpected recovery in February 1789 saved Pitt’s ministry and preserved the political status quo.


William Pitt the Younger (1759–1806) — Prime Minister. Faced the prospect of immediate dismissal if the Prince of Wales became Regent. His masterful handling of the crisis — asserting Parliament’s right to appoint and limit the Regent, and proposing severe restrictions on the Prince’s powers — preserved his ministry and strengthened his position.


Charles James Fox (1749–1806) — Leader of the Whig opposition. His assertion of the Prince’s inherent right to the Regency was a catastrophic political miscalculation that allowed Pitt to pose as the defender of parliamentary sovereignty. The crisis permanently linked Fox to the Prince of Wales in the King’s mind.


George, Prince of Wales (1762–1830) — The heir apparent. His close alliance with Fox and the opposition Whigs made him the natural alternative to Pitt. His dignified acceptance of Pitt’s restrictions under protest preserved his constitutional position, but his relationship with his father was permanently damaged.


Edmund Burke (1729–1797) — Whig MP and Fox’s ally. Participated in the Commons debates, denouncing the restrictions as a “solemn mockery of royalty.” His break with Fox over the French Revolution was still in the future, but the Regency crisis revealed growing tensions within the Whig party.


Richard Brinsley Sheridan (1751–1816) — Whig MP and orator. One of the sharpest critics of Pitt’s restrictions, arguing that the whole scheme was governed by party considerations and personal ambition. His eloquence in the crisis matched his performance in the Impeachment of Warren Hastings.


Lord Thurlow (1731–1806) — Lord Chancellor. Initially appeared to be preparing to join the Prince’s administration, but dramatically shifted course when signs of the King’s recovery emerged, declaring with theatrical piety: “When I forgot my king, may God forget me.”


Queen Charlotte (1744–1818) — The Queen. Pitt’s plan vested the care of the King’s person and the patronage of the royal household in her hands — a provision that made her, in effect, the political ally of the ministry against her own son.


Cross-References

George III — The King whose illness precipitated the crisis. See also the King’s later permanent breakdown (1810) and the Regency Act of 1811.
William Pitt the Younger — The Prime Minister who saved his ministry by asserting Parliament’s right over the Prince’s hereditary claim.
Charles James Fox — The Whig leader whose assertion of the Prince’s inherent right proved disastrous for his political career.
George IV — The Prince of Wales, whose prospect of the Regency was frustrated by his father’s recovery.
Edmund Burke — Whig orator and Fox’s ally, who denounced Pitt’s restrictions.
Richard Brinsley Sheridan — Whig MP whose eloquence was deployed in opposition to the restrictions.
French Revolution — The event that erupted just months after the King’s recovery, transforming British politics and completing the rupture between Burke and Fox.
Impeachment of Warren Hastings — The other great political drama of 1788, running in parallel with the Regency crisis in Westminster Hall.
Pitt’s India Act (1784) — The reform that had consolidated Pitt’s administration and provoked the Whig opposition that aligned the Prince with Fox.
Regency era — The period following the Regency Act of 1811, when the Prince finally became Regent during the King’s permanent incapacity.
Maria Fitzherbert — The Roman Catholic woman the Prince had secretly married in 1785, in violation of the Royal Marriages Act.
Lord North — Fox’s former coalition partner, now in opposition to Pitt; his rhetorical attacks on the Regency Bill were among the most memorable of the crisis.
Lord Thurlow — The Lord Chancellor whose dramatic reversal during the crisis signalled the King’s impending recovery.
Irish Parliament — The separate legislature whose swift and unqualified offer of the Regency to the Prince raised the spectre of constitutional divergence between the two kingdoms.
House of Commons and House of Lords — The two houses whose struggle over the right to appoint the Regent tested the constitutional balance.
St. Paul’s Cathedral — The venue of the King’s thanksgiving service following his recovery.

Sources

Belsham, William — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. IV — contains the most detailed contemporary account of the Regency crisis in this wiki. Book XXIII covers the King’s illness, the parliamentary proceedings, the Fox-Pitt duel over the right to the regency, the plan of limitations, the Prince’s response, and the King’s recovery (sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol4.md)
Belsham, William — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. V — covers the aftermath and the political realignments of 1793, when the crisis of war with revolutionary France superseded the constitutional questions raised by the Regency (sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol5.md)
Belsham, William — History of Great Britain, Vol. XI — covers the Irish dimension and the constitutional questions raised by the divergence of the Irish and English parliaments over the Regency (sources/belsham-history-vol11.md)

events/saratoga-campaign-1777.title: Saratoga Campaign (1777) and the Franco-American Alliance (1778)
events/saratoga-campaign-1777.content:
Saratoga Campaign (1777) and the Franco-American Alliance (1778)
Overview
The Saratoga Campaign (June–October 1777) was the pivotal military operation of the American Revolutionary War in the northern theatre. Designed by George III’s ministry under Lord North as a decisive blow to crush the rebellion, the campaign instead ended in the first surrender of a British army in the field — a catastrophe that transformed the war from a colonial insurrection into a global conflict. The surrender of General John Burgoyne’s entire army of 5,700 men at Saratoga, New York on 17 October 1777 ranks as the greatest British military disaster of the war and, by its diplomatic aftermath, one of the most consequential battles in modern history.

Background
By the spring of 1777, the war in America had reached a strategic stalemate. The British had evacuated Boston in March 1776 after the Siege of Boston, and General William Howe had captured New York City in the New York and New Jersey Campaign of 1776. Washington’s victories at Trenton and Princeton (December 1776 – January 1777) had revived American morale, but the rebellion remained unfinished. The Second Continental Congress had issued the American Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776, but no major European power had yet recognised the new nation. The British high command, confident that a single decisive campaign could end the war, devised an ambitious plan for 1777.
The British Plan
The architect of the northern plan was General John Burgoyne, a gambler, playwright, and soldier who had served with distinction in the Seven Years’ War and more recently in the Boston campaign. Burgoyne proposed a two-pronged invasion designed to sever the rebellious New England colonies from the rest of America by seizing the Lake Champlain–Hudson River corridor:

Burgoyne’s main force would advance south from Canada up Lake Champlain, capture Fort Ticonderoga, and push down the Hudson Valley to Albany.
Lieutenant Colonel Barry St. Leger would lead a secondary force from Lake Ontario eastward via the Mohawk Valley, clearing the way to Albany.
General William Howe, commanding the main British army in New York, was expected to advance north up the Hudson to meet Burgoyne at Albany.

The plan assumed co-ordination between forces separated by hundreds of miles of wilderness — an assumption that proved fatally flawed. Howe, who had operational independence from London, chose instead to launch his own campaign against Philadelphia, the rebel capital. He notified Burgoyne only after his departure, by which time the northern invasion was already in motion. Lord North and the cabinet in London, distracted by political difficulties at home and the King’s persistent ill health, failed to impose a unified command structure.

The Campaign
Advance from Canada
Burgoyne assembled a formidable invasion force at St. John’s, Quebec, in the spring of 1777: approximately 7,200 men, including British regulars, German Hessian auxiliaries under Baron Riedesel, Loyalist provincials, and Indigenous allies. The force moved south on Lake Champlain in June 1777, using a flotilla of boats to transport men, artillery, and supplies.
Capture of Fort Ticonderoga
On 2 July 1777, Burgoyne’s army arrived before Fort Ticonderoga, the key defensive position on Lake Champlain that Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold had famously captured in May 1775. The American garrison under General Arthur St. Clair quickly recognised that Burgoyne’s artillery, placed on the commanding heights of Mount Defiance (which the Americans had neglected to fortify), made the fort untenable. St. Clair evacuated Ticonderoga on the night of 5–6 July 1777, abandoning the fort without a fight.
The fall of Ticonderoga was a stunning success for Burgoyne — and a shock to the American cause. Nevertheless, the evacuation saved St. Clair’s army from encirclement and preserved a force that would later join General Philip Schuyler’s army to contest Burgoyne’s advance.
The Wilderness Bogs Down
After Ticonderoga, Burgoyne faced a choice: move south by water via Lake George or march overland through the dense wilderness toward the Hudson River. He chose the overland route, a decision that proved disastrous. Burgoyne’s army had to cut a road through 23 miles of virgin forest, cross swamps and ravines, and haul artillery and supply wagons over terrain that turned to mire under the autumn rains.
The American forces under Schuyler (and later Gates) employed a deliberate scorched-earth strategy: felling trees across the line of march, destroying bridges, diverting streams to flood the road, and driving off livestock. Burgoyne’s advance slowed to a crawl — rarely more than a mile per day. Supply lines stretched perilously back to Canada, and forage dwindled as the army advanced into increasingly hostile territory.
Meanwhile, St. Leger’s expedition through the Mohawk Valley was checked at the Battle of Oriskany (6 August 1777) and defeated at the Siege of Fort Stanwix, forcing him to retreat to Canada. And Howe, true to his own plans, had taken the main British army south by sea to attack Philadelphia. Burgoyne was alone.

The Battles of Saratoga
Freeman’s Farm (19 September 1777)
By early September, Burgoyne’s diminished and starving army had crossed the Hudson River and was encamped near the village of Saratoga (now Schuylerville), New York. Opposing him was the Northern Army under General Horatio Gates, who had replaced Schuyler on 19 August. Gates was a cautious, methodical commander, beloved by Congress and skilled in the politics of command, but not aggressive in battle.
Realising the urgency of breaking through to Albany before winter, Burgoyne launched an attack in three columns on the American positions south of Saratoga. The American advance force under Benedict Arnold and Colonel Daniel Morgan (commanding the riflemen of Morgan’s Rifle Corps) met the British centre at a clearing known as Freeman’s Farm.
The battle was a brutal, close-range engagement fought in the dense woods by men largely unable to see more than a few dozen yards. The British infantry, deploying in classic European linear tactics, were harassed by Morgan’s riflemen firing from cover. Arnold, restless and aggressive, fed reinforcements into the fight despite Gates’s orders to hold back. At the end of the day, the British held the field — but at dreadful cost. Of Burgoyne’s roughly 3,000 engaged, nearly 600 were killed or wounded. The Americans, who had fought from cover, lost about 300.
Tactically a British victory, Freeman’s Farm was strategically a disaster for Burgoyne. His army was now crippled, low on ammunition, and still south of the American main defensive line. Rather than withdrawing to a defensible position, Burgoyne fortified his camp and waited for news that would never come.
Bemis Heights (7 October 1777)
For three weeks, the two armies stared at each other across the wooded hills south of Saratoga while Gates’s army swelled with militia reinforcements to nearly 15,000 men. Burgoyne’s situation grew desperate: rations were down to half-allowance, desertion was rampant, and his Indian and Loyalist auxiliaries were melting away.
On 7 October 1777, Burgoyne ordered a reconnaissance-in-force to probe the American left flank near Bemis Heights. He committed approximately 1,500 men — a desperate gamble, not a full-scale assault. The Americans, sensing weakness, counter-attacked with devastating effect. Arnold, who had been stripped of field command by Gates after a bitter quarrel, galloped to the front and personally led the charge that broke through the British defences on the Breymann Redoubt — a pivotal moment commemorated in the famous legend of Arnold’s horse being shot from under him and his leg being crushed (though accounts vary).
The British line collapsed. General Simon Fraser, Burgoyne’s most able subordinate, was mortally wounded by a sniper. Baron Riedesel’s Germans were overrun. The survivors fell back in disorder to their fortified camp at Saratoga.
The Surrender (17 October 1777)
Burgoyne’s army was now surrounded, outnumbered, and starving. On the night of 8–9 October, he attempted to retreat northward, but Gates’s army blocked the route. The British fell back to Saratoga, where they were encircled. On 13 October, Burgoyne opened negotiations for surrender terms.
On 17 October 1777, Burgoyne’s army marched out of camp and laid down its arms in a formal ceremony. Approximately 5,700 men — British regulars, Hessians, Canadians, and Loyalists — surrendered as prisoners of war. Under the terms of the Convention of Saratoga, the troops were to be repatriated to Britain on condition they would not serve again in America. Congress, wary of British perfidy, later repudiated the terms and held the prisoners until the end of the war, a decision that poisoned further negotiations.

Consequences: The Greatest British Disaster
The surrender at Saratoga was without precedent in British military history. An entire British army — regulars, auxiliaries, and all — had been lost in the field. Lord North, upon hearing the news, is reported to have exclaimed, “Oh God! It is all over!” George III, characteristically stubborn, refused to accept defeat and resolved to continue the war, but the political damage was done.
Saratoga triggered a cascade of consequences:

Strategic collapse: The British abandoned the northern campaign and pulled back to defensive positions in Canada and New York City.
Parliamentary crisis: Lord North’s government came under withering attack in Parliament. The opposition, led by the Earl of Chatham (William Pitt the Elder), demanded an end to the war, though the King’s will prevailed.
Military redeployment: Britain was forced to evacuate Philadelphia in June 1778 to consolidate its defences in New York, marking a strategic withdrawal from the interior.
Loss of initiative: Never again would the British attempt a major offensive from Canada. The war shifted decisively to the southern colonies.


The Franco-American Alliance (1778)
French Diplomacy Before Saratoga
Since the outbreak of the rebellion, France had watched events in America with keen interest. The French foreign minister, the Comte de Vergennes, saw the American war as an opportunity to avenge France’s humiliating defeat in the Seven Years’ War (1756–1763), when Britain stripped France of its North American empire. As early as 1775, Vergennes had dispatched secret aid to the Americans through the front company Rodrigue Hortalez et Cie, operated by the playwright and adventurer Pierre Beaumarchais. By 1777, France had supplied the rebels with nearly 90% of their gunpowder.
However, the French court, still ruled by the cautious Louis XVI, was unwilling to commit to an open alliance until the Americans demonstrated they could win a decisive victory. The risk of joining a losing cause, only to face British retaliation alone, was too great.
The News of Saratoga
News of Burgoyne’s surrender reached London in late November 1777 and crossed the English Channel to Paris by early December. The impact on the French court was immediate and electric. Benjamin Franklin, the legendary American ambassador in Paris, played the diplomatic game masterfully. Through his reputation, wit, and careful cultivation of French salon society, Franklin had already made the American cause immensely popular among the French aristocracy. Saratoga provided the proof Vergennes needed.
The Treaty of Alliance (6 February 1778)
On 6 February 1778, France and the United States signed two treaties in Paris:

The Treaty of Amity and Commerce: A commercial agreement recognising the United States as a sovereign nation and establishing trade relations.
The Treaty of Alliance: A military pact in which both parties agreed to fight together until American independence was secured, and neither would make a separate peace.

The treaty was France’s first formal recognition of American independence. It included a remarkable clause: France renounced forever any claim to Canada or the territory captured from Britain in North America — a critical assurance that quieted American fears of a French territorial takeover.
War Becomes Global
France’s entry transformed the American Revolutionary War into a global conflict. The implications were enormous:

Spain entered the war in 1779 as a French ally (by the Treaty of Aranjuez), though Spain fought to recover Gibraltar and Florida, not to aid American independence. Spanish forces attacked British positions along the Mississippi, in West Florida, and in the Gulf of Mexico.
The Dutch Republic went to war with Britain in 1780 (the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War), driven by commercial rivalries and the British seizure of Dutch ships carrying naval supplies to France.
The League of Armed Neutrality (1780), led by Russia, Sweden, and Denmark, challenged Britain’s right to search neutral shipping, further isolating Britain diplomatically.

Britain, which had begun the war fighting a rebellion of its own colonists, now faced a European coalition on three continents. The Royal Navy, though still the world’s most powerful, was stretched thin defending against the combined French and Spanish fleets in the Channel, the Mediterranean, the Caribbean, and the Indian Ocean. French naval superiority in American waters would prove decisive at the Siege of Yorktown in 1781.
Military and Financial Strain on Britain
The cost of the war spiralled. The national debt, already swollen by the Seven Years’ War, rose from £127 million in 1775 to over £230 million by 1783. War taxes squeezed the British economy. The army, forced to send reinforcements to the West Indies, Florida, and Gibraltar, could never again concentrate overwhelming force in America. France’s intervention gave Washington’s Continental Army something it had never possessed: the prospect of decisive naval and military support.

Aftermath
The Franco-American Alliance held for the duration of the war. French troops under the Comte de Rochambeau fought alongside the Continental Army from 1780, and the French fleet under the Comte de Grasse played the indispensable role at the Siege of Yorktown in 1781. The alliance culminated in the final victory: the Treaty of Paris 1783, in which Great Britain formally recognised the independence of the United States.
Saratoga was thus the hinge of the war. Before Saratoga, the rebellion was an American crisis. After Saratoga, it was a world war — one Britain could not win.

Key Figures













































FigureRoleGeneral John BurgoyneBritish commander of the northern invasion force; a capable soldier undone by poor logistics, over-ambitious strategy, and the failure of the co-ordinated planGeneral Horatio GatesAmerican commander at Saratoga; cautious and political, he received the laurels of victory (and the Conway Cabal’s backing to replace Washington), but his tactical role was passiveMajor General Benedict ArnoldThe battlefield hero of Bemis Heights; wounded in the leg leading the decisive charge. His decision remains one of the most controversial of the warGeneral Philip SchuylerAmerican commander before Gates; organised the scorched-earth defence that slowed Burgoyne. events/septennial-act-1716.title: Septennial Act (1716)
events/septennial-act-1716.content:
Septennial Act (1716)
The Septennial Act (1716) — formally 1 Geo. I, st. 2, c. 38 — was an Act of the Parliament of Great Britain that extended the maximum duration of a Parliament from three to seven years. It was passed on 7 May 1716 by the Whig ministry of George I, led by Charles Townshend and James Stanhope, with the vigorous support of Robert Walpole. The Act remains one of the most consequential and controversial constitutional measures of the eighteenth century: it entrenched Whig oligarchy, reduced electoral contests, and became the cornerstone of Walpole’s system of political management for two decades (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2076–2542).
The Triennial Act (1694)
The Septennial Act repealed the Triennial Act 1694 (6 & 7 Will. & Mar., c. 2), which had been one of the key achievements of the post-Revolution settlement. That statute, passed under William III following the Glorious Revolution, declared that Parliament should be summoned at least once every three years and that no Parliament should continue longer than three years from the date of its first meeting. Its preamble recited that “by the ancient laws and statutes of this realm frequent parliaments ought to be held” and that “frequent NEW parliaments tend very much to the happy union and good agreement of the king and his people” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2476–2480).
The Triennial Act was widely regarded as a fundamental guarantee of English liberty. It ensured that the House of Commons, the elected element of the constitution, could not be perpetuated beyond its natural term by a ministry that had lost the confidence of the electorate. In the two decades of its operation, ten successive parliaments had been elected under its provisions, through two long and bloody wars and intense political faction.
Jacobite Context
The immediate precipitant of the Septennial Act was the Jacobite Rising of 1715, which had convulsed Britain within a year of the Hanoverian accession. The rebellion, led by the Earl of Mar in Scotland and supported by English Jacobites under Thomas Forster and the Earl of Derwentwater, was suppressed by February 1716 — but its psychological impact on the Whig ministry was profound.
The Whig leadership, who had impeached the former Tory ministers Robert Harley and Bolingbroke and driven the latter into Jacobite exile, had every reason to fear the verdict of a new election. The country remained deeply divided: Tory sentiment was strong in the counties, the landed gentry resented the new dynasty’s foreign entourage, and the Jacobite party, though militarily defeated, had not been extinguished. A general election in 1716 or early 1717 — the existing Parliament, elected in January 1715, was approaching the end of its three-year term — might well return a Tory majority, or at least a House of Commons hostile to the Whig programme of continental alliances, standing armies, and Hanoverian favour.
The preamble of the Septennial Bill itself acknowledged this context, declaring that “the Popish and Jacobite faction is so powerful as to threaten destruction to the present establishment” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2131–2133). The argument from security was the ministry’s principal justification: at a juncture so critical, with rebellion barely crushed and French and Swedish intrigues ongoing, a dissolution could be fatal. As Lord Carteret, the bill’s ablest defender in the Lords, put it, “this bill would fix the king and the present happy establishment on a lasting foundation” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2188–2190).
The Debate: Stability Versus Constitutional Violation
The bill, which originated in the House of Lords, provoked one of the most searching constitutional debates of the eighteenth century. It was opposed with extraordinary ability on both constitutional and prudential grounds.
In the House of Lords
The opposition in the Lords was led by the Earl of Nottingham (Daniel Finch), a former Tory who had broken with the Whigs over the intemperance of the administration’s prosecutions of the Jacobite lords. Nottingham argued that frequent parliaments were “of the essence of the English constitution, sanctioned by the practice of ages”; that the members of the lower house were “delegated by the body of the nation for a certain term of years, at the expiration of which they were no longer the representatives of the people”; and that by lengthening their own authority at pleasure, Parliament “deprived the people of the only remedy which the wisdom of our ancestors had provided against the ignorance and corruption of those who might be tempted to betray the trust reposed in them” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2107–2139).
Nottingham further warned that a long parliament would encourage every species of corruption: “the value of a seat would bear a determinate proportion to the legal duration of parliaments, and the purchase would rise accordingly”; that it would “both enhance the temptations, and multiply the opportunities, of a vicious ministry, to undermine the integrity and independency of parliaments”; and that the reasons urged for prolonging this particular parliament would apply with equal or greater force at the end of seven years, leading potentially to perpetual parliaments (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2140–2160).
Lord Carteret, then a rising Whig statesman, defended the bill with equal force. He acknowledged that frequent parliaments were a great security of the people’s rights, but insisted that the bill was directed against frequent elections, not frequent meetings. The Jacobite danger was real: “of all rebellions, this last was the most monstrous and unnatural — for all others were carried on under pretences of liberty, whereas the last was a rebellion for slavery” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2172–2179). On the question of commitment, the Lords voted 96 for, 61 against. Thirty peers — headed by the Duke of Somerset and the Duke of Shrewsbury — entered a formal protest (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2191–2195).
In the House of Commons
When the bill was transmitted to the Commons, opposition was “still more vehement and formidable” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2197–2198). Lord Guernsey (Heneage Finch) moved to reject the bill without reading it — a motion defeated, but a measure of the temper of the house.
The most celebrated Commons speech against the bill was delivered by William Shippen, the leader of the Jacobite Tories in the Commons and one of the finest parliamentary orators of the age. Shippen argued on multiple grounds. The claim that a new election might be dangerous was, he said, an insult to the king: “How is it that in the infancy of his reign, he hath deprived himself of the love and affection of a people who so lately received him with every expression of joy?” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2237–2239). The argument from foreign alliances was contemptible — to alter the constitution merely to gratify allies was to humble the nation’s dignity: “What emotions of indignation must not the insolence of this demand excite — especially if it happen to be urged by a state which owes its very being to England?” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2261–2265).
But Shippen’s most powerful argument was constitutional. The present parliament had been elected under the Triennial Act; its trust was a triennial trust. To extend it was to cease to be trustees of the people and to become their own electors: “I cannot discover by what rule of reason or law we, who are only representatives, can enlarge, to our own advantage, the authority delegated to us — or that by virtue of such delegated authority we can destroy the fundamental rights of our constitution” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2303–2309). The Triennial Act was a concession made to the people by William III “in the midst of his difficulties,” and to repeal it in the very commencement of the new reign was an act of astonishing ingratitude and impolicy (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2328–2342). He concluded with a memorable image: “A standing parliament… has been said to resemble a standing pool, the waters of which grow, for want of a fresh and free current, offensive and fetid. But the present parliament may more justly be compared to a torrent, which, in its furious and foaming course, desolates the land” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2361–2370).
The debate was concluded by Sir Robert Raymond, later Lord Raymond and Chief Justice of England, who delivered a comprehensive reply. He enumerated the arguments for the bill — the expense of elections, the divisions and animosities they excited, the advantages to enemies from domestic feuds, and the encouragement to allies — and refuted each in turn. Annual parliaments, not septennial, were the true constitutional remedy for electoral corruption. The expense argument proved too much: if men would bribe for a three-year seat, they would bribe proportionally more for seven. As for the allies: “Is it not to proclaim to the world that the king dare not call a new parliament? that he dare not trust the people in a new choice?” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2456–2458).
On the question of commitment, the Commons voted 284 for, 162 against — a majority of 122. Final passage was carried by 264 votes against 121, a “triumphant majority” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2510–2526). The bill received the royal assent on 7 May 1716.
Self-Extension Clause
A particularly contentious feature of the Act was that it not only fixed the maximum duration of future parliaments at seven years, but also extended the life of the existing parliament — which had been elected for three years under the Triennial Act — by an additional four years. As Belsham puts it with characteristic pungency: “being elected by the nation for three years, they elected themselves for four years more” (Belsham, vol. II, lines 2086–2087). This self-extension gave the measure an appearance of naked self-interest that its defenders never wholly refuted.
Consequences
Entrenchment of Whig Oligarchy
The immediate consequence of the Septennial Act was to secure the Whig ministry in power for the foreseeable future. The Parliament of 1715 continued until 1722 (when it was dissolved by the death of George I’s first Parliament), and the Whig-dominated electoral system that operated under the new seven-year cycle produced Commons after Commons that were amenable to Whig management. The Act effectively dismantled the electoral threat to Whig supremacy for a generation.
Reduction of Electoral Contests
One of the Act’s most remarked-upon effects was a dramatic reduction in the frequency and intensity of electoral contests. Under the Triennial Act, elections were a near-constant feature of political life, generating expense, local faction, and unpredictable shifts in the parliamentary balance. The longer interval dampened electoral activity: the cost of fighting elections increased (as Raymond had predicted), but the intervals were long enough that local interests consolidated rather than competed. This suited the Whig oligarchy, whose control of borough patronage and government placements could be exercised more effectively over a seven-year horizon.
Walpole’s Cornerstone
The Act became an essential element of Robert Walpole’s system of political management during his long ministry (1721–1742). A seven-year Parliament gave him the stability to build his patronage network, distribute places and pensions systematically, and maintain discipline over his followers without the constant disruption of electoral campaigns. His opponents — the “Patriot” opposition of William Pitt the Elder, Bolingbroke (after his return from exile), and the dissident Whigs — railed against the Septennial Act as the bulwark of “Robin’s” corruption, but were unable to muster sufficient force to repeal it. Belsham records a later “ineffectual attempt to repeal the septennial act” during the later years of the reign (Belsham, vol. II, line 479), suggesting that opposition to the measure never entirely subsided but never reached critical mass.
Endurance Until 1911
The Septennial Act remained in force for nearly two centuries. It was ultimately superseded by the Parliament Act 1911, which reduced the maximum duration of a Parliament to five years. During that long currency, the Act was defended on the same pragmatic grounds on which it had been passed: that frequent elections were disruptive, expensive, and destabilising, and that the mass of ordinary business could not be conducted under the shadow of a triennial dissolution. Critics, from John Wilkes in the 1760s to the Chartists in the 1840s, continued to argue that the Act had been a violation of constitutional principle and a self-interested power-grab by the Whig oligarchy — but the Septennial regime outlasted every attempt to restore the Triennial principle.
Constitutional Significance
The Septennial Act raised a question that troubled eighteenth-century constitutional thought: could Parliament limit its own duration? The Act’s opponents argued that the Triennial Act was a fundamental law, a compact between the sovereign and the people that could not be unilaterally altered by the representatives. Shippen and Raymond contended that a legislative body elected under one set of terms had no moral or legal authority to extend those terms without a fresh mandate from the electorate. The Act’s defenders, by contrast, relied on the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty — the principle that the King-in-Parliament was the supreme legislative authority and could not be bound by its predecessors. This doctrine prevailed, and the Septennial Act became a precedent for the view that Parliament’s powers over the constitution were unlimited. The Act thus marks a pivotal moment in the development of the modern British constitution: the victory of absolute parliamentary sovereignty over the older notion of a fundamental or ancient constitution.
Key Figures
The Whig Ministry (in favour)

Charles Townshend, 2nd Viscount Townshend — Secretary of State for the Northern Department and a leading figure in the Whig ministry that introduced the bill. Townshend was Walpole’s brother-in-law and political ally at this stage, though they would later fall out.
James Stanhope, 1st Earl Stanhope — Secretary of State for the Southern Department, a soldier-diplomat who was the ministry’s driving force in foreign affairs and a staunch supporter of the Septennial measure.
Robert Walpole — First Lord of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer (from 1715), whose parliamentary management was essential in steering the bill through the Commons. Walpole’s later long ministry would depend heavily on the Act’s provisions.
Lord Carteret — The bill’s most effective defender in the Lords, who argued that septennial parliaments would fix the Hanoverian establishment on a lasting foundation.

Opposition

Earl of Nottingham (Daniel Finch) — Former Tory secretary of state who led the opposition in the Lords with a powerful constitutional critique of the bill as violating the essence of the English constitution.
William Shippen — Jacobite Tory MP who delivered the most celebrated Commons speech against the bill, arguing that the House could not extend its own delegated authority.
Sir Robert Raymond — Future Chief Justice of England whose comprehensive speech refuted each argument for the bill point by point and called for annual, not septennial, parliaments as the constitutional remedy.
Charles Seymour, 6th Duke of Somerset — Whig grandee who nevertheless joined the protest against the bill in the Lords.
Charles Talbot, 1st Duke of Shrewsbury — Lord Chamberlain and former Lord Treasurer who also protested the bill despite his Whig credentials.

events/siege-of-yorktown-1781.title: Siege of Yorktown (28 Sept – 19 Oct 1781) and the Fall of the North Ministry
events/siege-of-yorktown-1781.content:
Siege of Yorktown (28 Sept – 19 Oct 1781)
The Siege of Yorktown (28 September – 19 October 1781) was the culminating military engagement of the American Revolutionary War in North America. After years of bloody stalemate in the northern colonies, the British high command adopted a southern strategy that initially met with dazzling success — the capture of Savannah (1778), Charleston (1780), and the crushing defeat of General Gates at Camden — only for Lieutenant General Charles, Earl Cornwallis to pursue an ultimately disastrous campaign that ended with the surrender of his entire army to a combined Franco-American force at Yorktown, Virginia. The news of the catastrophe reached London in November 1781, prompting Lord North’s legendary cry — “Oh God! It is all over!” — and precipitating the collapse of his ministry in March 1782.
Background: The Southern Strategy
Through the first three years of the war, British arms had failed to deliver a decisive blow in the northern theatre. The Saratoga Campaign of 1777 had ended in the catastrophic surrender of General John Burgoyne’s army at Saratoga, bringing France into the war on the American side. The British evacuation of Philadelphia in 1778 and the subsequent stalemate around New York convinced the ministry of George III and his chief minister Lord North that a new approach was needed.
The so-called southern strategy rested on the premise that the southern colonies — the Carolinas, Georgia, and Virginia — contained a larger proportion of loyalist sentiment than New England, and that a British military presence there would rally the King’s friends to restore royal government. In December 1778, a British expedition captured Savannah, Georgia, and by early 1780 the theatre had become the focus of the war.
The Fall of Charleston and Camden
In May 1780, after a six-week siege, a British army under Sir Henry Clinton and Lord Cornwallis compelled the surrender of Charleston, South Carolina — the worst American defeat of the war. Some 5,500 Continental troops and militia became prisoners of war, and General Benjamin Lincoln, the American commander, was subjected to the humiliation of marching out between the lines with colours cased. In August 1780, Cornwallis shattered a newly-formed American army under General Horatio Gates at Camden, killing or capturing over 2,000 men and driving the remnants into North Carolina.
Belsham records that these victories “excited the most sanguine expectations in England” that the southern colonies could be reduced to obedience. The ministry, intoxicated by success, anticipated a rapid end to the rebellion.
The Tide Turns in the Carolinas
But the British triumph at Camden proved to be the high-water mark of the southern campaign. American resistance, far from being crushed, re-emerged under new commanders. General Nathanael Greene, appointed to command the Southern Department after Camden, pursued a Fabian strategy of avoiding pitched battles while wearing down the British through attrition. At Cowpens (17 January 1781), Colonel Daniel Morgan’s force annihilated a British detachment under the dashing but impetuous Colonel Banastre Tarleton. Cornwallis, stung by the defeat, embarked on a relentless pursuit of Morgan and Greene across the rivers of North Carolina, a chase that Belsham describes as “bold and hazardous” and in which Greene had predicted that Cornwallis might “precipitate himself into some capital misfortune.”
The climax came at Guilford Court House (15 March 1781), where Cornwallis drove Greene from the field after a hard-fought engagement. But the victory was Pyrrhic: the British lost some 600 veteran troops, a quarter of their effective force, and Cornwallis found himself unable to sustain his army in the interior. “This was a victory,” Belsham observes, “very different from that of Camden, and dearly purchased on the part of the English.”
Compelled to march to Wilmington, North Carolina, to refit and resupply, Cornwallis now made the fateful decision that would lead to Yorktown: instead of following Greene back into South Carolina to protect the British posts there, he resolved to march north into Virginia, believing that the Chesapeake colonies were the decisive theatre.
Cornwallis’s Position: The Road to Yorktown
Lord Cornwallis entered Virginia in May 1781, joining forces with a British detachment under General William Phillips at Petersburg. The combined army, now some 7,000 strong, was formidable on paper, but the strategic situation was already deteriorating. The Marquis de Lafayette, commanding the American forces in Virginia, skillfully avoided battle while shadowing the British movements, earning Cornwallis’s contemptuous remark — “The boy cannot escape me!” — which Lafayette would later recall with satisfaction.
Throughout the summer of 1781, Cornwallis marched his army across Virginia — from Petersburg to Richmond, from Richmond to Williamsburg — in a series of operations that achieved little of lasting strategic value. He dispatched Tarleton on a daring raid that nearly captured Governor Thomas Jefferson and the Virginia Assembly at Charlottesville, but these were pinpricks against an enemy that refused to be drawn into a decisive battle.
In June, Cornwallis received dispatches from Sir Henry Clinton, the British commander-in-chief in New York, expressing alarm that New York itself might be threatened by the combined Franco-American army under George Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau. Clinton ordered the return of the troops he had detached to Virginia. Cornwallis, protesting but ultimately compliant, withdrew his army to the coast to facilitate embarkation.
After briefly considering Portsmouth, Cornwallis selected Yorktown, a small port on the York River near the Chesapeake Bay, as his base. The position, as Belsham notes, was unfavourable: Yorktown sat “nearly at the extremity of a narrow peninsula, enclosed between York River to the north and James River to the south,” and was easily invested by an enemy commanding the navigation of both rivers. Cornwallis himself had “so unfavourable an opinion of the port he occupied, that nothing but assurances of support would have induced him to attempt its defence.” But he trusted in the promise of the navy and the army in New York to relieve him.
The French-American Plan
While Cornwallis dug in at Yorktown, a grand strategic convergence was taking shape. The key to the plan was the French navy.
Washington and Rochambeau had spent the spring and early summer of 1781 in conference at Wethersfield, Connecticut, debating their next move. Washington’s instinct was to attack New York, the principal British base in North America. Rochambeau was sceptical. The question hung in the balance until a letter arrived from the Comte de Grasse, commanding a powerful French fleet of twenty-four ships of the line in the West Indies. De Grasse announced that his destination was unalterably fixed to the Chesapeake — he could operate there only until mid-October, when the hurricane season would compel his return to the Caribbean.
“We have no alternative,” Washington and Rochambeau replied. They would march south.
The plan required extraordinary secrecy and coordination. Washington maintained the appearance of preparing to besiege New York as late as 24 August, keeping Sir Henry Clinton guessing. Then, on that date, the allied army suddenly decamped, crossed the North River, and began a swift march through New Jersey and Pennsylvania. They passed through Philadelphia on 30 August, where the Continental Congress received the electrifying but still uncertain news. The fleet of the Comte de Grasse entered the Chesapeake Bay nearly simultaneously.
The Battle of the Capes (5 September 1781)
The strategic hinge of the campaign was a naval battle that would decide whether Cornwallis could be relieved. On 5 September 1781, a British fleet of nineteen ships of the line under Admiral Thomas Graves appeared off the Virginia Capes. De Grasse, expecting a reinforcement squadron from Rhode Island under the Comte de Barras, put to sea to meet them. A warm engagement followed, in which, as Belsham records, “the English appear not to have obtained the advantage.”
The outcome was decisive. De Grasse, joined by Barras’s squadron a few days later, was left “undisputed master of the Chesapeake.” The British fleet, having failed to break the French blockade, withdrew to New York. From this moment, relief of Cornwallis was “wholly impracticable.”
The Siege: 28 September — 19 October 1781
The allied army — some 9,000 Americans and 8,000 French — arrived before Yorktown in late September. Washington, Rochambeau, and the Comte de Grasse had trapped Cornwallis in a vice: the French fleet sealed the bay, while the Franco-American army closed the landward approaches.
The siege works were opened with classical eighteenth-century precision. The allies constructed a first parallel — a line of entrenchments — about two thousand yards from the British works, and began a heavy bombardment. Cornwallis, seeing his outer works untenable, pulled his troops back into the inner fortifications.
By 14 October, despite “the well directed and incessant fire of the enemy,” the besiegers had advanced far in their second parallel. Two British redoubts at a distance of two hundred yards from the British lines were causing particular trouble, enfilading the allied approaches. It was decided to storm them simultaneously — one by the French, the other by the Americans.
The assault was carried out “sword in hand with resistless impetuosity.” The Americans, Belsham notes, advanced with the cry “Remember New London!” — a reference to the destruction of that Connecticut port by the turncoat Benedict Arnold a month earlier. But when the British in the redoubts begged for quarter, the Americans granted it: “they could not tell how to put men to death while begging on their knees for quarter.”
By this time, the allied batteries mounted one hundred pieces of heavy ordnance. The British works, “enfiladed in almost every part, and nearly demolished, could scarcely mount a single gun.”
The Surrender
In desperation, Cornwallis attempted to transport his garrison across the York River to Gloucester Point on the opposite shore, where secondary British works were still held. A violent storm struck after the embarkation had actually commenced, “totally frustrating” the design.
Lord Cornwallis was left with no choice. On 17 October — the fourth anniversary of Burgoyne’s surrender at Saratoga — he dispatched a flag of truce. Negotiations followed, and on 19 October the articles of capitulation were signed.
The terms were hard. The honor of marching out with colours flying, which had been refused to General Lincoln at Charleston, was now refused to Cornwallis. General Benjamin Lincoln — the very officer who had surrendered at Charleston eighteen months before — was appointed to receive the submission of the army of Yorktown, “precisely in the same way his own had been conducted.” On 19 October, the British and Hessian troops, some 7,000 strong, marched out between the allied lines to the tune of a popular march called “The World Turned Upside Down.” Belsham records Cornwallis himself as pleading indisposition and sending his sword by a subordinate.
“The joy of the Americans on the capture of a second royal army was unbounded.” The Continental Congress ordered a marble column erected at Yorktown and appointed a solemn thanksgiving throughout all the states.
News Reaches London
The news of the catastrophe crossed the Atlantic in November 1781. The account that reached London was worse than anything the ministry had dared to fear: an entire British army — the second to have been lost in the war — had laid down its arms.
The famous exclamation attributed to Lord North — “Oh God! It is all over!” — captures the visceral shock with which the intelligence was received. North is said to have recoiled as if struck a physical blow. He had been the King’s minister for twelve years, the longest-serving prime minister of the reign, and had presided over the American war from its outbreak. The pillars of his political position — the confidence of the Crown and the support of Parliament — were both now crumbling.
Belsham records that the King’s Speech at the opening of the new session of Parliament on 27 November 1781 acknowledged “the events of it had been very unfortunate to his army in Virginia, having ended in the total loss of his forces in that province.” But George III, characteristically, insisted on the justice of his cause and called for “a vigorous, animated, and united exertion” to continue the war.
The Fall of the North Ministry: November 1781 — March 1782
The parliamentary session that opened on 27 November 1781 became the battleground on which the North ministry would be destroyed.
In the debates that followed, the Opposition — led by Charles James Fox, Edmund Burke, and the younger William Pitt — launched a sustained assault on the ministry’s conduct of the war. Burke, in a famous speech on army estimates, asked whether the American Secretary wished “to dispatch a third army to America, that General Washington might a third time receive them as prisoners of war.” The ministry survived the first divisions, but the majorities were shrinking: on a censorious motion concerning Lord Sandwich, the First Lord of the Admiralty, 217 members of the House of Commons voted him guilty of “shameful mismanagement of the naval affairs of Great Britain.”
The decisive blow fell in February and March 1782. On 22 February, General Henry Conway moved an address to the King imploring him to end offensive war in America. The ministry defeated it by a single vote — 193 to 192 — a “fearful majority of ONE voice only.” Fox immediately gave notice that the question would be revived. On 27 February, Conway moved again, and this time a ministerial attempt to substitute a bill for a truce was defeated 234 to 215. The original motion was then carried without a division, and on 1 March the House of Commons presented an address to George III, who responded that he would “take such measures as should appear to him most conducive to the restoration of harmony.”
This was not deemed sufficient. On 4 March, Conway moved a second address and a resolution declaring that the House would “consider as enemies to his Majesty and the country all those who should advise a prosecution of offensive war on the continent of North America.”
On 8 March, Lord John Cavendish moved a series of resolutions whose import was “that the chief cause of all the national misfortunes is want of foresight and ability in his Majesty’s Ministers.” Lord North’s government survived by only ten votes — 226 to 216. Sir John Rous, once a zealous ministerialist, moved that “the House could place no further confidence in the Ministers.” The motion was defeated 236 to 227, but with such a majority “victory was defeat.”
On 19 March 1782, the crisis reached its end. The Earl of Surrey was about to move a resolution of similar import when Lord North rose and addressed the Speaker. He declared, Belsham records, “that His Majesty had come to a determination to make an entire change of administration.” North thanked the House for its indulgence and declared himself ready to answer to his country for his conduct. The twelve-year ministry of Lord North — “this famous, or, to use a term more characteristically appropriate, this infamous Administration, so long the bane and curse of the British empire” — was “suddenly and totally dissolved, to the inexpressible joy of all ranks and orders of people.”
The Rockingham ministry was formed in its place, with the Marquis of Rockingham as First Lord of the Treasury and Charles James Fox and Edmund Burke in office. Peace negotiations with the American commissioners opened in Paris, culminating in the provisional articles of peace signed on 30 November 1782 and the definitive Treaty of Paris 1783, by which the thirteen colonies were recognised as free and independent states.
Key Figures
Lord Cornwallis (Charles, Earl Cornwallis): The British commander whose southern campaign, brilliant in its early stages, ended in disaster at Yorktown. Belsham portrays him as “generous, disinterested, and humane” as an individual, but fatally compromised by his adherence to a ruthless policy of war-making and by his subordination to orders from a distant commander-in-chief in New York.
George Washington: The American commander-in-chief, whose patient strategy of avoiding the destruction of his army while waiting for French assistance was vindicated at Yorktown. His decision to march south from New York was the decisive strategic move of the campaign.
Comte de Rochambeau: The French general who commanded the expeditionary force and coordinated with Washington. His loyalty to the plan and willingness to subordinate French strategic interests to the American theatre were essential.
Comte de Grasse: The French admiral whose fleet blockaded the Chesapeake and defeated the British naval relief attempt. His decision to sail north from the West Indies and his insistence on the Chesapeake as his destination determined the shape of the campaign.
Lord North: The British prime minister who had directed the war against America since 1775 and who fell from power in the aftermath of Yorktown. His reputation has been contested: Belsham treats him with a mixture of contempt for his policies and grudging respect for his parliamentary skill.
George III: The King, whose unyielding support for the American war and whose influence over the ministry through the “interior cabinet” (as the Duke of Richmond called it) was held by the Opposition to be the root cause of Britain’s misfortunes.
Aftermath and Consequences
The Siege of Yorktown effectively ended major combat operations in the American Revolutionary War. Although peace would not be formally concluded until the Treaty of Paris 1783 — and although fighting continued at sea and in other theatres — no further large-scale military operations took place in North America.
The principal consequences were:


American Independence: The military victory at Yorktown made American sovereignty a fact that even the most intransigent British ministers could no longer deny. The provisional articles recognising American independence were signed on 30 November 1782.


The Fall of the North Ministry: The political earthquake in London brought to power a ministry committed to peace, triggering a chain of events — the Rockingham ministry, the Shelburne ministry, and ultimately the Fox-North coalition of 1783 — that would reshape British politics for a generation.


The Loyalist Tragedy: The terms of the peace treaty left the American Loyalists — those colonists who had remained faithful to the Crown — exposed to confiscation and persecution. The Congressional recommendation that their estates be restored proved, as Belsham observes, “nugatory and useless.” Thousands migrated to Nova Scotia, the Bahamas, and other British possessions.


British Constitutional Development: The collapse of the North ministry and the subsequent political crisis stretched the boundaries of the eighteenth-century constitution. The King’s right to choose his ministers was constrained by the unmistakable verdict of the House of Commons; the principle that a ministry must command a parliamentary majority was established beyond dispute.


Contemporary Accounts
William Belsham, writing in the 1790s, presents the Yorktown campaign as the just conclusion of a war that was from the beginning unjust, impolitic, and ruinous. His narrative, while written from a distinctly Whiggish and critical perspective, draws on parliamentary debates, military dispatches, and published memoirs. He is scrupulous in recording the arguments of both sides — the ministry’s stubborn insistence on the justice of the cause, the Opposition’s denunciation of its folly — but his moral judgment is never in doubt: the war was a calamity brought on by the obstinacy of the King and the incompetence of his ministers, and Yorktown was its fitting epitaph.
Belsham’s account of the surrender itself is notably restrained, avoiding the triumphalism of American narratives while refusing to disguise the magnitude of the British defeat. He dwells on the pathos of the situation — the “eager hopes and sanguine expectations” that preceded the “final issue” — and on the irony that Cornwallis was compelled to surrender “precisely in the same way” as that in which he had compelled Lincoln at Charleston.
See Also

Saratoga Campaign — the earlier American victory that brought France into the war
American Declaration of Independence — the document that made the war a struggle for national sovereignty
Treaty of Paris 1783 — the peace treaty that formally ended the war
George III — the King whose stubborn prosecution of the war led to disaster
Lord North — the prime minister who fell with his policy
Charles James Fox — the great Opposition orator who led the attack on the ministry
Edmund Burke — the philosopher-statesman who denounced the war in parliament
Gordon Riots — the domestic crisis that had shaken the North ministry in 1780
Boston Tea Party — the act of colonial defiance that began the chain of events

events/south-sea-bubble-1720.title: South Sea Bubble (1720)
events/south-sea-bubble-1720.content:
South Sea Bubble (1720)
The South Sea Bubble of 1720 was the greatest financial catastrophe in eighteenth-century Britain — a speculative mania that gripped the entire nation, from the King’s court to the humblest tradesman, and ended in ruin for thousands. It began as a bold scheme to reduce the national debt, degenerated into an orgy of bribery, fraud, and corruption reaching into the highest offices of state, and concluded with the collapse of public credit, a parliamentary inquiry that exposed systemic rot, and the political extinction of the King’s first ministry. Out of the wreckage emerged Robert Walpole, whose masterful handling of the crisis made him indispensable and launched the longest premiership in British history.
The affair takes its name from the South Sea Company, a trading corporation whose stock rose from £128 in January 1720 to £1,050 in June, before crashing to £150 by September of the same year. It was the English counterpart to John Law’s Mississippi Scheme in France, and together they formed the twin pillars of the great European speculative bubble of 1719–1720.
Origins: The South Sea Company (1711–1719)
Foundation under Harley
The South Sea Company was incorporated in 1711 by Robert Harley, Earl of Oxford, as a centrepiece of his Tory ministry’s financial policy. The country had emerged from the War of the Spanish Succession burdened with a national debt of some £10 million — much of it in short-term, high-interest obligations that the government could not readily service. Harley’s plan was to convert these floating debts (some £9.47 million of “unprovided-for” debts, as Campbell records) into perpetual annuities at 6%, secured against the customs revenues, and to create a joint-stock company that would undertake this conversion in exchange for a monopoly of trade to the South Seas — the Spanish Americas.
The commercial logic was thin but seductive. The Bristol merchants who had sent the privateers Duke and Duchess under Captain Woodes Rogers and Captain Stephen Courtney to the South Seas in 1708 — with the famous navigator William Dampier as pilot — had returned in 1711 with rich prizes, “the wealth of the South Seas came to make a great noise” (Campbell). Harley’s ministry seized on this to argue that the trade could be made as lucrative as the East India trade. To fix the idea in the public mind, rumours were circulated in Holland that great profits were to be made, and several treatises were published in 1711–1712 advocating the scheme.
The charter of the new company vested in it the sole trade to the South Seas — a grant of enormous potential scope, encompassing the entire Pacific coast of the Americas. The debts were liquidated, the annuities granted, and the company incorporated “for carrying on a trade to the South Seas” (Campbell).
The Asiento (1713)
The company’s commercial prospects received a dramatic boost from the Treaty of Utrecht (1713). By the Asiento de Negros — the exclusive contract to supply the Spanish West Indies with enslaved Africans — Britain secured a thirty-year monopoly on one of the most profitable trades in the Atlantic world. The contract was vested in the South Sea Company by the King’s order, giving it the right not only to supply the Spanish colonies with 144,000 slaves over the term but also to send one “annual ship” of 500 tons to the trade fairs of Spanish America.
This gave the company a real, if limited, commercial foundation. But the annual ship was a pittance compared to the scale of the company’s capital, and the slave trade itself — though profitable — could never generate returns sufficient to justify the valuations that would soon attach to the stock. The company was, from the start, a financial engine disguised as a trading corporation.
The South Sea Scheme (1720)
After the collapse of the Jacobite rising of 1715 and the consolidation of Whig power under the Sunderland-Stanhope ministry, the national debt had grown still larger. In 1719, John Law’s Mississippi Company in France had successfully taken over much of the French national debt, sparking a speculative fever in Paris. The directors of the South Sea Company — led by the projector John Blunt, a man of “moderate talents” according to Smollett, but possessed of remarkable audacity — proposed to do for Britain what Law had done for France.
The plan, which became law as the South Sea Act in April 1720, was breathtaking in its scope. The company would take over the entire national debt — some £31 million — by exchanging its own stock for government annuities. In return, the government would reduce its annual interest payments from ~£1.5 million to ~£600,000, saving the Exchequer heavily. The company’s profit would come from the difference between the interest it received from the government and the dividends it paid to its stockholders — a profit that would be vastly multiplied if the stock could be driven to ever-higher prices.
The bill passed both Houses of Parliament with astonishing speed. Smollett, Belsham, and Campbell all record that the passage was secured by bribery on a massive scale. The directors created a fictitious stock of £574,000 — “fictitious stock” that had never been subscribed for but was distributed as gifts to those who could advance the bill.
The Mania (January–June 1720)
The Stock Rises
When the South Sea Act passed, the stock stood at about £128. It rose steadily through the spring. But a far more dramatic surge came when Blunt and the directors began to spread rumours calculated to inflame the imagination of the public. The most potent was the report — baseless — that Gibraltar and Port Mahon would be exchanged for places in Peru, by which means “the English trade to the South Sea would be protected and enlarged” (Smollett).

“This rumour, diffused by his emissaries, acted like a contagion. In five days the directors opened their books for a subscription of one million, at the rate of three hundred pounds for every hundred pounds capital. Persons of all ranks crowded to the house in such a manner, that the first subscription exceeded two millions of original stock. In a few days this stock advanced to three hundred and forty pounds; and the subscriptions were sold for double the price of the first payment.” — Smollett, Complete History of England, Vol. X

By June 1720, the stock had reached £1,050. The nation was seized by “a kind of national delirium” (Smollett). Exchange Alley was crowded with statesmen, clergymen, churchmen and dissenters, Whigs and Tories, physicians, lawyers, tradesmen, and multitudes of women. All other professions and employments were utterly neglected.
