The Flood of Bubble Companies
The mania was not confined to South Sea stock. Imitation companies — “Bubbles” — sprang up by the score, “under the countenance of the prime nobility” (Smollett). The Prince of Wales (the future George II) allowed himself to be constituted governor of the Welch Copper Company; the Duke of Chandos headed the York-Building Company; the Duke of Bridgewater formed a third for building houses in London and Westminster. About a hundred such schemes were projected and put into execution, “to the ruin of many thousands.”
The sums proposed to be raised by these expedients amounted to three hundred millions sterling — exceeding, as Smollett notes with evident horror, the value of all the land in England. One obscure projector, who refused to explain his scheme, simply took subscriptions of two guineas each, promising to disclose the project in a month. In one forenoon he received a thousand subscriptions; by evening he had left the kingdom.
The King, before departing for Hanover, issued a proclamation against these unlawful projects. The Lords Justices dismissed all petitions for charters, and the Prince of Wales renounced the company of which he had been elected governor. But the damage was done.
Bribery and Corruption
The most corrupt aspect of the mania was the systematic bribery of the political class. The committee of secrecy later discovered that, before any subscription could be made, a fictitious stock of £574,000 had been disposed of by the directors to facilitate the passing of the bill. Great part of this was distributed among:

Charles Spencer, 3rd Earl of Sunderland — First Lord of the Treasury and the King’s chief minister in England
James Craggs the elder — Postmaster-General
The Duchess of Kendal — the King’s German mistress (Melusine von der Schulenburg)
The Countess of Platen and her two nieces — the King’s half-sister and her circle
James Craggs the younger — Secretary of State
John Aislabie — Chancellor of the Exchequer

The directors also engaged in a massive fraud against the company itself, buying its own stock at artificially high prices on the pretence of supporting the market, while secretly selling their own holdings — “a notorious fraud and breach of trust” in the words of the House of Lords’ resolutions.
The Crash (September–December 1720)
Collapse of the Stock
The infatuation prevailed until 8 September 1720, when the stock began to fall. Then, as Smollett describes it, “some of the adventurers awake from their delirium.” The number of sellers daily increased. By 29 September, the stock had sunk to £150. Several eminent goldsmiths and bankers who had lent great sums upon the stock were obliged to stop payment and abscond.

“The ebb of this portentous tide was so violent, that it bore down everything in its way; and an infinite number of families was overwhelmed with ruin. Public credit sustained a terrible shock: the nation was thrown into a dangerous ferment; and nothing was heard but the ravings of grief, disappointment, and despair.” — Smollett, Complete History of England, Vol. X

The Bank of England and the Threat to National Credit
Some principal members of the ministry, deeply concerned in the fraudulent transactions, employed all their influence with the Bank of England to support the credit of the South Sea Company. The Bank reluctantly agreed to subscribe into the stock (valued at 400%) the sum of £3.5 million, which the South Sea Company was to repay at Lady Day and Michaelmas of the following year. Books were opened at the Bank to take in subscriptions for the support of public credit, and considerable sums came in.
By this expedient the stock was raised at first, and those who contrived it seized the opportunity to sell. But the bankruptcy of the goldsmiths and the Sword-Blade Company (the South Sea’s own banker) from the fall of the stock occasioned such a run upon the Bank that “the money was paid away faster than it could be received from the subscription” (Smollett). The stock fell again. The directors of the Bank, finding themselves in danger of being involved in the company’s ruin, renounced the agreement.
All expedients having failed, and the clamours of the people daily increasing, expresses were dispatched to George I at Hanover, pressing him to return. He shortened his stay in Germany and arrived in England on 11 November 1720.
The Parliamentary Inquiry (December 1720 – August 1721)
The Commons Acts
Parliament assembled on 8 December 1720. The King expressed his concern for “the unhappy turn of affairs, which had so deeply affected the public credit at home” and earnestly desired the Commons to consider the most effectual methods to restore credit. The lower house was too much interested in the calamity to postpone consideration.
The directors were ordered to produce an account of all their proceedings. Sir Joseph Jekyll moved for a select committee to examine the particulars. Robert Walpole, then Paymaster of the Forces, argued that such a method would protract the inquiry while public credit lay in a “bleeding condition.” He told the house he had formed a scheme for restoring public credit, but before communicating it, desired to know whether the subscriptions of the public debts, money subscriptions, and other contracts with the South Sea Company should remain in their present state. After a warm debate, the question was carried in the affirmative.
Walpole then produced his scheme: to ingraft nine millions of South Sea stock into the Bank of England, and a like sum into the East India Company, on certain conditions. The house voted that proposals should be received from these corporations, and a bill was passed into law.
A second bill restrained the sub-governor, deputy-governor, directors, treasurer, and other officers of the South Sea Company from quitting the kingdom, and provided for discovering their estates.
The Committee of Secrecy
A committee of secrecy was chosen by ballot to examine all books, papers, and proceedings relating to the execution of the South Sea Act. Their work produced devastating revelations. In the words of the committee’s report, they had discovered “a train of the deepest villainy and fraud that hell ever contrived to ruin a nation” (Smollett).
The persons of Sir George Caswell, Sir John Blunt, Sir John Lambert, Sir John Fellows, and Mr. Grigsby were taken into custody. Sir Theodore Janssen, Mr. Sawbridge, Sir Robert Chaplain, and Mr. Eyles were expelled from the House and apprehended. John Aislabie resigned his employment as Chancellor of the Exchequer and Lord of the Treasury. Orders were given to remove all directors of the South Sea Company from the places they possessed under the government.
The Lords and the Exposure of Political Corruption
The Lords, in the course of their examination, discovered that large portions of South Sea stock had been given to several persons in the administration and House of Commons for promoting the passage of the South Sea Act. The House immediately resolved that “this practice was a notorious and most dangerous species of corruption.”
Earl Stanhope distinguished himself by his vehemence. He declared that “the estates of the criminals, whether directors or not directors, ought to be confiscated to repair the public losses.” He was seconded by Lord Carteret, and even by the Earl of Sunderland himself — a man whose own hands were deeply stained. The Duke of Wharton declared he would give up his best friend if found guilty.
But the strain of the inquiry told on Stanhope. In a violent debate in the Lords, the Duke of Wharton made a speech that seemed to reflect on the ministry. Stanhope, “conceiving this reflection was aimed at him, was seized with a transport of anger. He undertook to vindicate the ministry; and spoke with such vehemence as produced a violent head-ach, which obliged him to retire.” He underwent proper evacuations and seemed to recover, but the next day — 5 February 1721 — he became lethargic, was seized with a suffocation, and “instantly expired” (Smollett).
A few days later (16 February), Secretary of State James Craggs the younger died of smallpox. The elder James Craggs died of lethargy before he could undergo the censure of the House. The House resolved, nevertheless, that he was “a notorious accomplice with Robert Knight, and some of the directors, in carrying on their scandalous practices,” and ordered that all his estate from 1 December 1720 be applied to the relief of the sufferers.
The Fate of the Directors
The committee of secrecy found that before any subscription could be made, the fictitious stock of £574,000 had been distributed. Among the recipients was the Earl of Sunderland, for whom £50,000 in stock had been taken by the cashier Knight. The House engaged in a violent dispute over Sunderland’s guilt. The whole strength of the ministry was mustered in his defence. The majority declared him innocent — “the nation in general was of another opinion” (Smollett). He resigned his place of First Commissioner in the Treasury, which was bestowed upon Robert Walpole.
Against John Aislabie, the evidence was overwhelming. The Commons resolved that he had “promoted the destructive execution of the South Sea scheme, with a view to his own exorbitant profit, and combined with the directors in their pernicious practices, to the ruin of public credit.” He was expelled from the House and committed to the Tower of London.
The directors delivered inventories of their estates, which were confiscated by Act of Parliament towards making good the damages sustained by the company, after a certain allowance was deducted for each according to his conduct and circumstances.
Robert Knight’s Flight
Knight, the cashier of the South Sea Company, who had been entrusted with the secrets of the whole affair, fled the kingdom. A proclamation was issued for his apprehension. He was seized at Tirlemont by the vigilance of Mr. Gandot, secretary to the British resident at Brussels, and confined in the citadel of Antwerp. The British government applied to the court of Vienna for his extradition, but the States of Brabant insisted on their privilege that no person apprehended for any crime in Brabant should be tried in any other country. Before the dispute could be resolved, Knight escaped from the citadel — and with him, the most damaging testimony against the inner circle of the ministry.
Walpole’s Scheme for the Restoration of Credit
Robert Walpole emerged as the dominant figure of the crisis. He had not been on the board of the South Sea Company and had publicly warned against the scheme during the mania — though it was later known that he had profited from stock dealings. More importantly, he had the necessary distance from the scandal and the financial acumen to devise a workable restoration plan.
His scheme — the “ingraftment” — was enacted into law in the summer of 1721. The total capital stock at the end of 1720 amounted to about £37.8 million. The stock allotted to all the proprietors did not exceed £24.5 million; the remaining capital belonged to the company in its corporate capacity. Walpole’s bill provided that:

£7 million should be paid to the public out of the company’s profits
Certain additions were made to the proprietors’ stock out of the company’s own stock
A particular distribution of stock amounting to £2.2 million was made
Upon remitting £5 million of the £7 million to the public, £2 million of the capital was annihilated
After these distributions, the remaining capital was divided among all the proprietors — a dividend of £33 6s 8d per cent
The company lost some £8.9 million in the process
All debtors to the company on loans advanced on stock (over £11 million) were discharged upon paying 10%
On this article, the company’s loss exceeded £6.9 million

The proprietors loudly complained of being deprived of £2 million, and the parliament eventually revived that sum. But the essential object was achieved: the South Sea Company was placed in a condition to fulfil its engagements with the public, the ferment of the people subsided, and “the credit of the nation was restored” (Smollett).
Aftermath and Significance
The Fall of the Sunderland Ministry
The South Sea Bubble destroyed the Whig ministry that had governed Britain since the accession of George I. The principal casualties were:

Earl Stanhope — dead of apoplexy provoked by the stress of the parliamentary inquiry (February 1721)
James Craggs the younger — dead of smallpox (February 1721)
James Craggs the elder — dead; his estate confiscated
John Aislabie — expelled from the Commons and imprisoned in the Tower
Charles Spencer, 3rd Earl of Sunderland — acquitted by a narrow majority in the Commons, but politically destroyed; forced to resign the Treasury
Sir John Blunt — taken into custody; fortune forfeited
The directors of the South Sea Company — stripped of their estates and forbidden to hold office in the Company, the Bank of England, or the East India Company

The Rise of Walpole
The great beneficiary of the catastrophe was Robert Walpole. He had been out of office when the South Sea Act was passed, having resigned from the ministry in 1717 during the Whig schism. He had been brought back into the ministry as Paymaster-General in June 1720 — too late to influence the South Sea Act but early enough to avoid contamination. When the crisis broke, he was the only senior figure with the financial competence, the parliamentary skills, and the personal integrity (or at least the appearance of it) to restore confidence.
The King, who deeply regretted the death of Stanhope, appointed Lord Townshend — Walpole’s brother-in-law — as Secretary of State in Stanhope’s place. Walpole himself became First Lord of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer in April 1721. He would remain the dominant figure in British politics for the next twenty-one years.
The irony was profound. The South Sea Bubble — the greatest financial scandal of the century — made Walpole indispensable. His restoration scheme demonstrated his mastery of finance and his capacity for practical, workable solutions. His refusal to pursue Sunderland to destruction displayed his political magnanimity (or calculation). His distance from the corrupt inner circle of the Company gave him the moral authority to clean up the mess.
The Restoration of Public Credit
By the end of 1721, the immediate crisis was over. The stock of the South Sea Company was reduced to manageable proportions. The Bank of England and the East India Company had absorbed the ingrafted stock. The directors had been punished, their estates confiscated, and the public’s anger — at least the most dangerous edge of it — had been satisfied.
The long-term consequences were more ambiguous. The Bubble discredited the very idea of joint-stock companies and public debt conversion schemes for a generation. The Bubble Act of 1720, which restricted the formation of joint-stock companies without a royal charter, was passed in the aftermath and remained law until 1825. But it also entrenched the Whig oligarchy. The crisis had demonstrated that the financial system — the Bank, the East India Company, the funded debt — was too important to be left to speculators and projectors. It needed management by men of substance, of property, of parliamentary weight. It needed Robert Walpole.

“Mr. Walpole, now paymaster of the forces, observed, that such a method would protract the inquiry, while the public credit lay in a bleeding condition. He told the house he had formed a scheme for restoring public credit.” — Smollett, Complete History of England, Vol. X

Key Figures
Sir John Blunt (1665–1733)
The projector of the South Sea Scheme. A former scrivener turned financier, Blunt was the driving force behind the Company’s operations. Smollett describes him as a man of “moderate talents” who nevertheless “was able to impose upon the whole nation, and make tools of the other directors, to serve his own purposes.” He was responsible for the fictitious stock distributions, the bribery of politicians, and the manipulation of the stock price. Arrested, his estate confiscated, he died in obscurity.
Charles Spencer, 3rd Earl of Sunderland (1675–1722)
First Lord of the Treasury and the King’s chief minister in England during George I’s frequent absences in Hanover. Sunderland was deeply implicated in the South Sea corruption — the committee of secrecy found that £50,000 in stock had been taken for his use by the cashier Knight. He was acquitted in the Commons by a narrow majority, but his reputation was destroyed. He resigned the Treasury to Robert Walpole in April 1721 and died the following year.
John Aislabie (1670–1742)
Chancellor of the Exchequer and a leading figure in the passage of the South Sea Act. Aislabie was the highest-ranking minister to be directly convicted. He was expelled from the House of Commons, committed to the Tower of London, and his estate forfeited. He retired to his Yorkshire estate, where he devoted himself to landscape gardening at Studley Royal.
Robert Walpole (1676–1745)
Paymaster of the Forces at the time of the crisis; First Lord of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer from April 1721. Walpole’s role in the South Sea affair was masterfully ambiguous: he had profited from stock dealings but had not been a director nor involved in the passage of the Act. His ingraftment scheme restored public credit, his parliamentary management secured the necessary legislation, and his refusal to pursue Sunderland to a fatal conclusion displayed both magnanimity and calculation. The crisis made him the indispensable man of the age.
James Craggs the Elder (1657–1721)
Postmaster-General and a principal conduit for the distribution of fictitious stock. He died of lethargy in February 1721 before the House could censure him, but the Commons resolved that he was “a notorious accomplice” with Knight and the directors, and ordered his entire estate from December 1720 to be applied to the relief of the sufferers.
James Craggs the Younger (1686–1721)
Secretary of State, son of the above. One of the most promising younger Whig politicians, Craggs died of smallpox on 16 February 1721 — cutting short a career that might have rivalled Walpole’s. His involvement in the South Sea corruption was less deep than his father’s, but the committee’s discoveries would likely have destroyed him politically had he lived.
George I (1660–1727)
King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1714. George was in Hanover for much of the crisis, leaving the ministry under Sunderland’s direction. The King’s German mistresses — particularly the Duchess of Kendal and the Countess of Platen — were among the chief recipients of South Sea bribes, a fact that tainted the court but which the inquiry did not press. George returned in November 1720, opened Parliament in December, and accepted the political destruction of his first ministry. His appointment of Walpole in 1721 was the most important decision of his reign.
Timeline of the South Sea Bubble (1720)





























































































MonthEventJan 1720South Sea Bill introduced in Parliament; stock at £128Feb 1720Bill passes Commons by large majority7 Apr 1720South Sea Act receives royal assent; stock at ~£300Apr–May 1720First and second money subscriptions; stock rises to ~£700May 1720King issues proclamation against bubble companies; flood of ~100 speculative schemesJun 1720South Sea stock peaks at £1,050Jul 1720Insiders begin selling; third subscription opensAug 1720Stock falling; Bank of England agreement to support at 400%8 Sep 1720Stock begins to fall decisively29 Sep 1720Stock collapses to £150; goldsmiths and bankers failSep–Oct 1720Bank of England renounces support agreement; Sword-Blade Company fails; run on the Bank11 Nov 1720George I returns from Hanover8 Dec 1720Parliament meets; King’s speech on restoration of creditDec 1720Walpole proposes his ingraftment scheme; Committee of Secrecy appointedJan 1721Directors arrested; Aislabie resigns; Aislabie expelled and committed to the Tower5 Feb 1721Earl Stanhope dies of apoplexy after violent debate in the Lords16 Feb 1721James Craggs the younger dies of smallpoxFeb–Mar 1721Sunderland acquitted in Commons but resigns; Walpole becomes First LordApr 1721Walpole appointed First Lord of the Treasury and Chancellor of the ExchequerJul 1721South Sea relief bill passed; directors’ estates confiscated1721–1722Restoration of credit; Walpole’s ingraftment scheme takes effect
Legacy
The South Sea Bubble stands as the archetypal financial mania in English history — the original cautionary tale of speculative excess, systemic corruption, and the entanglement of high finance and high politics. It destroyed one ministry and created another. It ruined thousands of families and laid the foundations of the Walpole system that governed Britain for two decades.
The Bubble left a permanent mark on British law and institutions. The Bubble Act 1720 (6 Geo. I, c. 18) restricted the formation of joint-stock companies and was not repealed until 1825. The scandal entrenched the practice of parliamentary inquiries into financial misconduct. And the disaster — unfolding simultaneously with John Law’s Mississippi Scheme in France — demonstrated to a generation of European statesmen and investors the catastrophic risks of debt conversion schemes that depended on rising stock prices.
In the longer arc of British history, the South Sea Bubble was the crucible in which the modern fiscal-military state was tested and strengthened. The Bank of England, the East India Company, and the funded national debt all survived the crisis — indeed, emerged from it more robust, having demonstrated their capacity to withstand the worst that speculation could inflict. The system proved more resilient than the men who had tried to game it.

events/stamp-act-crisis-1765.title: Stamp Act Crisis (1765–1766)
events/stamp-act-crisis-1765.content:
Stamp Act Crisis (1765–1766)
The Stamp Act Crisis (1765–1766) was the first great constitutional confrontation between Great Britain and its American colonies, arising from Parliament’s attempt to impose a direct tax on the colonies to help service the enormous national debt incurred during the Seven Years’ War. The crisis pitted the British doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty — the claim that Parliament could legislate for the colonies “in all cases whatsoever” — against the colonial claim that there could be “no taxation without representation.” It produced the Stamp Act Congress, the first coordinated inter-colonial protest, wide-scale civil disobedience and mob violence, a crippling non-importation movement, and ultimately the repeal of the Act — but only after Parliament had asserted its absolute authority in the Declaratory Act. The crisis settled nothing about the fundamental constitutional question of colonial representation, and it established the framework of arguments that would lead, within a decade, to the American Revolution.
Background: The Debt of Empire
The Seven Years’ War (1756–1763) had been, from the British perspective, a war of unparalleled success. By the Peace of Paris (1763), Great Britain had expelled France from Canada, secured Florida from Spain, established unchallengeable supremacy in India, and won a naval dominance that no European power could contest. But the cost of victory was staggering. Britain’s national debt had risen from approximately £72 million in 1754 to £133 million by 1763 — a sum so vast that the annual interest payment alone consumed more than half of the government’s peacetime revenue. Belsham records that the Annual Register of 1763 described this burden as “a debt which, in the ordinary course of affairs, could never be discharged.”1
The British taxpayer, already the most heavily taxed in Europe, could bear no further impositions. Parliament’s attention therefore turned to the American colonies, which had benefited from the war’s enormous expenditure — much of it spent in America itself for troop pay, provisions, and logistics — and which, it was argued, now enjoyed the protection of British arms without contributing proportionately to their cost. The colonies, far from a drain on the treasury, were in fact immensely profitable: Belsham notes that the profits to Great Britain from the trade of the colonies amounted to “two millions per annum,” and that this was “the fund which carried you triumphantly through the last war.”2 But George Grenville, who became First Lord of the Treasury in April 1763 upon the resignation of the Earl of Bute, was determined to make the colonies pay directly into the exchequer.
Grenville had already taken a first step in 1764 with the Sugar Act (the American Duties Act), which reduced the duty on foreign molasses imported into the colonies from sixpence to threepence per gallon — but added new enforcement mechanisms, gave the Admiralty courts jurisdiction over smuggling cases, and was clearly intended as a revenue measure rather than a regulation of trade. The colonies protested vigorously, but the Act passed with little parliamentary opposition.
In March 1764, Grenville announced in the House of Commons that he would propose a stamp tax on the colonies in the following session, giving the Americans a year to propose alternative means of raising revenue. None were forthcoming. When Parliament reconvened in January 1765, Grenville proceeded with his plan.
The Stamp Act
The Stamp Act was introduced in the House of Commons in February 1765 and passed on 22 March 1765, to take effect on 1 November 1765. It imposed a tax on virtually every piece of paper used in the American colonies: legal documents (deeds, mortgages, wills, contracts), newspapers, pamphlets, almanacks, licences, ship’s papers, playing cards, and dice. All such papers were required to bear a revenue stamp, purchased from official distributors appointed by the British government.
The declared purpose was, in the language of the Act, “raising a revenue in America in aid to the mother country.” Opposition in Parliament was “weak in respect to numbers,” Belsham records, but “unusually ardent and animated.”3 General Henry Conway protested against the right; Colonel Isaac Barré delivered a devastating reply to Charles Townshend’s claim that the Americans were “children planted by our care, and nourished by our indulgence”:

“They planted by your care! No — your oppressions planted them in America… They nourished by your indulgence! No — they grew by your neglect of them.”4

Barré’s speech — in which he first used the phrase “Sons of Liberty” to describe the American colonists — was widely circulated in America and contributed powerfully to the rising mood of resistance. But it could not stop the Act, which passed with comfortable majorities in both Houses and received the royal assent without controversy.
The Act was, in Belsham’s scathing judgment, a hideous specimen of despotism. The practical difficulties of enforcing it in a thinly settled continent were immense: in many parts of America, the cost of obtaining the necessary stamps from the distributors was said to be “tenfold the amount of the duty.” The Act permitted prosecutors to bring actions against supposed delinquents in courts more than fifteen hundred miles from where the alleged offence had been committed, while defendants who prevailed could recover no damages if the judge certified a probable foundation for the prosecution. The judge himself had a direct financial interest in conviction, being “allowed a large proportion of the penalty in case of conviction.”5

“Well might it be asked, whether the most abject vassals of the most tyrannic Government would passively submit to so humiliating a yoke!” — William Belsham6

Colonial Reaction
The Virginia Resolves
The news of the Stamp Act reached America in the spring of 1765. The first organised protest came from the Virginia House of Burgesses, where a young and relatively obscure member named Patrick Henry introduced a set of resolutions — the Virginia Resolves — in May 1765. Henry’s resolves declared that the colonists possessed all the rights of Englishmen, that the right of taxation was vested solely in the colonial assemblies, and that any attempt to vest that power elsewhere was a threat to colonial liberties. The most radical of the resolutions — which asserted that the General Assembly of Virginia had “the only and sole exclusive right and power to lay taxes and impositions upon the inhabitants of this colony” — passed by a single vote.
The Virginia Resolves were published in newspapers throughout the colonies, often with additional resolutions appended that were more extreme than anything Henry had actually proposed. They electrified the colonial resistance and set the pattern for similar declarations from other colonial assemblies. Belsham notes that the Provincial Assemblies, “far from taking any effectual measures to enforce submission to the act, passed resolutions in opposition to it, declaratory of their constitutional and unalienable rights.”7
The Loyal Nine and the Sons of Liberty
In Boston, resistance took a more direct and menacing form. A secret society called the Loyal Nine — artisans, merchants, and tradesmen — organised public protests against the Stamp Act. On the morning of 14 August 1765, an effigy of Andrew Oliver, the Massachusetts stamp distributor, was found hanging from a large elm tree on the Boston Common — the tree that would become famous as the Liberty Tree. That evening, a mob stormed Oliver’s office, demolished his building, and hanged his effigy. Oliver resigned his commission the next day.
On the night of 26 August, the violence escalated. A mob attacked the homes of William Story, Deputy Register of the Vice-Admiralty Court, and Benjamin Hallowell, the Comptroller of Customs. They then turned on the house of Thomas Hutchinson, the Lieutenant-Governor and Chief Justice of Massachusetts — a man who had privately opposed the Stamp Act but was determined to enforce the law. The mob gutted Hutchinson’s mansion, destroyed his furniture, scattered his papers and manuscript history of Massachusetts, and carried off his money and plate. Hutchinson barely escaped with his life.
The Loyal Nine evolved into the Sons of Liberty, a network of resistance organisations that would coordinate colonial opposition over the next decade. Similar disturbances broke out in cities from Portsmouth, New Hampshire, to Charleston, South Carolina.
The General Attack on the Stamp Distributors
Throughout the colonies, the appointed stamp distributors were forced to resign. Those who declined to resign faced mob violence. In New York, the stamp distributor James McEvers resigned within weeks of receiving his commission. In Rhode Island, the stamps were stored in a fortress but never distributed. In Maryland, the distributor was rescued from a mob by the sheriff and promptly resigned. Belsham records the scene:

“Those who had accepted commissions to act as distributors of stamps, were forced by public oath to renounce all concern in them at this or any future juncture; and in some instances the houses of those who were most obnoxious were demolished, and their effects plundered or destroyed.”8

The justices of the peace in many parts gave public notice “that they would never, by acting in that capacity, be instrumental to the subversion of their country’s liberties.” The gentlemen of the law, “fired by the same patriotic enthusiasm, universally renounced, in the exercise of their profession, the use of the British stamps.”9
The Stamp Act Congress
By the autumn of 1765, the colonial response had moved from spontaneous violence to organised political resistance. At the invitation of the Massachusetts House of Representatives, delegates from nine colonies — Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, and South Carolina — assembled in New York City in October 1765. This was the Stamp Act Congress, the first inter-colonial meeting ever convened in America.
The Congress met from 7 to 25 October 1765 at City Hall in New York. After extended debate — the more conservative delegates from the middle colonies restraining the fiercer spirits from Massachusetts and Virginia — the Congress adopted a Declaration of Rights and Grievances, composed of fourteen resolutions drafted largely by John Dickinson of Pennsylvania. The Declaration affirmed the colonists’ allegiance to the Crown and their “all due subordination” to Parliament, but insisted that the colonists possessed all the rights of Englishmen, that the right of taxation could only be exercised by representatives chosen by the people, and that trial by jury was a fundamental right that could not be infringed. Belsham records that the delegates “unanimously concurred in framing and publishing a sort of manifesto expressive of their grievances.”10
The Congress also petitioned the King and both Houses of Parliament for the repeal of the Stamp Act and the other revenue measures of the Grenville ministry.
Non-Importation and Economic Resistance
The most potent weapon of colonial resistance proved to be economic. In October 1765, merchants in New York City agreed to stop importing British goods until the Stamp Act was repealed. By December, merchants in Boston, Philadelphia, and other major ports had followed suit. The agreements were enforced by the Sons of Liberty, who published the names of merchants who continued to import British goods and, in some cases, intimidated them into compliance.
The effect on British trade was immediate and devastating. Belsham records that “the most alarming opposition was made by the merchants, who entered into solemn engagements not to import any more goods from Great Britain till the Stamp Act was repealed.”11 British exports to the colonies, which had been worth over £2 million annually, fell sharply. Petitions from the principal commercial cities of the kingdom — London, Bristol, Liverpool, Glasgow — began to pour into the House of Commons, demanding repeal.
By 1 November 1765, the date on which the Act was to take effect, “not a sheet of stamped paper was to be found throughout the Colonies; so that all business which could not be legally carried on without stamps was entirely at a stand.” Everywhere, “the courts of justice were shut, and the ports closed.”12 In Boston, the ships in the harbour hung out their colours half-mast high as a signal of deepest distress; the bells of the churches throughout the city, “being muffled, rang out a dumb peal.” The Act itself, as soon as it came from the King’s printing-house, “was burnt by the populace, with the effigies of the men most active in passing it.”13
The British Debate
The Fall of Grenville
The news of the American disturbances reached London in the autumn of 1765. By that time, however, the political landscape in Britain had changed. George III, who had endured months of Grenville’s lecturing and condescension — the minister treated the King, Belsham suggests, with something approaching insolence — had dismissed Grenville in July 1765 after the minister demanded the removal of all officials connected with the Earl of Bute. The King turned to the Marquis of Rockingham, a young Whig grandee of thirty-five, to form a ministry.
Rockingham’s ministry was composed of the great Whig families — the Cavendishes, the Bentincks, the Watsons-Wentworths — who had been excluded from power since the fall of the Duke of Newcastle. It was a ministry of amateurs and idealists, held together by the conviction that the Grenville system of American taxation was a disastrous mistake. The guiding intellectual force of the ministry was Edmund Burke, a young Irishman of dazzling abilities who served as Rockingham’s private secretary and who would become the great philosopher of the Whig party.
The Great Debates of 1766
Parliament convened on 14 January 1766, and the Stamp Act crisis immediately dominated its proceedings. The King’s speech expressed “firm confidence in their wisdom and zeal” to find resolutions that would “at once preserve the constitutional rights of the British Legislature over the Colonies, and to restore to them that harmony and tranquillity which have lately been interrupted by disorders of the most dangerous nature.”14
The great debate opened in the House of Commons when William Pitt the Elder — who had been absent from Parliament during the passage of the Stamp Act, lying ill in bed — rose to speak. His speech was the most celebrated of the entire crisis. He denounced every capital measure taken by the late ministry as entirely wrong, declared that Parliament had “NO RIGHT to lay a tax upon the Colonies,” and drew a sharp distinction between Parliament’s sovereign authority over commerce and legislation and its lack of authority over internal taxation:

“Taxation is no part of the governing or legislative power; the taxes are a voluntary gift and grant of the Commons alone… When in this House we give and grant, therefore, we give and grant what is our own; but can we give and grant the property of the Commons of America? It is an absurdity in terms. There is an idea in some, that the Colonies are virtually represented in this House. I would fain know by whom? The idea of virtual representation is the most contemptible that ever entered into the head of a man: it does not deserve a serious refutation.”15

Pitt went further: he defended the American resistance itself:

“Sir, I REJOICE that America has resisted; three millions of people so dead to all the feelings of liberty, as voluntarily to submit to be slaves, would have been fit instruments to make slaves of all the rest.”16

He concluded with a peroration that echoes through English constitutional history:

“It is my opinion, ‘That the Stamp Act be repealed ABSOLUTELY, TOTALLY, and IMMEDIATELY.‘”17

Grenville rose in reply, defending his measure with “all the systematic obstinacy of a sincere but cloudy and narrow mind.” He argued that taxation was “a branch of the sovereign power” that had been exercised over those who were never represented — the East India Company, chartered corporations, the Palatinate of Chester and the Bishopric of Durham before they sent representatives to Parliament. He warned that the American tumults bordered on rebellion and that if Pitt’s doctrines were confirmed, the colonists “would lose this name to take that of revolution.” He concluded with a bitter indictment of American ingratitude:

“The nation has run itself into an immense debt to give them protection; bounties have been extended to them… and now they are called upon to contribute a small share towards the public expence, they renounce your authority, insult your officers, and break out, I might almost say, into open rebellion.”18

Pitt, “fired with disdain and resentment,” immediately rose to reply. He was called to order by Lord Strange for speaking twice — but the House, crying “Go on,” allowed him to continue. He denounced Grenville’s accusation that gentlemen in the House had given birth to sedition in America: “The freedom with which they have spoken their sentiments against this unhappy Act, is imputed to them as a crime; but the imputation shall not discourage me.” He declared that Grenville “ought to have desisted from his project” and that the true blame lay with the minister who had passed the Act, not with those who now opposed it.19
Between Pitt’s absolute denial of Parliament’s right to tax and Grenville’s claim of unlimited parliamentary sovereignty, a middle ground was carved by the Marquis of Rockingham and his ministry. Rockingham’s position — the position that ultimately prevailed — was that the Stamp Act should be repealed as a matter of policy and prudence, while Parliament’s ultimate sovereignty over the colonies should be affirmed in the strongest possible terms. This was the logic of the Declaratory Act.
The petitions from the commercial cities were laid before Parliament. The late ministers and their partisans, Belsham records, “falsely and ridiculously represented” these petitions as “the effects of ministerial artifice,” exclaiming that “the distress of the mercantile part of the community be however what it may, it ought to be submitted to, rather than by a repeal of the act to hazard the total loss of the just superiority of Great Britain over the Colonies.”20
The Repeal and the Declaratory Act
After months of fierce debate, the Rockingham ministry carried the day. A bill for the repeal of the Stamp Act was brought in and, “after very vehement opposition,” passed both Houses by considerable majorities, receiving the royal assent on 18 March 1766.
But on the same day, Parliament passed the Declaratory Act — a measure that, in retrospect, was far more significant than the repeal itself. The Act declared that Parliament “had, hath, and of right ought to have, full power and authority to make laws and statutes of sufficient force and validity to bind the colonies and people of America, subjects of the crown of Great Britain, in all cases whatsoever.”
The conjunction of repeal and declaratory assertion was the essence of the Rockingham compromise: withdraw the offensive measure, but assert the principle on which it rested. Belsham’s judgment on the Declaratory Act is subtle:

“The Declaratory Act, however theoretically disputable, served to display their solicitude to sustain the honor of the nation.”21

The joy in America on receiving news of the repeal was extreme. Belsham records that the colonies were largely untroubled by the Declaratory Act: the mere declaration of “an abstract right, which they imagined to be with respect to the claim of taxation in fact relinquished, and which seemed chiefly intended as a salvo for the honor of Parliament, gave them little apprehension or uneasiness.”22 It was only years later, after a long series of vexations and encroachments on their established privileges, that the Assembly of Massachusetts formally voted the Declaratory Act to be a grievance.
The repeal was accompanied by a circular letter from Henry Seymour Conway, the Secretary of State, to the colonial governors, written “in that firm and temperate style which was at once calculated to maintain the honor of Government, and to appease the discontents and apprehensions of the People.” Conway particularly insisted that full compensation be made to those “who, from the madness of the people, have suffered for their deference to the Acts of the British Legislature.”23
Key Figures
George III (1738–1820)
King of Great Britain and Ireland. George III had supported Grenville’s American policy and believed the colonies ought to contribute to the costs of empire. He assented to the repeal reluctantly — his private conviction was that the Stamp Act was a legitimate exercise of parliamentary authority and that repeal would be seen as weakness. His personal relations with Grenville had soured badly by July 1765, but his reservations about Rockingham were almost equally strong: the new ministry contained too many of the old Whig families he distrusted. The King’s consistent position throughout the crisis was that Parliament’s authority over the colonies was absolute — a position he would maintain for the rest of his reign.
George Grenville (1712–1770)
Prime Minister from 1763 to 1765 and the author of the Stamp Act. Grenville was a man of “a sincere but cloudy and narrow mind” — an able administrator who was nevertheless “utterly destitute of those commanding talents” required of a first minister.24 His Stamp Act was, in Belsham’s judgment, the product of a narrow fiscal logic that took no account of the constitutional sensibilities it would affront. Grenville never held office again after his dismissal in July 1765. He opposed the repeal in the 1766 debates, arguing with bitterness that it would be seen as a surrender, and spent his remaining years in impotent opposition.
William Pitt the Elder (1708–1778)
The great wartime leader, now in opposition, whose speeches in the 1766 repeal debates were among the most celebrated of his career. Pitt drew the sharpest constitutional line of any British statesman: Parliament had sovereign authority over the colonies in all matters of legislation and commerce, but it had no right to tax them. His distinction between internal and external taxation — however logically questionable — became the constitutional foundation on which the colonial case rested. His declaration that he “rejoiced” America had resisted became a watchword of the American cause. Pitt returned to office in July 1766 as Lord Privy Seal and Earl of Chatham, but his health was already failing, and his second ministry was a disaster.
Charles Watson-Wentworth, 2nd Marquis of Rockingham (1730–1782)
The young Whig nobleman who formed a ministry in July 1765 and carried the repeal of the Stamp Act. Rockingham was not a man of brilliant intellect — Edmund Burke called him “a man of great honour and integrity” but not of commanding abilities — but he had the good sense to surround himself with talented advisors. His ministry’s achievement was the repeal of the Stamp Act; its flaw was the Declaratory Act, which affirmed a principle that made future conflict inevitable. Rockingham fell from power in July 1766 when Pitt abandoned him.
Edmund Burke (1729–1797)
The Irish-born philosopher and politician who served as Rockingham’s private secretary during the crisis and who emerged, in the course of the Stamp Act debates, as the most powerful intellect in the Whig party. Burke’s thinking on America — developed fully in his later speeches and writings — was grounded in the conviction that the colonies should be governed by conciliation rather than coercion, and that Britain’s imperial authority rested ultimately on the consent of the governed. His influence on Rockingham’s policy was profound, though his greatest contributions lay ahead.
Patrick Henry (1736–1799)
The young Virginia lawyer and orator whose resolutions in the House of Burgesses in May 1765 inaugurated the colonial resistance to the Stamp Act. Henry’s speech — in which he is said to have cried “Caesar had his Brutus, Charles the First his Cromwell, and George the Third…” before being called to order, to which he replied “…may profit by their example” — became the founding legend of American revolutionary oratory.
Charles Townshend (1725–1767)
President of the Board of Trade under Grenville and later, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, the author of the Townshend Duties. In the 1766 debates, Townshend took a characteristically complex position: nominally supporting the Rockingham government’s policy of repeal, he made speeches that seemed to concede the Americans’ position while simultaneously embracing the claim of unlimited parliamentary sovereignty. His performances baffled friend and foe alike.
Henry Seymour Conway (1721–1795)
Secretary of State for the Southern Department in the Rockingham ministry. Conway had distinguished himself in the 1765 parliamentary debates by protesting alone against the passage of the Stamp Act. As Secretary of State, he oversaw the communication of the repeal to the colonies and drafted the conciliatory circular letter to the colonial governors. He was one of the few British statesmen of the era who consistently advocated a conciliatory policy toward America.
Significance
The Stamp Act Crisis was the pivotal moment in the disintegration of the first British Empire. It established the constitutional framework within which the American Revolution would be fought: Parliament claimed unlimited sovereignty; the colonies claimed that their assemblies were co-ordinate legislatures with exclusive authority over internal taxation. The crisis settled nothing.
The repeal, so joyfully received in America, was in fact the beginning of the tragedy. The Americans believed they had won a permanent concession on the principle of representation; the British believed they had, through the Declaratory Act, preserved the principle of sovereignty while tactically retreating on a particular measure. Both sides were wrong, and neither understood the position of the other. As Belsham observed, the repeal produced “all the happy and beneficial effects which had been previously expected or predicted” — but only temporarily. Within eighteen months, Charles Townshend would rekindle the crisis with a new set of duties, and the Declaratory Act would ensure that the ensuing conflict would be fought not over a particular tax but over the nature of the empire itself.25
Belsham, writing from the perspective of the 1790s, saw the Stamp Act crisis as the first step on a road that led inevitably to American independence. His judgment on Grenville is severe but revealing:

“Little, certainly, did this Minister imagine how fertile would be the invention of his successors in office, or how thoroughly subdued by time and custom the spirit of the people.”26

Key Events

events/treaty-of-aix-la-chapelle-1748.title: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748)
events/treaty-of-aix-la-chapelle-1748.content:
Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748)
The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, signed on 18 October 1748, was the peace settlement that ended the War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748). It was a treaty of status quo ante bellum — a mutual restitution of conquests that restored the pre-war territorial status quo while leaving the fundamental questions that had provoked the war entirely unresolved. Widely regarded even at the time as a truce rather than a final peace, the treaty satisfied none of the principal belligerents and set the stage for the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756 and the Seven Years’ War (1756–1763).
The negotiations were conducted at the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle (March–October 1748), with the Earl of Sandwich (John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich) and Sir Thomas Robinson acting as British plenipotentiaries, and the comte de Saint-Séverin representing France. The central bargain was a general restoration of all conquests — a solution that infuriated British colonists who had captured Louisbourg in 1745, gratified Frederick the Great who kept Silesia, and left Maria Theresa nursing a grievance that would reshape the alliances of Europe.
Background: The Exhaustion of the Combatants
By 1747, the War of the Austrian Succession had run for seven years with no decisive result. The war had expanded far beyond its original issue of Maria Theresa’s succession to the Habsburg dominions, embracing the separate conflicts of the War of Jenkins’ Ear (1739–1748) between Britain and Spain, the Jacobite Rising of 1745 in Britain, and the Italian campaigns of Spain and Austria.
The military situation on the continent was unfavourable to the allies. Marechal de Saxe, the greatest French commander of the age, had won a brilliant series of victories in Flanders — Fontenoy (1745), Raucoux (1746), and Lauffeld (1747) — and had overrun the Austrian Netherlands. The Duke of Cumberland, despite his victory at Culloden (1746), had proved no match for Saxe in open battle. By 1747, the French had penetrated into Dutch Brabant and Flanders, and the Dutch Republic was in real danger of invasion.
Yet France, too, was exhausted. The war had been ruinously expensive; the French navy had been driven from the seas; and the British blockade had crippled French commerce. Britain, for its part, had seen its Jacobite rebellion crushed, its continental campaigns stalled, and its colonial war in India produce mixed results — Madras had fallen to the French under La Bourdonnais in 1746, while Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island had been captured by New England colonial forces under William Pepperrell and Commodore Peter Warren in 1745.
Neither side could deliver a knockout blow, and both faced mounting domestic pressure for peace. In the winter of 1746–1747, Louis XV made direct and repeated advances of accommodation to the courts of London and The Hague.
The Congress at Aix-la-Chapelle (March–October 1748)
The congress opened in March 1748 at the free imperial city of Aix-la-Chapelle (modern Aachen). The chief negotiators were:

Earl of Sandwich (John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich) and Sir Thomas Robinson — British plenipotentiaries
Comte de Saint-Séverin (Alphonse Marie Louis, comte de Saint-Séverin d’Aragon) — French plenipotentiary
Count von Kaunitz (later prince) — Austrian representative, already laying the groundwork for his celebrated diplomatic revolution
Count Podewils — Prussian representative
The Marquess of Tablada — Spanish representative

While the diplomats deliberated, hostilities continued. Marechal de Saxe, in a final show of strength, invested the fortress of Maastricht in April 1748. The allies, under the Duke of Cumberland and the Prince of Waldeck, were unable to prevent the investment, and the fortress seemed doomed. But the preliminaries of peace were signed in the space of a few weeks, and a suspension of arms was agreed. Maastricht was preserved, largely through the skilful defence of the governor, Baron d’Alva, and the unexpected speed of the diplomatic resolution.
The negotiations proceeded with unusual rapidity by the standards of eighteenth-century diplomacy. The basis had been agreed in principle between Britain and France before the congress formally opened: a mutual restitution of conquests. The detailed terms were hammered out over the spring and summer of 1748, and the definitive treaty was signed on 18 October.
Terms of the Treaty
The treaty was a complex of bilateral instruments rather than a single document. The essential provisions are summarised below.
Summary of Terms





















































ProvisionDetailsMutual restitution of conquestsAll conquests made during the war, whether in Europe, the East Indies, or the Americas, were to be mutually restored. This was the central bargain.Louisbourg returned to FranceThe fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island, captured by New England forces in 1745 after a celebrated seven-week siege, was restored to France — the most controversial provision from the British perspective.Madras returned to BritainThe settlement of Madras on the Coromandel Coast of India, captured by the French under La Bourdonnais in September 1746, was restored to Britain in exchange for Louisbourg.Prussia confirmed in possession of SilesiaFrederick the Great was confirmed in his conquest of Silesia, along with the county of Glatz — the principal gain of the war for Prussia, secured at Maria Theresa’s expense.Parma, Piacenza, and Guastalla to Don PhilipThe Duchy of Parma (with Piacenza and Guastalla) was ceded to Don Philip, younger son of Philip V of Spain and Elisabeth Farnese, creating a new Bourbon state in northern Italy.Sardinia gainsThe Kingdom of Sardinia received portions of the Milanese, including Vigevano and other territories.Asiento renewedThe Asiento de Negros — the exclusive right to supply slaves to the Spanish American colonies — was renewed for four years, continuing the contract originally granted to Britain at the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) and administered by the South Sea Company.Restoration of the Duke of ModenaThe Duke of Modena, a French ally, was restored to his dominions.HostagesFrance required British hostages to reside in France pending the full execution of the mutual restitution of conquests. The Earls of Sussex and Cathcart were nominated for this purpose — a point seized upon by the opposition as humiliating.Boundary commissionsThe disputed boundaries between French and British territory in North America were referred to the decision of commissaries — a provision that effectively deferred the question to future conflict.Spanish grievances unmentionedThe original cause of the War of Jenkins’ Ear — the Spanish right of search and seizure on the high seas — was passed over in complete silence. Not a syllable was mentioned on the subject that had provoked such clamour in 1738–1739.
What the Treaty Did Not Settle

The boundaries of Nova Scotia and the Ohio Valley — a question referred to commissioners who never agreed
The right of search — the original casus belli of the Anglo-Spanish war
Maria Theresa’s claim to Silesia — she never recognised Frederick’s possession and resolved on revenge
The French and British claims in India — left to the rivalry of Dupleix and Robert Clive in the years that followed

The British Reaction: “The Peace Without Honour”
The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle was received in Britain with a mixture of relief and fury — relief from a war-weary nation that had borne crushing taxes, but fury from those who saw the terms as a betrayal of British and colonial sacrifice.
The most explosive grievance was the return of Louisbourg. The fortress on Cape Breton Island had been captured in 1745 by a volunteer force of New England militiamen under William Pepperrell, co-operating with Commodore Peter Warren of the Royal Navy. The siege had been a triumph of colonial enterprise — six thousand raw but determined provincials had taken one of the strongest fortresses in North America in a campaign of only eight weeks. The conquest was celebrated throughout the colonies and in Britain as proof of the rising importance of the American colonies.
The news that Louisbourg was to be handed back to France struck the New England colonies like a thunderbolt. The colonists felt, with bitter justice, that their blood and treasure had been thrown away. Belsham records that “the nation had reason to recollect the coarse but sagacious political adage of Hyde, Earl of Rochester, ‘that to attack France in Flanders was to take a bull by the horns.‘” The sacrifice of Cape Breton was the price of recovering Madras — a calculus that made strategic sense from London’s imperial perspective but carried no weight in the town halls of Boston and New England.
In Parliament, the opposition denounced the peace as “disgraceful to the nation.” The requirement that British hostages reside in France gave the patriots a particular handle for attack. Yet the nation at large, Belsham notes, “who were with reason wearied with the expenses and disasters of the war, were well satisfied with the terms of the peace, and it was celebrated with great and universal rejoicings.” The judgment was divided between popular relief and colonial outrage — a division that would deepen as the century progressed.
The Treaty as a Truce: Significance and Legacy
The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle has been described by almost every historian who has examined it as a truce masquerading as a peace. The status quo ante bellum formula restored the territorial map of 1740 with two decisive exceptions: Silesia remained in Prussian hands, and Parma passed to the Spanish Bourbons. But it settled nothing.
For Britain, the treaty was a disappointment. The colonial question in North America — the boundaries of Nova Scotia, the Ohio Valley, the hinterland of the French and British possessions — was left to commissioners who never resolved it. The war with Spain had produced no mention of the right of search. The capture of Louisbourg had been thrown away. The peace was bought at the price of returning a fortress that would prove enormously costly to retake (it fell again to Edward Boscawen and James Wolfe in 1758). The interval between Aix-la-Chapelle and the outbreak of the Seven Years’ War in 1756 was not a period of genuine peace but of armed truce, during which both Britain and France prepared for a renewal of the struggle they knew was inevitable.
For Austria, the treaty was a humiliation. Maria Theresa had lost Silesia, the richest province of the Habsburg monarchy, and received nothing in exchange. She emerged from the congress with a burning determination to recover her lost territory and a cold recognition that Britain — her traditional ally — was an unreliable partner. Her great minister, Count von Kaunitz (later Prince Kaunitz), who represented Austria at the congress, had already begun the diplomatic work that would produce the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756 — the reversal of alliances by which Austria abandoned Britain and allied with her ancient enemy France.
For Prussia, the treaty was a triumph. Frederick the Great was confirmed in the possession of Silesia, the conquest that had begun the war and that would remain the foundation of Prussian power. The treaty gave Frederick a breathing-space to consolidate his new province, drill his army, and prepare for the next round — which he knew would come when Austria had found a new ally.
For France, the treaty was a missed opportunity. Marechal de Saxe had given France military dominance in Flanders, yet the negotiators gave back all the conquered territory. The French court was divided between the war party, which wanted to press the advantage, and the peace party, led by Madame de Pompadour and the finance minister, which recognised that France could not afford to continue. The result satisfied no one and left France with the worst of both worlds: the resentment of maintaining a vast war establishment without territorial gain.
For Spain, the treaty was a modest success: the Asiento was renewed, and Don Philip received the rich duchy of Parma, satisfying Elisabeth Farnese’s long-standing ambition to establish her younger sons in Italian states.
The Diplomatic Revolution
The discontent of the principal powers created the conditions for the most dramatic realignment in eighteenth-century European diplomacy. Maria Theresa, deeply alienated from Britain, which she felt had abandoned her at Aix-la-Chapelle, authorised Kaunitz to pursue a rapprochement with France. Kaunitz’s diplomacy, conducted with extraordinary patience and secrecy, culminated in the Treaty of Westminster (January 1756) between Britain and Prussia — a defensive convention that astonished Europe — and the First Treaty of Versailles (May 1756) between France and Austria, reversing the alliances that had endured for nearly two centuries. The Seven Years’ War (1756–1763) that followed was, in large part, the war that Aix-la-Chapelle had failed to prevent.
Key Figures
George II
King of Great Britain and Ireland, and Elector of Hanover. George II had commanded personally at the Battle of Dettingen (1743), the last British monarch to lead troops in battle. By 1748, he was weary of war and eager for peace, though he shared his subjects’ dismay at the return of Louisbourg. His attachment to his Hanoverian electoral interests had been a persistent source of political controversy throughout the war.
Earl of Sandwich (John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich, 1718–1792)
British plenipotentiary at Aix-la-Chapelle and a rising figure in the Pelham ministry. Sandwich had already distinguished himself as a naval administrator and diplomat. At Aix-la-Chapelle, he steered the British negotiation through the complexities of the mutual restitution clause and the exchange of Louisbourg for Madras. He later served as First Lord of the Admiralty during the Seven Years’ War and again during the American Revolutionary War. His name would become synonymous with the food-item he was said to have invented to sustain himself at the gaming table.
Sir Thomas Robinson (1695–1770)
British co-plenipotentiary and a career diplomat who had served as ambassador to Vienna during the early years of the war. Robinson was a capable but unspectacular negotiator; his greatest fame came later when, as Secretary of State, he proved unequal to the parliamentary rough-and-tumble and was famously destroyed in debate by William Pitt the Elder.
Comte de Saint-Séverin (Alphonse Marie Louis, comte de Saint-Séverin d’Aragon, 1705–1757)
The chief French negotiator. Saint-Séverin was a skilled diplomat who extracted the maximum advantage from France’s strong military position. He secured the return of Louisbourg and preserved the French position in North America, but could not persuade his government to retain the Austrian Netherlands — a territorial prize that would have fundamentally altered the European balance.
Maria Theresa (1717–1780)
Empress-Queen of Hungary and Bohemia. The War of the Austrian Succession had begun with the challenge to her succession; it ended with her confirmed on her thrones but stripped of Silesia. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle left her with a bitter sense of betrayal by Britain and a cold determination to recover her losses. Her resentment set the stage for the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756 and the great reform of the Habsburg monarchy that she and Kaunitz carried out in the following decade.
Frederick the Great (1712–1786)
King of Prussia, who had seized Silesia in December 1740 and defended it through three hard-fought wars. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle confirmed his conquest — the single most important territorial gain of the war. Frederick spent the peace years consolidating his new province, building the palace of Sanssouci, and preparing the Prussian army for what he correctly anticipated would be a renewed struggle with Austria. He was the only major sovereign to emerge from the treaty entirely satisfied.
Duke of Cumberland (William Augustus, Duke of Cumberland, 1721–1765)
Captain-General of the British army, hero of Culloden, but thoroughly outgeneralled by Marechal de Saxe in Flanders. His inability to prevent Saxe’s conquest of the Austrian Netherlands was one reason the allies could not negotiate from strength at Aix-la-Chapelle.
Count (later Prince) von Kaunitz (1711–1794)
Austrian plenipotentiary at the congress, already the architect of the diplomatic strategy that would produce the Franco-Austrian alliance. Kaunitz’s reading of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle was coldly realistic: Britain would not fight for Silesia, and only France could help Austria recover it. His embassy to Paris (1750–1753) and his subsequent direction of Austrian policy produced the diplomatic revolution that reshaped Europe.
Cross-References
