Related people: Queen Anne, Robert Harley, Henry St John Bolingbroke, Marlborough, George Rooke, Duke of Ormond, Prince Eugene of Savoy, Marshal Villars, George I
Related places: Gibraltar, Minorca, Port Mahon, Dunkirk, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Hudson’s Bay, Utrecht
Related institutions: South Sea Company, House of Hanover, House of Bourbon, House of Habsburg
Related documents: Act of Settlement (1701), Barrier Treaty (1709/1713), Treaty of Ryswick (1697), Treaty of the Pyrenees (1659)

events/war-of-jenkins-ear-1739.title: War of Jenkins' Ear & Capture of Porto Bello (1739)
events/war-of-jenkins-ear-1739.content:
War of Jenkins’ Ear & Capture of Porto Bello (1739)
The War of Jenkins’ Ear (1739–1748) was a conflict between Great Britain and Spain that originated in long-standing commercial disputes in the West Indies and was triggered by a notorious incident of Spanish brutality against a British merchant captain. The war is best remembered for Admiral Edward Vernon’s stunning capture of Porto Bello (modern Portobelo, Panama) in November 1739 with only six ships — an achievement that made him the most popular man in Britain and gave London one of its most famous street names. The war would soon merge into the wider War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748) and produce, in its turn, the disastrous Cartagena expedition of 1741.
Background: Spanish Depredations in the West Indies
The Treaty of Utrecht (1713), which ended the War of the Spanish Succession, had granted Britain the asiento — the exclusive right to supply slaves to Spanish America — together with permission to send one annual trading ship (navío de permiso) to the Spanish colonies. These concessions were the source of endless friction. British merchants exploited them as a cover for widespread contraband trade, while the Spanish authorities responded with increasingly aggressive enforcement.
The instrument of Spanish enforcement was the Guarda Costas — armed vessels commissioned by the Spanish colonial authorities to patrol the coasts of the West Indies and the Spanish Main, intercepting smugglers and searching British merchant ships for contraband. In practice, the Guarda Costas operated with little restraint. According to John Campbell’s Lives of the British Admirals, they “boarded and plundered every English ship they met, under a pretence of searching for contraband goods” and “seized several English vessels, confiscated their cargoes, and threw the sailors into prison” (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 431). The British government received a constant stream of petitions and complaints from merchants, ship-owners, and sailors who had been abused in the Caribbean.
As early as March 1731, “several masters and sailors of merchant-ships, who had been taken by the Spanish Guarda Costas, came to London to give an account to parliament of the cruel treatment they had received from the Spaniards” (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 430). The House of Commons addressed the King in 1733 demanding satisfaction, and though some minor reparations were made — one Guarda Costa was sold at Santiago de Cuba and the proceeds paid to the South Sea Company factors — the underlying problem persisted. The Spanish authorities, moreover, began to dispute Britain’s right to cut logwood in the Bay of Campeachy or gather salt on the island of Tortugas, adding territorial grievances to the catalogue of commercial disputes.
The Jenkins’ Ear Incident (1731)
The single incident that inflamed British public opinion above all others occurred in 1731, though it did not become a political cause célèbre until 1738. Captain Robert Jenkins, master of the Scottish merchant vessel Rebecca, was stopped in the West Indies by a Spanish Guarda Costa. The Spanish boarding party, suspecting him of smuggling, subjected him to a brutal search. According to the account later presented to Parliament, the Spaniards tore off one of Jenkins’s ears, declaring they would do the same to his king. They then tortured him with “wanton inhumanity” and threatened him with instant death (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 432).
Jenkins preserved his severed ear and, seven years later, in 1738, appeared before a committee of the House of Commons to give evidence. He stood at the bar of the House holding his ear in his hand. When a member asked him what his thoughts were while in the hands of the Spaniards, he replied: “I recommended my soul to God, and my cause to my country.” This dramatic answer, reported and reprinted across the country, produced a sensation. The incident became a symbol of Spanish insolence and cruelty, and the cry for war became irresistible.
Public Clamour and Walpole’s Reluctance
Throughout the 1730s, the government of Sir Robert Walpole had pursued a consistent policy of peace. Walpole, Britain’s first and longest-serving Prime Minister (1721–1742), believed that war was ruinous to trade and to the public finances that his entire system of government depended upon. He had maintained peace with Spain through a series of diplomatic expedients — the Treaty of Seville (1729) and the Convention of El Pardo (1739) — the latter of which provided for Spanish payment of £95,000 in compensation for captured British ships.
But by 1738, the public mood had turned decisively against Walpole. The opposition, led by William Pitt the Elder, Lord Carteret, and the “Patriot” faction, used the Jenkins’ Ear incident to rally the country. Petitions poured into Parliament from merchants and maritime communities. The press, including The Craftsman and other opposition journals, fanned the flames. “The nation in general was too much exasperated to afford any hopes of preventing a war with Spain” (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 432). Even as Walpole secured a majority in Parliament against the most bellicose motions, he could not contain public fury.
The turning point came when the Spanish government failed to make the payments stipulated by the Convention of El Pardo. Lord Carteret moved in the Lords that this failure was “a high indignity to the king, and an injustice to the nation.” Though the motion was lost, the damage was done. Walpole, against his better judgment, was forced to yield. Letters of marque and reprisal were issued against Spanish shipping; the army was augmented; an embargo was laid on outward-bound vessels; and a fleet was assembled at Spithead. By the summer of 1739, Britain was effectively at war, even before the formal declaration.
The Declaration of War (October 1739)
On 23 October 1739, Great Britain formally declared war against Spain. The British navy at that time had eighty-four men-of-war in commission, with another thirty-two ready to be fitted out. The entire Spanish navy numbered only thirty-three ships of war, including the flota merchant vessels (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 432). The disparity in naval power was enormous, and the British public expected swift and decisive results.
Vernon’s Expedition
Among the most vocal proponents of war in the House of Commons was Edward Vernon, a blunt-speaking naval officer and MP for Ipswich. Vernon had served in the West Indies and knew the Spanish Caribbean intimately. In a parliamentary debate on Spanish depredations, he declared — with characteristic bravado — that he could take the fortified Spanish port of Porto Bello on the Isthmus of Darien with six ships only.
The boast was seized upon by the opposition, who echoed it through the country. Walpole, perhaps hoping to remove a troublesome critic from the Commons, appointed Vernon to command the West Indies squadron and gave him the opportunity to make good his word. There was a suspicion, recorded even by contemporary historians, that the ministry was “not without hopes that the admiral might disgrace himself and his party by not succeeding in the adventure” (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 433).
Vernon sailed from England on 20 July 1739 with nine men-of-war. He arrived at Port Royal, Jamaica, on 23 October — the very day war was proclaimed in England. Upon arrival he had the satisfaction of seeing the Diamond man-of-war standing into harbour with two Spanish prizes, one a register ship carrying 120,000 pieces of eight and clothing for 6,000 men.
The Capture of Porto Bello (21–22 November 1739)
Vernon sailed from Jamaica on 5 November with six ships:















































ShipGunsMenCommanderBurford70500Vice-Admiral Vernon / Capt. WatsonHampton Court70495Captain MainWorcester60400Captain WaterhouseStrafford60400Captain TrevorLouisa60400Captain HerbertNorwich50300
After encountering contrary winds, the squadron came in sight of Porto Bello on the evening of 20 November. Porto Bello — so called from the beauty of its harbour — was situated on the north coast of the Isthmus of Darien, in what is now Panama. The town stood at the bottom of a small bay, defended by three fortifications: the Iron Fort (Fuerte del Hierro) at the mouth of the harbour on the north side; Castle St. Jeronimo near the town, with a battery facing the bay entrance; and the Castle Gloria on the west side of the town, a massive structure garrisoned by 400 men.
On the morning of 21 November, Vernon weighed anchor and formed line of battle. The ships entered the bay in order, with the Hampton Court leading. As she came within a cable’s length of the Iron Fort, she was suddenly becalmed by the high land to windward and exposed to a smart fire before she could bring her guns to bear. Once she anchored and returned fire, she “seemed, in a moment, a cloud of perpetual thunder” — firing 400 balls in the space of twenty-five minutes (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 435).
The Norwich and Worcester came up next and engaged with “vast alacrity.” Vernon himself, aboard the Burford, perceived the Spaniards beginning to flee from parts of the fort. He ordered a landing. The boats full of sailors and marines passed the admiral, who called out to them to land immediately under the walls of the fort, though no breach had been made. The sailors scaled the wall, pulled the soldiers up after them, struck the Spanish colours, and hoisted the British ensign on the lower battery.
The garrison of the Iron Fort, originally 300 men, had been reduced to only 35 privates and 5 officers by the time they surrendered. Observing the English flag on the lower battery, the upper garrison hoisted a white flag and surrendered at discretion.
On the morning of 22 November, Vernon called a council of war to plan an attack on Gloria Castle, but the Spaniards anticipated him by sending a boat with a flag of truce. Articles of capitulation were agreed and signed on board the Burford that day between Vernon and Commodore Brown on one side, and Governor Don Francisco Martinez de Retez and Commandant Don Francisco de Abarea on the other. The British troops took immediate possession of Gloria Castle and St. Jeronimo.
Two Spanish guarda-costas of twenty guns each and an armed snow were found in the harbour. The Spanish crews, having first plundered the town and committed outrages on the inhabitants, were relieved by the disciplined behaviour of the British sailors, who received 10,000 dollars (the Spanish troop payroll, captured intact) as a reward.
Vernon spent three weeks demolishing the fortifications, using 122 barrels of Spanish gunpowder, and took on board 40 brass cannon, 10 brass field-pieces, 4 brass mortars, 18 brass pattereroes, and spiked 80 pieces of iron ordnance. He sailed for Jamaica on 13 December.
The Popular Celebration
The news of Porto Bello’s capture reached England in March 1740. Captain Rentone, dispatched in the Triumph sloop, arrived on 12 March — though news had preceded him by a day via a merchant ship from Jamaica. The nation “became frantic with joy” (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 438).
Parliament voted congratulatory addresses. The cities of London, Bristol, and others followed suit. The Commons granted every demand of the crown: 28,000 land forces, 6,000 marines, and a powerful naval expansion. Vernon became the most celebrated man in Britain. Medals were struck in his honour. Inn- and tavern-keepers renamed their establishments “The Admiral Vernon” or “Porto Bello.” The most lasting tribute came in London, where the street Portobello Road (originally Porto Bello Road, later corrupted to its modern spelling) was laid out on the Portobello estate in Paddington, named to commemorate the victory. The name survives to this day as one of London’s most famous markets.
More significantly, the victory inspired the composition of “Rule, Britannia!” — the patriotic song by James Thomson with music by Thomas Arne, first performed at Cliveden in 1740 for the Prince of Wales. Though the song celebrates British naval supremacy in general, its composition in the year of Porto Bello — with the line “Britannia, rule the waves” — was unmistakably informed by Vernon’s astonishing triumph. The contemporary ballad “Hosier’s Ghost” by Richard Glover, recounting the death of Admiral Francis Hosier off Porto Bello in 1726 and contrasting it with Vernon’s success, also became immensely popular.
The praise was not unqualified. Campbell’s history notes that the victory, while honourable to the British navy, was “in part attributed to the cowardice of the Spaniards in surrendering the first fort before a breach was made, and the other two before they were attacked” — adding that Gloria Castle was so regularly fortified that it “might have sustained a long siege” (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 437–438).
Aftermath: Cartagena and the Widening War
The capture of Porto Bello proved to be the high-water mark of British success in the war. Emboldened by Vernon’s victory, the government planned a far more ambitious operation: the capture of Cartagena de Indias (in modern Colombia), the most formidable Spanish fortress in the Americas.
In 1741, a massive expedition assembled at Jamaica under Vernon’s command. Sir Chaloner Ogle arrived in January with reinforcements, giving Vernon a fleet of thirty ships of the line, numerous frigates, bomb-ketches, and fire-ships, with 15,000 seamen and 12,000 soldiers (including four battalions raised in America and 500 Jamaican negroes). “This very formidable armament,” Campbell writes, “doubtless the most tremendous that ever appeared in those seas, was certainly equal to any attempt against the Spanish settlements” (Campbell, Vol. IV, p. 444).
Yet the Cartagena expedition was a disaster. The fleet had been delayed at Spithead for months by the ministry; Vernon himself delayed at Jamaica until the season was dangerously advanced; the Spanish, forewarned, reinforced the garrison under the great military engineer Blas de Lezo; disease ravaged the British troops; and coordination between Vernon and the army commander, Brigadier-General Thomas Wentworth, was catastrophic. After two months of siege and desperate fighting, the British withdrew with staggering losses — over 9,000 men dead, mostly from yellow fever and other diseases. Vernon’s reputation never fully recovered.
The war with Spain merged into the general European conflict of the War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748), triggered by the death of Emperor Charles VI and the disputed succession of Maria Theresa of Austria. Britain found herself fighting France and Spain simultaneously across multiple theatres. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) ended the war on broadly status quo terms — Porto Bello, which had been evacuated immediately after its capture, remained in Spanish hands. As one historian observed, “In the whole course of a war which had continued nine years, nothing had been lost, and nothing gained, Porto Bello excepted, which had been immediately evacuated.”
Key Figures

Robert Walpole (1676–1745) — Prime Minister, reluctantly pushed into war by public clamour against his pacific policy. His ministry fell in 1742, partly as a consequence of the war’s mismanagement.
Edward Vernon (1684–1757) — Admiral, hero of Porto Bello, inventor of “grog” (diluted rum issued to sailors), and later disgraced by the Cartagena disaster. He served as MP for Ipswich and was a fierce critic of the Admiralty.
Captain Robert Jenkins — Scottish merchant captain whose severed ear became the rallying cry for war. His subsequent career is obscure; he is remembered only for this single, dramatic appearance in history.
King George II (1683–1760) — The reigning monarch. The last British king to lead troops in person (at Dettingen, 1743), he supported the war against Spain despite Walpole’s reservations.

Cross-References

West Indies — the theatre of operations
South Sea Company — whose commercial interests were entangled with the dispute
Treaty of Utrecht (1713) — granted the asiento and created the framework for Anglo-Spanish commercial conflict
War of the Austrian Succession — the larger European war into which this conflict was subsumed
Cartagena expedition — the disastrous follow-up to Porto Bello (1741)
George Anson — whose circumnavigation (1740–1744) was originally conceived as part of the war strategy
Jacobite rising of 1745 — which diverted British military resources from the Spanish war

Sources

Campbell, John. Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. IV (New Edition, 1817). Chapter III (George II). campbell-lives-admirals-vol4.md
Campbell, John / Stevenson, William. Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. VI (New Edition, 1817). Memoir of Admiral Edward Vernon (p. 240). campbell-lives-admirals-vol6.md
Smollett, Tobias. A Complete History of England, Vol. X (3rd ed., 1759). Book Ninth (George II, section on War of Jenkins’ Ear). smollett-history-england-vol10.md

events/war-of-the-first-coalition-1793.title: War of the First Coalition (1793–1797)
events/war-of-the-first-coalition-1793.content:
War of the First Coalition (1793–1797)
The War of the First Coalition (1793–1797) was the opening phase of the French Revolutionary Wars, in which the monarchies of Europe — led by Pitt’s Britain, Austria, and Prussia — combined to contain and destroy the revolutionary government of France. It was the longest and most expensive war Britain had ever fought, and it ended in the complete military triumph of the French Republic. By 1797, the coalition had collapsed piecemeal, leaving only Britain and Austria still in arms. The war transformed British politics, demolished the fiscal system that Pitt had so carefully constructed, and set the stage for the global struggle against Napoleonic France that would dominate the next two decades.
The Road to War
The French Revolution and the European Reaction
The French Revolution of 1789 had initially been welcomed by much of British public opinion. Charles James Fox and the Whig opposition hailed the fall of the Bastille as the dawn of a new era of liberty; even Pitt, cautious and fiscal-minded, declared in 1792 that the situation in France offered an opportunity for “uninterrupted peace” and predicted “fifteen years of tranquillity.” But the revolution radicalised rapidly. On 21 September 1792, the French National Convention declared France a republic. In November, it issued the Edict of Fraternity (the Decree of 19 November 1792), which promised “fraternity and assistance to all peoples wishing to recover their liberty” — a direct threat to every throne in Europe. The Convention invited the subject nations of the continent to revolt, declared that France would treat as enemies any powers that remained neutral, and ordered its generals to carry the revolution beyond France’s borders.
On 21 January 1793, the Convention executed Louis XVI by the guillotine. The event sent a shock through every court in Europe. In London, the king’s ministers recalled their ambassador; the French ambassador, M. Chauvelin, was ordered to depart the kingdom. But the point of no return had already been reached.
The Scheldt Crisis and the Invasion of the Austrian Netherlands
The immediate casus belli was the French invasion of the Austrian Netherlands (modern-day Belgium). In November 1792, French armies under General Charles Dumouriez crushed the Austrian forces at the Battle of Jemappes and overran the entire province. The French Convention, in a flagrant violation of the Treaty of Westphalia (1648), decreed the opening of the Scheldt River to international navigation. The Scheldt had been closed by treaty for over a century; its opening struck directly at the commercial interests of the Dutch Republic and Great Britain, for whom the closure of the Scheldt was a fundamental guarantee of Dutch independence and British strategic security.
Britain had guaranteed the independence of the Dutch Republic by treaty. The French occupation of the Netherlands — and the French refusal to give any security that the province would be evacuated at the conclusion of war — made the question one of national honour and vital interest. Pitt, who had worked so hard in the 1780s to restore British finances and avoid continental entanglements, found himself forced into a war he did not want but could not avoid.
The Parliamentary Debate (February 1793)
On the day that France declared war — 1 February 1793 — the British Parliament was already debating the crisis. Pitt rose to deliver what Belsham describes as “an eloquent harangue, evidently calculated to prepare the minds of his auditors for war.” He denounced the execution of the French king as a crime that “the present age must be for ever contaminated with the guilt and ignominy of having witnessed.” He catalogued French aggression: the annexation of Savoy, the Edict of Fraternity, the invasion of the Netherlands, the opening of the Scheldt. The French, he argued, had demonstrated that “the wild and destructive ambition of the present rulers in France was limited only by their power.” He moved an address of thanks to the king, preparing the nation for war.
Charles James Fox rose in opposition, in what Belsham records as the most powerful speech of the debate. Fox “allowed that the trial and execution of the French monarch were acts of the grossest inhumanity and injustice,” but argued that “crimes perpetrated in one independent state were not cognisable in another.” He identified three grounds on which the ministry based its case for war — the opening of the Scheldt, the Edict of Fraternity, and the danger to the European balance of power — and demolished each in turn. The Dutch had made no request for British assistance. The Edict of Fraternity had been accompanied by an explanation that took away its sting. As for the balance of power: “We had seen the entire conquest of Poland, and the invasion of France, with such marked indifference, that it would be difficult now to take it up with the grace of sincerity.”
Edmund Burke, who had broken with Fox over the French Revolution and whose Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) had made him the intellectual champion of European counter-revolution, spoke in terms of apocalyptic urgency. He “pronounced a vehement Philippic, affording a melancholy contrast to the speeches of his better days.” He denounced the opposition as men who “could neither vindicate the principles nor deny the power of France, yet impeded the measures taken to secure us against that power.” For Burke, the war was not a diplomatic dispute but a crusade: “No man had a more lively sense of the evils of war than himself. A war with France, in present circumstances, must be terrible; but peace much more so.”
France Declares War (1 February 1793)
Before the British Parliament could vote, France acted. On 1 February 1793, the French National Convention declared war on Great Britain and the Dutch Republic. The British declaration of war followed immediately. The long struggle had begun.
The First Coalition
The coalition that assembled against France in the spring of 1793 was the most formidable alliance Europe had seen since the Seven Years’ War. Its members were:

Great Britain — the paymaster, providing financial subsidies to every continental ally, and the naval arm, commanding the seas
Austria — the principal military power on the continent, with armies in the Netherlands and on the Rhine
Prussia — a reluctant and unreliable ally, whose king was more interested in the partition of Poland than in the war in the west
Spain — a Bourbon monarchy that feared the contagion of revolution
Holland (the Dutch Republic) — the Stadtholder’s government, bound to Britain by treaty
Sardinia-Piedmont — the Italian kingdom that faced French expansion across the Alps
Portugal — a minor but consistent ally
The Kingdom of Naples and various Italian states

The coalition was united by nothing but fear. Austria and Prussia were traditional rivals. Britain and Spain were still smarting from the wounds of the American war. The alliance had no common strategic objective beyond the defeat of France, and no agreed plan for the settlement of Europe after a victory. It was, as one historian put it, a coalition of monarchies against a revolution, not a coalition of states with a shared interest.
The Military Struggle (1793–1794)
The Flanders Campaign
The main theatre of operations in 1793 was the Austrian Netherlands and northern France, where a combined British, Austrian, and allied army under the Prince of Coburg and the Duke of York — the second son of George III — aimed to invade France. The Duke of York was appointed commander of the British and auxiliary troops on the continent.
The campaign opened with remarkable success. In the spring and summer of 1793, the allies captured the French border fortresses of Valenciennes, Condé, Mentz (Mainz), and Le Quesnoy in rapid succession. The French armies, demoralised by the defection of General Charles Dumouriez to the Austrians after the Battle of Neerwinden (18 March 1793), seemed on the verge of collapse. The court of London, Belsham writes, was filled with “elation” — it was widely believed that the war would be over in a single campaign.
But the coalition’s triumphs were squandered by disunity and strategic disagreement. The Austrians, under Coburg, were more interested in recovering the Netherlands for themselves than in invading France. The British, under the Duke of York, favoured an advance on Paris. The result was a “fatal separation”: Coburg turned south to besiege the fortress of Maubeuge, while York, with 37,000 men, besieged the port of Dunkirk — a decision of catastrophic folly.
The siege of Dunkirk was a disaster. The French, galvanised by the revolutionary levée en masse that had raised hundreds of thousands of conscripts, concentrated their forces against York’s isolated army. On 8 September 1793, the French under General Houchard attacked at the Battle of Hondschoote and inflicted a severe defeat. The Duke of York was forced to raise the siege and retreat, losing his artillery and baggage. Belsham records the defeat in a single terse sentence: “Duke of York totally defeated at Dunkirk.”
The campaign of 1794 was worse. The French, now under the direction of the Committee of Public Safety and the revolutionary zeal of the Reign of Terror, had reorganised their armies and found brilliant young commanders. The Battle of Fleurus (26 June 1794) was the decisive engagement: the French under General Jourdan defeated the Austrian army under Coburg, and the Austrian Netherlands were lost for good. The Duke of York’s army, now reduced to a fraction of its original strength, retreated northwards through Holland, harried by the French and the winter. By the spring of 1795, the “shattered remains of the Duke of York’s army” — Belsham’s phrase — embarked for England. The Flanders campaign had cost Britain £6 million and the lives of tens of thousands of soldiers, and had achieved nothing.
Toulon (August–December 1793)
The one British success of 1793 came in the Mediterranean. In August, the French royalist and federalist inhabitants of Toulon, in revolt against the Jacobin Convention, surrendered their city and its naval arsenal to a British fleet under Admiral Lord Hood. The port was the most important naval base in the Mediterranean; its capture gave Britain control of the French Mediterranean fleet — thirty ships of the line — and a strategic foothold in southern France.
The occupation of Toulon was brief and glorious. A young artillery officer named Napoleon Bonaparte — then unknown outside the army — was given command of the siege artillery. He arrayed his guns on the heights commanding the harbour, and on 17 December 1793, after a ferocious bombardment, the British and Spanish garrison evacuated the town. The British fleet under Hood sailed out of the harbour under fire, carrying thousands of royalist refugees. Among the British officers present was a young captain named Horatio Nelson, serving with the naval brigade. It was the first meeting of the two men who would dominate the coming epoch.
Toulon was the pattern of the war: a brilliant opportunity thrown away by the incompetence of the coalition; a French recovery made possible by the revolutionary energy that the allied monarchies could not match.
The Naval War: The Glorious First of June (1794)
If the land war was a catalogue of disaster, the naval war brought one of the most celebrated British victories of the age. In the spring of 1794, a French grain convoy of over 130 ships was expected from America, vital to feed a France starving under the Terror and the revolutionary governance. The French Atlantic fleet put to sea under Admiral Villaret-Joyeuse to cover the convoy’s passage. The British Channel Fleet, under Admiral Lord Howe — “Black Dick” to the sailors — intercepted them on the morning of 1 June 1794, about 400 miles west of the French coast.
The Glorious First of June was a battle of extraordinary ferocity, fought in the classic style of the line of battle. Howe, in his flagship the Queen Charlotte, broke the French line — a daring tactical innovation — and engaged at close quarters. Six French ships of the line were captured; one was sunk. The British loss was 290 killed and 858 wounded; the French lost over 3,000 killed and wounded plus the captured crews.
Yet the strategic result was ambiguous. The French grain convoy, the real object of the campaign, had escaped — the British frigates had missed it in the fog, and it reached Brest safely. The French fleet, though battered, was not destroyed; within weeks it was ready for sea again. The Channel remained contested. But the victory gave Britain its first great naval triumph of the war, and Howe was rewarded with the thanks of Parliament and — after years of neglect by the Admiralty — overdue recognition. The battle established a moral ascendancy that the Royal Navy would never lose.
The Financial Strain
The war was an economic catastrophe for Britain. Pitt had spent the 1780s restoring the national finances after the disaster of the American war. His Sinking Fund — a device by which surplus revenue was set aside to redeem the national debt — was the centrepiece of his fiscal policy, and he had boasted that under his management the debt would be paid off within a generation.
The war destroyed that dream. In 1793 alone, Pitt borrowed £6 million for the war effort. In 1794, another £11 million. By 1795, the national debt had more than doubled from its pre-war level. The Sinking Fund was suspended in 1795 — formally abandoned, though Pitt continued to use the mechanism as a fiscal fiction. The “extravagant loan of the minister” became a regular theme of the opposition’s attacks.
Belsham records that commercial credit collapsed in the first months of the war: “An unparalleled number of bankruptcies in London” followed the declaration of war, and it required the government’s intervention — the issuance of exchequer bills to support commercial credit — to prevent a general financial crash. The Bank of England itself came under severe pressure, and in 1797 it would be forced to suspend cash payments — the famous Bank Restriction Act.
Pitt’s response to the financial crisis was to raise taxes to levels unprecedented in British history. He introduced the first income tax in British history in 1799, but even before that, in the period of the First Coalition, he had imposed heavy new duties on imports, raised the land tax, and borrowed at ruinous rates of interest. The cost of the war in the first four years alone was estimated at over £50 million — more than the entire cost of the Seven Years’ War.
The Collapse of the Coalition (1795–1797)
The First Coalition did not break in battle; it dissolved by mutual exhaustion and diplomatic betrayal.
Prussia, the first to falter, signed the separate Peace of Basel with France on 5 April 1795. The Prussian king, Frederick William II, had never been enthusiastic about the war; his eyes were fixed on Poland, where the third and final partition was in progress. France recognised Prussia’s Polish acquisitions; Prussia recognised French conquests on the left bank of the Rhine. The price of Prussian withdrawal was the abandonment of all the German princes whose territories lay west of the river.
Spain, the second to defect, signed its own Peace of Basel on 22 July 1795. The Spanish Bourbon monarchy, after two years of defeat and exhaustion, abandoned the coalition and — in 1796 — became an ally of France, bound by the Treaty of San Ildefonso. The defection of Spain was a strategic catastrophe for Britain: it opened the Mediterranean to the combined French and Spanish fleets, forced the British evacuation of Corsica, and made the sea route to India and the East Indies vulnerable to enemy attack.
Holland, or rather the Batavian Republic that the French had established after their conquest of the Netherlands in the winter of 1794–95, had been forced out of the coalition and into an alliance with France. The Dutch fleet, which had been Britain’s ally, was now a hostile force in the North Sea.
By the summer of 1796, the First Coalition had shrunk to two members: Great Britain and Austria. Britain had the navy and the money but no army capable of engaging the French on the continent. Austria had the army but was reeling under the blows of a young general named Napoleon Bonaparte, who had taken command of the French Army of Italy in March 1796 and was, in the space of a year, destroying the Austrian position in Italy in a campaign of unparalleled brilliance — Montenotte, Lodi, Castiglione, Arcole, Rivoli.
The Invasion Threat and Hoche’s Irish Expedition (1796–1797)
The collapse of the coalition brought the war directly to the shores of Britain and Ireland. With France triumphant on the continent, the French Directory resolved to strike at the heart of British power by an invasion of the British Isles.
The principal threat was directed at Ireland. Lazare Hoche, one of the ablest of the French revolutionary generals, assembled a fleet at Brest in December 1796: fifteen ships of the line, some forty transports, and 14,000 veteran troops. The plan was to land in Bantry Bay, in the south-west of Ireland, where the French hoped to unite with the United Irishmen under Lord Edward Fitzgerald and Wolfe Tone — the revolutionary society preparing an insurrection against British rule.
The expedition sailed on 15 December 1796. It was scattered by the worst winter storms in living memory. Hoche’s flagship became separated from the fleet; the ships that reached Bantry Bay — under Admiral Bouvet — found themselves unable to land troops in the mountainous seas. After a week of indecision, the fleet turned back for France. Not a single French soldier set foot on Irish soil.
The failed expedition was a narrow escape, but it was not an end to the danger. The French would try again in 1798 — and this time, in the summer of that year, they would land a small force at Killala Bay, too late to save the Irish Rebellion from defeat. The threat of invasion hung over Britain until the Peace of Amiens in 1802, and — after a brief interval — returned with the great invasion camps of 1803–1805.
The End of the First Coalition and the Peace Offensive (1797)
By 1797, Britain stood alone. Austria, after Bonaparte’s relentless Italian campaign and the preliminary Peace of Leoben (April 1797), sued for peace, confirmed by the Treaty of Campo Formio (October 1797). The First Coalition was dead.
Britain’s position in 1797 was the most perilous it had faced since the American war. The navy was shattered by the mutinies at Spithead and the Nore — the greatest breakdown of discipline in the history of the Royal Navy. The Bank of England had suspended cash payments. The national debt was staggering. The Opposition, led by Fox and Grey, was demanding peace. Pitt himself, in February 1797, authorised secret peace feelers through Lord Malmesbury — the first of several abortive attempts to negotiate with the Directory. The negotiations at Lille broke down over irreconcilable differences: the Directory demanded the return of the French colonies that Britain had captured, and Britain demanded the evacuation of Belgium and the Rhineland.
The war would go on. The Second Coalition — Britain, Russia, Austria, and Naples — was already being assembled. But the character of the war had changed. It was no longer a war against revolutionary principles; it was a war of national survival against a military power that threatened the very existence of the British state.
Significance
The War of the First Coalition was the formative experience of Pitt’s second ministry and the crucible in which the fiscal-military state of the Napoleonic Wars was forged. It taught the British government four hard lessons that would shape strategy for the next twenty years:
First, Britain could not fight a continental war with a continental army. The Duke of York’s Flanders campaign demonstrated that British troops, however brave, were no match for the mass armies of revolutionary France when commanded by allied incompetence and coalition politics. Britain’s strength was naval and financial.
Second, the coalition system was fragile. The allies had no common strategic objective, no command structure, and no shared commitment to the war. Prussia and Spain peeled off the moment it suited them.
Third, revolutionary France could mobilise resources that the old regime could not match. The levée en masse, the Committee of Public Safety, the brutal efficiency of the Terror — the French Republic was capable of concentrating national power in a way that the monarchies of the old regime could not replicate.
Fourth, the war would be decided at sea and in the empire, not in Flanders. The Glorious First of June, the capture of the Cape of Good Hope (1795), the capture of Ceylon from the Dutch, the conquest of Trinidad, the successful defence of the West Indian colonies — these were the achievements that sustained Britain’s will to fight. And in the Mediterranean, a new generation of naval commanders — Horatio Nelson, Sir John Jervis, Adam Duncan — was learning the craft that would culminate in the Nile (1798), Copenhagen (1801), and Trafalgar (1805).
Key Figures


William Pitt the Younger (1759–1806) — Prime Minister. Architect of the war strategy, manager of the coalition’s finances, and the man who reluctantly led Britain into the longest war of his generation. His fiscal system was shattered by the war he was forced to fight.


Charles James Fox (1749–1806) — Leader of the Whig opposition. The most eloquent critic of the war, who argued from the first that it was unnecessary, provoked by British policy, and doomed to fail. Political isolation after his break with Burke; his consistent advocacy of peace was vindicated only by later history.


Edmund Burke (1729–1797) — The apostate Whig who broke with Fox over the French Revolution. His Reflections and his parliamentary speeches provided the intellectual justification for the war as a crusade against the principles of revolution. His death in 1797 deprived the war party of its most powerful voice.


Prince Frederick, Duke of York (1763–1827) — Second son of George III, appointed commander of the British expeditionary force in Flanders. His campaign was a catastrophic failure. The nursery rhyme “The Grand Old Duke of York” is thought to be a satirical memorial of his futile marches.


Admiral Lord Howe (1726–1799) — “Black Dick,” victor of the Glorious First of June. The most respected British naval commander of his generation.


Henry Dundas (1742–1811) — Pitt’s secretary of state for war (from 1794). The manager of the war effort, the organiser of the colonial expeditions, and the patron of Scottish patronage in the British government.


Horatio Nelson (1758–1805) — A young captain at the siege of Toulon, the blockade of Genoa, and the Battle of Cape St. Vincent (1797). The First Coalition was the apprenticeship of the man who would become the greatest naval commander in British history.


Lazare Hoche (1768–1797) — The French general who led the attempted invasion of Ireland (December 1796). His death in 1797 deprived France of one of its most capable commanders.


Wolfe Tone (1763–1798) — The Irish revolutionary who accompanied Hoche’s expedition as a French officer. The leader of the United Irishmen, whose alliance with France gave the British government its greatest fear: insurrection in Ireland combined with invasion from France.

events/wilkes-affair-1763.title: The Wilkes Affair (1763–1769)
events/wilkes-affair-1763.content:
The Wilkes Affair (1763–1769)
The Wilkes Affair was the most serious domestic political crisis of the early reign of George III, a protracted constitutional struggle that convulsed British politics from 1763 to 1769 and raised fundamental questions about the liberty of the press, the legality of general warrants, the scope of parliamentary privilege, and the right of electors to choose their representatives. At its centre was John Wilkes — MP for Aylesbury, journalist, libertine, and demagogue — a man whose personal dissoluteness never diminished his hold on the popular imagination or the potency of the causes he championed.
The affair unfolded in two distinct phases. The first (1763–1764) turned on Wilkes’s arrest and prosecution for seditious libel after the publication of The North Briton No. 45, and established landmark legal precedents against general warrants. The second (1768–1769) — the Middlesex election crisis — escalated the quarrel from a personal prosecution into a constitutional confrontation between the House of Commons and the electors of the largest county in England, and gave birth to the mass politics of extra-parliamentary agitation that would define British radicalism for the next half-century.

The North Briton No. 45
John Wilkes entered Parliament as MP for Aylesbury in 1757 as a follower of William Pitt the Elder, but he made his name not as a debater but as a journalist. In June 1762 he founded The North Briton, a weekly newspaper designed to attack the ministry of the Earl of Bute (John Stuart, 3rd Earl of Bute) and the peace negotiations that would end the Seven Years’ War. The paper was scurrilous, personal, and wildly popular — it gave voice to a London radicalism that the governing classes had long dismissed as beneath notice, and its success rested on Wilkes’s genius for invective and his willingness to name names.
The crisis came on 23 April 1763. King George III had delivered the speech from the throne at the close of the parliamentary session, in which he praised the recently concluded Peace of Paris as “honourable to my crown and beneficial to my people.” On the same day, Wilkes published The North Briton No. 45, in which he denounced the speech as containing “the most abandoned instigations of falsehood.” He accused the King’s ministers — and by implication the King himself — of having deceived Parliament and the nation with a peace that sacrificed the true interests of Britain.
No. 45 was not Wilkes’s most brilliant piece of writing, nor his most scurrilous. But the timing and the target were explosive. The Bute ministry had already resigned (Bute had stepped down on 8 April 1763, replaced by George Grenville), but Wilkes’s attack seemed to strike at the Crown itself. The new Grenville ministry, stung by the insult and eager to demonstrate its authority, determined to crush him.
The General Warrant
On 29 April 1763, the Earl of Halifax (George Montagu-Dunk, 2nd Earl of Halifax), as one of the two Secretaries of State, issued a general warrant — a warrant that named no specific individual but ordered the arrest of “the authors, printers, and publishers” of The North Briton No. 45. Under this warrant, the Secretary of State’s messengers arrested forty-nine people over the course of several days — compositors, pressmen, news vendors — before they finally reached Wilkes himself. His house was entered, his personal papers were seized, and he was committed to the Tower of London.
The use of general warrants was not unprecedented, but it had always been controversial. Such warrants had been employed against Jacobite printers in earlier decades, and the Secretaries of State had long claimed the right to issue them in cases of seditious libel. But no court had ever definitively ruled on their legality. The sheer sweep of the arrests — forty-nine people for a single anonymous article — shocked public opinion and turned the case from a prosecution of a libeller into a test of the limits of executive power.
The Legal Battle: Chief Justice Pratt’s Judgment
Wilkes was brought before the Court of Common Pleas on a writ of habeas corpus. His counsel argued two points: first, that the general warrant was illegal, as it did not name the person to be arrested; second, that as a Member of Parliament, Wilkes was protected by parliamentary privilege from arrest for libel during a session of Parliament.
On 6 May 1763, Lord Chief Justice Charles Pratt (later created Lord Camden) delivered his judgment. It was a landmark of English constitutional law. Pratt ruled that Wilkes was entitled to privilege of Parliament and must be discharged from custody. More importantly, he declared that general warrants — warrants that did not name the person to be arrested — were “unconstitutional, illegal, and absolutely void.” He ordered the Secretary of State’s messengers to be prosecuted for trespass.
The judgment was a sensation. The City of London voted the freedom of the City to Chief Justice Pratt, presented to him in a golden box; his portrait was placed in Guildhall. Belsham records that Pratt “became the idol of the nation.” For the first time, the principle that a man could not be arrested without a warrant naming him was established as a matter of law — a victory for English liberty that Wilkes, whatever his personal defects, had made possible.
The Expulsion and Flight
The ministry, however, did not surrender. While Pratt’s judgment freed Wilkes from the Tower, it did not prevent Parliament from taking its own action. The Commons was a jealous guardian of its privileges, and the ministry had a comfortable majority. On 24 November 1763, after a protracted debate, the House of Commons voted by a great majority “that THE NORTH BRITON, No. 45, is a false, scandalous, and seditious libel, manifestly tending to alienate the affections of the people.” On the same day, the Commons resolved that John Wilkes was guilty of writing and publishing the libel, and ordered his expulsion from the House.
Wilkes had already fled to France — not only to escape the parliamentary prosecution but because a second charge had been prepared against him. During the original search of his papers, the ministry had seized a copy of an obscene and blasphemous poem, the Essay on Woman, which Wilkes had printed privately for his amusement among a small circle of friends. The poem, which parodied Pope’s Essay on Man, was of no political significance, but its publication gave the ministry a weapon against him that Pratts judgment could not touch.
Wilkes was tried in absentia in the Court of King’s Bench, found guilty of publishing both the North Briton No. 45 and the Essay on Woman, and outlawed. He remained in France for four years, moving restlessly through the literary and political salons of Paris, corresponding with his English supporters, and waiting for his moment.
The Return and the Middlesex Elections
In February 1768, after four years of exile, Wilkes returned to England. The political mood had shifted. The Grenville ministry had fallen in 1765; the Rockingham ministry that followed had repealed the Stamp Act but lasted barely a year; the Chatham ministry (with Pitt now Earl of Chatham in the Lords) was in disarray, with the Duke of Grafton effectively managing the government. The great popular currents that had swirled around the North Briton had not dissipated — they had only deepened.
Wilkes presented himself to the Court of King’s Bench to be discharged from his outlawry. The court confirmed his conviction but refused to hear his appeal against outlawry on a technicality, and he was sentenced to twenty-two months’ imprisonment. He was carried to the King’s Bench Prison in St. George’s Fields, Southwark.
His imprisonment became the occasion for the mass politics that defined the second phase of his career. Crowds gathered outside the prison, chanting “Wilkes and Liberty!” — the slogan that became the cry of the London mob and the emblem of the movement. On 10 May 1768, a crowd estimated at fifteen thousand assembled in St. George’s Fields. Soldiers of the Scottish regiment stationed nearby — an inflammatory choice in itself — were called out. They fired into the crowd, killing several people. The Massacre of St. George’s Fields, as it became known, turned a political crisis into a popular insurgency.
In the general election of March 1768, while still a prisoner and an outlaw in the eyes of the law, Wilkes had stood for Parliament. He was defeated in the City of London but then stood for the County of Middlesex — the most populous and politically conscious constituency in the kingdom, encompassing the northern and western suburbs of London. He was elected by a overwhelming majority.
The Crisis of 1769
Parliament refused to seat him. On 3 February 1769, the House of Commons voted to expel him for the libels of 1763. The freeholders of Middlesex immediately re-elected him. The House expelled him again. The freeholders returned him a second time. When the House expelled him a fourth time and declared Wilkes incapable of being elected to the present Parliament, Middlesex returned him yet again.
At this point, the ministry under the Duke of Grafton determined on a drastic course. Rather than allow the cycle of expulsion and re-election to continue indefinitely, the House declared on 17 March 1769 that Wilkes’s opponent, Henry Luttrell, was the duly elected member for Middlesex — despite Luttrell having received fewer than 300 votes to Wilkes’s 1,143.
This was the decisive moment. The question was no longer whether John Wilkes was a fit person to sit in Parliament — a question on which reasonable people could disagree — but whether the House of Commons could nullify the votes of a free constituency and install a candidate whom the electors had rejected. The principle at stake was the right of election itself.
Popular Support: Wilkes and Liberty
The Middlesex election crisis transformed Wilkes from a journalist and libertine into a popular hero, the symbol of resistance against an overbearing executive. The cry of “Wilkes and Liberty!” swept through London and the provinces. Effigies of Lord Bute and the Earl of Halifax were burned. Wilkes’s prison in the King’s Bench became a place of pilgrimage. Subscriptions poured in from across the country to pay his debts and finance his campaigns.
The Society of the Supporters of the Bill of Rights was founded in February 1769, initially to defray Wilkes’s enormous legal expenses — estimated at £20,000 — but quickly expanding into the first organised extra-parliamentary pressure group in British politics. The Society published accounts of its expenditures, circulated petitions, organised public meetings, and agitated for parliamentary reform. It was the prototype of the radical clubs and associations that would transform British politics over the following half-century.
The crisis also produced a torrent of pamphlets and essays. Edmund Burke, who had entered Parliament in 1765 as secretary to the Marquess of Rockingham, published his Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents in 1770 — a work that, while not directly about Wilkes, analysed the same constitutional disease: the growth of the influence of the Crown and the corruption of Parliament by the “king’s friends.” Lord Chatham (as Pitt had become) supported Wilkes’s cause in the Lords, though his health was failing and his interventions were intermittent.
The city of London — the great commercial and financial heart of the kingdom — stood solidly behind Wilkes. The Common Council voted him its thanks, and the Livery of London made him their champion. The freedom of the City was voted to him. London’s support gave the Wilkesite movement a base of wealth and institutional power that no amount of ministerial pressure could break.
The Aftermath and the Constitutional Crisis
The Middlesex election crisis was unresolved. The Grafton ministry had triumphed in the short term: Luttrell sat in the Commons, and the principle of virtual representation — that the Commons could judge the qualifications of its own members — was upheld by the ministerial majority. But the cost was immense. The crisis had exposed the unreformed electoral system to public scrutiny as never before. The case of the Middlesex electors — 1,143 voters whose choice had been set aside by an oligarchical House — became the rallying cry of every reform movement for the next half-century.
The constitutional question was fundamental: could the House of Commons, by a simple majority vote, exclude a member duly elected by a free constituency? If it could, then the Commons was not a representative body but a self-perpetuating oligarchy, accountable to no one but itself. The Wilkesites argued that the House’s claim to be “the judge of its own elections” — a claim traditionally used to protect the Commons against the Crown — had been perverted into a weapon against the electors themselves.
The crisis also had a profound effect on the American colonies. American newspapers followed the Wilkes affair with intense interest. The struggle against general warrants and the cry of “Wilkes and Liberty” resonated powerfully in Boston and New York, where comparable issues of executive power and the rights of Englishmen were being contested. The Middlesex election seemed, from an American perspective, a warning of what parliamentary supremacy might mean — a House of Commons that could nullify the votes of Englishmen at home could surely do the same to colonists abroad. When the American crisis escalated in the 1770s, Wilkes — by then Lord Mayor of London — became one of the colonists’ most prominent British allies, presenting their petitions to the King and denouncing the Coercive Acts.
The Resolution
The crisis did not come to a formal conclusion until 1774, five years after the expulsion. In the general election of that year, Wilkes — now serving as Lord Mayor of London, to which dignity he had been elected in 1774 — was again returned unopposed for Middlesex. This time, with a new Parliament and a changed political mood, the House allowed him to take his seat. He had been a member in exile for six years; he was now, at last, a member in possession.
The resolutions that had declared Luttrell elected and Wilkes incapable of sitting were eventually expunged from the Journals of the House of Commons in 1782 — a posthumous vindication of the principle for which the Middlesex electors had fought.
Key Figures
John Wilkes (1725–1797)
The central figure of the affair — MP, journalist, libertine, and radical demagogue. Wilkes was not a systematic thinker nor a principled reformer; he was a wit, a rake, and a man of immense personal courage whose battles against authority established precedents that became foundations of English liberty. His ugliness was legendary, his charm irresistible, and his resilience extraordinary.
George III (1738–1820)
The King whose Speech provoked Wilkes’s attack, and whose prerogative was indirectly challenged by the crisis. George III gave his full support to the ministries that prosecuted Wilkes and expelled him from the Commons. The crisis deepened the King’s conviction that the press was licentious and that the popular agitation against his government was the work of faction and sedition.
The Earl of Bute (John Stuart, 3rd Earl of Bute, 1713–1792)
The prime minister whose ministry was the target of Wilkes’s attacks in The North Briton. Bute had resigned before the arrest, but his shadow hung over the affair. The popular hatred of “the Scots favourite” — the King’s former tutor, a Scot, and a man of inexperience — gave Wilkes’s journalism much of its venom and appeal.
The Earl of Halifax (George Montagu-Dunk, 2nd Earl of Halifax, 1716–1771)
The Secretary of State who issued the general warrant against Wilkes. Halifax was a hard-liner on questions of executive authority and colonial policy, and his willingness to use the full power of the state against Wilkes turned the case into a test of the limits of that power.
Charles Pratt, Lord Camden (1714–1794)
Lord Chief Justice of the Common Pleas, later Lord Chancellor. Pratt’s judgment in May 1763 — declaring general warrants illegal and parliamentary privilege applicable to libel — was the most important judicial victory of the affair and a landmark of English constitutional law. He was raised to the peerage as Lord Camden in 1766 and became Lord Chancellor in the Chatham ministry.
William Pitt the Elder (1708–1778)
Wilkes’s early political patron, who had brought him into Parliament for Aylesbury. By 1763 Pitt had resigned from office and was in the political wilderness; he spoke in defence of Wilkes’s cause but was constrained by his own complicated relationship with the King and the ministry. He returned to office in 1766 as Earl of Chatham, by which time the Wilkes affair had moved into its second phase.
Edmund Burke (1729–1797)
The great Whig philosopher-politician, who entered Parliament in 1765 and became the Rockingham Whigs’ most brilliant spokesman. Burke’s Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770), written in the wake of the Wilkes crisis, analysed the constitutional disease that the affair had exposed: the growth of the influence of the Crown and the corruption of the representative system. Burke also defended the principle that the House of Commons should respect the choice of electors, though he distrusted Wilkes personally as a demagogue.
The Duke of Grafton (Augustus FitzRoy, 3rd Duke of Grafton, 1735–1811)
Prime Minister during the Middlesex election crisis (1768–1770). Grafton, a grandson of the second duke and a protege of Chatham, led the ministry that expelled Wilkes and declared Luttrell elected. His government never recovered from the damage, and he resigned in January 1770, to be replaced by Lord North — a change that did not, however, alter the ministry’s Wilkes policy.
Henry Luttrell (1737–1821)
The defeated candidate whom the House of Commons declared elected for Middlesex. A soldier and placeman, Luttrell’s name became a byword for parliamentary corruption. He was awarded £500 for his “trouble” by the Treasury, sat in Parliament for the remainder of the term, and lived under a cloud of popular contempt for the rest of his life.
