Related sources: William Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. I (covers the North Briton crisis, the general warrant, and Pratt’s judgment); Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. II (covers the aftermath and the American dimension); History of Great Britain, Vol. VI (covers the Middlesex election crisis and the popular movement)


“The liberty of the press is the great bulwark of all the liberties of the people; and should ever be sacred and inviolable.” — John Wilkes


“The question is not whether John Wilkes is a fit person to sit in this House — the question is whether the freeholders of Middlesex have a right to send whom they please.” — Attributed to Sergeant Glynn, Wilkes’s counsel and later MP for Middlesex

index.title: index
index.content:
Great Britain 18th Century Wiki
A narrative-research knowledge base on 18th-century and early 19th-century British history, covering naval power, maritime affairs, war, trade, politics, and colonial expansion from the closing years of William III through the Peace of Amiens.
Total pages: 143
Sources

Campbell, John — Naval History of Great Britain (Vol. III, 1818). Covers 1697–1714, from the closing years of William III through the full reign of Queen Anne, including the War of the Spanish Succession, the capture of Gibraltar, and the Union of 1707. Read source page
Campbell, John — Lives of the British Admirals (Vol. IV, 1817, New Edition). Covers 1707–1763, from Queen Anne’s later reign through George I and George II, including the War of Jenkins’ Ear, the War of the Austrian Succession, the Jacobite risings, and the Seven Years’ War. Read source page
Campbell, John — Lives of the British Admirals (Vol. V, 1817, New Edition). Covers 1756–1779, from the Seven Years’ War through the Peace of Paris (1763) and into the American Revolutionary War. Features the Byng execution, Quiberon Bay, the fall of Quebec, and the outbreak of the American conflict. Read source page
Campbell, John — Lives of the British Admirals (Vol. VI, 1817, New Edition). A biographical volume with extended memoirs of 13 naval commanders: Dampier, Leake, Byng of Torrington, Norris, the Berkley family, Wager, Vernon, Barnett, John Byng, Anson, Boscawen, Hawke, and Byron. Read source page
Campbell, John — Lives of the British Admirals (Vol. VII, 1817, New Edition). Covers 1780–1802, from the close of the American Revolutionary War through the French Revolutionary Wars to the Peace of Amiens. Features Rodney, Yorktown, Cook’s third voyage, the Glorious First of June, Cape St. Vincent, the Nore mutinies, the Nile, Copenhagen, and the death of Cook. Read source page
Smollett, Tobias — A Complete History of England (Vol. X, 1759, 3rd ed.). A general history covering from Queen Anne’s reign through the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748). Covers the War of the Spanish Succession, the South Sea Bubble, the Walpole ministry, the ‘15 and ‘45 Jacobite risings, and the War of the Austrian Succession. Complements the Campbell naval volumes with political and military context. Read source page
Belsham, William — History of Great Britain (Vol. XII, 1805). The final volume covering 1800–1802, from the breakdown of armistice negotiations through the Peace of Amiens. Features the Armed Neutrality, the Battle of Copenhagen, the fall of Pitt, the conquest of Egypt, the death of Abercrombie, and the Treaty of Amiens. Read source page
Belsham, William — Memoirs of the Reign of George III (Vol. IV, c. 1806, 6th ed.). Covers 1784–1792, from Pitt’s consolidation of power through the Nootka Sound crisis and the early French Revolution. Features the India Bill, the Hastings impeachment, the Regency crisis, the Burke-Paine pamphlet war, and the abolition debates. Fills the post-American-Revolution gap. Read source page
Belsham, William — Memoirs of the Reign of George III (Vol. III, c. 1790s). Covers 1779–1793, from the crisis of the North ministry through the Gordon Riots, the fall of Yorktown, the peace with America, the Fox-North coalition, and Pitt’s rise to power. Provides the domestic political context for the American Revolutionary War period. Read source page
Belsham, William — Memoirs of the Reign of George III (Vol. V, 6th ed.). Covers 1793–1796, the opening years of the French Revolutionary War from the British domestic perspective. Features the war debates, Toulon, the treason trials, the Habeas Corpus suspension, the Two Acts, and the capture of the Cape of Good Hope. Read source page
Belsham, William — History of Great Britain (Vol. IV, 1805). Covers 1738–1760, from the crisis of Walpole’s last years through the Seven Years’ War. Features the War of Jenkins’ Ear, the ‘45 Jacobite rising, the capture of Quebec, Plassey, and the death of George II. Provides political and diplomatic context for the mid-century wars. Read source page
Belsham, William — History of Great Britain (Vol. XI, 1804). Covers 1798–1800, from the Income Tax debates through the Union with Ireland. Features the siege of Acre, Suvaroff’s Italian campaign, the fall of Tippoo Sultan, and the passage of the Act of Union. Read source page
Belsham, William — Memoirs of the Reign of George III (Vol. II, c. 1790s). Covers c. 1767–1774, the pre-Revolutionary crisis in America from the British political perspective. Features the Townshend duties, the Boston Massacre, the Tea Party, the Coercive Acts, and the meeting of the First Continental Congress. Read source page
Belsham, William — Memoirs of the Reign of George III (Vol. I, c. 1790s). Covers 1760–1766, from the accession of George III through the Peace of Paris and the Stamp Act crisis. Features the end of the Seven Years’ War, the fall of Pitt, the Wilkes affair, the Stamp Act, and its repeal. Read source page
Belsham, William — History of Great Britain (Vol. X, 1805). Covers 1795–1798, from the Two Acts through the Battle of the Nile. Features the Treason and Sedition Bills, Bonaparte’s Italian campaign, the Peace of Leoben, the Irish Rebellion, and Nelson’s victory at Aboukir Bay. Read source page
Belsham, William — History of Great Britain (Vol. VI, 1805). Covers 1768–1778, from the Boston Massacre through the American Revolutionary War to the French alliance. Features Lexington, Bunker Hill, the Declaration of Independence, Saratoga, and the surrender of Burgoyne. Read source page
Belsham, William — History of Great Britain (Vol. II, 1805). Covers 1714–1727, the reign of George I. Features the Jacobite rising of 1715, the Septennial Act, the South Sea Bubble, the Atterbury plot, and the rise of Walpole. Read source page
Burnet, Gilbert — History of His Own Time (Vol. II, 1734). A contemporary account covering 1688–1713, from the Glorious Revolution to the Treaty of Utrecht. Features William III, Queen Anne, the Nine Years’ War, and the War of the Spanish Succession. Read source page
Thurston, Robert H. — History of the Growth of the Steam-Engine (1878). Covers the development of the steam engine from Hero to the late 19th century. Major 18th-century content on Newcomen’s atmospheric engine, Watt’s separate condenser, the Boulton & Watt partnership, and early steamboats. Read source page
Malcolm, John — Life of Robert, Lord Clive (Vol. I, 1836). Covers Clive’s life and the establishment of British power in India. Features the siege of Arcot, the Battle of Plassey, the capture of Chandernagore, and the settlement of Bengal. Read source page
Malcolm, John — Life of Robert, Lord Clive (Vol. II, 1836). Covers Clive’s later career 1758–1767. Features the siege of Madras by Lally, the defeat of the Dutch in Bengal, the acquisition of the Diwani, and Clive’s reforms of the Bengal civil service. Read source page
Malcolm, John — Life of Robert, Lord Clive (Vol. III, 1836). Covers Clive’s final years 1766–1774. Features the white mutiny of the Bengal army, the salt monopoly controversy, the parliamentary inquiry, and Clive’s death. Read source page
Colquhoun, Patrick — A Treatise on Indigence (1806). A comprehensive analysis of poverty and poor relief in England, with historical data on population, poor rates, and the cost of relief from the Reformation through 1803. Features Gregory King’s 1688 social table. Read source page
Fleetwood, William — Chronicon Preciosum; or, An Account of English Gold and Silver Money, the Price of Corn and other Commodities, and of Things, before and after the Conquest (first published 1707; this edition 1745). Written to answer how much a fixed money sum (£5) in the reign of Henry VI was worth in the commodities of the day; establishes that £5 in Henry VI’s reign was of somewhat better value than £11 in 1745. Contains the history of English gold and silver coinage, a six-hundred-year price series of corn and other commodities, a survey of clerical stipends and wages, and an appendix with an Historical Account of Coins including tables of coin weights and finenesses and plates. A foundational reference in English numismatics and price history. Read source page
Massie, Joseph — An Essay on the Natural Rate of Interest (1750). A systematic refutation of Locke and Petty on interest, arguing the rate is governed by the profits of trade, not the quantity of money. Contains a table of wheat prices and interest rates across five periods (1444–1748) disproving Locke’s theory, and traces falling profits to increased competition among traders. Anticipated the classical theory of interest later developed by Adam Smith. Read source page
Hume, David — Of Money (1752). A classic essay on monetary theory, arguing money is merely a medium of exchange and developing the price-specie-flow mechanism. A foundational text of classical economics. Read source page
Hume, David — Political Discourses (1752). Hume’s collected economic and political essays, including Of Commerce, Of Money, Of Interest, Of the Balance of Trade, Of Public Credit, Of the Original Contract, and Idea of a Perfect Commonwealth. A foundational text of classical economics. Read source page
Smith, Adam — An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776). The foundational treatise of classical political economy: division of labour and extent of the market; real, money, natural, and market price; wages, profits, and rent; capital and productive labour; historical progress of opulence after Rome; critique of the mercantile system (restraints, bounties, drawbacks, treaties, colonies); physiocratic agricultural systems; sovereign expenses, taxes, and public debts. Full five-book working extract (pandoc plain, ~376k words). Read source page
Postlethwayt, Malachy — Britain’s Commercial Interest Explained and Improved (2 vols., 1757). A collection of 19 dissertations on British trade, agriculture, colonial administration, and the proposed union with Ireland, written during the Seven Years’ War. Features detailed analysis of the American colonies (£1.5M annual exports), Anglo-French rivalry, the case for Irish union (44 years before the 1801 Act), neutral trade and naval power, and the argument that cultivating waste lands (only half of England’s productive land was in use) would restore Britain’s competitiveness. Opens with Britain “reduced to a very melancholy state” in 1757. Read source page
Postlethwayt, Malachy — The Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce (4th ed., 2 vols., 1774). The first comprehensive English commercial dictionary, containing alphabetical entries on every branch of trade, manufacturing, navigation, and commercial law. Covers British and international commerce with extensive extracts from French edicts, Spanish regulations, and Dutch shipping practices. Updated to reflect the Treaty of Paris (1763). A primary source for mid-to-late 18th-century commercial knowledge, cited by Adam Smith in the Wealth of Nations. Read combined source page · Vol. I (A–K) · Vol. II (L–Z)
Burke, Edmund — Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770). Burke’s classic defence of party government, analysing the influence of the Crown and the “king’s friends” under George III. Read source page
Wakefield, Gilbert — A Reply to Some Parts of the Bishop of Landaff’s Address (1793). A radical critique of the war with Revolutionary France and the loyalist clergy, by the imprisoned Unitarian scholar. Read source page
Knox, Vicesimus — The Spirit of Despotism (written 1794–1795; published 1821/1822). A 41-section liberal Anglican critique of Crown influence, war, corruption, and the Pitt government’s repression of reform. Suppressed by Knox himself; published posthumously by William Hone. Read source page
Uglow, Jenny — The Lunar Men: The Friends Who Made the Future 1730–1810 (Faber and Faber, 2002). Group biography of the Lunar Society of Birmingham — Darwin, Boulton, Watt, Wedgwood, Priestley, and others — driving the industrial, chemical, and canal revolutions of the late eighteenth century. Read source page
Irving, Washington — The Life of Oliver Goldsmith, with Selections from His Writings, Vols I–II (A. L. Fowle, New York, 1900). Complete dual package: continuous biographical sketch (birth 1728–death 1774; Trinity, Edinburgh/Leyden wanderings, Griffiths & Newbery, Johnson circle, Traveller, Vicar, Deserted Village, She Stoops, Retaliation, Abbey monument) plus poetical extracts, Bee essays, full Citizen of the World selection (early letters in Vol. I; continued + Hingpo/Zelis strand in Vol. II), and miscellany (Hypatia, Asem, Shenstone, political frugality, national prejudice, taste). Read source page

Entities
Naval Commanders

George Anson, 1st Baron Anson (1697–1762) — Circumnavigator, victor of Cape Finisterre (1747), and reforming First Lord of the Admiralty. Read entity page
Edward Boscawen (1711–1761) — “Old Dreadnought,” captor of Louisbourg (1758) and victor at Lagos (1759). Read entity page
John Byng (1704–1757) — Admiral executed after the loss of Minorca (1756). Read entity page
George Byng, 1st Viscount Torrington (1663–1733) — Victor of Cape Passaro (1718), destroyer of the Spanish fleet, and First Lord of the Admiralty. Read entity page
John Byron (1723–1786) — “Foul-weather Jack,” circumnavigator, grandfather of the poet, West Indies commander. Read entity page
Adam Duncan, 1st Viscount Duncan (1731–1804) — Victor of Camperdown (1797), held the North Sea during the Nore mutiny. Read entity page
Edward Hawke, 1st Baron Hawke (1705–1781) — Victors of Quiberon Bay (1759) and master of the Western Squadron blockade. Read entity page
Richard Howe, 1st Earl Howe (1726–1799) — “Black Dick,” victor of the Glorious First of June (1794), negotiator of the Nore mutiny. Read entity page
John Jervis, 1st Earl of St Vincent (1735–1823) — Victor of Cape St Vincent (1797), reforming First Lord of the Admiralty, mentor of Nelson. Read entity page
Sir John Leake (1656–1720) — Captor of Sardinia and Minorca (1708), commander-in-chief in the Mediterranean. Read entity page
Horatio Nelson, 1st Viscount Nelson (1758–1805) — Victors of the Nile (1798), Copenhagen (1801), and Trafalgar (1805). Read entity page
Sir John Norris (c. 1660–1749) — Admiral of the Fleet, the longest-serving naval commander of the era, five Baltic commands. Read entity page
George Brydges Rodney, 1st Baron Rodney (1718–1792) — Victor of the Battle of the Saintes (1782), breaker of the line, reliever of Gibraltar. Read entity page
Sir George Rooke (1650–1709) — Captor of Gibraltar (1704) and victor at Vigo Bay (1702). Read entity page
Sir Cloudesley Shovel (1650–1707) — Mediterranean commander, Toulon blockade, drowned in the Scilly naval disaster. Read entity page
Edward Vernon (1684–1757) — Captor of Porto Bello (1739), controversial commander at Cartagena, and inventor of grog. Read entity page
Sir Charles Wager (1666–1743) — Captor of the Spanish treasure fleet (1708), First Lord of the Admiralty. Read entity page

Monarchs

Queen Anne (1665–1714, r. 1702–1714) — Last Stuart monarch, Act of Union 1707, War of the Spanish Succession. Read entity page
George I (1660–1727, r. 1714–1727) — First Hanoverian, Jacobite rising of 1715, South Sea Bubble, the Walpole era. Read entity page
George II (1683–1760, r. 1727–1760) — Last British monarch to lead troops in battle, the ‘45, Seven Years’ War. Read entity page
George III (1738–1820, r. 1760–1820) — Farmer George, loss of the American colonies, the Regency crisis, patronage of agriculture and the arts. Read entity page

Politicians and Statesmen

Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke (1678–1751) — Tory statesman, architect of the Treaty of Utrecht, Jacobite exile, author of The Idea of a Patriot King. Read entity page
Edmund Burke (1729–1797) — Political philosopher of party government, Reflections on the Revolution in France, impeachment of Warren Hastings. Read entity page
Charles James Fox (1749–1806) — Whig statesman, rival of Pitt, supporter of the American and French Revolutions. Read entity page
George Grenville (1712–1770) — Prime Minister, author of the Stamp Act (1765), champion of parliamentary sovereignty over the colonies. Read entity page
Robert Harley, 1st Earl of Oxford (1661–1724) — Moderate Tory Lord Treasurer under Anne, rival of Bolingbroke, South Sea Company director. Read entity page
John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough (1650–1722) — Captain-General of the Grand Alliance, victor of Blenheim, Ramillies, Oudenarde, and Malplaquet. Read entity page
Frederick North, 2nd Earl of Guilford (1732–1792) — Prime Minister during the American Revolutionary War, loss of the American colonies. Read entity page
William Pitt, 1st Earl of Chatham (1708–1778) — “The Great Commoner,” architect of the Seven Years’ War strategy that delivered British global supremacy. Read entity page
William Pitt the Younger (1759–1806) — Youngest Prime Minister, financial reform, French Revolutionary Wars, Union with Ireland. Read entity page
Charles Townshend (1725–1767) — Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Townshend Acts (1767), “Champagne Charley.” Read entity page
Robert Walpole, 1st Earl of Orford (1676–1745) — First de facto Prime Minister, master of the South Sea Bubble crisis, twenty-year Whig supremacy. Read entity page
John Wilkes (1725–1797) — Radical politician, the North Briton No. 45, Middlesex elections, champion of English liberties. Read entity page

Colonial and Military Commanders

Robert Clive, 1st Baron Clive (1725–1774) — “Clive of India,” victor of Plassey (1757), architect of British dominion in Bengal. Read entity page
Sir Eyre Coote (1726–1783) — Victor of Wandiwash (1760), Commander-in-Chief in India, the ablest British officer of his generation in the East. Read entity page
Prince William Augustus, Duke of Cumberland (1721–1765) — “Butcher Cumberland,” victor of Culloden (1746), commander at Dettingen and Fontenoy. Read entity page
Warren Hastings (1732–1818) — First Governor-General of Bengal, impeached by Burke, defender of the Company’s Indian empire. Read entity page
Charles Edward Stuart (1720–1788) — “Bonnie Prince Charlie,” Jacobite claimant, leader of the ‘45 Rising, Culloden and the escape to Skye. Read entity page
General James Wolfe (1727–1759) — Victors of Quebec (1759) and the Plains of Abraham, died securing British Canada. Read entity page

Intellectuals and Historians

William Belsham (1752–1827) — Whig historian, Memoirs of the Reign of George III (5 vols.) and History of Great Britain (12 vols.). Read entity page
Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715) — Bishop of Salisbury, Whig historian of the Glorious Revolution, History of His Own Time. Read entity page
John Campbell (1708–1775) — Scottish naval historian, Lives of the Admirals, Naval History of Great Britain. Read entity page
Patrick Colquhoun (1745–1820) — Scottish merchant, magistrate, and statistician; Treatise on the Police of the Metropolis, pioneer of poverty measurement. Read entity page
David Hume (1711–1776) — Philosopher, historian, and economist; Political Discourses (1752), History of England, and the price-specie-flow mechanism. Read entity page
Joseph Massie (d. 1784) — Economic pamphleteer, Essay on the Natural Rate of Interest (1750), pioneer of data-driven economics. Read entity page
Malachy Postlethwayt (c. 1707–1767) — Economic writer, Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce, mercantilist theorist and critic of the slave trade. Read entity page
Adam Smith (1723–1790) — Moral philosopher and father of political economy; The Wealth of Nations (1776), division of labour, free trade. Read entity page
Tobias Smollett (1721–1771) — Scottish novelist and historian, Complete History of England, Humphry Clinker, Tory historiographer. Read entity page
James Watt (1736–1819) — Scottish engineer, inventor of the separate condenser, partner in Boulton & Watt, transformed steam power. Read entity page

Institutions

Bank of England (1694) — Founder of modern central banking, manager of the national debt, lender of last resort. Read entity page
East India Company (1600–1874) — From trading monopoly to territorial empire, Clive and the Diwani, the Hastings impeachment. Read entity page
The Lunar Society (c. 1765–1813) — The “Lunar Men” of Birmingham, informal circle of industrialists and thinkers driving the Industrial Revolution. Read entity page
South Sea Company (1711–1853) — Harley’s financial innovation, the South Sea Bubble (1720), and the crisis that made Walpole. Read entity page

Places

Bengal — Richest Mughal province, centre of British Indian empire, site of Plassey, the Diwani, and the Great Famine of 1770. Read entity page
Gibraltar — British fortress since 1704, the Great Siege (1779–83), key to Mediterranean naval dominance. Read entity page
Plassey — Village in Bengal, site of the Battle of Plassey (1757) where Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah. Read entity page
Quebec — Capital of French Canada, captured by Wolfe in 1759, defended against American invasion in 1775. Read entity page

Concepts
Political, Constitutional, and Financial

The Anglo-French Rivalry — The central geopolitical conflict: four great wars with France from 1702 to 1802, fought across Europe, America, India, and the seas for imperial and commercial supremacy. Read concept page
The British Constitution — The mixed and balanced constitution of king, lords, and commons; the Glorious Revolution settlement; the 18th-century understanding of liberty, law, and parliamentary sovereignty. Read concept page
The Fiscal-Military State — The system of taxation, borrowing, and military administration that underwrote Britain’s rise as a great power — excise, land tax, the Admiralty, Pitt’s income tax. Read concept page
The Jacobite Threat and the Highlands — The Stuart claim to the throne, the ‘15 and ‘45 risings, the Highland clan system, Culloden, and the post-‘45 destruction of the clan order. Read concept page
The National Debt and Public Credit — The funding system, the South Sea crisis, Walpole’s restoration, Pitt’s Sinking Fund, and the century-long debate over the sustainability of public borrowing. Read concept page
Parliamentary Patronage and Old Corruption — The system of crown patronage, placement, rotten boroughs, treasury influence, and sinecures that shaped 18th-century political life. Read concept page
Party Government and the Court-Country Divide — From Bolingbroke’s Patriot King to Burke’s defence of party; the Whig supremacy, the Fox-North coalition, and Pitt’s Tory revival. Read concept page
Radicalism and Popular Politics — The Wilkesite movement, Wyvill’s county associations, the London Corresponding Society, Paine’s Rights of Man, and the government crackdown of the 1790s. Read concept page

Imperial, Economic, and Social

The Atlantic System and Colonial Trade — The Navigation Acts, triangular trade, the American colonies as market, the West Indies, and the economic structure of the first British Empire. Read concept page
British India and the Company Raj — The transformation of the East India Company from merchant to sovereign; Plassey, the Diwani, the Hastings impeachment, and Pitt’s dual system of 1784. Read concept page
The Industrial Transformation — Newcomen and Watt’s steam engines, the Lunar Society, iron and coal, the textile revolution, and the emergence of the factory system. Read concept page
Ireland and the Protestant Ascendancy — The penal laws, Grattan’s Parliament, the United Irishmen, the 1798 Rebellion, and the Act of Union 1800. Read concept page
Naval Power and Maritime Strategy — The Royal Navy: dockyards, impressment, the Western Squadron, the line of battle, prize money, and the administrative infrastructure of sea power. Read concept page
Political Economy — From Massie and Hume’s critique of mercantilism to Smith’s Wealth of Nations; the quantity theory of money, free trade, and the economic debates of the century. Read concept page
Poverty and the Poor Laws — The parish poor relief system, the Laws of Settlement, the workhouse, Speenhamland, friendly societies, and the growth of the poor rates from 1601 to 1803. Read concept page
Slavery and the Abolition Movement — The British slave trade, the plantation system, Dolben’s Act, Wilberforce’s parliamentary campaign, and the moral and economic debates over abolition. Read concept page

Events
Union and Succession (1707–1716)

Act of Union 1707 (1707) — The union of England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain. Diplomatic negotiations, Scottish parliamentary debate, the securing of Presbyterian and Episcopal settlements, and the creation of a united parliament and free trade area. Read event page
Treaty of Utrecht (1713) — The Peace of Utrecht ending the War of the Spanish Succession. Britain gained Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, the Hudson Bay territory, and the Asiento slave trade monopoly. Marked Britain’s emergence as a global power. Read event page
Jacobite Rising of 1715 (1715–1716) — The ‘Fifteen — the first major Jacobite attempt to restore the Stuart line. The Earl of Mar raised the standard at Braemar, the indecisive Battle of Sheriffmuir, the surrender at Preston, and the collapse of the rising upon the arrival of the Pretender too late. Read event page
Septennial Act 1716 (1716) — Extended the maximum duration of Parliament from three to seven years. Passed by the Whig government after the ‘15 rising to reduce electoral instability, it entrenched Whig dominance for a generation. Read event page

Walpole Era and Mid-Century Conflict (1718–1748)

Battle of Cape Passaro (11 August 1718) — Admiral George Byng’s destruction of the Spanish fleet off Sicily. Fought before the formal declaration of war, it established British naval supremacy in the Mediterranean and ended Spanish ambitions in Italy. Read event page
South Sea Bubble (1720) — The spectacular rise and catastrophic collapse of the South Sea Company’s share price. A mania of speculation that engulfed the political class, led to a parliamentary inquiry, and propelled Robert Walpole to power as the first de facto Prime Minister. Read event page
Excise Crisis (1733) — Walpole’s proposed excise tax on tobacco and wine provoked a furious popular and parliamentary opposition. Walpole was forced to withdraw the bill — it was the first great test of his ministry and a rare defeat for the Robinocracy. Read event page
War of Jenkins’ Ear (1739–1742) — The war with Spain triggered by Captain Jenkins’s severed ear. The popular clamour for revenge forced Walpole into an unwanted war. Vernon’s capture of Porto Bello (1739) raised British spirits, but the disastrous Cartagena expedition (1741) demoralised the nation. Read event page
Cartagena Expedition (March–April 1741) — The largest amphibious expedition of the 18th century, 27,000 men against the Spanish fortress of Cartagena. A catastrophic failure due to disease, poor co-ordination, and Spanish defences under Blas de Lezo; 80–90% of the British force died. Read event page
Jacobite Rising of 1745 (1745–1746) — The ‘Forty-Five — Prince Charles Edward Stuart’s daring march from the Highlands to Derby, the Jacobite army’s retreat, and the final defeat at Culloden. The most serious threat to the Hanoverian succession. Read event page
Battle of Culloden (16 April 1746) — The final battle of the Jacobite rising of 1745. Cumberland’s disciplined government forces destroyed the exhausted Jacobite army in 40 minutes. The brutal pacification of the Highlands followed. Read event page
Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) — The peace ending the War of the Austrian Succession. Britain returned Louisbourg to France in exchange for Madras, a deeply unpopular concession that produced the cry ‘No peace without Louisbourg!’ Read event page

The Seven Years’ War (1756–1763)

Loss of Minorca (1756) — The French capture of the British Mediterranean base of Minorca. The subsequent court-martial and execution of Admiral John Byng for failing to ‘do his utmost’ — Voltaire’s pour encourager les autres. Read event page
Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757) — Robert Clive’s victory over Siraj-ud-Daulah in Bengal. A small engagement that established British military supremacy in India and laid the foundation of the British Raj. Read event page
Capture of Louisbourg (1758) — The siege and capture of the French fortress of Louisbourg, the key to the St Lawrence. A major amphibious operation led by Boscawen and Amherst that opened the seaway to Quebec. Read event page
Capture of Quebec (September 1759) — Wolfe’s daring ascent of the cliffs at Anse-au-Foulon and the Battle of the Plains of Abraham. Both Wolfe and the French commander Montcalm died. The battle decided the fate of Canada. Read event page
Battle of Quiberon Bay (20 November 1759) — Hawke’s daring pursuit of the French Brest fleet into the rocky Bay of Quiberon in a winter gale. The Royal Navy’s most brilliant tactical victory of the century; it destroyed French invasion plans and secured British naval supremacy for the remainder of the war. Read event page
Peace of Paris 1763 (1763) — The treaty ending the Seven Years’ War. Britain gained Canada, Florida, and supremacy in India; France ceded the Mississippi Valley. The peace marked Britain’s zenith as a global power — and planted the seeds of the American Revolution. Read event page

The American Crisis (1763–1776)

Wilkes Affair (1763–1774) — John Wilkes’s North Briton No. 45, his successive expulsions from Parliament, and the Middlesex election dispute. A landmark struggle for the liberty of the press, the right of electors, and the authority of Parliament. Read event page
Stamp Act Crisis (1765–1766) — Grenville’s Stamp Act provoked the first great colonial protest, the Stamp Act Congress, and the cry of ‘no taxation without representation.’ Repealed by the Rockingham ministry, but the Declaratory Act affirmed Parliament’s supremacy. Read event page
Boston Massacre (5 March 1770) — British soldiers fired into a Boston crowd, killing five. The ‘massacre’ became a defining propaganda event for the American patriot cause; Captain Preston and his men were defended by John Adams. Read event page
Boston Tea Party (16 December 1773) — American colonists dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston Harbour to protest the Tea Act. The British response — the Coercive Acts — drove the colonies toward revolution. Read event page
Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776) — The Second Continental Congress declared the Thirteen Colonies independent states, no longer part of the British Empire. Jefferson’s Declaration articulated the principles of the American Revolution and permanently severed the colonial bond. Read event page

The American War of Independence (1776–1783)

Saratoga Campaign (September–October 1777) — Burgoyne’s invasion from Canada ended in disaster at Saratoga. The American victory persuaded France to enter the war as an ally of the United States, transforming a colonial rebellion into a global conflict. Read event page
Gordon Riots (2–9 June 1780) — The most destructive urban riots in 18th-century London. Lord George Gordon’s Protestant Association marched on Parliament to protest Catholic relief; six days of arson and looting, 285 killed, the Bank of England and Newgate Prison attacked. Read event page
Siege of Yorktown (September–October 1781) — Washington and Rochambeau trapped Cornwallis’s army at Yorktown, Virginia, while de Grasse’s fleet blockaded the Chesapeake. The surrender effectively ended the American Revolutionary War and signalled the loss of Britain’s first empire. Read event page
Treaty of Paris 1783 (3 September 1783) — The definitive peace ending the American War of Independence. Britain recognised American independence, ceded Florida to Spain, Tobago and Senegal to France. Shelburne’s settlement was attacked as too generous. Read event page

Pitt’s Ministry and Reform (1784–1793)

Pitt’s India Act 1784 (1784) — Pitt’s East India Act established the Board of Control, creating the dual government of India by Company and Crown. It followed the Fox-North India Bill’s defeat and the King’s dismissal of the coalition. The system lasted until 1858. Read event page
Impeachment of Warren Hastings (1788–1795) — Burke’s seven-year impeachment of the former Governor-General of Bengal before the House of Lords. The greatest state trial of the century, Hastings was eventually acquitted, but the trial established that imperial officials were accountable to Parliament. Read event page
Regency Crisis (1788–1789) — George III’s first episode of mental illness (porphyria). Pitt’s ministry faced the prospect of a Foxite Regency under the Prince of Wales. The King’s dramatic recovery in February 1789 saved Pitt and damaged Fox. Read event page
French Revolution: British Reaction (1789–1793) — The fierce British debate over the French Revolution. Burke’s Reflections against Paine’s Rights of Man; the Revolution Controversy; the London Corresponding Society; the government crackdown — the Treason Trials, Habeas Corpus suspension, and the Two Acts. Read event page

The French Revolutionary Wars (1793–1801)

War of the First Coalition (1793–1797) — The first great coalition against Revolutionary France. Britain, Austria, Prussia, Spain, and Holland against the French Republic. From Pitt’s declaration of war, through the Flanders disaster and the fall of Toulon, to the Glorious First of June and the collapse of the coalition. Read event page
Glorious First of June (1 June 1794) — The first major naval battle of the French Revolutionary Wars. Admiral Lord Howe’s Channel Fleet defeated the French Atlantic fleet under Villaret-Joyeuse, capturing or destroying seven French ships. Though the French grain convoy escaped, the battle established British naval dominance. Read event page
Irish Rebellion of 1798 (May–September 1798) — The United Irishmen’s rising against the Anglican Ascendancy. Wexford, Antrim, and Down rose; French landings at Killala; Vinegar Hill; government brutal suppression. Wolfe Tone captured and died by suicide. The rebellion drove Pitt toward the Act of Union. Read event page
Act of Union 1800 (1800, effective 1 January 1801) — The union of Great Britain and Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The Irish Parliament voted itself out of existence after a campaign of systematic bribery; 100 Irish MPs and 32 peers went to Westminster. Pitt resigned when George III vetoed Catholic emancipation. Read event page

Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. X
William Belsham (1752–1827) — History of Great Britain, from the Revolution, 1688, to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Amiens, 1802. — In Twelve Volumes. Volume X. Printed for R. Phillips, London, 1805.
This is Volume X of Belsham’s 12-volume History of Great Britain, covering 1795–1798 — the middle years of the French Revolutionary War. It fills the gap between Belsham Memoirs Vol. V (1793–1796) and Belsham History Vol. XI (1798–1800).

Scope: Covers 1795–1798 — the Two Acts (Treason and Sedition Bills), the King attacked by the mob, the Italian campaign of the young Bonaparte (Lodi, Arcole, Rivoli), the Peace of Leoben, the destruction of Venice, the Irish Rebellion of 1798, and the Battle of the Nile.
Book-by-Book Summary
BOOK XXII — The Two Acts and the Italian Campaign (1795–1796)

The session of 1795–6 — the King attacked by the mob, the public alarm
The Treason and Sedition Bills (the “Two Acts”) — Pitt’s crackdown on radical meetings and speech, the great Fox-Sheridan opposition, the county petitions
Mr. Whitbread’s bill to fix the price of labour
Pitt’s extravagant loans — the financial strain of the war, the sinking fund
The French campaign in Italy (1796) — Bonaparte’s first Italian campaign, the victories at Montenotte, Millesimo, Lodi
The King of Sardinia compelled to peace
The French occupy Leghorn, Bologna, Urbino, Ferrara
Bonaparte’s victories at Castiglione, Arcole — Wurmser takes refuge in Mantua
The Cispadane Confederacy
Lord Malmesbury’s failed peace mission to Paris

BOOK XXIII — The Peace of Leoben and the First Coalition’s Collapse (1796–1797)

The session of 1796–7 — the continuation of the war
The capitulation of Mantua — the fall of the last Austrian stronghold in Italy
Bonaparte enters the Ecclesiastical States — the plunder of Loretto
The Peace of Tolentino with the Pope
The Preliminaries of Leoben (April 1797) — the Austrians sue for peace
The subversion of the Venetian Republic — Bonaparte’s destruction of the ancient republic
The subversion of the Genoese government — the foundation of the Cisalpine Republic
The naval mutinies at Spithead and the Nore
The Irish crisis — the Earl of Moira’s motion, the growing rebellion in Ireland
The French descent on the Welsh coast

BOOK XXIV — The Irish Rebellion and the Nile (1797–1798)

The session of 1797–8 — the secession of the opposition majority
The restrictions on the Bank continued — the financial crisis
The Irish Rebellion of 1798 — the arrest of the Irish Directory, the Battle of New Ross, the defeat of the rebels at Enniscorthy
The suppression of the rebellion in the south and north
Lord Cornwallis appointed Chief Governor
The French landing in Killala Bay — the French force in the west
The rebellion suppressed by Cornwallis
The trial of Arthur O’Connor
The prosecution of Gilbert Wakefield
Bonaparte’s expedition to Egypt (1798) — the victory of the Pyramids, the capture of Cairo
The Battle of the Nile (Aboukir Bay, August 1798) — Nelson’s total destruction of the French fleet
The extraordinary effects of Nelson’s victory — the Second Coalition formed, the isolation of Bonaparte’s army in Egypt
Mr. Fox struck out of the Privy Council — the political fall-out

sources/belsham-history-vol11.title: Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. XI
sources/belsham-history-vol11.content:
Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. XI
William Belsham (1752–1827) — History of Great Britain, from the Revolution, 1688, to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Amiens, 1802. — In Twelve Volumes. Volume XI. Printed for G. & J. Robinson, London, 1804.
This is Volume XI of Belsham’s comprehensive 12-volume History of Great Britain, covering 1798–1800 — the climactic middle years of the French Revolutionary War. It fills the gap between the end of Belsham Memoirs Vol. V (1796) and the start of Belsham History Vol. XII (1800).
The volume contains 456 page-files (OCR’d from the New York Public Library copy, barcode 33433066658638), extracted as 15,267 lines (~615 KB) of plain text.
Scope: Covers 1798–1800 — the Irish Rebellion and the Act of Union, the Second Coalition, Suvaroff’s campaigns in Italy, the siege of Acre, the Battle of the Nile’s aftermath, the Income Tax, the fall of Tippoo Sultan at Seringapatam, and the political crisis over the Union with Ireland.
Book-by-Book Summary
BOOK XXXI — The Income Tax and the Union Debates (1798–1799)

The session of Parliament 1798–9 — the King’s speech, the address, the war situation
Tierney’s motion for peace — the Opposition’s attempt to negotiate with France
The Habeas Corpus suspension renewed — the debate on the state prisoners, the case of Colonel Despard
The Income Tax imposed — Pitt’s revolutionary new tax on income, the principle of raising supplies within the year, the debates on the commercial clauses
The loan of £15 million — the financing of the war
The Union with Ireland — the King’s message recommending the Union, Pitt’s great speech in favour, the proposed terms, the resolutions
The campaign in Europe — Suvaroff’s victories in Italy, the Battle of the Adda, the entry into Milan, the Battle of Zurich, Massena’s triumphs
The siege of Acre (1799) — Sir Sydney Smith’s defence, Bonaparte’s repeated assaults, the failure of the siege, the French retreat into Egypt
Bonaparte’s victory over the Turks at Aboukir
Tippoo Sultan — his deceitful professions of friendship, Lord Mornington’s (Wellesley) remonstrance, the assembling of forces at Vellore

BOOK XXXII — The War and the Union (1799)

The continuation of the military campaign — Suvaroff in Switzerland, the Battle of Constance, the Battle of Genola
The surrender of Ancona and Coni
The junction of the French and Spanish fleets
The Irish Union debates in detail — the speeches of Grattan, the opposition in the Irish Parliament
The government determined to persevere despite Irish hostility
The affairs of India — the crisis with Tippoo Sultan

BOOK XXXIII — The Conclusion of the Campaign (1799–1800)

The final stages of the European campaign
The Legislative Union debate and passage
The affairs of India resolved
The volume closes with the situation at the end of 1799, leading into the events covered by Vol. XII (1800–1802)

sources/belsham-history-vol12.title: Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. XII
sources/belsham-history-vol12.content:
Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. XII
William Belsham (1752–1827) — History of Great Britain, from the Revolution, 1688, to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Amiens, 1802. — In Twelve Volumes. Volume XII. Printed for Richard Phillips, No. 6, Bridge-Street, Black-Friars, London, 1805.
This is the final volume (XII) of Belsham’s comprehensive history of Great Britain, covering the climactic closing years of the French Revolutionary Wars (1800–1802) , from the breakdown of armistice negotiations through the Peace of Amiens. It is the latest chronological source in this wiki, pushing coverage into the first years of the 19th century.
Belsham was a noted English political and historical writer, a dissenter and supporter of parliamentary reform, whose 12-volume work provides a detailed Whig-leaning account of British affairs from the Glorious Revolution to the Peace of Amiens.
The volume contains 662 page-files (OCR’d from the Waukesha Public Library copy, via the University of Wisconsin system), extracted as 23,962 lines (~1 MB) of plain text.
Scope: This volume covers barely three years (1800–1802) but they are among the most eventful of the war — the change of ministry from Pitt to Addington, Nelson’s victory at Copenhagen, the dissolution of the Armed Neutrality, the conquest of Egypt, the assassination of Kleber, the Peace of Amiens, and the brief interval of European peace.
Book-by-Book Summary
BOOK XXXIV — Armistice Negotiations and the Egyptian Campaign (line 523, ~7,000 lines)
Opens with the peace negotiations between Lord Grenville and M. Otto, the French agent in London. Key topics:

Negotiation for a naval armistice (1800) — the diplomatic contest between Grenville and Otto, the French demand for a maritime truce as a condition for extending the continental armistice, the British refusal
The Convention of Hohenlinden — the French victory over Austria, the collapse of the Second Coalition on the continent
The blockade of Malta — the two-year siege of the French garrison at La Valette, the British naval blockade, the surrender of the island (September 1800)
Loss of the Queen Charlotte — Lord Keith’s 120-gun flagship destroyed by fire off Leghorn (March 1800), one of the finest vessels in the navy lost
Actions off the French coast — Sir Edward Pellew’s cruise off Bretagne, the capture of French store-ships
The vengeance on Cesenatico — a punitive expedition against the Italian town for harbouring French privateers
The abortive attempt on Ferrol and the unsuccessful demonstration at Cadiz
The Egyptian campaign in retrospect — the march of the Grand Vizier from Syria, Kleber’s attempt to negotiate the evacuation of Egypt
The Convention of El Arisch (January 1800) — the agreement for the French evacuation of Egypt, its subsequent repudiation
The Battle of Heliopolis (March 1800) — Kleber’s stunning victory over the Turkish army
The assassination of General Kleber (June 1800) — the death of Napoleon’s most capable general in Egypt
The election of Pope Pius VII and the death of Field-Marshal Suvaroff
Public honours paid to Lord Nelson for his Mediterranean victories
The Battle of Hohenlinden (December 1800) — Moreau’s decisive victory over the Austrians, leading to the Convention of Steyer and the effective end of the war on the continent
The misunderstanding between Great Britain and Denmark — the seeds of the Armed Neutrality crisis

BOOK XXXV — The Armed Neutrality, the Change of Ministry, and the Conquest of Egypt (line ~9,500, ~7,500 lines)
The most eventful book in the volume. Key topics:

The Armed Neutrality of the North (1800–1801) — the revival of the League by Tsar Paul I of Russia, joined by Sweden, Denmark, and Prussia; the British embargo on Russian, Swedish, and Danish shipping
The rupture with the Baltic powers — the grounds of the war with the Northern Confederacy, the British decision to force the Sound
The Battle of Copenhagen (2 April 1801) — Nelson’s victory over the Danish fleet, his famous disregard of Parker’s signal, the armistice, the dissolution of the League
The death of the Emperor Paul (March 1801) — the assassination of the Tsar, the accession of Alexander I, the complete reversal of Russian policy
The Treaty of Luneville (February 1801) — the peace between France and Austria, confirming the Rhine frontier
The King of Prussia seizes Hanover — the Prussian occupation of the Electorate, the British response
The change of ministry (1801) — Pitt’s resignation over Catholic Emancipation and the Union with Ireland, the formation of Addington’s ministry
The first session of the Imperial Parliament (1801) — the first Parliament of the united Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
The expedition to Egypt (1801) — Sir Ralph Abercrombie’s amphibious landing, the Battle of Alexandria (March 1801), the death of Abercrombie, the arrival of General Baird’s Indian army
The surrender of Alexandria and the final conquest of Egypt from the French
The preliminaries of peace signed (October 1801) — the framework for the Peace of Amiens
The reduction of the Danish West India islands
Victory of Sir James Saumarez in the Mediterranean
The heroic defence of Porto Ferrajo (Elba)
The threats of invasion — the French flotilla at Boulogne, the British counter-attacks

BOOK XXXVI — The Peace of Amiens and the Postwar Settlement (line ~14,500, ~9,500 lines)
The final book, covering the negotiation, ratification, and aftermath of the Peace of Amiens. Key topics:

The session of Parliament 1801–1802 — the address, the preliminary debates
The violent debates on the preliminaries of peace — the opposition’s attack on the terms, the government’s defence
The Definitive Treaty of Amiens (March 1802) — the terms of the peace between Britain and France, Spain, and the Batavian Republic
Observations on the Treaty of Amiens — Belsham’s own critical assessment of the peace
The income tax repealed — Addington’s popular measure
The state of the national finances — the cost of the war, the debt
Bonaparte elected President of the Italian Republic — the extension of French influence in Italy
The King’s debts a sixth time paid — the ongoing royal financial controversies
The claim of the Prince of Wales as Duke of Cornwall
Debates on the definitive treaty in both houses of Parliament
The disastrous expedition to St. Domingo — the French attempt to reconquer Haiti, the yellow fever catastrophe
The abdication of the King of Sardinia and the annexation of Piedmont to France
The critical situation of Malta — the dispute over the evacuation of the island, the seed of the next war
The civil dissensions in Switzerland — the French armed mediation
Bonaparte declared First Consul for Life (August 1802) — the consolidation of Napoleonic power
The plot of Colonel Despard — the conspiracy against the British government
The ratification and celebration of the Concordat — the reconciliation between France and the Catholic Church
Mr. Fox visits Paris — the famous opposition leader’s tour of Napoleonic France
The election of Mr. Jefferson to the Presidency of the United States
The appendix containing statistical and documentary material

Key Data Points

























































AttributeDetailAuthorWilliam Belsham (1752–1827)Full titleHistory of Great Britain, from the Revolution, 1688, to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Amiens, 1802VolumeXII (final volume)Year published1805PublisherRichard Phillips, Bridge-Street, Black-Friars, LondonSource libraryWaukesha Public Library / University of Wisconsin (barcode 89007051949)Raw filewiki/raw/belsham-history-vol12.txtLines23,962Page files662Period covered1800–1802StyleWhig-leaning parliamentary history with detailed political analysisOCR qualityGood. Text is readable. Some library stamps on early pages.
Relationship to Other Sources
This is the latest chronological source in the wiki — covering the very end of the 18th century / first years of the 19th. It picks up where Campbell Vol. VII leaves off:




















SourcePeriodFocusCampbell Vol. VII1780–1802Naval operations of the French Revolutionary Wars, to Peace of AmiensBelsham Vol. XII1800–1802Political, diplomatic, and military history — the Armistice negotiations, Copenhagen, the change of ministry, the conquest of Egypt, the Peace of Amiens
While Campbell Vol. VII covers the same period from a naval perspective (the Glorious First of June, Cape St. Vincent, the Nile, Copenhagen), Belsham provides the political and diplomatic context — the Addington ministry, the Parliamentary debates, the armistice negotiations, the Egyptian campaign from the army’s perspective, and the domestic impact of the war. The two volumes are complementary for building entity pages (Pitt, Addington, Nelson, Abercrombie, Bonaparte) and concept pages (the Armed Neutrality, the Peace of Amiens, the Union of 1801).

Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. II
William Belsham (1752–1827) — History of Great Britain, from the Revolution, 1688, to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Amiens, 1802. — In Twelve Volumes. Volume II. Printed for R. Phillips, London, 1805.

sources/belsham-history-vol4.title: Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. IV
sources/belsham-history-vol4.content:
Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. IV
William Belsham (1752–1827) — History of Great Britain, from the Revolution, 1688, to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Amiens, 1802. — In Twelve Volumes. Volume IV. Printed for R. Phillips, London, 1805.
This is Volume IV of Belsham’s comprehensive 12-volume History of Great Britain (the same series as Vol. XII already in this wiki). It covers the reign of George II (1727–1760) in detail, from the crisis of 1738 that led to the War of Jenkins’ Ear through the death of George II and the accession of George III.
The volume contains 594 page-files (OCR’d from the University of Wisconsin / Waukesha Public Library copy, barcode 89095774774), extracted as 20,725 lines (~830 KB) of plain text.
Scope: Covers 1738–1760 — the fall of Walpole, the War of Jenkins’ Ear, the War of the Austrian Succession, the Jacobite rising of 1745, the Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle, the diplomatic revolution, and the Seven Years’ War (including Plassey, Quebec, and Quiberon Bay). It overlaps with Campbell Vol. IV’s period but provides the general political, diplomatic, and land-warfare perspective.
Book-by-Book Summary
BOOK X — The Fall of Walpole and the War of Jenkins’ Ear (1738–1744)

Session of January 1738 — the debate on the land forces, the growing opposition to Walpole
Spanish depredations in the West Indies — the guarda-costas, the ear of Jenkins, the merchants’ grievances
The Convention of the Prado (1739) — the attempt at diplomatic settlement, the £95,000 indemnity
The debate on the convention — Walpole’s reluctant defence, Pitt’s attack, the Opposition’s fury
War declared against Spain (October 1739) — “no search, no seizure”
Vernon’s capture of Porto Bello (November 1739) — the overwhelming popular enthusiasm
The disastrous Cartagena expedition (1741) — Vernon and Wentworth’s failure, the devastating losses to disease
Anson’s circumnavigation — the capture of the Manila galleon
The War of the Austrian Succession begins (1740) — Frederick the Great’s invasion of Silesia, Maria Theresa’s appeal to Hungary, “Moriamur pro rege nostro Maria Theresa!”
The fall of Sir Robert Walpole (1742) — the end of the longest ministry in British history
The schism among the Patriots — the collapse of the opposition coalition
The Battle of Dettingen (1743) — George II at the head of the army, the last British monarch to command in battle
The naval engagement off Toulon (1744) — the failure of Admiral Mathews, the subsequent court-martial
Lord Carteret’s resignation and the formation of the Pelham ministry

BOOK XI — The ‘45 and the Peace (1744–1748)

The Jacobite rising of 1745 — Charles Edward Stuart’s landing in Scotland, the march to Derby
The Battle of Prestonpans — the Highland charge destroys Cope’s army
The retreat from Derby — the fateful decision to turn back
The Battle of Falkirk — the second Jacobite victory
Cumberland’s campaign — the brutal suppression, the Battle of Culloden (April 1746)
The aftermath — the trials and executions, the pacification of the Highlands
The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) — the return of Louisbourg, the general peace

BOOK XII — The Peace and the Prelude to the Seven Years’ War (1748–1754)

The administration of Henry Pelham — peace and economy
The Regency Act of 1751 — the crisis after the death of the Prince of Wales
The reform of the calendar — the adoption of the Gregorian calendar (1752)
The foundation of Halifax, Nova Scotia
The Convention of Madrid — settling the Spanish disputes
The interest on the public funds reduced
The act for the encouragement of the British fisheries
The rise of William Pitt — his emergence as a leading Commons figure
The death of Henry Pelham (1754) and the succession of the Duke of Newcastle

BOOK XIII — The Seven Years’ War (1755–1760)

The diplomatic revolution — the reversal of alliances, the Treaty of Westminster with Prussia, the Franco-Austrian alliance
Braddock’s defeat in America — the disaster on the Monongahela
The loss of Minorca (1756) — Admiral Byng’s failure, his court-martial and execution
The fall of Newcastle (1756) — the formation of the Devonshire-Pitt ministry
The campaign of 1757 — the Rochefort expedition, the Battle of Hastenbeck, the Convention of Klosterzeven, the fall of Hanover
Pitt’s return to power (1757) — the Pitt-Newcastle coalition
The capture of Louisbourg (1758) — Boscawen’s triumph, the opening of the St. Lawrence
The Battle of Plassey (1757) — Clive’s victory, the foundation of British India
The operations in Germany — the Battles of Rossbach and Leuthen, Frederick’s survival
The Battle of Wandewash and the capture of Pondicherry — the destruction of French power in India
The capture of Quebec (1759) — Wolfe’s victory and death, the annus mirabilis
The Battle of Quiberon Bay (1759) — Hawke’s destruction of the French fleet
The conquest of Canada — the fall of Montreal (1760)
The death of George II (October 1760) — a character of the king, the state of literature and the arts during his reign

sources/belsham-history-vol6.title: Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. VI
sources/belsham-history-vol6.content:
Belsham — History of Great Britain, Vol. VI
William Belsham (1752–1827) — History of Great Britain, from the Revolution, 1688, to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Amiens, 1802. — In Twelve Volumes. Volume VI. Printed for R. Phillips, London, 1805.
This is Volume VI of Belsham’s 12-volume History of Great Britain, covering the American Revolutionary crisis and the first years of the war (1768–1778) . It fills the 1775–1778 gap between Belsham Memoirs Vol. II (ending 1774) and Belsham Memoirs Vol. III (starting 1779).
The volume contains 572 page-files (OCR’d from the University of Wisconsin / Waukesha Public Library copy, barcode 89095774782), extracted as 20,336 lines (~840 KB) of plain text.
Scope: Covers 1768–1778 — from the Boston Massacre and the Townshend crisis through the Declaration of Independence, the campaign of 1776–77, and the surrender of Burgoyne at Saratoga, to the French alliance and the opening of the global war.
Book-by-Book Summary
BOOK XVI — The Road to Revolution (1768–1774)

Review of American transactions — the deterioration of relations after the Townshend duties
The Massachusetts Circular Letter (1768) — the assembly’s defiance, Lord Hillsborough’s demand to rescind, the dissolution of the assembly
The occupation of Boston by British troops (1768) — 14 ships of war in the harbour, troops landing with bayonets fixed
The Virginia Resolves and the non-importation agreements
The partial repeal of the Townshend duties — Lord North’s retention of the tea duty
The Boston Massacre (March 1770) — the killing of five civilians, the trial of Captain Preston, the defence by John Adams
The Gaspee affair (1772) — the burning of the British revenue schooner
The Committees of Correspondence — the colonial network of resistance
The Hutchinson letters affair — Franklin’s exposure of the governor’s private correspondence, Wedderburn’s attack on Franklin
The Tea Act and the Boston Tea Party (December 1773) — the destruction of 342 chests
The Coercive Acts (1774) — the Boston Port Act, the Massachusetts Government Act, the Administration of Justice Act
The Quebec Act (1774) — extending Quebec’s boundaries, the colonial fury
The First Continental Congress — the Declaration of Rights, the Continental Association
Lord Chatham’s and Burke’s speeches for conciliation
The Petition to the King from the City of London presented by Wilkes

BOOK XVII — The Outbreak of War (1775–1776)

Hostilities commenced at Lexington (April 1775) — the shot heard round the world
The Battle of Bunker Hill (June 1775) — the British Pyrrhic victory
Lord North’s conciliatory proposition — his offer to exempt any colony from taxation if it contributed to imperial defence
Burke’s conciliatory proposition — his great speech on conciliation with America
The Congress Petition rejected — the Olive Branch Petition
America declared to be in rebellion — the Prohibitory Act, the closure of American trade
The Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776)
The British campaign of 1776 — the evacuation of Boston, the capture of New York, the Battle of Long Island
The Battle of Trenton and Princeton — Washington’s counter-stroke

BOOK XVIII — The War Expands (1776–1778)

Military operations in the Jerseys — the campaign of 1777
General Howe’s expedition to the Chesapeake — the Battle of Brandywine, the capture of Philadelphia
The second engagement at German-Town
General Burgoyne’s campaign from Canada — the capture of Ticonderoga, the advance to the North River
The disasters at Bennington and Fort Stanwix
The surrender of Burgoyne at Saratoga (October 1777) — the turning point of the war
The French alliance (1778) — the Treaty of Alliance between France and America
The British evacuation of Philadelphia
The opening of the global war — France enters the conflict
The war with Spain and the siege of Gibraltar — the Spanish entry into the war, the great siege begins

sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol1.title: Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. I
sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol1.content:
Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. I
William Belsham (1752–1827) — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, to the Session of Parliament Ending A.D. 1793. — Volume I. Printed for G. G. and J. Robinson, Paternoster-Row, London.
This is Volume I of Belsham’s Memoirs of the Reign of George III (the G. G. & J. Robinson edition, same as Vols. II and III already in this wiki). It covers from the accession of George III (1760) through the Stamp Act crisis and its repeal (1766) .
The volume contains 374 page-files (OCR’d from the UCLA Library copy, from the collection of C. K. Ogden), extracted as 13,333 lines (~535 KB) of plain text.
Scope: Covers 1760–1766 — the accession of George III, the end of the Seven Years’ War, the fall of Pitt, the Bute ministry, the Peace of Paris (1763), the Wilkes affair, the Grenville ministry, the Stamp Act (1765) and the American colonial resistance, the Rockingham ministry and the repeal of the Stamp Act.
Content Summary
The volume opens with the death of George II and the accession of the new king, then follows the events chronologically through the parliamentary sessions. Key topics:

The accession of George III (October 1760) — the young king’s character, his upbringing under the Princess Dowager and Lord Bute, his first speech (“I glory in the name of Briton”)
The end of the Seven Years’ War — the negotiations with France, the Family Compact between France and Spain
The resignation of Pitt (October 1761) — Pitt’s demand for immediate war with Spain, the Cabinet’s refusal, his resignation on a pension
The Bute ministry — the King’s favourite, the political opposition, the prosecution of the war against Spain
The Peace of Paris (1763) — the terms: Canada, Florida, and India ceded to Britain, the return of Guadeloupe and Martinique to France
The fall of Bute and the formation of the Grenville ministry
The Wilkes affair (1763) — John Wilkes’s North Briton No. 45, the general warrant, Wilkes’s arrest and parliamentary expulsion
The Stamp Act (1765) — Grenville’s measure to tax the American colonies, the colonial resistance, the cry of “no taxation without representation”
The Rockingham ministry (1765–1766) — the change of government, the debate over the Stamp Act
The repeal of the Stamp Act (1766) — Pitt’s great speech in favour of repeal, the Declaratory Act asserting parliamentary sovereignty
The volume closes with the formation of the Chatham (Pitt) ministry

sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol2.content:
Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. II
William Belsham (1752–1827) — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, to the Session of Parliament Ending A.D. 1793. — Volume II. Printed for G. G. and J. Robinson, Paternoster-Row, London.
This is Volume II of Belsham’s Memoirs of the Reign of George III (the earlier G. G. & J. Robinson edition, same as Vol. III we already have). It covers the pre-Revolutionary crisis in America from the Townshend duties through the outbreak of the American Revolutionary War.
The volume contains 362 page-files (OCR’d from the UCLA Library copy, from the collection of C. K. Ogden), extracted as 12,610 lines (~530 KB) of plain text.
Scope: Covers approximately 1767–1774, from the imposition of the Townshend duties through the Boston Massacre, the Tea Act, the Boston Tea Party, the Coercive Acts, the Quebec Act, and the meeting of the First Continental Congress. It is the best source in the wiki for the political background to the American Revolution from the British perspective.
Content Summary
The volume follows the American crisis chronologically through the parliamentary sessions. The OCR uses 18th-century long-s typography throughout. Key phases covered:
Phase 1 — The Townshend Crisis (1767–1770)

The imposition of the Townshend duties (glass, paper, paints, tea)
The American non-importation agreements
The Massachusetts Circular Letter
The arrival of British troops in Boston
The Boston Massacre (March 1770) — the shooting of civilians by British soldiers, the trial of Captain Preston, the defence by John Adams
The partial repeal of the Townshend duties (the tea duty retained)
The re-establishment of a committee of correspondence in Massachusetts

Phase 2 — The Drift to Conflict (1770–1773)

The Gaspee affair (1772) — the burning of the British revenue schooner by Rhode Island colonists
The Hutchinson letters affair — Benjamin Franklin’s leaking of Governor Hutchinson’s private letters, the Privy Council hearing, Wedderburn’s diatribe against Franklin
The formation of Committees of Correspondence throughout the colonies
The Massachusetts Assembly’s remonstrances against the royal government
British determination to maintain parliamentary sovereignty

Phase 3 — The Tea Crisis and the Coercive Acts (1773–1774)

The Tea Act (1773) — the East India Company’s attempt to sell tea directly to America
The Boston Tea Party (December 1773) — the destruction of 342 chests of tea in Boston harbour
The British reaction — Lord North determined on coercion
The Coercive Acts (1774) — the Boston Port Act, the Massachusetts Government Act, the Administration of Justice Act, the Quartering Act
The Quebec Act (1774) — extending Quebec’s boundaries, recognising Catholicism
The debate in Parliament — Chatham’s and Burke’s speeches against coercion
The meeting of the First Continental Congress (September 1774)
The American Declaration of Rights and Grievances
The volume closes on the eve of armed conflict

sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol3.title: Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. III
sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol3.content:
Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. III
William Belsham (1752–1827) — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, to the Session of Parliament Ending A.D. 1793. — Volume III. Printed for G. G. and J. Robinson, Paternoster-Row, London.
This is Volume III of Belsham’s Memoirs of the Reign of George III — an earlier edition of his work on the reign, from a different publisher (the 6th edition 8-volume set was published by R. Phillips). This volume covers from November 1779 through approximately 1793, covering the climactic years of the American Revolutionary War, the domestic political crisis in Britain, and the aftermath of the war.
The volume contains 370 page-files (OCR’d from the UCLA Library copy, from the collection of C. K. Ogden), extracted as 13,133 lines (~540 KB) of plain text. It is smaller than the other Belsham volumes.
Scope: Covers the last years of the North ministry, the Gordon Riots, the military campaigns of 1780–1781 in America, the fall of the North government, the Rockingham and Shelburne ministries, the peace negotiations, the Fox-North coalition, and Pitt’s rise to power. This volume overlaps with Campbell Vol. V (ending 1779) and Campbell Vol. VII (starting 1780) but from a domestic political and parliamentary perspective rather than a naval one.
Content Summary
The volume is structured as a continuous parliamentary history of the reign, closely tracking each session and the major debates. Since the OCR uses 18th-century long-s typography, the chapter/book markers are not cleanly separated in the raw text, but the narrative follows these key phases:
Phase 1 — The North Ministry in Crisis (1779–1781)

The 6th Session of Parliament (November 1779) — the King’s speech, the amendment by Lord Rockingham against the ministry’s American policy
The Economy movement — Burke’s plans for economical reform, the county petitions, the Commission of Accounts
Dunning’s resolution (April 1780) — “the influence of the Crown has increased, is increasing, and ought to be diminished” — a landmark parliamentary declaration
The Gordon Riots (June 1780) — Lord George Gordon’s anti-Catholic petition, the Protestant Association, the mob’s destruction of Newgate prison, the arson and looting across London, the military suppression under the King’s personal direction
The Armed Neutrality (1780) — Catherine the Great’s league, the Dutch crisis, the British seizure of Dutch ships, the rupture with Holland
Rodney’s Moonlight Battle (January 1780) — the relief of Gibraltar, the victory off Cape St. Vincent, the capture of the Spanish convoy
The American war in 1780 — Arnold’s treason, the execution of Major Andre, the Battle of Camden, Gates’s defeat, Cornwallis’s advance
The declaration of war against Holland — the Dutch treaty with the Americans, the British ultimatum
Burke’s Establishment (Reform) Bill — the attack on sinecures and royal patronage
The emergence of William Pitt the Younger — the young MP’s first major speeches in Parliament

Phase 2 — The Fall of North and the Peace (1781–1783)

The campaign of 1781 — Cornwallis in Virginia, the Battle of the Chesapeake, the surrender at Yorktown (October 1781)
The parliamentary crisis (1782) — the Opposition’s attacks on the ministry, the vote of no confidence, the resignation of Lord North (March 1782)
The Rockingham ministry — the brief government of the Marquis of Rockingham, his death (July 1782)
The Shelburne ministry — Shelburne’s peace negotiations with the Americans
The preliminary peace with America (1782) — the recognition of American independence
The Fox-North coalition — the unlikely alliance of Fox and North against Shelburne
The fall of the coalition — George III’s refusal to accept the India Bill, the dismissal of the coalition (December 1783)
Pitt becomes Prime Minister (December 1783) at the age of 24

Phase 3 — Pitt’s First Years (1784–c. 1793)

The general election of 1784 and Pitt’s consolidation of power
India legislation, reform debates
The early French Revolution and the British reaction
The session of Parliament ending in 1793

sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol4.title: Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. IV
sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol4.content:
Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. IV
William Belsham (1752–1827) — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, from His Accession, to the Peace of Amiens. — In Eight Volumes. Volume IV. The Sixth Edition. Printed for R. Phillips, 1795–1808 (Vol. I published 1806). London.
This is Volume IV of Belsham’s Memoirs of the Reign of George III, a different (shorter) series from his 12-volume History of Great Britain. While there is some thematic overlap, this volume focuses exclusively on the reign of George III and covers the domestic political history of the 1780s and early 1790s — a period that was previously a gap in this wiki (Campbell Vol. V ends at 1779, and the next sources start with the French Revolutionary Wars in 1793).
The volume contains 600 page-files (OCR’d from the UCLA Library copy, from the collection of C. K. Ogden), extracted as 22,913 lines (~925 KB) of plain text.
Scope: Covers approximately 1784–1792, from Pitt’s consolidation of power after the 1784 election through the early French Revolution, the Nootka Sound crisis with Spain, and the intensifying debate over the Revolution in Britain. It fills the post-American-Revolution peacetime period that the Campbell naval volumes skip over.
Book-by-Book Summary
BOOK XXII — Pitt’s Ministry, India, and Reform (line 500, ~5,987 lines)
Covers the political landscape from 1784, after Pitt’s victory in the general election that followed the Fox-North coalition’s fall. Key topics:

State of parties after the 1784 election — the triumph of Pitt’s Tories over the Fox-North Whig coalition, the ideological realignment of the parties
The Westminster election scrutiny — the bitter contested return between Fox and Sir Cecil Wray
Mr. Sawbridge’s motion for parliamentary reform — the perennial attempt to shorten parliaments and broaden the suffrage
Pitt’s Second India Bill (1784) — the establishment of the Board of Control, the restructuring of the East India Company’s governance
Burke’s crusade against abuses in India — the gathering campaign against Warren Hastings
The Smuggling Prevention Bill — Pitt’s customs reforms
The commutation of the window tax — the financial debates
Pitt’s plan for redeeming the national debt — the Sinking Fund
The King’s debts discharged a fifth time — the ongoing controversy over royal finances
The bill for disarming the Scottish Highlands — the lifting of restrictions on Highland clans
Irish affairs — the volunteer convention at Dublin, the reform debates in the Irish Parliament
The Westminster scrutiny continues — the parliamentary inquiry into the conduct of the High Bailiff

BOOK XXIII — European Diplomacy, India, and the Slave Trade (line 6,487, ~6,279 lines)
Covers the mid-to-late 1780s, shifting from domestic policy to foreign affairs and imperial governance. Key topics:

State of Europe — the diplomatic situation after the Peace of Paris (1783)
Political commotions in Holland — the Patriot revolt against the Stadtholder, the Prussian army’s intervention, the British role
The Prussian alliance — England arms in support of Prussia, the alliance treaty between Britain, Prussia, and Holland
The unpopular naval promotion — controversies in the Admiralty
The resignation of Lord Howe from the Admiralty
The resignation of the Earl of Mansfield as Lord Chief Justice
The India Declaratory Act — clarifying British sovereignty in India
Proceedings against Sir Elijah Impey — the impeachment of the former Chief Justice of Bengal
The bill for regulating the African slave trade — the early abolition movement, Dolben’s Act regulating the conditions on slave ships
The alarming illness of the King (1788) — the Regency crisis, the political scramble over who would govern if George III became permanently incapacitated
The French financial crisis — the prelude to the Revolution, the Assembly of Notables
The ambitious projects of the Emperor Joseph II — the Austrian policies in the Netherlands and Germany

BOOK XXIV — Nootka Sound, the French Revolution, and the Crisis of the 1790s (line 12,766, ~10,147 lines)
Covers from 1789 through approximately 1792, the most eventful period in the volume. Key topics:

The Nootka Sound dispute with Spain (1790) — the Spanish seizure of British ships and settlement on the Northwest Coast, the British naval mobilisation, the Convention of the Escurial
Death of Charles III of Spain and the accession of Charles IV
France’s reluctance to support Spain — the impact of the Revolution on the Franco-Spanish alliance
The anniversary of the French Revolution celebrated — the first anniversary of the fall of the Bastille
Burke publishes his Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) — the great counter-revolutionary manifesto, its impact on British politics
The pernicious and fatal consequences of the Reflections — Belsham’s own critical assessment of Burke’s influence
The Reflections answered by Thomas Paine — the Rights of Man, its explosive popularity
The wonderful effects of Paine’s pamphlet — the mass circulation, the radical societies, the government’s alarm
The Church and King riots at Birmingham (1791) — the mob attack on Joseph Priestley and the dissenting community
The dissolution of the National Constituent Assembly — the end of the first phase of the French Revolution
Mr. Whitbread’s motion of censure respecting Russia — the Ochakov affair
Wilberforce’s second motion for the abolition of the slave trade (1791) — the defeat of the abolition bill
The second partition treaty of Poland — the Russian and Prussian dismemberment of the Polish state
The assassination of the King of Sweden — Gustavus III’s death
The recall of the English ambassador from France — the deteriorating diplomatic relations
The terrors of innovation — the British government’s growing fear of revolutionary contagion
The volume closes with the political situation on the eve of the war with Revolutionary France

Key Data Points

Relationship to Other Sources
This volume fills a critical gap in the wiki’s coverage — the period between the end of the American Revolutionary War (1783, covered by Campbell Vol. V and Vol. VII) and the French Revolutionary Wars (1793 onward, covered by Campbell Vol. VII and Belsham Vol. XII):
