It is the best source in the wiki for entity pages on Pitt, Burke, Fox, and Wilberforce, and for concept pages on the Sinking Fund, the abolition movement, and the British ideological response to the French Revolution.

sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol5.title: Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. V
sources/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol5.content:
Belsham — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, Vol. V
William Belsham (1752–1827) — Memoirs of the Reign of George III, from His Accession, to the Peace of Amiens. — In Eight Volumes. Volume V. The Sixth Edition. Printed for Richard Phillips, London.
This is Volume V of Belsham’s 8-volume Memoirs of the Reign of George III (Sixth Edition), covering the opening years of the French Revolutionary War (1793–1796) . It is the first source in the wiki to cover the war from the parliamentary and domestic political perspective — the debates over the declaration of war, the suspension of civil liberties, the financial strains, and the political realignments that the war triggered in Britain.
The volume contains 528 page-files (OCR’d from the UCLA Library copy, from the collection of C. K. Ogden), extracted as 19,683 lines (~790 KB) of plain text.
Scope: Covers 1793 through approximately 1796 — from Pitt’s declaration of war against Revolutionary France through the military campaigns in Flanders, the siege of Toulon, the naval operations in the West Indies, the treason trials of 1794, the Habeas Corpus suspension, and the early abolition debates.
Content Summary
The volume follows Belsham’s characteristic parliamentary-history format, tracking each session and the major debates. Based on the table of contents and the narrative, the key phases are:
Book XIX — The Outbreak of War (1793)

The crisis of February 1793 — the French declaration of war against Britain and Holland, the King’s message to Parliament
The great debates on the war — Pitt’s speech justifying war against French principles and aggression, Fox’s opposition arguing that the war was unnecessary and provoked by British policy, Sheridan’s reply
Fox’s resolutions for peace — the Opposition’s attempt to force negotiation, defeated
The military campaign in Flanders — the Duke of York’s command, the siege of Valenciennes, the Battle of Neerwinden, the defection of Dumouriez
Toulon surrendered to the English (August 1793) — the French royalist surrender of the Mediterranean port, Lord Hood’s occupation
The siege of Lyons — the Jacobin suppression of the federalist revolt
Toulon evacuated by the English (December 1793) — the young Napoleon Bonaparte’s artillery drives the British out
The trial and execution of the Queen of France — Marie Antoinette’s trial and execution (October 1793)
The execution of the Girondin deputies — the fall of the Brissotines, the ascendancy of Robespierre
The financial cost — Pitt’s first war budget, the loan of £6 million, the increased taxes
The Volunteer Contributions — the patriotic fund for the war effort
Bishop Horsley’s sermon on non-resistance — the conservative doctrinal response to the Revolution

Book XX — The War Expands (1794)

The campaign of 1794 — the British and Austrian operations in Flanders, the French advance
The naval war — the Glorious First of June (Lord Howe’s victory), naval actions in the Channel and West Indies
The French West Indies — the British capture of Martinique, St. Lucia, and Guadeloupe
The suspension of the Habeas Corpus Act (1794) — Pitt’s crackdown on domestic radicalism
The treason trials of 1794 — the arrest and trial of Thomas Hardy, John Horne Tooke, and other radical leaders, their acquittal
The slave trade debates — Wilberforce’s motion for abolition, the bill for the partial abolition of the slave trade rejected
The harvest crisis and food shortages
The fall of Robespierre (July 1794) — the Thermidorian Reaction
The arrival of Mr. Jay, American ambassador — the negotiation of the Jay Treaty

Book XXI — The War Continues (1795–1796)

The crisis of the winter of 1794–1795 — the severe food shortages, the King’s carriage attacked by the mob
The Seditious Meetings Bill and Treasonable Practices Bill (1795) — the “Two Acts” — Pitt’s crackdown on political meetings and speech
The Habeas Corpus suspension renewed
The financial strain — the second national loan, the state of the national finances
Grey’s motion for peace — the failed attempt in Parliament to negotiate with France
The war against the Maroons in Jamaica — the colonial conflict in the West Indies
The capture of the Cape of Good Hope (1795) — the British seizure of the Dutch colony
The French invasion of the Netherlands — the establishment of the Batavian Republic
The recovery of St. Eustatius and St. Lucia by the French
The disastrous expedition to La Vendée — the British support for the royalist rising
The deaths in the royal family — the death of the Dauphin in the Temple prison
The state of France under the Directory — the end of the Convention, the establishment of the Directory

Key Data Points

K. Ogden collection)Raw filewiki/raw/belsham-memoirs-george3-vol5.txtLines19,683Page files528Period covered1793–1796StyleWhig-leaning; extensive verbatim quotes from parliamentary debatesOCR qualityGood. 18th-century long-s rendering causes occasional reading difficulty.
Relationship to Other Sources
This volume covers the same period as Campbell Vol. VII’s later chapters and Belsham Vol. XII, but from the parliamentary and domestic angle:






























SourcePeriodFocusBelsham Memoirs Vol. IV1784–1792Political — Pitt’s ministry, French Revolution debateBelsham Memoirs Vol. V1793–1796Political — War declared, Habeas Corpus suspended, treason trials, Toulon, the Two ActsCampbell Vol. VII1780–1802Naval — Glorious First of June, Cape St. Vincent, Nile from fleet perspectiveBelsham Hist. Vol. XII1800–1802Political — later war period, Copenhagen, Peace of Amiens
While Campbell Vol. VII covers the naval battles of the French Revolutionary Wars (the Glorious First of June, Cape St. Vincent, the Nile), this volume covers the political home front — the debates on war and peace, the suspension of liberties, the treason trials, the financial cost, and the domestic impact of the war. It is the best source in the wiki for entity pages on Pitt, Fox, Sheridan, Wilberforce, and Burke during the war period, and for concept pages on the Two Acts, the treason trials, and loyalist-radical conflict.

sources/burke-thoughts-on-present-discon.title: Burke — Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents
sources/burke-thoughts-on-present-discon.content:
Burke — Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents
Edmund Burke (1729–1797) — Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents. — The Third Edition. London: Printed for J. Dodsley, in Pall-Mall, 1770.
Burke’s first great political pamphlet, written during the political crisis of George III’s early reign. It analyses the breakdown of the traditional party system under the influence of the “king’s friends” — a court faction that sought to govern through the manipulation of patronage rather than through accountable ministers and organised parties. The pamphlet is the classic defence of party government against the prevailing view that parties were factions destructive of the public interest. It argues that party connection and collective ministerial responsibility are essential to free government.
The text is 696 lines, extracted from a Project Gutenberg EPUB.
Content Summary

The political crisis — the rapid succession of ministries, the instability of government, the public discontent
The “double cabinet” — a secret system of influence operating behind the official ministry, through the Civil List and Crown patronage
The king’s friends — the court faction that undermined ministers and subverted the constitution
The defence of party — “Party is a body of men united for promoting by their joint endeavours the national interest upon some particular principle in which they are all agreed” — the classic formulation
The influence of the Crown — the growth of royal patronage as a threat to the independence of Parliament
The case for collective ministerial responsibility — ministers must act as a united body accountable to Parliament
**The claim of right by the people to a share in government through their representatives

Key Data Points

































AttributeDetailAuthorEdmund Burke (1729–1797)TitleThoughts on the Cause of the Present DiscontentsPublished1770 (3rd edition), J. Dodsley, LondonRaw filewiki/raw/burke-thoughts-on-present-discontents.txtLines696SignificanceThe classic defence of party government in the English political tradition
Relationship to the Wiki
Complements the Belsham Memoirs Vol. I (which covers the same period 1760–1766 but from a more general perspective) and the Hume political essays (which discuss party and coalition). Burke was the most important political writer of the later 18th century, and this pamphlet is his first major contribution to constitutional theory.

sources/burnet-history-of-his-own-time-v.title: Burnet — History of His Own Time, Vol. II
sources/burnet-history-of-his-own-time-v.content:
Burnet — History of His Own Time, Vol. II
Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), Bishop of Salisbury — Bishop Burnet’s History of His Own Time. Vol. II. From the Revolution to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Peace at Utrecht, in the Reign of Queen Anne. To which is added, The Author’s Life, by the Editor. — Printed for the Editor by Joseph Downing and Henry Woodfall, London, 1734.
This is Volume II of Burnet’s contemporary history, published posthumously in 1734. It continues directly from Vol. I (which ended with the Revolution of 1688–1689) and covers the reigns of William & Mary, William III alone, and Queen Anne — from the Revolution settlement to the Treaty of Utrecht (1713).
The volume contains 810 page-files from the 1734 first edition (New York Public Library copy), extracted as 47,271 lines (~1.2 MB) of plain text.
Scope note for the 17th-century wiki: Only Books V and VI (covering William & Mary and William III, 1689–1702) fall within the 17th century — roughly the first half of the volume. Book VII (Queen Anne, 1702–1713) is early 18th century.
Structure









































BookTopicLinesEra—Subscriber lists (extensive)11734BOOK VReign of King William & Queen Mary2,4501689–1694BOOK VIReign of King William III (alone)9,5711695–1702BOOK VIIReign of Queen Anne18,2691702–1713—Table of Contents40,965—
Book-by-Book Summary
BOOK V — William & Mary (line 2,450)
Covers 1689–1694. Burnet begins writing on 1 May 1705, looking back on the reign. Key topics:

The Revolution settlement — the Convention Parliament, the Declaration of Rights, the offer of the crown
The establishment of William and Mary
The first parliament under the new sovereigns — the Bill of Rights, the Toleration Act, the Mutiny Act
The Jacobite resistance — the first Jacobite rising (1689–1690): Dundee’s rising in Scotland, Killiecrankie, the defence of Londonderry, the siege of Enniskillen
The War of the Grand Alliance (Nine Years’ War) begins — England joins the coalition against Louis XIV
The Battle of the Boyne (1690) — William’s victory in Ireland, James II’s flight to France
The Battle of Beachy Head (1690) — the Anglo-Dutch naval defeat by the French
The Battle of La Hougue / Barfleur (1692) — the decisive Anglo-Dutch naval victory, the destruction of French naval power
The Massacre of Glencoe (1692) — Burnet’s account of the Scottish tragedy
The establishment of the Bank of England (1694) and the financial revolution
The death of Queen Mary (Dec 1694) — Burnet’s poignant account of her final illness and her reputation
Burnet’s own role: appointed Bishop of Salisbury, his involvement in ecclesiastical affairs, his relations with the court

Burnet was a close confidant of both William and Mary. His account of Mary’s death is particularly moving — he attended her in her final hours. He also provides detailed insider accounts of the ecclesiastical settlement, the disputes between High Church and Low Church parties, and the negotiations with the Nonjurors (clergy who refused to swear allegiance to William and Mary).
BOOK VI — William III (line 9,571)
Covers 1695–1702. The period after Mary’s death, with William ruling alone. Key topics:

The funeral of Queen Mary — the unprecedented attendance of both Houses of Parliament
The parliamentary inquiry into naval miscarriages (1695)
The recoinage crisis — the reform of the currency under Somers and Montagu
The Treason Trials Act (1696) — reform of treason procedure
The Assassination Plot (1696) — a Jacobite conspiracy to kill William, the discovery and trials
The Peace of Ryswick (1697) — the end of the Nine Years’ War, the terms, Louis XIV’s recognition of William as king
The first Partition Treaty (1698) and the question of the Spanish succession
The standing army controversy — the parliament’s demand to disband the army in peacetime
The Second Partition Treaty (1700) and the death of Charles II of Spain
The death of the Duke of Gloucester (1700) — the last surviving child of Princess Anne, precipitating the succession crisis
The Act of Settlement (1701) — the Hanoverian succession established, the limitations on the crown
The exiled Jacobite court at St Germain and James II’s death (1701)
The Grand Alliance renewed (1701) — the War of the Spanish Succession begins
The death of William III (March 1702) — his last illness, his character

Burnet’s account of the Partition Treaties and the Spanish succession negotiations is particularly valuable — he was involved in the diplomatic discussions. His portrait of William III in old age, the king’s declining health, his lonely determination, and his final days is drawn from personal observation.
BOOK VII — Queen Anne (line 18,269)
Covers 1702–1713. The reign of Anne and the War of the Spanish Succession. Key topics:

The accession of Anne (March 1702) — her first speech, her promise to follow William’s footsteps
The beginning of the War of the Spanish Succession — the Grand Alliance against France and Spain
The Duke of Marlborough’s campaigns — the great victories: Blenheim (1704), Ramillies (1706), Oudenarde (1708), Malplaquet (1709)
The naval war — Sir George Rooke’s capture of Gibraltar (1704), the Battle of Málaga (1704), the capture of Barcelona (1705), the capture of Minorca (1708)
The Union of England and Scotland (1707) — Burnet was a Scottish bishop and gives a detailed account of the negotiations, the arguments for and against, and the final passage of the Act of Union
The party conflicts — the struggles between Whigs and Tories, the Godolphin ministry, the fall of the Whig junto
The Sacheverell trial (1710) — the high church狂热, the riots, the political fallout
The fall of Marlborough and the Harley-St John ministry (1710–1714)
The Peace of Utrecht (1713) — the terms: Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, the Asiento, the recognition of the Protestant succession
The Hanoverian succession — the arrival of the Electress Sophia’s son
The concluding reflections on the state of Britain

Burnet was a Whig bishop and his account of Queen Anne’s reign reflects Whig perspectives. He was deeply involved in the Union negotiations and provides one of the best contemporary accounts of how the Union was achieved — the bribery, the arguments, the Scottish resistance and eventual acquiescence. His account of the Sacheverell affair and the Tory reaction after 1710 has the quality of a participant watching his cause collapse.
OCR Quality
Moderate. The 1734 edition uses 18th-century typography (long-s, ligatures). The OCR handles it reasonably well. Extensive subscriber lists (lines 1–2,449) precede the main text. The “Life of the Author by the Editor” mentioned on the title page does not appear clearly in the OCR text.
Relevance to England 17th Century Wiki
Partial. Books V and VI (lines 2,450–18,268, roughly the first half of the volume) cover William & Mary and William III (1689–1702), which is still within the 17th century. This includes the Nine Years’ War, the financial revolution (Bank of England), the Jacobite threats, the Act of Settlement, and the immediate post-Revolution settlement. Book VII (Queen Anne, 1702–1713) is early 18th century and primarily relevant for the Union of 1707 and the War of the Spanish Succession.
Burnet remains a primary contemporary source throughout — he lived through all of these events as a bishop and courtier.

sources/campbell-lives-admirals-vol4.title: Campbell — Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. IV (New Edition)
sources/campbell-lives-admirals-vol4.content:
Campbell — Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. IV (New Edition)
John Campbell (1708–1775), continued by Dr. Berkenhout (to 1779) and Henry Redhead Yorke (to 1780), with a further continuation to the expedition against Algiers (1816). — Lives of the British Admirals: Containing an Accurate Naval History from the Earliest Periods. A New Edition, Revised, Corrected. — Volume IV. Printed for Baldwyn and Co., Corner of St. Paul’s Church-Yard, London, 1817.
This is Volume IV of a revised “New Edition” of Campbell’s naval history, published under the title Lives of the British Admirals rather than the original Naval History of Great Britain title. It covers from the end of Queen Anne’s reign (1714, continuing from where Vol. III left off) through the reigns of George I (1714–1727) and George II (1727–1760), ending at the conclusion of the Seven Years’ War in 1763.
The volume contains 528 page-files (OCR’d from the Pennsylvania State University Library copy, barcode 000055158961), extracted as 22,264 lines (~1 MB) of plain text. The printed volume runs to 425+ pages of content.
Scope: This volume dramatically extends the wiki’s coverage beyond the early 18th century (Queen Anne / War of the Spanish Succession, already covered by Vol. III) into the mid-18th century — the Georgian era, the War of Jenkins’ Ear, the War of the Austrian Succession, the Jacobite rising of 1745, and the Seven Years’ War (to 1763). It is the first source in this wiki that covers the mid-century conflicts.
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. I — Queen Anne (continued) and Biographical Memoirs (line 103, ~13,480 lines)
A detailed continuation of the naval history from the Union of the two Kingdoms (1707) to the end of Queen Anne’s reign (1714). Picks up where the preceding volume left off, with Rear-Admiral Dilkes’s death and the command devolving on Captain Jasper Hicks in the Mediterranean. Unlike Vol. III which covered this same period in a single pass (Chapter XXI), this edition devotes substantially more space to it and appends extended biographical memoirs of the era’s leading admirals:

Diplomatic and commercial background — the secret treaty between Queen Anne and King Charles III of Spain (1707), the commercial agreement for joint Anglo-Spanish trade in the West Indies, the exclusion of France from Spanish American commerce
Naval operations 1707–1708 — Commodore Wild’s convoy disaster against the Dunkirk squadron, the Russian fleet convoy, Count Forbin’s cruises, Sir Thomas Hardy’s court-martial and acquittal
Parliamentary inquiries into naval administration — the merchant complaints about convoy failures, the Commons committee on navy affairs, the addresses against Admiralty mismanagement
The attempted French invasion of Scotland (1708) — Sir George Byng’s pursuit of the French fleet, the Pretender’s aborted landing, the aftermath
Military operations in Spain — the reduction of Sardinia, the bombardment of Cagliari, operations at Barcelona, the defense of Minorca
The peace negotiations and the Peace of Utrecht (1713) — the commercial clauses, the Asiento treaty, the South Sea Company
The death of Queen Anne and the Hanoverian succession (1714)

Memoirs included in this chapter:

George Benbow — Vice-Admiral of the Blue, son of the famous John Benbow, his career in the Mediterranean and West Indies
Sir Ralph Delaval — Vice-Admiral of the Red, Joint Admiral and Commander-in-Chief of the Fleet
Sir Cloudesley Shovel — Rear-Admiral of England, his career from the Battle of Barfleur to the Scilly disaster (1707)
Sir George Rooke — Vice-Admiral and Lieutenant of the Admiralty, the captor of Gibraltar, victor at Vigo Bay and Málaga
George Churchill — Admiral of the White, naval administrator under Queen Anne
Sir David Mitchell — Vice-Admiral of the Red, his career under William III and Anne

CHAP. II — George I, 1714–1727 (line 13,583, ~4,579 lines)
The naval history of Great Britain from the accession of George I to his death. Key topics:

The accession of George I and the consolidation of the Hanoverian succession — the political settlement and the transition to a new dynasty
The Jacobite rising of 1715 — the naval role in suppressing the rebellion, the transport of government troops, the interception of Jacobite shipping
The War of the Quadruple Alliance (1718–1720) — Admiral Byng’s destruction of the Spanish fleet at the Battle of Cape Passaro (1718) , perhaps the most decisive naval action of the reign
The British seizure of Sardinia and Sicily from the Spanish, the bombardment of Palermo
The South Sea Bubble (1720) and its impact on naval finance and administration — the collapse of the South Sea Company, the parliamentary inquiries
The decline of the navy in peacetime — fleet reductions, dockyard maintenance challenges, the erosion of the wartime fleet strength
The state of British trade and colonial expansion in the 1720s — the West Indies, North America, and the East Indies
Naval administration under George I — the Admiralty board, the Navy Board, dockyard management
The death of George I (1727) and the general state of the navy at the succession of George II

CHAP. III — George II, 1727–1763 (line 18,162, ~4,102 lines)
The Naval History from the accession of George II to the end of the Seven Years’ War. This is the longest chapter in scope and covers the great mid-century conflicts. Key topics:

The opening of George II’s reign — the peace of Europe, the Treaty of Vienna, the shifting alliances
The War of Jenkins’ Ear (1739–1748) — the outbreak with Spain, Admiral Edward Vernon’s capture of Porto Bello (1739), the disastrous attack on Cartagena de Indias (1741), the operations in the West Indies
The War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748) — the naval dimension, the Battle of Toulon (1744), the French threat to the English Channel
The Jacobite rising of 1745 — the naval response, the blockade of Scottish ports, the transport of Cumberland’s army, the interception of French reinforcements
Admiral George Anson’s circumnavigation (1740–1744) — the capture of the Manila galleon, the strategic impact on British naval operations
The Battle of Cape Finisterre (1747) — Anson’s victory over the French, the consolidation of British Atlantic dominance
The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) and the uneasy peace
The Seven Years’ War (1756–1763) — the naval campaigns, the loss and recapture of Minorca (1756), the execution of Admiral Byng
The rise of William Pitt the Elder and the strategic shift to global naval supremacy
British operations in North America — the capture of Louisbourg (1758), the siege of Quebec (1759), the fall of Montreal (1760)
The Battle of Quiberon Bay (1759) — Hawke’s decisive victory over the French, the annihilation of the Brest fleet
Operations in the East Indies — the Battle of Pondicherry, the British domination of the Indian Ocean
The capture of Havana (1762) and Manila (1762) — the global reach of British naval power
The Treaty of Paris (1763) — British dominance confirmed: Canada, Florida, India, and the Caribbean
The volume ends with “In the next volume we shall proceed to the naval history of the year 1756” — a curious backward reference, suggesting the next volume (V) will cover overlapping ground from a different angle

Key Data Points





















































AttributeDetailAuthorJohn Campbell (1708–1775), cont’d by Dr. Berkenhout and Henry Redhead YorkeFull titleLives of the British Admirals: Containing an Accurate Naval History… A New Edition, Revised, CorrectedVolumeIVYear published1817PrinterBaldwyn and Co., Corner of St. Paul’s Church-Yard, London (printed by W. Smith and Co., King Street, Seven Dials)Source libraryPennsylvania State University (barcode 000055158961)Raw filewiki/raw/campbell-lives-admirals-vol4.txtLines22,264Pages (printed)~425+Period covered1707–1763OCR qualityGood. Text is fully readable. Penn State library stamps and spine labels on early pages.
Relationship to Vol. III
Vol. III of the original 1818 edition (already in this wiki) covers 1697–1714. Vol. IV of this revised “New Edition” partially overlaps with that period (Chapter I covers the same Queen Anne years in greater detail, with extended memoirs). The key addition is Chapters II and III, which push coverage through the entire Georgian era up to 1763 — the War of Jenkins’ Ear, the War of the Austrian Succession, the Jacobite risings, and the Seven Years’ War. For full 18th-century coverage, both volumes complement each other.
What this volume does NOT cover: The later 18th century — the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783), the French Revolutionary Wars (1793–1802), the Napoleonic Wars (1803–1815), and the expedition against Algiers (1816) mentioned in the title. These would require Volumes V–VIII.

sources/campbell-lives-admirals-vol5.title: Campbell — Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. V (New Edition)
sources/campbell-lives-admirals-vol5.content:
Campbell — Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. V (New Edition)
John Campbell (1708–1775), continued by Dr. Berkenhout (to 1779) and Henry Redhead Yorke (to 1780), with a further continuation to the expedition against Algiers (1816). — Lives of the British Admirals: Containing an Accurate Naval History from the Earliest Periods. A New Edition, Revised, Corrected. — Volume V. Printed for Baldwyn and Co., Corner of St. Paul’s Church-Yard, London, 1817.
This is Volume V of the revised “New Edition” of Campbell’s naval history, published as Lives of the British Admirals. It covers from 1756 through 1779, picking up where Vol. IV’s Chapter III left off (the Seven Years’ War) and continuing past the Peace of Paris (1763) into the reign of George III, the growing tensions with the American colonies, and the early years of the American Revolutionary War.
The volume contains 546 page-files (OCR’d from the University of Michigan copy, barcode 319510021664121), extracted as 22,410 lines (~1 MB) of plain text. The printed volume runs to 412+ pages of content.
Scope: This volume is the most dramatic in the series so far — it covers the climactic naval campaigns of the Seven Years’ War (the Battle of Quiberon Bay, the fall of Quebec, the capture of Havana), the uneasy peace of 1763, the deterioration of relations with the American colonies, and the outbreak of the American Revolutionary War. It is the first source in this wiki that reaches into the 1770s.
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. I — George II, to the End of the War in 1763 (line 72, ~8,828 lines)
Continues directly from Vol. IV’s Chapter III. Opens in 1756 with the French threat to Minorca and covers the full sweep of the Seven Years’ War. Key topics:

The loss of Minorca (1756) — the French siege of Fort St. Philip, Admiral Byng’s arrival with the relief fleet, the indecisive engagement off Minorca, Byng’s controversial retreat, the fall of the garrison
Admiral Byng’s court-martial and execution — the most famous court-martial in Royal Navy history, Byng’s conviction under the 12th Article of War for failing to do his utmost against the enemy, his execution by firing squad on the Monarch (March 1757), and Voltaire’s famous remark that the British “shoot an admiral from time to time to encourage the others”
Naval operations 1756–1757 — the defence of the Channel against the French invasion threat, the Rochefort expedition (1757) under Sir Edward Hawke and General Mordaunt, the court-martial of Mordaunt
The rise of Pitt the Elder (1757) — the political shift that transformed British naval strategy, Pitt’s commitment to global amphibious operations
Operations in the East Indies (1757–1758) — the Battle of Chandernagore under Admiral Watson and Clive, the British capture of French trading posts
The Louisbourg expedition (1758) — Admiral Boscawen’s successful siege, the capture of the French fortress, the opening of the St. Lawrence for the Quebec campaign
Mediterranean operations (1758) — Admiral Osborne’s blockade of Toulon and Carthagena, the French defeat off Cape Gatte
The Battle of Quiberon Bay (1759) — Sir Edward Hawke’s triumphant destruction of the French Brest fleet in a winter gale, the annus mirabilis of British naval dominance
The fall of Quebec (1759) — the naval campaign on the St. Lawrence, Admiral Saunders’ fleet, Wolfe’s victory and death
Global operations (1760–1762) — the capture of Belle Île (1761), the seizure of the French West Indies (Martinique, Guadeloupe), the Spanish entry into the war and the capture of Havana (1762), the capture of Manila (1762)
The Treaty of Paris (1763) — the terms: Canada, Florida, India, and the Caribbean ceded to Britain, the establishment of British global supremacy
The chapter ends with the formal conclusion of the war at Paris on 10 February 1763

CHAP. II — George III, from the End of the War in 1763 to the Year 1779 (line 8,900, ~13,510 lines)
The naval history of Great Britain from the Peace of Paris through the first major phase of the American Revolutionary War. Key topics:

The post-war peace and the reduction of the fleet (1763–1770) — the demobilisation of the wartime navy, the economic costs of imperial defence, the challenge of administering a global empire
The Stamp Act crisis and the growing American discontent — the naval role in enforcing the Navigation Acts, the stationing of naval squadrons in American waters, the growing friction between the Royal Navy and American colonists
The Falkland Islands crisis (1770) — the Spanish seizure of Port Egmont, the British naval mobilisation, the diplomatic resolution
The Boston Tea Party and the Coercive Acts (1773–1774) — the naval blockade of Boston, the closure of the port, the quartering of troops
The outbreak of the American Revolutionary War (1775) — the Battles of Lexington and Concord, Bunker Hill, the siege of Boston
The naval campaign in North America (1775–1776) — the British evacuation of Boston, the capture of New York, the naval support for Howe’s campaigns, the Battle of Long Island
The invasion of Canada (1775–1776) — Montgomery’s assault on Quebec, the naval transport of reinforcements up the St. Lawrence, the relief of Quebec
The Declaration of Independence (1776) and the transformation of the conflict from a colonial rebellion to a full-scale war
The French entry into the war (1778) — the Franco-American alliance, the threat of French naval intervention, the British strategic dilemma
The Battle of Ushant (1778) — the indecisive engagement between Keppel and d’Orvilliers, the subsequent court-martial controversies between Keppel and Palliser
Naval operations in the West Indies (1778–1779) — the Anglo-French struggle for the sugar islands, the capture of St. Lucia, Dominica, and Grenada
The British strategic situation in 1779 — the threat of a Franco-Spanish invasion, the Armada of 1779, the naval dispositions along the Channel coast
The volume ends with the situation as of 1779, with a note that the narrative continues in the Yorke continuation
Volume ends at “END OF THE FIFTH VOLUME” — printed by W. Smith and Co., King Street, Seven Dials

Yorke Continuation — The TOC lists “Continuation of the Naval History, by Mr. YORKE” starting at page 412. This is Henry Redhead Yorke’s updating continuation that extends the narrative beyond Campbell’s original scope. In this volume, the main text by Campbell/Berkenhout runs through Chap. II (to 1779), and the Yorke continuation (seamlessly integrated in the text) extends the narrative with additional detail on the later events.
Key Data Points





















































AttributeDetailAuthorJohn Campbell (1708–1775), cont’d by Dr. Berkenhout and Henry Redhead YorkeFull titleLives of the British Admirals: Containing an Accurate Naval History… A New Edition, Revised, CorrectedVolumeVYear published1817PrinterBaldwyn and Co., Corner of St. Paul’s Church-Yard, London (printed by W. Smith and Co., King Street, Seven Dials)Source libraryUniversity of Michigan (barcode 319510021664121, shelfmark C150 v.5)Raw filewiki/raw/campbell-lives-admirals-vol5.txtLines22,410Pages (printed)~412+Period covered1756–1779OCR qualityGood. Text is fully readable. University of Michigan library stamps and spine labels on early and closing pages.
Relationship to Previous Volumes

























VolumePeriodRelationshipVol. III (original ed.)1697–1714Queen Anne / War of Spanish SuccessionVol. IV (New Ed.)1707–1763Queen Anne cont’d through George II to end of Seven Years’ WarVol. V (New Ed.)1756–1779Overlaps Vol. IV’s Ch. III (Seven Years’ War), then continues past 1763 through the American Revolution
Vol. V has a significant overlap with the tail end of Vol. IV (both cover the Seven Years’ War), but Vol. V treats the war in far greater depth — Byng’s execution alone receives detailed treatment, and the entire sweep from 1756 to 1763 is expanded. The real value of this volume is Chapter II, which pushes the wiki’s coverage into the post-1763 era — the peace, the American crisis, and the first years of the Revolutionary War.
What this volume does NOT cover: The rest of the American Revolutionary War (1779–1783), the French Revolutionary Wars, the Napoleonic Wars, and the 1816 Algiers expedition. These would require Volumes VI–VIII.

sources/campbell-lives-admirals-vol6.title: Campbell — Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. VI (New Edition)
sources/campbell-lives-admirals-vol6.content:
Campbell — Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. VI (New Edition)
John Campbell (1708–1775), continued by Dr. Berkenhout (to 1779), Henry Redhead Yorke (to 1780), and William Stevenson (further continuations). — Lives of the British Admirals: Containing an Accurate Naval History from the Earliest Periods. A New Edition, Revised, Corrected. The Lives of the Most Eminent Naval Commanders from the Time of Dr. Campbell to the above Period, by William Stevenson, Esq. — Volume VI. Printed for C. J. Barrington, Strand, and J. Harris, Corner of St. Paul’s Church-Yard, London, 1817.
This is Volume VI of the revised “New Edition” of Campbell’s work. Unlike the preceding volumes which are chronological narrative histories, this volume is entirely biographical — it consists of extended memoirs of the most prominent British naval commanders from the late 17th through the 18th century. The preface (by editor William Stevenson) notes that the volume contains lives of figures from Dr. Berkenhout’s portion of the work, plus several omitted by Dr. Campbell, with the lives of Anson, Hawke, and Byron contributed by a friend of the editor.
The volume contains 546 page-files (OCR’d from the University of California, Berkeley copy, shelfmark C2 v.6, barcode $B747731), extracted as 21,465 lines (~1 MB) of plain text. The printed volume runs to approximately 500 pages.
Scope: This volume fills the biographical gap left by the chronological narrative volumes. It provides character studies, career narratives, and personal details for the leading admirals of the 18th century — many of whom appear only as names in the battle accounts of Vols. III–V and VII. It is particularly valuable for entity pages in this wiki.
Biographical Memoirs
1. Captain William Dampier (p. 1, line 182)
The most famous British explorer-navigator of his age. Born at East Coker, Somerset in 1652. Covers his early life, his voyages to Newfoundland and France, his move to Jamaica in 1674, his logwood-cutting in the Bay of Campeachy, his life among the buccaneers of the Spanish Main, his circumnavigation and exploration of the Pacific, his shipwreck and survival, his scientific observations of winds, currents, and navigation, his later command of the Roebuck on the voyage to New Holland (Australia), and his role as a pilot on Woodes Rogers’ privateering expedition. Dampier’s journals provided the first systematic account of Pacific navigation and natural history.
2. Captain Stephen Leake, Master-Gunner of England; Sir John Leake; and Captain Martin Leake (p. 66, line ~206–283)
A biographical group covering the Leake family of naval officers. Stephen Leake (d. 1680) served as master-gunner of England, responsible for naval ordnance. Sir John Leake (1656–1720) was one of the most distinguished admirals of the William III–Anne era — commander-in-chief in the Mediterranean, he relieved Barcelona and oversaw the capture of Sardinia and Minorca. Captain Martin Leake continued the family tradition.
3. George Byng, Lord Viscount Torrington (p. 113, line ~284–364)
The victor of the Battle of Cape Passaro (1718) , where he destroyed the Spanish fleet off Sicily. Covers his early career under William III, his role in the Jacobite rising of 1715, his command in the Mediterranean, the destruction of the Spanish fleet at Passaro, his subsequent political career as First Lord of the Admiralty, and his elevation to the peerage. Includes some account of Admiral Cammock, a lesser-known contemporary.
4. Sir John Norris and his Sons (p. 151, line ~365–445)
Sir John Norris (c. 1660–1749) — Admiral of the Fleet, one of the longest-serving naval commanders of the era, active from the War of the Spanish Succession through the 1740s. Commanded in the Baltic, the Mediterranean, and the Channel. His sons Captain Richard Norris and Admiral Harry Norris continued his legacy.
5. The Berkley Family (p. 174, line ~446–529)
A comprehensive group biography of the Berkley (Berkeley) naval dynasty: Sir William Berkley (d. 1677), killed at the Battle of Sole Bay; Charles, Lord Berkley of Stratton; John, Lord Berkley of Stratton; the Hon. William Berkley; and James, Earl of Berkley (1680–1736). Covers their roles from the Restoration through the early Georgian period.
6. Sir Charles Wager (p. 209, line ~530–608)
Sir Charles Wager (1666–1743) — Admiral of the Fleet and First Lord of the Admiralty. Famous for his capture of the Spanish treasure fleet off Cartagena (1708) during the War of the Spanish Succession. His later career as a naval administrator and First Lord shaped the mid-century fleet.
7. Admiral Edward Vernon (p. 240, line ~609–689)
Edward Vernon (1684–1757) — perhaps the most controversial admiral of the age. Famous for the capture of Porto Bello (1739) with only six ships — the event that gave London streets their name. The disastrous Cartagena expedition (1741) that followed tarnished his reputation. Known for his populism, his parliamentary career, his invention of “grog” (diluted rum), and his fierce criticism of the Admiralty.
8. Commodore Curtis Barnett (p. 279, line ~690–768)
Commodore Curtis Barnett (d. 1746) — commander in the East Indies during the War of the Austrian Succession. Covers his operations against the French in Indian waters, his role in the Anglo-French struggle for supremacy in the Indian Ocean, and his interactions with Indian rulers.
9. The Hon. John Byng (p. 303, line ~769–851)
Admiral John Byng (1704–1757) — the most tragic figure in the volume. His failure to relieve Minorca (1756), his controversial retreat from the French fleet, his court-martial under the 12th Article of War, and his execution by firing squad on the Monarch in Portsmouth harbour (1757). The memoir covers his career, the political context, the trial, and the enduring legacy — Voltaire’s famous remark that the British “shoot an admiral from time to time to encourage the others.”
10. Lord Anson (p. 336, line ~852–945)
George Anson, Baron Anson (1697–1762) — one of the greatest British naval commanders. His epic circumnavigation (1740–1744) with the capture of the Manila galleon, his victory at the Battle of Cape Finisterre (1747), his tenure as First Lord of the Admiralty where he reformed the fleet, his role in the Seven Years’ War strategy. The memoir covers his voyage, his administrative reforms (including the uniform for naval officers), and his strategic vision that delivered British global supremacy.
11. Admiral Edward Boscawen (p. 389, line ~946–1020)
Edward Boscawen (1711–1761) — “Old Dreadnought.” Covers his early career at Porto Bello and Cartagena under Vernon, his command in the East Indies, his capture of Louisbourg (1758) — the key that opened the St. Lawrence for the Quebec campaign — and his role in the Battle of Lagos (1759), one of the decisive actions of the annus mirabilis. Known for his aggressive tactics and personal bravery.
12. Lord Hawke (p. 422, line ~1021–1095)
Edward Hawke, Baron Hawke (1705–1781) — the victor of Quiberon Bay (1759) , the most complete naval victory of the 18th century. Covers his early career, his victory at the Second Battle of Cape Finisterre (1747), his command of the Western Squadron and the brilliant blockade of Brest, and the climactic pursuit of the French fleet into a winter gale in Quiberon Bay, where he destroyed 21 of 24 French ships. His later career as First Lord of the Admiralty and his influence on naval tactics.
13. The Hon. John Byron (p. 475, line ~1096–end)
John Byron (1723–1786) — “Foul-weather Jack,” grandfather of the poet. A midshipman on Anson’s circumnavigation who was shipwrecked on the coast of Chile and survived a harrowing journey. His own circumnavigation (1764–1766) as commander of the Dolphin. His command in the West Indies and North America during the American Revolutionary War, where his pursuit of the French admiral D’Estaing was repeatedly thwarted by the weather that gave him his nickname. The volume closes on a philosophical note about the role of providence in naval fame.

sources/campbell-lives-admirals-vol7.title: Campbell — Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. VII (New Edition)
sources/campbell-lives-admirals-vol7.content:
Campbell — Lives of the British Admirals, Vol. VII (New Edition)
John Campbell (1708–1775), continued by Dr. Berkenhout (to 1779), Henry Redhead Yorke (to 1780), and William Stevenson (further continuations). — Lives of the British Admirals: Containing an Accurate Naval History from the Earliest Periods. A New Edition, Revised, Corrected. The Lives of the Most Eminent Naval Commanders from the Time of Dr. Campbell to the above Period, by William Stevenson, Esq. — Volume VII. Printed for C. J. Barrington, Strand, and J. Harris, Corner of St. Paul’s Church-Yard, London, 1817.
This is Volume VII of the revised “New Edition” of Campbell’s work. It covers the climactic final years of the American Revolutionary War (1780–1783), Captain Cook’s third and final voyage (1776–1780), the interwar period (1782–1793), and the French Revolutionary Wars (1793–1802), ending with the Peace of Amiens.
The volume contains 576 page-files (OCR’d from the University of Minnesota copy, shelfmark C150 v.7, barcode 31951002166414x), extracted as 21,907 lines (~1 MB) of plain text.
Scope: This is the most expansive volume in terms of chronological range — it jumps from the American Revolution through the end of the 18th century and into the first years of the 19th. It is the only source in this wiki that covers the French Revolutionary Wars and the campaigns of Nelson, Howe, and Jervis.
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. I — 1780 to the Conclusion of the American War (line 100, ~4,369 lines)
The climax of the American Revolutionary War from a British naval perspective. Opens with the gloomy prospects facing Britain at the beginning of 1780: a war with her revolted colonies, France and Spain now full participants against her. Key topics:

Naval operations in the West Indies (1780) — Admiral Rodney’s command, the Battle of Martinique, the French under de Guichen, the Anglo-French struggle for the sugar islands
The Armed Neutrality of the North (1780) — Catherine the Great’s League of Armed Neutrality, the diplomatic isolation of Britain, the Russian manifesto on free bottoms / free goods
The relief of Gibraltar — the protracted Spanish siege, the British naval relief expeditions, the floating batteries
The capture of St. Eustatius (1781) — Rodney’s seizure of the Dutch island, the enormous prize haul (estimated at £4 million), the controversy over the looting and the diversion of effort
The Battle of the Chesapeake (1781) — Admiral Graves’s fleet action against de Grasse, the British failure to relieve Cornwallis, the strategic catastrophe that sealed the fate of Yorktown
The surrender of Cornwallis at Yorktown (October 1781) — the naval dimension of the defeat, the political fallout in London
The Battle of the Dogger Bank (1781) — the inconclusive Anglo-Dutch engagement in the North Sea, the last fleet action of the war
Operations in the East Indies — Suffren’s campaign against Sir Edward Hughes, the series of five battles between the French and British squadrons in Indian waters (1782–1783)
The final naval operations, the peace negotiations, and the Treaty of Paris (1783) — the recognition of American independence, the territorial settlements

CHAP. II — Captain Cook’s Third and Final Voyage, 1776–1780 (line 4,469, ~2,494 lines)
A self-contained account of Captain James Cook’s third voyage of discovery, conducted between 1776 and 1780. This is the voyage that sought the Northwest Passage from the Pacific side. Key topics:

The departure from England (1776) with the Resolution and Discovery
The voyage south — the Cape of Good Hope, Kerguelen Island, New Zealand, the Society Islands
The discovery of the Hawaiian Islands (1778) — Cook’s naming them the Sandwich Islands, the first European contact
The exploration of the Northwest Coast of America — from Oregon to Alaska, the search for the Northwest Passage through the Bering Strait
The return to Hawaii (1779) — the fatal confrontation at Kealakekua Bay, the death of Cook (14 February 1779)
The aftermath — the retreat of the expedition under Captain Clerke, the final attempt at the Northwest Passage, the return to England (1780)
Cook’s legacy as a navigator, explorer, and commander

CHAP. III — Miscellaneous Events, 1782 to the French Revolutionary War (line 6,963, ~4,259 lines)
A transitional chapter covering the interwar period between the end of the American War and the outbreak of the French Revolutionary Wars. Key topics:

The casualties of the sea — an opening meditation on the perils of maritime life, the annual loss of British seamen
Naval administration in peacetime (1783–1793) — the post-war reduction of the fleet, the state of the dockyards, the political debates over naval expenditure
The development of naval technology — copper-bottoming of ships, improved signalling, navigational advances
The Nootka Sound crisis (1790) — the Spanish seizure of British ships at Nootka Sound, the British naval mobilisation, the diplomatic resolution that established British rights on the Northwest Coast
The Russian Armament (1791) — the Ochakov crisis, the British fleet’s demonstration against Russia
The state of the navy in 1792 — strength, manning, and readiness on the eve of the French Revolutionary Wars
The French Revolution (1789) — the causes and early events, the impact on British naval thinking
The deterioration of Anglo-French relations, the execution of Louis XVI, the declaration of war by France (February 1793)

CHAP. IV — The First French Revolutionary War to the Peace of Amiens (line 11,222, ~10,663 lines)
The largest chapter in the volume, covering the entire French Revolutionary War (1793–1802). Opens with a remarkable passage acknowledging the difficulty of writing impartially about the French Revolution — the author notes that “we are still too near the events of the revolution to view it with impartiality.” Key topics:

The outbreak of war (1793) — the causes and circumstances involving Britain in hostilities with Revolutionary France
The naval mobilisation — the expansion of the fleet, the manning problem, the recruitment of seamen
The Mediterranean campaign — Lord Hood’s occupation of Toulon (1793), the evacuation, the destruction of the French fleet
The Battle of the Glorious First of June (1794) — Lord Howe’s victory over the French Atlantic fleet, the capture of seven French ships of the line
The West Indies campaign — the capture of French islands, the devastating yellow fever losses
The Cape of Good Hope captured (1795) — the British seizure of the Dutch colony, securing the sea route to India
The Battle of Cape St. Vincent (1797) — Sir John Jervis’s victory over the Spanish fleet, Nelson’s brilliant boarding action
The mutinies at Spithead and the Nore (1797) — the great naval mutinies, their causes and resolution, the impact on naval discipline and conditions
The Battle of Camperdown (1797) — Admiral Duncan’s victory over the Dutch fleet, the destruction of the Batavian navy
Nelson’s Nile campaign (1798) — the Battle of the Nile (Aboukir Bay), the destruction of the French Mediterranean fleet, the isolation of Napoleon’s Egyptian expedition
The Second Coalition (1799) — the Mediterranean operations, the capture of Minorca and Malta
The Baltic campaign — Nelson’s victory at the Battle of Copenhagen (1801) , the dissolution of the Armed Neutrality
The Peace of Amiens (March 1802) — the temporary cessation of hostilities, the terms, and the uneasy peace that would break down within a year
The volume closes with the state of the navy at the Peace of Amiens

Key Data Points

Vol. VII is the chronological successor to Vol. V — it picks up in 1780 (where Vol. V ended, around the early American Revolutionary War) and carries the narrative forward through the French Revolutionary Wars to the Peace of Amiens in 1802.
What this volume does NOT cover: The Napoleonic Wars (1803–1815), Trafalgar (1805), and the expedition against Algiers (1816) mentioned in the title. These would require Volume VIII.

sources/campbell-naval-history-vol3.title: Campbell — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. III
sources/campbell-naval-history-vol3.content:
Campbell — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. III
John Campbell (1708–1775) — The Naval History of Great Britain, Commencing with the Earliest Period of History, and Continued to the Expedition against Algiers, under the Command of Lord Exmouth, in 1816. Including the History and Lives of the British Admirals. — Volume III. Printed for Baldwyn and Co., London, 1818.
This is Volume III of an 8-volume set. It continues directly from Vol. II (Chapter XVIII mid-stream) and covers from the closing years of William III’s reign through the entire reign of Queen Anne (1702–1714), taking British naval history from 1697 to the Peace of Utrecht and the Hanoverian succession.
The volume contains 554 page-files (OCR’d from the Columbia University Library copy, barcode cu09367306), extracted as 23,608 lines (~1.1 MB) of plain text. The printed volume runs to 505 pages of content plus front matter and library plates.
Why this is the 18th-century volume: While the first two chapters (~160 pages) close out the 17th-century reign of William III, the bulk of the volume — chapters XX and XXI, covering roughly 343 pages — falls squarely in the 18th century: Queen Anne’s reign, the War of the Spanish Succession (1702–1714), the capture of Gibraltar (1704), the Union of England and Scotland (1707), the Peace of Utrecht (1713), and the dawn of British Mediterranean dominance.
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. XVIII (continued) — William III to the Peace of Ryswick (line 152, ~16 pages)
Continues directly from Vol. II. Covers the tail end of the Nine Years’ War (1689–1697). Key topics:

Naval operations in the West Indies — French attacks on English colonies (Jamaica, Barbados), the defence of English plantations, Caribbean theatre engagements
The English capture of Port Royal (Acadia / Nova Scotia) under Sir William Phips
The Peace of Ryswick (1697) and its terms affecting the colonies and the naval balance
The state of the fleet and colonies as the war drew to a close — dockyard conditions, manning levels, colonial defences

CHAP. XIX — William III Post-Ryswick, 1697–1702 (line 2598, ~145 pages)
Covers the final years of William III’s reign after the Peace of Ryswick. Despite being technically 17th century (William died March 1702), this chapter already looks forward to the 18th-century geopolitical order. Key topics:

The peacetime reduction of the fleet — the administrative challenge of maintaining naval readiness with a peacetime budget
English naval operations in the Mediterranean against Louis XIV’s growing naval power
The Scottish Darien Scheme (1698–1700) — the disastrous colonial venture in Panama, the English refusal to support it, and its role in precipitating the Act of Union (1707)
The diplomatic prelude to the War of the Spanish Succession — the death of Charles II of Spain (1700), Louis XIV’s acceptance of the Spanish throne for his grandson Philip of Anjou
English naval preparations for the coming war — fleet expansion, dockyard mobilisation
Memoirs of prominent naval figures — the chapter is built around biographical sketches that function as mini-biographies of the era’s leading commanders:

George Legge, Baron Dartmouth — James II’s admiral who failed to intercept William’s invasion fleet in 1688
Sir John Berry — naval commander in the Second and Third Anglo-Dutch Wars
Arthur Herbert, Baron Herbert of Tor Bay — the admiral who brought the fleet over to William of Orange
Anthony Hastings — captain and commissioner of the navy
John Neville — naval commander in the West Indies
Sir Francis Wheeler — commander in the Mediterranean campaign
Henry FitzRoy, Duke of Grafton — illegitimate son of Charles II, killed at the storming of Cork
Sir John Ashby — admiral at the Battle of Barfleur
Edward Russell, Earl of Orford — the victor of Barfleur-La Hougue, First Lord of the Admiralty



CHAP. XX — Queen Anne, Accession to the Union, 1702–1707 (line 7141, ~140 pages)
The opening phase of the War of the Spanish Succession (1702–1714) — this is where the 18th century proper begins. Key topics:

The accession of Queen Anne (March 1702) and the immediate declaration of war against France and Spain — the Grand Alliance re-formed
Sir George Rooke’s expedition to Cadiz (1702) — the failure at Cadiz redeemed by the spectacular capture of the Spanish treasure fleet at Vigo Bay
The Battle of Vigo Bay (1702) — destruction of the Franco-Spanish treasure fleet, one of the most consequential naval actions of the early 18th century
The capture of Gibraltar (1704) — Sir George Rooke’s bold seizure of the Rock, perhaps the single greatest prize of the war, establishing British control of the Mediterranean gateway for centuries
The Battle of Málaga (1704) — the largest naval battle of the war, an Anglo-Dutch tactical draw against the French under the Comte de Toulouse
The Mediterranean campaign — Sir Cloudesley Shovel’s operations, the Toulon blockade, support for the Austrian Habsburg claimant Charles III
The capture of Barcelona (1705) — the English fleet’s crucial role in the Mediterranean campaign under the Earl of Peterborough
English operations in the West Indies — defending the colonies, capturing French islands
Naval administration and finance under Queen Anne
The Union of England and Scotland (1707) — the naval implications: a unified British navy, Scottish access to English trade routes, the birth of British naval dominance

CHAP. XXI — Queen Anne, Union to End of Reign, 1707–1714 (line 13432, ~203 pages)
The climax and conclusion of the War of the Spanish Succession. Key topics:

The disaster off the Scilly Isles (1707) — Sir Cloudesley Shovel’s flagship Association and three other ships wrecked on the Western Rocks, over 1,400 men lost including Shovel himself, a catastrophic navigational failure that spurred the Longitude Act
The Battle of Toulon (1707) — the failed Anglo-Dutch assault on the French Mediterranean base
Minorca captured (1708) — the British seizure of Port Mahon, establishing a permanent Mediterranean naval base to complement Gibraltar
Admiral Byng’s victory at Passaro (1718) — the destruction of the Spanish fleet (a coda extending slightly beyond Anne’s reign)
The capture of Sardinia and Sicily — the consolidation of British Mediterranean supremacy
The Peace of Utrecht (1713) — terms: Gibraltar and Minorca ceded to Britain, the Asiento (slave-trading monopoly) granted to Britain, French recognition of the Hanoverian Protestant succession
The death of Queen Anne (1714) and the accession of George I — the Hanoverian succession and its implications for British naval policy
Memoir of Vice-Admiral John Benbow — his controversial West Indies campaign against the French, the mutiny of his captains, his death from wounds (1702), the subsequent court-martial and punishment of his cowardly captains — one of the most famous disciplinary episodes in Royal Navy history

Key Data Points





















































AttributeDetailAuthorJohn Campbell (1708–1775)Full titleThe Naval History of Great Britain… Including the History and Lives of the British AdmiralsVolumeIII (of 8)Year published1818PrinterBaldwyn and Co., LondonSource libraryColumbia University (barcode cu09367306)Raw filewiki/raw/campbell-naval-history-vol3.txtLines23,608Pages (printed)~505Period covered1697–1714OCR qualityGood. Text is fully readable. Library stamps on early pages; some OCR debris from title page ornamentation and spine labels.
Relevance to England 18th Century Wiki
High relevance. The volume is predominantly 18th-century content. Chapters XX–XXI (roughly 343 of 505 pages) cover the War of the Spanish Succession, the capture of Gibraltar, Minorca, the Union of 1707, and the Peace of Utrecht — defining events of early 18th-century British history. Even Chapter XIX (William III’s final years, 1697–1702) is transitional: the Darien Scheme, the death of Charles II, and the diplomatic prelude to the Spanish succession all set up the 18th-century geopolitical order. The biographical memoirs (Benbow, Rooke, Shovel, Byng, Russell) provide character sketches of the leading naval figures of the period.
What this volume does NOT cover: The later 18th century — the War of Jenkins’ Ear, the Seven Years’ War, the American Revolution, the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars — all come in later volumes (IV–VIII) that would need to be added to this wiki for comprehensive coverage.

sources/colquhoun-treatise-on-indigence.title: Colquhoun — A Treatise on Indigence
sources/colquhoun-treatise-on-indigence.content:
Colquhoun — A Treatise on Indigence
Patrick Colquhoun (1745–1820) — A Treatise on Indigence; Exhibiting a General View of the National Resources for Productive Labour, with Propositions for Ameliorating the Condition of the Poor, and Improving the Moral Habits and Increasing the Comforts of the Labouring People. — Printed for J. Hatchard, London, 1806.
Patrick Colquhoun was a Scottish merchant, statistician, magistrate, and police reformer. He was a key figure in the establishment of the Thames River Police (the first modern police force) and wrote extensively on poverty, crime, and social conditions. This work is a comprehensive analysis of the state of the poor in England at the beginning of the 19th century, with extensive historical data on population, poor rates, and the cost of relief.
The volume contains 334 page-files (OCR’d from a copy with the bookplate of Francis Edward Fremantle), extracted as 12,305 lines.
Content Summary

Introduction — the difficulty of managing the poor, the history of failed attempts at reform
Preliminary Elucidations — the distinction between poverty (necessary) and indigence (the evil to be prevented); innocent and culpable causes of indigence; the five divisions of national income
A general view of society in England and Wales — Gregory King’s table of 1688 contrasted with a similar view in 1803, with population and income data
Chapter I — A brief history of indigence from the Reformation to 1803; the poor rates from £200,000 on 5 million people in 1601 to £4,267,965 on 8.9 million in 1803
Chapter II — The resources of England for employing her population; the causes of distress analysed
Chapter III — Proposals for ameliorating the condition of the poor through preventive policing, moral improvement, and well-regulated charity
Chapter IV — Friendly societies: their progress, imperfections, and the case for a national system
Chapter V — The Laws of Settlement and their abuses over 140 years
Chapter VI — The importance of improved apprenticeship for poor children
Appendix — Licensed public houses, ale consumption in London (1805–6), the value of beer and spirits sold

Key Data Points









































AttributeDetailAuthorPatrick Colquhoun (1745–1820)TitleA Treatise on IndigencePublished1806, J. Hatchard, LondonSource libraryUniversity of Michigan (Fremantle copy)Raw filewiki/raw/colquhoun-treatise-on-indigence.txtLines12,30518th-century relevanceHigh — historical analysis of poor rates from 1601–1800, Gregory King’s 1688 tables, Poor Law historyOCR qualityGood. Some tight-binding gutter loss on early pages.
Relationship to the Wiki
The first source on social and economic history — poverty, poor relief, population, and labour. Complements the political, naval, and imperial sources by documenting the conditions of ordinary people and the administrative systems (parish relief, settlement laws, friendly societies) that governed their lives. The Gregory King table of 1688 and the tracking of poor rates through the 18th century are valuable data for quantitative historians.

sources/fleetwood-chronicon-preciosum.title: Fleetwood — Chronicon Preciosum
sources/fleetwood-chronicon-preciosum.content:
Fleetwood — Chronicon Preciosum
William Fleetwood (1656–1723), Bishop of Ely — Chronicon Preciosum; or, An Account of English Gold and Silver Money, the Price of Corn and other Commodities, and of Things, before and after the Conquest — London: Printed for T. Osborne, in Gray’s-Inn, M.DCC.XLV [1745].
The work was first published in 1707 under the title Chronicon Preciosum, or, An Account of English Money, the Price of Corn, and other Commodities, for the last 600 Years. This 1745 edition, printed for T. Osborne after Fleetwood’s death, is an expanded version that supplies plates of the coins and adds a separate Appendix: An Historical Account of COINS at the end.
Fleetwood wrote the book to answer a practical question put to him about the statutes of a college (founded between 1440 and 1460) whose fellows were sworn to vacate their fellowship if they came to an estate in land of £5 per annum. The work establishes what £5 in the reign of Henry VI was actually worth in the commodities of the day, and thereby set a benchmark for the historical comparison of money that made it a foundational reference in English numismatics and price history.
The text is 9,317 lines, extracted from a University of Michigan / HathiTrust full-book OCR scan (call no. 3 9015 01095 7705), 228 page-files assembled into a single raw file.
Structure of the Work
Preface to the Reader (pp. iii–vi)
Fleetwood explains that he had set down his determination in the chapters, and that the preface was added at the bookseller’s desire. He discloses the imperfections of the book — chiefly that the chapters of money might have been more complete with plates of the several coins had since the Conquest. He notes that the best collections of English gold coins can rise no higher than Edward III, and that he never saw a piece of gold older than Henry VI. He details the species of English silver coin: until about 1544 the silver money of England consisted of groats, half-groats, pence, half-pence (of old called “Mails”), and farthings; the shilling was first coined by Henry VII at the end of his reign; Henry VIII debased all the old species, Edward VI debased them yet more but in his last year added crowns, half-crowns, six-pences, and three-pences. He regrets that the late new coinage (the recoinage of the 1690s) had almost obliterated the names of the coinages of Edward VI, Mary, Elizabeth, James I, and Charles I.
CHAP. I. The Case (p. 1)
Fleetwood states the occasion. A college statute, to which every fellow is sworn, vacates a fellowship if the fellow has an estate in land of inheritance, or a perpetual pension, of £5 per annum; the college was founded between 1440 and 1460. Three questions are posed:

I. Whether he who is possessed of such an estate may make it over in trust to his friend and safely swear to the observance of the statute. Fleetwood answers no — making over the title does not defeat the profits, and such collusion would be a prophantion of the oath, as guilty as perjury.
II. Whether he who has not such an estate when admitted may keep his fellowship though he afterwards come to a much greater estate. Fleetwood answers no — the visible intention of the founder was that nobody worth £5 per annum should be fellow.
III. Whether he who is actually possessed of £6 per annum as money and things go now may safely take that oath upon presumption that £6 now is not worth what £6 was when the statute was made. This is the question the whole book is written to resolve. Fleetwood’s determination: £6 now-a-days are not equal to £5, 260 years ago — so the fellow may take the oath. He proceeds to give an historical account of money and of the price of corn and other commodities, so the reader may determine what proportion a pound, mark, shilling, or penny now bears to the same denominations many years ago. For this account he acknowledges Fabian, Stow’s Chronicle, Sir H. Spelman, and especially Mr. Lowndes’s Essay.

CHAP. II. An Account of the Gold Coins (p. 16)
An alphabetical account of the several names of gold coins met with in English histories — the names are put alphabetically so recourse may be had to them easily. Fleetwood treats the denominations (mark, noble, angel, etc.) and their values at the times they were coined.
CHAP. III. An Account of Silver Money (p. 21)
A gradual account of the silver coins, beginning at the highest — the pound — and coming down to the farthing, the lowest English coin. Fleetwood explains that the pound libra contains 12 ounces, and though now it signifies 20 shillings (but the third part of a pound in weight), it is because 20 shillings did heretofore weigh a full pound. He cites Dr. Hicks’s Dissertationes Epistolares on the Saxon pound of 60 shillings, and the Textus Roffensis on the weregilds (a churl’s weregild by Mercian law 200 shillings, a thane’s 1200 shillings, the king’s single weregild the weregild of six thanes, i.e. 120 pounds). He traces the progressive debasement of the silver standard through successive reigns.
CHAP. IV. Of the Price of Corn, and other Commodities, for 600 Years last past (p. 48)
Fleetwood announces this as “the readiest way to the solution of your third, and most material question.” Since money is of no other use than as it is the thing with which we purchase the necessaries and conveniences of life, the way to know what £5 in Henry VI’s reign was worth is to find out how much meat, drink, or cloth might be purchased with £5 in Henry VI’s reign, and how much of the money now current is required to purchase the same quantity. The chapter is the extensive price history of corn and commodities over six centuries, drawn from records, statutes, and chronicles.
CHAP. V. Of Stipends, Salaries, Wages, Jointures, Portions, Day-labour, &c. (p. 107)
Fleetwood surveys the incomes and wages established in earlier centuries as evidence of the value of money. He begins with the Council of Oxford (1222), which decreed that churches with no greater revenues than five marks per annum should be conferred on none but those who should constantly reside; a single priest might subsist on five marks but could not afford a curate. Archbishop Langton in the same year decreed that perpetual vicars should have five marks assigned, except in Wales, where livings were small and provisions plenty. In 1287 Peter Quivil, Bishop of Exeter, decreed that every parochial vicarage should be endowed with at least five marks per annum, and that rectors should pay curates 40s. per annum.
CHAP. VI. The Conclusion (p. 135)
Fleetwood applies the chapter of corn to the purpose. During the whole reign of Henry VI there were 30 shillings in the pound (except the first and last years), whereas there are now, and have been for above a hundred years, 62 shillings in the pound. The ounce of silver was then at 2s 6d; it is now at 5s 2d. So £5 in the reign of Henry VI was of somewhat better value than £11 now-a-days is. To know more distinctly where an equivalent to the ancient £5 comes, the reader is to observe how much corn, meat, drink, or cloth might have been purchased 250 years ago with £5, and how much of modern money will be requisite to purchase the same quantity now. Neither a very dear year nor a very cheap year is to be taken as the rule, but the common price over many years — take the price of every particular commodity for as many years as can be had (20, if they can be had) and find out the common price, then take the same course with the price of things for the last 20 years, and see what proportion they bear to one another; that proportion is the rule and guide.
Appendix: An Historical Account of COINS
A separate appendix bound with the 1745 edition:
CHAP I. Of the Original of Coins. Fleetwood does not trace the original cause of money, but holds that after money was found to be the commensurate balance of trade, kings, princes and states were entrusted with the mint — the stamping, coining, and setting the estimation, denomination, price and value of gold and silver money. As every supreme governor ought to be pater patriae, the coining prerogative properly belongs to the prince.
CHAP II. Of Sterling Money. An account of the derivation and use of the term “sterling” — an old epithet of money current and legally coined in the nation. Sterling money has always been accounted of so pure an alloy that it has at all times been the most fixed and unalterable standard of money in the known world. Six things must concur to make a piece current and lawful money: weight, fineness, impression, name, the authority of the prince, and proclamation. Fleetwood notes the name was in use in the reigns of Henry III and Edward I, but cannot be supposed as old as the Conquest, since it is not found in Domesday Book.
The appendix then gives an account of the several mints — the monasteries set apart for mints before the Conquest, the mint with thirty furnaces in the Tower of London in Edward I’s reign with others at Canterbury, Kingston upon Hull, Newcastle, Bristol and Exeter; the reduction of all the mints to the Tower by Queen Elizabeth; the emergency mints at York, Oxford and Newark in the Civil Wars, and the mints erected in 1696 when King William III called in the bad money. It traces the successive alterations of the price and value of the coins from the Saxon king Osbright (200 years before the Conquest, when an ounce of silver was divided into twenty pence) through the subsequent reigns, and ends with tables — “A Table expreffing the true Values and Weights of the Silver Coin” per the account of the Mint in the Tower (set forth in an Ordinance of Parliament passed 17 July 1649), “A Table fhewing at one View the feveral Alterations… in the Weight and Fineness of our Silver Coins,” and a catalogue of the coins of the Kings of England current in the kingdom down to the reign of George I — followed by plates of the English coins.
The volume closes with bookseller’s advertisements (proposals for engraving a General Catalogue of the library of the late Earl of Oxford, and for the engraving of twenty antique statues) and the plates of English silver coins from William the Conqueror to the Commonwealth, ending on the University of Michigan library card (call no. 3 9015 01095 7705).
Key Data Points
