Relationship to the Wiki
This is the most sustained contemporary critique of the Pitt government’s conduct during the French Revolutionary Wars from a liberal Anglican perspective. It complements the high-political narratives of the Belsham histories and the Burke pamphlets by providing the view from the reformist opposition. Knox writes as a mainstream clergyman and educator, not a radical — which makes his indictment of the “Spirit of Despotism” all the more striking. The work is a key source for the domestic political climate of the 1790s, the repression of reform movements, the debate on the French Revolution, and the constitutional arguments around Crown influence, parliamentary reform, and civil liberties.

sources/lunar-men.title: Uglow — The Lunar Men
sources/lunar-men.content:
Uglow — The Lunar Men
Jenny Uglow — The Lunar Men: The Friends Who Made the Future 1730–1810. — Faber and Faber, London, 2002. — 588 pp. + plates.
A group biography of the Lunar Society of Birmingham — the informal circle of provincial manufacturers, doctors, clergymen, inventors, and gentlemen that gathered around the full moon from the 1760s to the 1790s. Uglow traces the intertwined lives of Erasmus Darwin, Matthew Boulton, James Watt, Josiah Wedgwood, Joseph Priestley, James Keir, William Small, William Withering, Richard Lovell Edgeworth, Thomas Day, John Whitehurst, and others as they drive the Industrial Revolution, the chemical revolution, the canal age, and the radical politics of the late eighteenth century.
The book is structured in five parts (Waxing, First through Fourth Quarter, and Waning), covering the chronological sweep from the birth of the first Lunatic (Erasmus Darwin in 1731) through the dispersal of the group after the Priestley Riots of 1791 and the deaths of the last survivors in the 1810s–1820s.
The text is 12,407 lines, extracted from the Faber and Faber ebook edition (2010).

Part I: WAXING
Prologue: ‘Surprise the world’
Introduces the Lunar Society as a small, informal club meeting on the Monday nearest the full moon. Uglow argues that this provincial group of manufacturers, professionals, and amateurs — unlike aristocrats or university men — collectively pushed British society over the threshold of modernity. Five core figures are introduced (Darwin, Boulton, Watt, Wedgwood, Priestley) alongside supporting characters (Keir, Whitehurst, Small, Withering, Edgeworth, Day). Sets the context of eighteenth-century scientific enthusiasm, collecting mania, and the overlap between popular science and industrial ambition.

Part II: FIRST QUARTER (Chapters 1–9)
1. Earth, Elston & Electricity
Erasmus Darwin’s birth at Elston, Nottinghamshire in 1731. Childhood in the severe winter of 1739–40. The Darwin family’s yeoman background and Dissenting milieu in the Midlands. Education: Chesterfield School, then St John’s College, Cambridge (1746), and medical study in Edinburgh (1750–52). Sets up practice in Lichfield (1756). Darwin’s early experiments in electricity, his stammer, his huge appetite for knowledge — and actual food — and his first marriage to Mary Howard in 1757.
2. Toys
Matthew Boulton’s birth in Birmingham (1728), son of a silver-stamper and buckle-maker. Boulton’s apprenticeship and inheritance of the family business. His marriage to Mary Robinson; her early death. Boulton’s expansion of the Soho Manufactory, founded in 1762 on Handsworth Heath outside Birmingham. Boulton’s flamboyant personality, business ambition, and skill at entertaining aristocratic customers and foreign visitors. His obsession with quality, his growing reputation as the leading toy-maker (metalwork, buttons, buckles, steel jewellery) in England.
3. Scotland
The Scottish Enlightenment’s influence on the Lunar circle. William Small’s arrival in Birmingham — Small had been Professor of Natural Philosophy at William and Mary College, Virginia, where he taught Thomas Jefferson. Small’s role as the key link between Darwin, Boulton, and the Birmingham circle. James Watt’s early life in Greenock, his ‘trading’ in mathematical instruments in Glasgow, his friendship with Joseph Black and discovery of latent heat. Small and Watt’s correspondence.
4. The Doctor’s Bag
Erasmus Darwin’s medical practice and reputation in Lichfield. His consultations, his bluntness with patients, and his innovative treatments. Darwin’s work on the evolution of the species in Zoonomia (1794–96), begun much earlier. His friendships with fellow doctors and his role as physician to the Lunar circle. Darwin the poet — translations of Linnaeus, The Botanic Garden, the ‘crushes’ and love letters of his romantic life after Mary’s death. Marriage to Elizabeth Pole (1781) and move to Derby.
5. Pots
Josiah Wedgwood’s birth in Burslem, Staffordshire (1730). The Wedgwood family of potters. Smallpox at age eleven left him with a permanently weakened leg. Apprenticeship to his brother Thomas. Partnership with Thomas Whieldon (1754–59), the leading Staffordshire potter. Experiments in glazes and clays. Wedgwood’s scientific approach to ceramics, his meticulous notebooks. The establishment of his own works at Ivy House, Burslem (1759). His marriage to Sarah Wedgwood (1764). The beginnings of Etruria (1769).
6. Heading for Soho
Boulton’s Soho Manufactory — the largest and most advanced factory in England. Boulton’s search for skilled craftsmen and his cultivation of aristocratic clients. Boulton’s ‘renaissance in metal’: ormolu vases, silverware, Sheffield plate, steel jewellery. The financial strains of the Manufactory. Boulton’s partnership with John Fothergill. His quest for a suitable engine partner — the search for a better steam engine that led to James Watt.
7. Ingenious Philosophers
The formation of the Lunar Society as a regular meeting group (1765–68). Key members: Small, Darwin, Boulton, Whitehurst, Keir. The eclectic experiments they conducted — electrical, pneumatic, chemical, mechanical. The informal, ludic character of their meetings: ‘a little philosophical laughing’. The role of correspondence: the Lunar men wrote constantly to each other, their letters forming the true record of the group’s collective mind.
8. Reaching Out
The Lunar Society’s expansion. Thomas Day enters the circle — Rousseau’s disciple, eccentric, wealthy. Day’s failed experiment raising two foundling girls to be his ideal wife (Sabrina and Lucretia), as described in Edgeworth’s memoirs. Richard Lovell Edgeworth joins — engineer, inventor, educational theorist, serial husband. Edgeworth’s many projects: land improvement, telegraphs, wheel carriages. The group grows: James Keir the chemist; John Whitehurst the clockmaker and geologist.
9. Steam
Watt’s improvement of the Newcomen engine. The separate condenser (1765), Watt’s decisive insight. The partnership of Watt and Boulton (1775). Financial backing from Boulton. Watt’s anxiety and perfectionism versus Boulton’s optimism and salesmanship. The first engines installed at Soho, Shropshire, and Cornwall. ‘I sell here, Sir, what all the world desires to have — Power.’ The patent battles. The engine’s revolutionary impact on mining, manufacturing, and transport.

Part III: SECOND QUARTER (Chapters 10–19)
10. They Build Canals
The canal mania of the 1760s–70s. James Brindley, the self-taught engineer. The Bridgewater Canal (1761) and its impact. The Grand Trunk Canal linking the Mersey, Trent, and Severn. Wedgwood’s strategic interest: canals meant cheap transport of clay and finished pottery. Wedgwood and Boulton as promoters of canal schemes. The Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal. Erasmus Darwin as canal investor and poet of the ‘Navigation’ in The Botanic Garden.
11. Painting the Light
Joseph Wright of Derby — the painter of the Lunar circle. Wright’s great conversation pieces: ‘A Philosopher giving that Lecture on the Orrery’ (1766), ‘An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump’ (1768). Wright’s technique — the dramatic use of candlelight and moonlight. His portraits of Darwin, Whitehurst, and others. The connection between the Lunar circle’s experiments and Wright’s artistic vision of science as awe and mystery.
12. Magic & Mechanics
The overlap between science and mesmerism, entertainment and demonstration. Itinerant lecturers and electrical demonstrations. John Canton, Joseph Priestley’s early electrical work. The psychological dimension of the new science: where does experiment end and magic begin? The Lunar men’s performance of science for audiences.
13. Derbyshire Explorata
The Lunar men as explorers and field geologists. Whitehurst’s Inquiry into the Origin and Formation of the Earth (1778). Whitehurst’s work on the strata of Derbyshire, his systematic study of the Peak District. Exploration of the limestone caves (Mam Tor, Castleton, the Blue John mines). John Whitehurst’s clockwork: his famous astronomical clock for the King of Portugal.
14. Chemical Reactions
James Keir’s chemical experiments. Keir’s Dictionary of Chemistry (1789) and his translation of Macquer’s Chemical Dictionary. Keir’s glassworks at Stourbridge and later chemical works near Tipton. The group’s engagement with the new chemistry of Black, Lavoisier, and Priestley. Keir’s defence of phlogiston. The Lunar men’s debates over the nature of heat, air, and chemical combination.
15. Trials of Life
Personal lives of the Lunar men in the 1770s. Darwin’s grief after Mary’s death (1770) and his second courtship. Wedgwood’s leg — the amputation (1768) that nearly killed him. Edgeworth’s complicated domestic life — four wives, twenty-two children. Deaths and disruptions: Small’s early death (1775) deeply affected the group. Boulton’s loss of his first wife; his second marriage to Mary’s sister. The challenges of balancing philosophical friendship with business imperatives.
16. Rousseau & Romance
Thomas Day’s philosophical romance with the ideas of Rousseau. Day’s Emilius and Sophia (translation of Emile). His attempt to raise an ideal wife — the foundling experiments. The failure of the experiment, his eventual marriage to Esther Milnes. Edgeworth’s friendship with Day and their shared educational ideals. The tension between Rousseauan simplicity and the commercial-industrial drive of the other Lunar men.
17. Vases, Ormolu, Silver & Frogs
Boulton’s ormolu vases and the Soho metalwork. Boulton’s campaign to capture the luxury market. The Frog Service — Catherine the Great’s great dinner service from Wedgwood (1773–74), 952 pieces decorated with 1,244 views of British scenes and country houses. The rivalry and mutual support between Wedgwood and Boulton. The Portland Vase — Wedgwood’s four-year struggle to reproduce it in jasper.
18. Running the Show
The management of the great Lunar businesses. Boulton at Soho — managing 700+ workers, organising production from raw metal to finished goods. Wedgwood at Etruria — division of labour, discipline, pricing strategy, the showroom in London. Watt’s struggle to supervise engine installations across England, Scotland, and Cornwall. The financial organisation: partnership agreements, patent fees, customer credit, and cash flow.
19. Eddies
The late 1770s: slow years and personal setbacks. The American War’s impact on trade. Boulton’s financial difficulties. Watt’s depressive moods. Wedgwood’s expansion into new markets. Darwin’s literary ambitions taking shape. Priestley’s growing reputation as writer and theologian.

Part IV: THIRD QUARTER (Chapters 20–29)
20. Experiments on Air
Priestley’s discovery of ‘dephlogisticated air’ (oxygen) in August 1774, using a burning glass to heat mercuric oxide. The mouse experiment (March 1775). Priestley’s attachment to phlogiston theory. His publication Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air (1774–77). The debate with Lavoisier over the nature of oxygen and the overthrow of phlogiston. Priestley’s refusal to abandon phlogiston — a rare instance of the circle’s experimental openness becoming intellectual obstinacy.
21. ‘What All the World Desires’
Boulton and Watt’s triumph with the rotative steam engine (1781). The sun-and-planet gear, the double-acting engine. William Murdoch’s contributions. The Cornish engine market. The boom in orders for draining mines, driving mills, and powering factories. Boulton’s aggressive marketing — sending Watt’s engines across England, Scotland, and to continental Europe. The patent extended by Act of Parliament (1775) to 1800.
22. ‘Bandy’d Like a Shuttlecock’
The struggle over Watt’s patent extension. Competitors, pirates, and imitators. The lawsuits — Boulton and Watt v. Bull, Hornblower, and others. Legal battles that nearly broke them. The role of the older Lunatic members in defending Watt’s priority. The social costs: Watt’s obsessive secretiveness, his resentment at the ‘bandying’ of his reputation in the press and Parliament.
23. Plants & Passions
Erasmus Darwin’s greatest literary work — The Botanic Garden (1791), a scientific poem in two parts: ‘The Economy of Vegetation’ and ‘The Loves of the Plants’. Darwin as poet and populariser of Linnaean botany — the sexual system of plants rendered in poetic form with considerable erotic charge. The controversy — conservative critics attacked Darwin for combining sex, science, and atheism. The poem’s spectacular success among progressive readers.
24. Conquering Cornwall
Boulton and Watt’s Cornish engine campaign. The Cornish mining district — deep tin and copper mines requiring powerful pumps. The competition with other engine builders. The ‘duty’ measurements (Smeaton’s improved engine tests). Watt’s perfectionism in engine design. The Cornwall agents and engineers. The personal costs: Watt’s absences from home, his rivalry with his own partner Murdoch.
25. Dull Earth & Shining Stones
Mineralogy and geology in the Lunar circle. Whitehurst’s geological map of Derbyshire. Wedgwood’s use of local clays and minerals. Keir’s work on glass and alkali manufacture. The Lunar men’s interest in mining, mineral rights, and the industrial applications of geological knowledge. Fossils, crystals, and the age of the earth — speculations that challenged biblical chronology.
26. Creative Copying
The relationship between art, design, and industry in the Lunar circle. Wedgwood’s reproduction of the Portland Vase — the crowning achievement of four years of experimentation in jasper-ware (1786–1790). Boulton’s copying of antique vases in ormolu and silver. The aesthetic of industrial production: did copying cheapen art or democratise beauty? The Lunar men saw no contradiction between mechanical reproduction and artistic achievement.
27. Sons & Daughters
The children of the Lunar men. The education and careers of the next generation: Josiah Wedgwood II, John Wedgwood, Tom Wedgwood. James Watt Jr., Gregory Watt. Robert Darwin (Erasmus’s son, Charles Darwin’s father). Maria Edgeworth, the novelist. The Lunar daughters: Anne Boulton, Susannah Darwin. The tension between the fathers’ ambitions for their children and the children’s own desires. Tom Wedgwood’s brilliant but tragic life.
28. Bringing on the Artists
The Lunar men as patrons of the arts. Wedgwood’s employment of John Flaxman, George Stubbs, and others to design pottery. Boulton’s commissioning of Robert Adam for architectural and decorative designs. Wright of Derby’s portraits of Lunar figures. Erasmus Darwin’s influence on William Blake (illustrations for The Botanic Garden). John Hill, the botanical artist. The Birmingham Academy of Arts. The Lunar circle as patrons bridging Enlightenment science and Romantic art.
29. From the Nation to the Land
The Lunar men and the American Revolution. Many of the group sympathised with the American colonists: Priestley, Price, and the radical politics of the 1770s–80s. Boulton and Watt’s correspondence with Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson. William Small’s American connections — his teaching of Jefferson at William and Mary. The larger political context: the loss of the American colonies, the reshaping of British commercial policy. The Lunar men’s focus on domestic improvement, canals, and manufactures as Britain rebuilt.

Part V: FOURTH QUARTER (Chapters 30–40)
30. Fire
The Birmingham Riots of 1791 (the ‘Priestley Riots’). Priestley’s political and religious radicalism — his support for the French Revolution, his Unitarianism, his attacks on the Church of England. The ‘Church and King’ mob’s three-day rampage. The destruction of Priestley’s house, laboratory, and library at Fair Hill. Priestley’s escape. The failure of local authorities to intervene. The psychological impact on the Lunar circle: the end of the group’s confident, open-handed Enlightenment optimism.
31. Boulton’s Blazing Skies
Birmingham in the aftermath of the riots. Boulton’s position: a loyalist manufacturer who nonetheless protected his friends. The retrenchment of the Liberal cause. The emergence of reaction — Pitt’s repression, the suspension of habeas corpus. Boulton’s continued business success, overshadowed by fear and division. The growing tension between the older members over politics.
32. The Linnaean Row
The quarrel within the Lunar circle over Linnaean classification and Darwin’s poetic treatment of botany. The moral and philosophical disagreements. Wedgwood’s discomfort with the erotic aspect of The Loves of the Plants. The wider public debate over sexual language in science. The cooling of some friendships.
33. Protecting Our Interests
The patent extension fight reaches its climax. Boulton’s lobbying of Parliament. The counter-petitions from engine users, particularly in Cornwall. The compromise: the patent extended but with lower royalty rates. The immense wealth that followed. Watt’s growing fortune and his retreat into land purchases and gentlemanly life at Heathfield Hall. The transformation of the inventor into a landed proprietor.
34. Family & Feeling
The personal lives of the Lunar circle in the 1790s. Wedgwood’s declining health. Darwin’s controversies — his materialist philosophy attacked as atheistic. Edgeworth’s educational writings. The marriages of the next generation. Withering’s medical career, his work on digitalis (foxglove) in treating dropsy and heart conditions. The growing distance between the Lunatics as age, politics, and geography separated them.
35. Grand Projects
The Lunar men’s visionary schemes. Darwin’s speculations on steamships, manned flight, and global weather control. Edgeworth’s telegraph, his land improvement in Ireland, his educational theories. Wedgwood’s plans for improving the conditions of the working classes. The canal network — the Lunar men’s dream of a Midlands connected by waterways to every corner of Britain. The cutting of the Grand Junction Canal.
36. Turning
The division of the Lunar circle. Priestley’s emigration to America (1794). Watt’s withdrawal from active business. Keir’s chemical works flourishing. Boulton’s Soho Mint — his greatest late achievement, using steam power for coin striking. The Boulton and Watt sons taking over the engine business. The meetings becoming rarer, the correspondence thinner.
37. Riots
The repression of the 1790s intensifies. Pitt’s Treason Trials (1794). The suspension of habeas corpus. The persecution of Dissenters and Reformers. The Lunar men’s experience of surveillance and suspicion. The end of their public optimism. The French Revolution’s betrayal of its ideals — terror, war, the execution of Lavoisier (1794), a chemist dear to the Lunar circle.
38. Handing On
The Lunar sons in the 1790s. James Watt Jr. in Paris — mingling with Jacobins and being denounced by Burke. Tom Wedgwood’s experimental work on photography (silver nitrate and light), though he never fixed the images. Josiah Wedgwood II’s management of Etruria. The younger generation’s different values, their distance from their fathers’ cooperative ideals. The closing of the Soho Manufactory gates to visitors: the end of open-handed display.
39. ‘Fire Engines & Sundry Works’
The later careers of the surviving Lunatics. Boulton’s Soho Mint — steam-driven coin presses that struck millions of coins for the East India Company, the Bank of England, and foreign governments. William Murdoch’s gas lighting — lighting Soho with coal gas (1802). Boulton and Murdoch’s Nelson medallion for Trafalgar veterans (1805). Watt’s retirement to Heathfield — his workshop, his hobbies, his melancholy.
40. ‘Time Is! Time Was! …’
The closing years. Boulton’s last campaign: building Birmingham’s first theatre (1807) against Nonconformist opposition. The deaths: Priestley 1804, Boulton 1809, Edgeworth 1817, Watt 1819, Keir 1820. Only Samuel Galton lived to see the Reform Act of 1832. Maria Edgeworth’s final visits to the families, carrying her father’s memoirs. The legacy: a world of steam, iron, canals, gaslight, and chemically-founded industry — all imagined and brought into being by a handful of friends meeting by the light of the full moon.

Part VI: WANING
Epilogue: ‘Fiddledum, Diddledum’
Uglow’s concluding reflections on the Lunar Society’s legacy. The men who had been provincial outsiders became, in retrospect, the architects of modern industrial Britain. The Lunar Society’s informal, cross-disciplinary, collaborative model — Uglow draws a parallel with the collaborative culture of the internet age. The Lunar men’s extraordinary combination of science, art, commerce, and friendship. Their belief in progress, in the power of knowledge to improve the human condition. The quiet end: by the 1820s, the last survivors had scattered and died, but the world they made — industrial, interconnected, powered by steam — was permanent.

Endmatter

Chronology (from line ~7100): A year-by-year timeline of key events in the Lunar men’s lives and the wider historical context, 1709–1832.
Abbreviations and Sources: Full bibliography with abbreviations used in the endnotes, covering manuscript sources (Birmingham City Archives, Wedgwood Museum, James Watt papers, Darwin papers, Edgeworth papers, Priestley papers) and printed primary and secondary works.
List of Illustrations: 31 plates and numerous in-text illustrations, including portraits by Joseph Wright of Derby, George Stubbs, and others; views of Birmingham and Soho; Wedgwood’s jasper-ware and vases; and Wright’s great scientific conversation pieces (Orrery, Air Pump).


Key Figures (Principal Lunar Men)






































































NameLifespanRoleErasmus Darwin1731–1802Physician, poet, naturalist, evolution theoristMatthew Boulton1728–1809Manufacturer, Soho, steam-engine partner, mint masterJames Watt1736–1819Engineer, steam-engine inventorJosiah Wedgwood1730–1795Potter, industrialist, porcelain pioneerJoseph Priestley1733–1804Chemist, theologian, radical DissenterJames Keir1735–1820Chemist, glassmaker, alkali manufacturerWilliam Small1734–1775Physician, philosopher, group catalystWilliam Withering1741–1799Physician, botanist, digitalis pioneerRichard Lovell Edgeworth1744–1817Engineer, educational theorist, land improverThomas Day1748–1789Writer, Rousseau disciple, eccentricJohn Whitehurst1713–1788Clockmaker, geologist, scientific instrument makerSamuel Galton1753–1832Gunmaker, Quaker, last surviving member

Key Themes

Collaborative science across disciplines: The Lunar model — manufacturers, doctors, clergymen, and gentlemen meeting informally, sharing experiments and ideas across every branch of natural philosophy.
The marriage of science and industry: Every discovery was immediately tested for practical application — chemistry to pottery glazes, steam power to mining, electricity to medicine.
The Enlightenment in the provinces: The Lunar men showed that Britain’s intellectual ferment was not confined to London and Edinburgh — the Midlands became a powerhouse of innovation precisely because it was outside the old institutional structures.
The political dimension: The Lunar men were generally liberal, Dissenting, and sympathetic to the American and French Revolutions — Priestley’s house was destroyed for this. The book traces the shift from Enlightenment optimism to conservative reaction in the 1790s.
Science, art, and the sublime: Wright of Derby’s paintings, Wedgwood’s ceramics, Darwin’s poems — the Lunar men produced not just industrial technology but an aesthetic of the industrial sublime.
The human cost: The stress on Watt, the tragedy of Tom Wedgwood, the failure of Day’s idealistic schemes, Priestley’s exile — Uglow never loses sight of the personal costs of their ambitions.
The generation gap: The Lunar sons (James Watt Jr., Tom Wedgwood, the Edgeworth children) belonged to a different world — more political, more conflicted, more Romantic.
The Lunar legacy: The book positions the Lunar Society as the crucible of modern industrial Britain — the first time that scientific research, engineering, manufacturing, and commerce were systematically integrated by a group of friends.


Sources Referenced

Manuscript collections: Birmingham City Archives (Boulton & Watt papers), Wedgwood Museum archives, James Watt papers (Birmingham), Darwin papers (Cambridge University Library), Priestley papers, Edgeworth papers
Primary printed: Erasmus Darwin, Zoonomia, The Botanic Garden, Phytologia, The Temple of Nature; Joseph Priestley, Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air; James Watt, correspondence and notebooks; Josiah Wedgwood, Experiment Book; John Whitehurst, Inquiry into the Origin and Formation of the Earth; Richard Lovell Edgeworth, Practical Education; James Keir, Dictionary of Chemistry
Biographical: Lives of Erasmus Darwin (by Anna Seward, Desmond King-Hele), Matthew Boulton (H. W. Dickinson, A. E. Musson, Eric Robinson, Jennifer Tann), James Watt (H. W. Dickinson, Richard Hills), Josiah Wedgwood (Eliza Meteyard, Robin Reilly), Joseph Priestley (Anne Holt, F. W. Gibbs, Robert Schofield), Thomas Day (Peter Rowland), John Whitehurst (Maxwell Craven)
Secondary works on the Lunar Society: Robert E. Schofield, The Lunar Society of Birmingham; R. M. & A. M. W. Rees, The Lunar Society; Desmond King-Hele, The Lunar Men: The Story of the Lunar Society
General historical context: E. P. Thompson, The Making of the English Working Class; J. H. Plumb, England in the Eighteenth Century; Roy Porter, Enlightenment: Britain and the Creation of the Modern World; Paul Langford, A Polite and Commercial People; John Brewer, The Pleasures of the Imagination

sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol1.title: Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. I
sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol1.content:
Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. I
Major-General Sir John Malcolm, G.C.B., F.R.S. (1769–1833) — The Life of Robert, Lord Clive: Collected from the Family Papers Communicated by the Earl of Powis. — In Three Volumes. Volume I. John Murray, Albemarle Street, London, 1836.
The first volume of Sir John Malcolm’s biography of Robert Clive (1725–1774), the soldier and statesman who established British East India Company rule in Bengal. Written by a fellow Indian army officer and diplomat who served in India during the same era (Malcolm was a key figure in the later Anglo-Maratha wars, and had access to the Powis family papers).
The volume contains 9,913 lines, extracted from a CreateSpace reprint (2016) of the 1836 original.
Chapter Summary
INTRODUCTION — General View of the State of India in 1746. The decline of the Mughal Empire since Aurungzebe (1707), the rise of the Marathas, the European trading companies, the Portuguese decline, the English and French East India Companies, the Carnatic and its rulers, Dupleix and La Bourdonnais, the outbreak of the War of the Austrian Succession in India, the capture of Madras (1746), the siege of Pondicherry, the peace of 1748.
CHAPTER I — Clive’s family and boyhood. His early life in India. History of the Carnatic to 1750. Clive’s arrival at Madras as a writer (clerk) in the Company’s service, his depression and attempted suicide, his transfer to the military branch.
CHAPTER II — Wars in the Carnatic. The siege of Arcot (1751) and subsequent operations of Clive till 1752. Clive’s defence of Arcot with 200 men against 10,000, his sorties and eventual relief — the feat that made his reputation.
CHAPTER III — Clive returns to England (1753). Again sent to India in 1755. The capture of Gheriah. Operations in Bengal. Calcutta retaken from Suraj-ud-Daulah, and the peace forced upon the Nawab.
CHAPTER IV — The surrender of Chandernagore (the French settlement in Bengal). The quarrel with Suraj-ud-Daulah.
CHAPTER V — The intrigues at the court of Murshidabad. The conspiracy of Mir Jafar. The Battle of Plassey (June 1757) — Clive’s victory with 3,000 men against 50,000. Suraj-ud-Daulah deposed, Mir Jafar raised to the throne.
CHAPTER VI — Transactions subsequent to the Battle of Plassey. The settlement of Bengal, the imposition of the Company’s authority.
CHAPTER VII — State of parties in Bengal and at the court of Mir Jafar. Clive proceeds to Patna. He accepts the government of Bengal.
CHAPTER VIII — Clive’s expedition to occupy the Northern Circars. Intrigues at the court of Murshidabad. The Shahzada’s invasion of Bihar repelled by Clive. Clive receives a jaghir (land grant).
Key Data Points

Relationship to the Wiki
The first in-depth source on British India in the wiki. Covers the Carnatic Wars (1740s–1750s) and the establishment of British power in Bengal (1757–1760). Complements Campbell Vol. IV (naval operations in Indian waters) and Belsham History Vol. IV (which covers Plassey and Wandewash from a distance).

sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol2.title: Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. II
sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol2.content:
Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. II
Major-General Sir John Malcolm — The Life of Robert, Lord Clive. — Volume II. John Murray, London, 1836.
Covers Clive’s later career from 1758 through his second administration of Bengal and his final return to England. The key events are the defence of Madras against Lally, the defeat of the Dutch in Bengal, Clive’s first return to England, his political battles at the India House, his return to Bengal as governor, and the acquisition of the Diwani (the revenue administration of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa) for the East India Company.
Chapter Summary
CHAPTER IX — The Northern Circars expedition under Colonel Forde (1758). The siege of Madras by the French Count de Lally. Clive’s correspondence and strategic direction from Bengal.
CHAPTER X — The Dutch armament against Bengal (1759), destroyed by Clive’s decisive action. Proceedings in England regarding the government of Bengal. Clive’s famous letter to Pitt the Elder proposing that the Crown take over the Indian possessions. Clive returns to England (1760).
CHAPTER XI — Clive in England. His private life and character — the Indian nabob in London, his wealth and estates, his peerage, his parliamentary career.
CHAPTER XII — Clive’s politics. His quarrel with Laurence Sulivan, the chairman of the East India Company. His right to the jaghir (land grant) disputed. The parties at the India House. The disasters in India during his absence. Clive called upon to resume the government of Bengal. He consents and sets out for India (1764).
CHAPTER XIII — State of India during Clive’s absence (1760–1765). Vansittart’s government. The deposition of Mir Jafar. The elevation of Mir Qasim. The massacre of Patna (1763) — the killing of 150 British prisoners by Mir Qasim. The restoration of Mir Jafar. The disorders in Bengal.
CHAPTER XIV — Clive assumes the government of Bengal (1765). The state of the country and the various services. Military arrangements. Negotiations with the Nawab of Bengal. Treaty with the Nawab-Vizier of Oudh. The settlement with the Emperor Shah Alam II. The Diwani acquired for the Company — the grant of revenue administration over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, making the East India Company the de facto ruler of 20 million people. Discontents in the civil service and Clive’s reforms.
Key Data Points

Continues directly from Vol. I. Covers the climax of Clive’s career — the acquisition of the Diwani (1765), which laid the foundation for the British Raj. Also covers the French siege of Madras under Lally, complementing Campbell Vol. IV’s naval coverage of the same period.

sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol3.title: Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. III
sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol3.content:
Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. III
Major-General Sir John Malcolm — The Life of Robert, Lord Clive. — Volume III. John Murray, London, 1836.
The final volume of Malcolm’s biography, covering Clive’s last years in India (1766–1767) and his final return to England, the parliamentary attacks on his reputation, and his death in 1774.
Chapter Summary
CHAPTER XV — The mutinous combination among the officers of the Bengal army (1766). Clive’s suppression of the “white mutiny” over the reduction of double batta — nearly 200 officers resigned their commissions. Clive’s display of resolve, the collapse of the mutiny, the punishment of the ringleaders.
CHAPTER XVI — Clive’s other reforms in Bengal. The salt monopoly controversy — Clive’s allocation of its profits to senior civil and military officers as a legitimate allowance. The administrative reforms, the regulation of trade, the suppression of private trading by Company servants.
CHAPTER XVII — Clive returns to England (July 1767). His shattered health, the waters at Bath. His welcome by the Court of Directors and the public. His correspondence with Orme the historian, providing materials for the continuation of the history of India. His retirement from active service.
CHAPTER XVIII — The parliamentary attacks on Clive (1772–1773). The inquiry into the East India Company’s affairs, the accusations of corruption against Clive. Clive’s great parliamentary defence — “I stand astonished at my own moderation.” His acquittal and vindication by the House of Commons. His declining health, his death by suicide (November 22, 1774). The assessment of his character and achievements.
Key Data Points

Relationship to the Wiki
Completes the three-volume biography of Clive. Covers Clive’s final years — the administrative consolidation of the East India Company’s rule in Bengal, the battle over corruption and reform, and the parliamentary reckoning that defined the Company’s relationship with the British state. Complements Belsham Memoirs Vols. I–II (which cover the same period from the British domestic angle) and Belsham History Vol. IV (covering the India Acts).

sources/massie-natural-rate-of-interest.title: Massie — An Essay on the Natural Rate of Interest
sources/massie-natural-rate-of-interest.content:
Massie — An Essay on the Natural Rate of Interest
Joseph Massie (d. 1784) — An Essay on the Governing Causes of the Natural Rate of Interest; Wherein the Sentiments of Sir William Petty and Mr. Locke, on that Head, are considered. — London: Printed for W. Owen, at Homer’s Head, near Temple Bar, 1750. Reprinted as Joseph Massie on the Natural Rate of Interest, 1750, edited by Jacob H. Hollander, The Lord Baltimore Press, Baltimore, 1912.
A seminal mid-18th-century economic pamphlet by the little-known but influential writer Joseph Massie. Massie was a prolific economic pamphleteer in the 1750s–1760s and compiled the celebrated Alphabetical and Chronological Index of Commercial Books and Pamphlets — a bibliography of 2,377 items by 1764 that remains the most important guide to English economic literature before Adam Smith. He proposed (unsuccessfully, to the Treasury in 1760) writing a “commercial history of Great Britain” and a treatise on the “elements of commerce illustrated by Applications,” but the present essay is his most important theoretical work.
The text is 2,350 lines, extracted from the 1912 Johns Hopkins reprint (which itself reproduces the original 1750 edition, 62 pages + preface, at “Price One Shilling”). The original was out of print by 1758.
Structure of the Essay
Preface (pp. iii–iv)
An apologia for questioning Locke’s authority on interest. Massie professes great veneration for Locke but argues that the subject “cannot be too particularly considered.”
1. Extracts from Petty and Locke (pp. 11–18)
Massie reproduces verbatim the key passages he intends to criticise:
From Sir William Petty’s Political Arithmetic (3rd ed., 1699):

Petty claims the natural fall of interest is “the Effect of the Increase of Money”

From John Locke’s Treatise on Interest (Works, 1740 ed., Vol. 2):

Locke defines “natural Use” as the rate “which the present Scarcity of [Money] makes it naturally at, upon an equal Distribution of it”
Interest is raised in two ways: (1) when Money is little in proportion to Debts; (2) when Money is little in proportion to Trade
The borrower’s Profit is what makes interest possible — and this profit increases “the less Quantity of Money, in Proportion to Trade”
The natural Value of Money (as yielding interest) depends on the whole Quantity of Money in proportion to the whole Trade
Locke’s historical example: in Queen Elizabeth’s time high interest coincided with thriving trade

2. Critique of Locke on Debts (pp. 19–28)
Massie’s first major argument: Locke’s position that debts govern interest is contradicted by the facts.

If debts raised interest, the enormous increase in both private and public debts since 1600 should have made interest far higher — not lower. National debt alone rose from 45 to 78 million pounds between 1740 and 1750.
“Publick Faith is like a Merchant, whose Credit falls and rises, as his Trade declines or prospers” — the government pays more in wartime due to risk (the 1745 rebellion), not debt quantity.
Key distinction: what looks like high interest for risky borrowers is partly a “Praemium of Risque” (insurance premium), not pure interest. Calling it interest is “as improper as it would be to call that Praemium Interest, which a Merchant gives an Insurer to have his Ship or Merchandise insured against the Dangers of the Sea or Enemies.”
Borrowing and lending are not caused by scarcity of money but by its unequal distribution — when wealth concentrates in few hands, the rich must lend to the industrious rather than employ it themselves.

3. Critique of Locke on the Quantity of Money (pp. 35–45)
Massie’s second critique: the proportion of money to trade does not govern interest either.

Locke’s own rule for how much money a country needs (one-fiftieth of labourers’ wages, one-fourth of landholders’ revenue, one-twentieth of brokers’ returns) is circular — these quantities themselves vary with the value of money.
The price-of-wheat test: Massie compiles a systematic table of wheat prices and interest rates across five periods:
















































PeriodWheat price (per quarter)Legal interestNatural interestLocke’s predicted rate1444–146012s 1d (in present money)Not fixed~10%9.5%1646–1665£2 17s 5.5d8%7%2%1666–1685£2 6s 3.75d6%5%2.5%1686–1705£2 5s 9.75d6%5%2.5%1729–1748£1 8s 6d5%4%(baseline)

If money’s proportion to trade governed interest (using wheat price as proxy), interest should have been only 2% in 1646–1665 — but it was actually 7%. In the 1666–1705 periods, when money was becoming scarcer relative to trade, interest should have risen — instead it fell. The rule is contradicted by every period except the earliest.
A reductio ad absurdum: if the rule held, interest would have been 14%, 28%, 56%, even 112% at earlier periods when wheat was cheaper. “No one can imagine any Man ever paid 112 l. for the Use of 100 l. for a Year.”

4. Massie’s Positive Theory: Interest is Governed by Profits of Trade (pp. 45–54)
Massie’s central argument, presented with a clear theoretical structure:
First principle: Interest is founded on the profit that borrowed money is capable of producing. “He who borrows 100 l. in Money of his Neighbour for a Year, by the Use of which in Trade or otherwise … his Neighbour could, and he may, make a Profit of 5 l. … is as much 105 l. in his Neighbour’s Debt, as he would have been if he had actually borrow’d so much Money.”
The rule: “The natural Rate of Interest is governed by the Profits of Trade to Particulars.” This is not just a statement about individual borrowers — it is a general rule: what matters is the profit rate typical merchants can make, not extraordinary profits from special skill.
The equitable division: Following Locke’s own suggestion (Extract 4), Massie accepts that lenders and borrowers divide profits equally — one half to the lender as interest, the other half to the borrower as the reward for his labour and risk.
Proof from cross-country comparison:



































CountryInterest rateExplanationHolland3%Most traders per capita, lowest profitsGreat Britain4%Next-highest proportion of tradersFrance, Germany, Portugal5–6%Fewer traders relative to populationWest & East Indies7–9%Higher risk from distance, climateTurkey10–12%Fewest traders, highest profits
5. The Superior Causes: What Governs Profits of Trade (pp. 49–58)
Massie traces profits back to their root causes:
First law of profit: “The Profits of Trade in general, are governed by the Proportion which the Number of Traders bears to the Quantity of Trade.” More competitors chasing the same trade = lower profits = lower interest. Fewer traders (or more trade) = higher profits = higher interest.
Why profits have fallen across Europe: Three causes:

Increase of traders: constant influx of new competitors, especially young men underselling established merchants to build their business
Decrease of trade relative to traders: the rise of rival trading nations (France, Sweden, Denmark, etc.) competing with England and Holland for foreign trade
The East-India trade: the drain of silver to Asia reduces the quantity of trade available to European merchants — “The Riches of the West-Indies, are by the trading Nations of Europe carried to the East-Indies, without Producing any Advantages to the Trade of Europe in general”

Second law — the ultimate cause of trade itself: “The first and greatest Motive to trade is Necessity” — the inability of any man to procure all the necessities of life by his own labour. But beyond this, the quantity of trade depends on government and security of property.
Massie’s explicit argument: it is Government, and not Nature, which makes nations industrious or idle. Free governments that preserve “Men’s private Rights” (like Holland and Britain) produce more traders per capita, lower profits, and lower interest — because men “extend their Cares to Futurity” only when they have “a Prospect of enjoying hereafter the Fruits of their present Industry.” Despotic governments (Turkey, Spain) produce fewer traders, higher profits, and higher interest.
6. On Public Credit and the National Debt (pp. 29–35)
An extended digression on why government borrowing rates are irrelevant to the natural rate of interest:

“All Reasoning about natural Interest from the Rate which the Government pays for Money, is, and unavoidably must be fallacious”
The government’s rate is “founded in Necessity” (which has no bounds), while natural interest is “founded in Profit” (which does)
In peacetime, the government can borrow below the natural rate (public faith is “more extensively known” than private security)
Counter-intuitive claim: paying off the national debt would raise interest, not lower it — because the portion owed to foreigners (Dutch, Swiss) must be paid in coin or bullion, draining money from trade

Key Data Points





































AttributeDetailAuthorJoseph Massie (d. 1784)TitleAn Essay on the Governing Causes of the Natural Rate of InterestPublished1750; reprinted 1912 (Johns Hopkins)Raw filewiki/raw/massie-natural-rate-of-interest.txt (2,350 lines)Original collationTitle + preface [iii]–iv + pp. 5–62, octavo; price 1 shillingPeriod1750 (primary source in economic thought)SignificanceAnticipated the classical theory of interest (profit-driven) later developed by Adam Smith; provided the most systematic empirical refutation of Locke’s quantity-of-money theory of interest before Hume (1752)
Significance in the History of Economic Thought
Massie’s essay ranks as an important element in the pre-Smithian discussion of profits. The German economist Wilhelm Roscher credited Massie with refuting the direct association of the rate of interest with the amount of money — a refutation that “two years later Hume repeated with greater simplicity but no more force.” Massie established that:

Interest is a share of profit, not a monetary phenomenon
The rate of profit is determined by the ratio of traders to trade (a rudimentary theory of competition)
The ultimate determinants of commercial activity are institutional — the security of property under free government

The tract was out of print within eight years of publication (by 1758), suggesting limited contemporary circulation, though it was rediscovered and valued by later historians.

sources/postlethwayt-britains-commercial.title: postlethwayt-britains-commercial-interest
sources/postlethwayt-britains-commercial.content:
Postlethwayt — Britain’s Commercial Interest Explained and Improved (1757)
Author: Malachy Postlethwayt (1707–1767)
Title: Britain’s Commercial Interest Explained and Improved; In a Series of Dissertations on Several Important Branches of her Trade and Police: Containing a Candid Enquiry into the Secret Causes of the Present Misfortunes of the Nation, with Proposals for their Remedy. Also the Great Advantages which would accrue to this Kingdom from an Union with Ireland
Edition: First edition, printed for D. Browne (London), 1757
Format: Two volumes; Vol. I only in this source (548 pp.)
OCLC: 6290741
Raw text: postlethwayt-britains-commercial-interest.txt (21,004 lines, 743 KB)

Summary
Postlethwayt’s Britain’s Commercial Interest Explained and Improved (1757) is a collection of nineteen political-economic dissertations written during the early years of the Seven Years’ War. Unlike his earlier prospectus for the Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce (1749), this is a full-length policy treatise — 548 pages — offering Postlethwayt’s analysis of Britain’s commercial decline and his proposed remedies. The entire work is framed as a sustained address to John Manners, Marquess of Granby (later Duke of Rutland), a prominent military commander and statesman.
The preface opens by declaring that “the nation is, at present, reduced to a very melancholy state” and that Britain is “destitute, at this juncture, of all maritime allies.” The central argument is structural: high domestic costs — driven by under-cultivation, high rents, and excessive taxes — undermine Britain’s ability to compete with France. Postlethwayt argues that the only path to recovery is agricultural improvement, legislative union with Ireland (following the Scottish model of 1707), colonial integration, and fiscal discipline.

Contents
Volume I
Dissertation I (pp. 1–55) — Of the Landed Interest, in relation to the cultivation of waste land
Postlethwayt opens his treatise with the fundamental proposition that “every essential object of traffic and commerce, requisite to the sustenance and convenience of human life being produced by the earth,” the more land that is cultivated, the greater the national prosperity. His core argument is that cultivating waste lands will lower grain prices, reduce the cost of labour and manufactures, and restore Britain’s competitive position against foreign rivals.
Contains the book’s most important quantitative calculation: England contains approximately 62,000 square miles of productive land (after deducting “irregularity, towns and rivers” from a gross area of 92,800), of which only about 31,000 square miles are currently under cultivation. Postlethwayt calculates that 86 square miles of new land should be brought into cultivation each year just to keep pace with the natural increase of population.
A central paradox explored: high rents appear to benefit landlords in the short term but ultimately impoverish them, because they drive up the price of everything the landlord must buy — labour, manufactures, provisions. A gentleman with £1,000 per annum who spends £500 and saves £500 “will be deceived” if he thinks rising rents increase his real wealth, because the purchasing power of his savings falls proportionally. Postlethwayt calculates that a 20–30% fall in rents (from increased cultivation) would make everything correspondingly cheaper, so that “70 or 80 l. would purchase more” than 100 l. does at present — the landlord would actually be better off.
Dissertation II (pp. 56–73) — The Productions and trade of England compared with those of Scotland and Ireland, and the British plantations
Extends the argument of Diss I by comparing Britain’s position with its constituent kingdoms and colonies. Postlethwayt argues that however great the advantages England has over its other territories, “when duly considered, they will be found to be less considerable than is commonly imagined” — because the same problems of under-cultivation and high costs affect all parts of the British dominions. The dissertations throughout enforce the theme that each part of the empire should serve the whole rather than compete internally.
Dissertation III (pp. 74–101) — A summary of various general principles of agriculture, founded on experience, for the improvement of lands
A practical agricultural manual embedded within the policy framework. Postlethwayt discusses drainage techniques for wet lands (“such as lye on a slope are drained by cutting trenches”) and distinguishes three types of wet land requiring different treatment. Covers soil improvement, crop rotation, and the management of waste grounds. This is the most “hands-on” section of the book, drawing on practical agricultural experience rather than political arithmetic.
Dissertation IV (pp. 102–123) — Farther considerations on the establishment of public granaries
Proposes state-managed grain stores modelled on French practice (“as recommended to the practice of France, by some of their ablest writers”). Postlethwayt notes that the French law forbidding merchants to keep corn above three years was well-intentioned but counter-productive — it prevented speculation that could stabilise prices across good and bad harvests. He argues that “three or four plentiful harvests running are no new thing” and that “great scarcities have not happened till after such repeated plenty,” making public granaries essential to prevent the cycle of glut and dearth.
Dissertation V (pp. 124–142) — Further considerations on trade, agriculture, and public granaries
Continues the argument for state intervention in grain markets. Postlethwayt addresses objections to his scheme and provides comparative examples from European practice.
Dissertation VI (pp. 143–172) — Farther considerations on the connections of Trade between Great Britain and Ireland and the British plantations
Analyses the trading relationships among the British Isles and American colonies. Postlethwayt argues that Ireland and the plantations should function as complementary parts of a single imperial economy, with each territory specialising in what it produces best. The current system of trade restrictions — particularly those against Irish exports — undermines this natural complementarity.
Dissertation VII (pp. 173–196) — Of such productions, manufactures, and trades, as England, Scotland, Ireland, and the British plantations should chiefly cultivate
A division-of-labour argument for specialisation within the British imperial system. Postlethwayt argues that the various parts of the empire should be directed toward productions in which they have natural advantages, so they “rival and compete with foreign nations, and not with each other.” This anticipates the classical argument for free trade within an imperial customs union.
Dissertation VIII (pp. 197–203) — Of the connection between the landed and trading interests of the kingdom
A brief but pointed treatment of the interdependence of agriculture and commerce. Postlethwayt argues that the supposed conflict between “landed” and “trading” interests is a fallacy — each depends on the other, and policies that benefit one at the expense of the other ultimately harm both.
Dissertation IX (pp. 204–244) — An abstract of some philosophic remarks, relating to the cultivation of land
Draws on philosophical and practical writings on agricultural improvement. Postlethwayt compiles observations from various authors to support his case that agricultural improvement is the foundation of national wealth.
Dissertation X (pp. 245–267) — The landed and trading interests connectively considered
Addresses the gentry and planters directly, urging them to adopt improved agricultural methods as a patriotic duty. Postlethwayt argues that “country gentlemen and planters may promote the benefit of their estates, in conjunction with that of the nation” — private profit and public good coincide when estates are efficiently managed.
Dissertation XI (pp. 268–290) — The union of Great Britain and Ireland, considered
Opens the major second-half theme of the book. Postlethwayt’s immediate motivation is revealing: “One motive to the drawing up of these papers is, the late great scarcity of grain, and the deplorable distress and calamity of the bulk of the people in consequence thereof” — this is the famine of 1756–57. He argues that the grain shortage is inseparable from the broader question of Irish union. A legislative union (modelled on the Anglo-Scottish union of 1707) would integrate Irish agriculture with British markets, solve the grain problem, and give both kingdoms a common interest in prosperity.
Dissertation XII (pp. 291–334) — The foregoing subject farther considered
A historical survey of proposals for Irish union from the reign of Queen Anne to the present. Postlethwayt draws on earlier writers who had urged union, noting that the arguments have been made repeatedly but never acted upon. The historical record — “from the beginning of the reign of Queen Anne to the present time” — shows that every generation has recognised the benefits of union but lacked the political will.
Dissertation XIII (pp. 335–376) — The union of England and Ireland continued
Focuses on the illicit wool trade from Ireland to France — the single most damaging leak in the British commercial system. Postlethwayt writes that “Long experience has shewn, that no laws hitherto enacted, however severe, have been sufficient to prevent the people of Ireland from running their raw wools to France, and their manufactured goods to foreign countries.” Only union can stop this, he argues, because it would make it “the interest of Ireland to discourage that practice” — substituting Irish commercial interest for British legislative coercion. The wool smuggling directly undermines the British textile industry, Britain’s most valuable export.
Dissertation XIV (pp. 377–400) — Of the union of England and Ireland continued
Examines two capital errors in British policy toward Ireland: 1) the Act to prohibit Irish cattle imports, and 2) the destruction of the woollen manufacture of that kingdom. Postlethwayt describes both as “destructive” and argues that “England has scarce ever exercised her power in commercial affairs but she has suffered for it.” The cattle acts (passed in the 1660s prohibiting Irish livestock from English markets) are now “generally allowed destructive.” The suppression of Irish woollen manufacturing (under William III) drove Irish wool to France, where it fed the very rival whose textile exports now competed with England’s.
Dissertation XV (pp. 401–420) — Of the union of the Isle of Man with England
Discusses the Isle of Man’s role as a smuggling entrepot. Postlethwayt writes that “it is too notorious to be doubted, that this Isle has many years been, and still continues to be, a common storehouse for all manner of foreign goods and merchandises that pay high duties in Great Britain or Ireland, or are prohibited to be imported into these kingdoms.” Its merchants have “constant supplies of large quantities of tobacco” and other contraband. Incorporation into the British customs system would close this loophole. (The Isle of Man was indeed brought under British customs control through the Isle of Man Purchase Act 1765, eight years after this work.)
Dissertation XVI (pp. 421–460) — A succinct view of the constitution of the British plantations in America
The most extensive treatment of the American colonies in the book. Postlethwayt categorises the colonies by their form of government:

Crown colonies — Nova Scotia, New Hampshire, the Jerseys, New York, Virginia, the two Carolinas, Bermuda, the Summer Islands, the Bahamas, Jamaica, Barbados, and the Leeward Islands
Proprietary colonies — Pennsylvania and Maryland
Charter governments — Massachusetts Bay (the chief of which is “the province of Massachusetts-Bay, commonly called New England”)

He analyses the causes of the colonies becoming “the present seat of war” (the Seven Years’ War in North America) and proposes measures to restore their “strength and stability.” The key problem: the colonies, left to their own devices, have developed in ways that undermine imperial unity, and the French have exploited these divisions.
Dissertation XVII (pp. 461–480) — Further considerations on the causes of the present state of our affairs in America
Argues explicitly for greater imperial cohesion. Postlethwayt writes that “our great aim tends towards such a union amongst all his Majesty’s dominions, as will promote the mutual strength and vigor, as well as the mutual prosperity of them all; for the happy general union that we would cement, is no less constitutional than commercial.” This is among the earliest systematic arguments for what would later be called imperial federation.
Dissertation XVIII (pp. 481–500) — The cause of the present state of our affairs in America farther considered
Contains the book’s most valuable trade data. Postlethwayt provides a detailed enumeration of colonial produce exported to Europe from the continental colonies:

“The produce of his majesty’s colonies on the continent of America, shipped to Europe, from South and North Carolina, Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, New-Jersey, New-York, Connecticut, Massachusetts-Bay, New-Hampshire, and Newfoundland, chiefly consisting of corn, rice, pitch, tar, turpentine, skins, furs, tobacco, timber, masts and yards, fish, oil, ships for sale, etc. are computed yearly to amount to the value of £1,500,000 sterling and upwards; and the freight hereof, many of them being bulky commodities, amounts to £350,000 sterling at least.”

This gives a concrete picture of the economic value of the mainland colonies on the eve of the Seven Years’ War — roughly £1.85 million annually in produce and freight.
Dissertation XIX (pp. 501–548) — A short review of the conduct of France, in relation to her North American colonies
The culminating dissertation, comparing French and British colonial administration. Postlethwayt examines the Crozat grant in Louisiana (the monopoly granted to Antoine Crozat in 1712), noting that France’s claim covered territory bounded by “New Mexico, and the lands of the English of Carolina, west and east; and by the river Illinois, and the gulf of Mexico, north and south.” He warns that the French claim “will take in more than two thirds of the gulf” if France means to claim all lands not actually possessed by Spain or England.
Postlethwayt argues that French colonial administration has been more effective than British — the French crown has invested systematically in its American colonies while Britain has left hers largely to their own devices. “How far the limits of the country the French intended to possess in North-America, before the war, might extend, was not known; and to what degree they design to carry their conquests, if they are able, no one will doubt.” The work ends with Britain at a critical juncture, needing to reform both its domestic economy and its imperial structure to meet the French challenge.

Historical Context
The book was published in 1757 — the third year of the Seven Years’ War, and arguably the lowest point of the war for Britain. The opening years had brought a catalogue of disasters: the loss of Minorca (May 1756), the execution of Admiral Byng (March 1757, shot “to encourage the others”), Braddock’s defeat on the Monongahela (July 1755), the fall of Oswego (August 1756), and the fall of Fort William Henry (August 1757). The ministry was unstable — the Newcastle ministry had fallen in November 1756, replaced by the short-lived Devonshire-Pitt ministry, which itself collapsed in April 1757, leading to the formation of the Pitt-Newcastle coalition just as the book appeared.
Postlethwayt writes in the preface that the nation is “destitute, at this juncture, of all maritime allies” — a reference to the diplomatic revolution of 1756, in which France and Austria became allies, leaving Britain isolated in Europe. His argument that neutral trade benefits France more than it harms her reflects the specific problem of the 1750s: Spain, the Dutch Republic, and other neutrals carried French goods, effectively nullifying Britain’s naval superiority.
The work also engages with the Irish famine of 1756–57, the last major pre-Famine food crisis in Ireland, which killed tens of thousands. Postlethwayt’s opening of Diss XI — attributing his motive to “the late great scarcity of grain, and the deplorable distress and calamity of the bulk of the people” — places the book in the context of this immediate humanitarian crisis.

Key Themes
Agricultural Improvement as National Policy
Postlethwayt’s central claim is that Britain’s competitive decline stems from under-cultivation of land. His calculation that only half of England’s productive land is cultivated is the empirical foundation of the entire work. The solution is not mercantilist regulation but supply-side agricultural reform: more land in cultivation → cheaper food and raw materials → lower labour costs → cheaper manufactures → restored export competitiveness.
Imperial Specialisation vs. Internal Competition
The British empire’s various parts should not compete with each other but should be directed toward different productive activities based on comparative advantage. This argument appears in Diss VII and recurs throughout the Ireland-America dissertations.
The Case for Irish Union
The longest sustained argument in the book (Diss XI–XV, nearly 200 pages) is the case for legislative union between Great Britain and Ireland — 44 years before the Act of Union of 1801. Postlethwayt’s argument is thoroughly economic:

Prevents Irish wool smuggling to France
Integrates Irish agriculture into British markets
Removes the destructive trade restrictions that harm both kingdoms
Follows the successful model of Anglo-Scottish union (1707)

Colonial Administration and the French Threat
Postlethwayt’s analysis of the American colonies (Diss XVI–XIX) diagnoses a structural weakness: Britain has left its colonies to develop without systematic support, while France invests heavily in its American empire. The closing comparison of French vs. British colonial administration is a direct warning about the stakes of the Seven Years’ War.
Neutral Trade and Naval Power
A distinctive argument: neutral carriers in wartime do not preserve British commerce but instead undermine British naval superiority. By carrying French goods, neutral states “extend the commerce of France in time of war, more than she herself does in times of peace,” and enable French merchant ships “to be converted into private ships of war” and even become “a part of the royal navy of France.” The policy of neutral trade “augments the maritime force of France.”
Public Debt and Fiscal Reform
Postlethwayt argues for raising supplies to carry on wars within the year, without further increasing the public debts — a radical position in the midst of a war that would ultimately double the national debt. He references his own earlier tract on this subject and argues that perpetual taxes and mounting debt are a structural drag on British competitiveness.
Ministerial Instability
The preface alludes directly to “our ministerial distractions” which “have disturbed and distracted the whole nation, as well as quite alienated the regard of our foreign friends, and given spirit and influence to our enemies.” The work is partly an appeal to the Duke of Rutland to “become the happy instrument of uniting the wisest and the ablest men in the nation in the service of their king and country.”

Sources Referenced by Postlethwayt

William Petty — political arithmetic; the area and population calculations for England follow Petty’s methods
John Locke — on money, interest, and property
Charles Davenant — on the balance of trade and public revenue
Joshua Gee — The Trade and Navigation of Great Britain Considered (1729), a key influence on Postlethwayt’s colonial arguments
French writers on public granaries — unnamed but referenced in Diss IV
Bishop Fleetwood — Chronicon Preciosum (1707), referenced by Massie (not directly by Postlethwayt, but both writers draw on the same sources)
Various agricultural writers — the source of the practical farming advice in Diss III and IX


Significance
Postlethwayt’s Britain’s Commercial Interest Explained and Improved is the most comprehensive single treatise on British commercial policy published during the Seven Years’ War. It bridges the period between the older mercantilist writers (Child, Davenant, Gee) and the classical economists (Smith, who would cite the Universal Dictionary in the Wealth of Nations). Its arguments for agricultural improvement, Irish union, and imperial integration anticipate policies that would be enacted in the decades following — the Isle of Man Purchase Act (1765), the Free Trade movement, and the Act of Union with Ireland (1801).
The work is particularly valuable for its on-the-ground view of the British imperial crisis in 1757 — before Pitt’s victories at Plassey, Quebec, and Quiberon Bay transformed Britain’s fortunes. It captures Britain at its lowest point in the war, and its analysis of neutral trade, ministerial instability, and colonial vulnerability reflects genuine concerns that were widely shared by contemporaries.
