sources/postlethwayt-universal-dictionar.content:
Postlethwayt — Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce, Vol. I (A–K)
Author: Malachy Postlethwayt (1707–1767)
Title: The Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce, Vol. I
Edition: Fourth edition, London: W. Strahan, J. and F. Rivington, J. Hinton, et al., 1774
Format: Folio, 273,340 lines (~12 MB OCR text)
Raw text: Vol. I
Part of: postlethwayt-universal-dictionary (combined entry covering both volumes)

Contents
Volume I contains all the front matter of the work — the extended “General Idea of the Contents,” the Introduction, and two substantial Preliminary Discourses addressed to Parliament — followed by the alphabetical entries from A through the letter K (ending with KINCARDINSHIRE, KALI, and KENT). This volume carries the bulk of the work’s theoretical and analytical framework; the alphabetical entries in the second half of the alphabet are in postlethwayt-universal-dictionary-vol2.

Front Matter
”A General Idea of the Contents”
An extended analytical table of contents — approximately 100 numbered sections — that functions as a self-contained prospectus for the dictionary. It is divided across the following broad purposes:
For British traders — from the supreme merchant to every subordinate class of respectable traders; the practical conduct of commercial affairs.
For persons of distinction — who desire a political knowledge of trade and commerce, the nature of the national finances, and the political systems of commerce in the several states and empires of the world.
Commercial policy — the emolument arising from the labour, industry, and ingenuity of all commercial artists; the mutual advantage of Great Britain and her American plantations; the reciprocal benefit of Great Britain and Ireland; the landed and trading interests harmonised; the moneyed interest compared with the landed and trading — reductions of interest, stockjobbing, bubbling, and gaming as the destruction of trade and traders.
Public finance — the immensity of the national debts and tax-incumbrances and their destructive consequences to the trade of the kingdom; the qualifications of the British senator; the commercial constitution of parliament; the pernicious consequences of taxes on native commodities; the revenue from the Conquest to the reign of George III.
Trade theory and practice — importation and exportation in a practical and political light; the balance of trade; augmentation and diminution of coin; the several societies for the discovery of new arts, trades, and manufactures; the utility of the Royal Society to trade; the jurisdiction of the admiralty relative to commercial concerns; the office of ambassadors, residents, and consuls in foreign states; the computation of annuities on lives, leases, and reversions; commercial arithmetic and the foreign exchanges and their arbitration; the whole art of banking.
The Mercantile College — a proposed new institution for training young British merchants; also a new institution for the education of young persons of distinction for parliamentary business; the constitution of the several banks throughout Europe; the standard of gold and silver throughout Europe; the intrinsic value of foreign coins; trading in bullion to advantage.
Marine affairs and insurance — insurances of shipping and merchandise, with great variety of curious cases, including the political discussion of the point of injuring the ships and merchandise of enemies in time of war; foreign weights and measures; laws, customs, and usages of merchants regarding foreign and inland bills of exchange; freight, bills of lading, masters and owners of ships, charter parties, averages, barratries, bottomry, shipwrecks, demurrage; the business of the custom-house and its several departments; the Act of Navigation; account of the foreign shipping frequenting the ports of England.
London as the trading metropolis — the superior importance of the city of London and its commercial connections over the whole kingdom; the commercial power of the trading citizens over the nation on all state emergencies; the supreme dignity of London as a corporation, showing that the greatest families in the kingdom originally sprang from trading citizens who distinguished themselves as chief magistrates; the bad policy of want of harmony between the court and the city; anecdotes of eminent citizens; the incorporated city companies and the bodies of trade in Paris.
French commercial regulation — all the material French edicts, arrêts, and laws concerning the chief trades in France, extracted from Savary; the peculiar regulations of French trading corporations requiring a masterpiece of workmanship as proof of qualification; Colbert’s wise and political measures while superintendent of the commerce and navigation of France.
Circulation and credit — the circulating cash requisite to carry on the trade of a nation; the nature and effect of paper credit in commercial states and empires; the par and equation between gold and silver; Sir Isaac Newton’s representation on the necessity of lowering the price of guineas from 31s 6d to 21s; the state of the coin and coinage of England from the Revolution to George III; the practical arts of assaying gold and silver; the art of assaying gold and silver from their ores, with knowledge of all metallurgical operations to judge of mines and minerals upon true philosophical principles; subterranean treasures and the art of mineralogy.
Natural productions — the vegetable productions of nature as the great objects of traffic geographically and commercially described; philosophical experiments to judge of the quality of natural productions; the productions of art, including capital commodities and manufactures in other countries, to whet the invention of British artists; the judges, inspectors, and overseers of manufactures in France compared with the woollen manufactories of Great Britain, which are “shamefully neglected.”
World commerce — public fairs throughout Europe; the Asiatic and African caravans; the commerce of the Chinese and the East Indies; the Turkey, Arabian, and Persian trades; the African trade and the inland trade; monopolies in general.
Political arithmetic and public debt — the funds of Great Britain; the consequences of “the destructive practice of funding and borrowing in times of war”; the injurious effects of becoming tributaries to foreigners; the excessive dearness of all English commodities as the principal cause of this nation being undersold at all the markets in Europe by the French and Dutch; the connection between dear English commodities and universal smuggling.
The great ends of the work — to promote a happy and lasting commercial union between Great Britain and her American colonies “at this critical juncture”; to suggest ways and means whereby the commercial grievances may be relieved; to save the nation the future expense of engaging in the Continental Wars of Europe.

The Introduction
A philosophical essay in its own right — running over 100 lines — arguing that the exercise of trade and commerce is “the soul of the whole British empire.” Postlethwayt surveys world history to demonstrate that idleness and luxury bring ruin to great empires: the Assyrian monarchy, “degenerating into a libidinous and intemperate course of life,” was conquered by Cyrus the Great; the Persian monarchy was “over-run with ease, luxury, and riot”; Alexander the Great, “no sooner devoted himself to pleasures, and to soften himself in idleness and immoderate excess,” became “the scorn and contempt of his own soldiers”; the Roman monarchy fell when the Turks, “constantly inured to hardships and perpetual toil, found the others a people uneasy with their plenty.” Even Mahomet, “like a subtle legislator, enjoined it as a law, which even their very emperors were not to be exempted from — namely, to eat no more than the labour of his hands could purchase every day.”
Postlethwayt argues that commerce civilises: “What would our gentry, our nobility, or our sovereign be better than those of Barbary, was it not for our superiority of traffic and navigation?” He recounts the remarkable true story of a young German nobleman who, told by his prospective father-in-law that he would not give his daughter to a man without a manual trade, learned basket-making in six months — and when the wars of the Palatinate drove both families from their estates, maintained them in Holland by his craft. This story illustrates the contrast between German and English practice: “amongst their nobility, the younger of whole families are employed in their armies, there is rarely found one of them destitute of some manual art.”
The introduction draws extensively on Bishop Spratt’s History of the Royal Society to urge the English nobility and gentry to devote themselves to practical and experimental philosophy. Their country seats give them “the best opportunity and freedom of observation”; their “familiar way of conversing with their neighbourhood will always supply them with intelligence.” The introduction concludes with a passage on English naval greatness: “the English greatness will never be supported or increased in this age by any other wars but those by sea.”

Preliminary Discourse the First
“The Present Commercial Grievances of the Nation Delineated: With their Causes and Cure briefly attempted. Also Strictures upon the Ill State of the Finances of the Kingdom; and a Plan to cement a more interesting Commercial Union between Great Britain and her American Colonies. Humbly Addressed to the Parliament.”
A sustained economic argument — approximately 2,600 lines — that the excessive dearness of all English commodities at foreign markets is caused by the weight of the national debt and the “oppressions of taxes in consequence thereof.” The argument proceeds in several stages:
On the competitiveness of English manufactures — To sell abroad, English commodities must be as cheap as those of rival nations. The Dutch exempt their exports from all port-duties; France has nearly followed their example. Though the Statute of 8 Geo. I c. 15 (1722) removed port-duties on British manufactures, and drawbacks are allowed on inland duties, the compound effect of multiple taxes continues to burden English goods at their exportation. France has been able to undersell England in staple woollen manufactures by ten to twelve per cent since 1735, and by twelve to sixteen per cent after the Seven Years’ War.
On the cascade of taxes — A pane of glass costing one shilling before a penny-per-pound tax was immediately advanced to eighteen pence — “600 per cent advance on account of this tax.” A pair of shoes rose two shillings on account of a twopenny-per-pound leather tax — above 1,000 per cent. When Parliament added three shillings per barrel on beer (one farthing a pot), brewers and victuallers doubled the duty into their own pockets, and journeymen raised their wages threepence per day; the public paid above eight times what the government received. The conclusion: taxes on necessaries, multiplying through every tradesman’s hands in the chain of production, may enhance prices to the consumer at “five hundred, and sometimes even a thousand fold” above the original tax.
On the land tax — The four-shilling land tax in time of peace raises rents upon tenants, who reimburse themselves by advancing the price of the produce of their lands; the land tax also terminates ultimately on the consumer, just as all other taxes do.
On smuggling — The excessive dearness of English commodities is the chief cause of smuggling throughout Great Britain and her American colonies.
Proposed remedies — The work is intended to suggest ways and means to relieve the commercial grievances of the kingdom; one great end is to promote a commercial union with the American colonies that would reduce the need for Continental wars, which have hitherto contributed so greatly to the enhancement of taxes.

Preliminary Discourse the Second
“Animadversions on the Foundation laid for a more interesting Commercial Union between Great Britain and British America, by the Definitive Treaty of Peace concluded at Paris, 10th February 1763.”
Takes up from the first discourse to consider the terms of the Treaty of Paris and their implications for British-American commercial union. Addresses the national ferments caused by ministerial instability, arguing that ministers cannot govern comfortably while the people experience unredressed grievances. Urges that the post-war settlement provides an opportunity to put British-American commercial relations on a new and lasting footing, and that the nation should avoid future Continental entanglements which drain resources needed at home. The discourse also animadverts on the conduct of alliances with European potentates and the balance of benefit from the Seven Years’ War.

Alphabetical Entries: A through K
A
The letter A — the largest single section in the volume — opens with a cascade of minor terms, foreign coins, and weights and measures, followed by entries of mounting commercial importance:
ABASSI — a silver coin in Persia, described in shape and size with its current rate of exchange.
ACCEPTANCE — a term in the traffic of inland and foreign bills of exchange; the act of accepting a bill drawn upon a party, creating a legal obligation.
ACCOUNT / ACCOMPT — an extended treatment of all commercial accounts: account current, account of sales, account of charges, account in joint partnership.
ADMIRAL / ADMIRALTY — the office of admiral, the jurisdiction of the English Admiralty over commercial concerns at sea; the French Ordonnance de la Marine and its provisions for commercial jurisdiction; cognizance of prizes, wreck, bottomry disputes, and maritime contracts.
AFRICA — a major geographical and commercial survey of the continent, organised by region: West Africa (Guinea, the Gold Coast, the Slave Coast, the Kingdom of Benin, the Cape Verde Islands), North Africa (Barbary), and East Africa; trade in gold, ivory, gum, and slaves; the British African trade and the policy question of the inland trade; the Royal African Company and the separate traders; the Senegal River trade after the Treaty of Paris.
AGIO — a bank term for the premium at which bank money circulates above current coin; the varying agios at Amsterdam, Venice, Hamburg.
AMERICA — on the American plantations and their mutual advantage with Great Britain; the articles of commerce; the Treaty of Paris and the territorial changes; the policy of commercial union and the avoidance of measures that would drive the colonies toward independence.
ANNUITIES — the computation of annuities on lives, leases, and reversions; the parliamentary funds; tables of compound interest (five separate tables appearing in the middle of the volume).
ARABIA — the commerce of Arabia Felix, including the frankincense and coffee trades, the Red Sea route to India.
ASIENTO — the South Sea Company’s contract for supplying enslaved Africans to the Spanish American colonies; the history of the Asiento from its granting to Britain under the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) through its operation; the terms, including the annual ship (the “permission ship”), the factories at Porto Bello, Panama, and other ports; the disputes with Spain that led to the War of Jenkins’ Ear.
ARTS AND TRADES — of the several regulated trades and crafts in France; the French system of masters and journeymen; the masterpiece examination required for admission to corporate freedom.

B
BANK / BANKSTOCK — one of the longest and most detailed entries in the volume. Defines the three kinds of banks: (1) public banks such as Amsterdam, where magistrates manage depositors’ bullion and never lend it out (a magistrate at Amsterdam was sentenced to death for borrowing money for a single day); payments are by transfer on the bank’s books, commanding an agio of 3–6% above current money; (2) incorporated joint-stock banks such as the Bank of England, whose security rests on large sums lent to government on parliamentary faith, and which is praised for “exquisitely well kept” accounts “with a variety of checks” making fraud nearly impossible; (3) private bankers in Lombard Street, individuals or partnerships trading on their own stock.
The BANKSTOCK sub-entry is the most remarkable feature: a complete double-entry ledger for a model banking business, showing every account a banker would keep:

Opening capital: Cash £20,000, South Sea Stock at 115, India Stock at 187, Bank Stock at 139½
Loans on pledged stock at 5%
Bills of exchange: a specimen bill drawn on Clifford & Sons, Amsterdam, for 6,000 florins at 35s 4d per £, discounted at 4½% for 1 month 10 days
Bottomry: a loan to a Captain of an Indiaman at 40%
Privateer adventure: £5,000 for a ¼ share in the “Duke and Prince Frederic Privateer,” returning £30,000 in prize money
Gold and silver bullion at £3:17:10–11 per oz; pillar pieces of eight at 5s 5½d per oz
Lottery tickets, jewels, promissory notes — all with specimen DR/CR entries

The entry also contains a lengthy critique of land-bank schemes (“absurd and chimerical; land is immovable and cannot return capital like money”), notes on financing new inventions (especially after Royal Society certification), and a discussion of the difference between domestic and foreign banking (called “remitters” in England). Cross-references to banks at London, Amsterdam, Genoa, Venice, Hamburg, and Paris.
BILLS OF EXCHANGE — a comprehensive legal treatise — approximately 5,440 lines — covering the law and practice of bills across England, Scotland, France, the Holy Roman Empire, the Netherlands, and Italy:

English law: built around the statutes (particularly 9 & 10 Will. III) and leading cases including Jackson v. Pigot on negotiability
Scottish law: extensive treatment of acceptance, protest, re-exchange, horning and caption (the Scottish debt-enforcement process), annualrent, and prescription, with reported Scottish cases
French law: the complete Ordonnance de Commerce of 1673 (Tit. V, arts. I–XXVII), reproduced verbatim
Imperial cities of the Holy Roman Empire: Hamburgh (exchange rules at the Hamburgh Bank), Frankfurt (two imperial edicts of 1666 and 1676), Augsburg (14 articles on acceptance and usage), Leipzig/Saxony (Electoral decree of John George)
Amsterdam: negotiating bills at Amsterdam, the role of bank transfers, agio, and brokers
Bologna: 17 articles on Italian exchange practices

BOHEMIA — the commerce and productions of the kingdom of Bohemia; its glass manufactures and linen trade.
BOOK-KEEPING — the art of debtor and creditor “exhibited in a new concise light”; the method of double-entry accounts for a merchant’s business.
BOUNTIES — the British system of export bounties and fishery bounties; the herring bounty of 23 Geo. II c. 24 (£3 per annum per £100 employed, plus a ship bounty of £1 10s per ton); mandatory rendezvous at Shetland and Scotland; crew requirements; sworn certification on return.
BROKAGE / BROKERAGE — the fees payable to a broker for negotiating commercial transactions; the regulation of brokers in England and France.
BRUNSWICK-LUNENBURG — the duchy and its commerce; the cities of Hamburgh, Harburg, and Lunenburg and their trade.

C
CALLICOE-PRINTING — the trade in printed, painted, and stained calicoes; the statutory prohibitions against wearing East Indian, Chinese, and Persian printed silks and calicoes in Great Britain; the regulations for warehousing and re-exporting them; the rules for domestic calico printing.
CAPTAIN of Merchantmen — the duties, liabilities, and legal position of the master of a merchant vessel; his obligations in regard to cargo, crew, and owners; the laws of barratry.
CARIBBEE ISLANDS — the commerce of the British, French, Dutch, and Danish Caribbean colonies; sugar, rum, molasses, and the provisions trade.
COMPANIES — a major entry covering both the Livery Companies of the City of London and the great trading companies of England:
Livery Companies — the twelve principal companies in order of precedence, with their incorporation dates and founding monarchs: the Mercers (1393, Richard II), the Grocers (1345, Edward III, “formerly called pepperers”), the Drapers (Henry VI, tracing to Edward III’s admission of Flemish weavers), the Fishmongers (united 1536, Henry VIII, formerly two companies), the Goldsmiths, the Skinners (1327, Edward III), the Merchant Taylors (1501, Henry VII, “formerly called taylors and linnen-armourers”), the Haberdashers, the Salters, the Ironmongers, the Vintners, the Clothworkers. A second tier of companies is listed in full: Dyers, Brewers, Leathersellers, Pewterers, Barbers, Surgeons, Armourers, Bakers, and some fifty more, all noted as fraternities incorporated with charters of privilege.
Trading companies — from the Merchant Adventurers (Edward IV) through the Muscovy Company (Edward VI), the Turkey/Levant Company (Elizabeth I), the East India Company (Elizabeth I, 1600), the Virginia and West India Merchants, and the Greenland and Eastland companies. Postlethwayt notes the historical shift from exclusive companies to free trade: “experience hath shewn, that the trade of the nation has advanced, in proportion as monopolies have been laid aside.”
CUSTOM-HOUSE — among the longest entries in the entire dictionary, functioning as a complete administrative manual for the English customs service. Organised alphabetically (the article continues across multiple letters C through I), it covers:
Specimen forms (with originals from Southampton, 17 January 1730): a sufferance for passenger Moses Wharton on the Providence of London from Rotterdam (baggage: 30 ells plain hollands linen, 1½ lb Dutch wrought silk, 3 lb tea, an Indian damask gown — the dutiable items noted for entry, the prohibited items for prosecution); the sufferance entry book; an over-entry certificate for James Cross (33 lbs thrown silk, with detailed repayment calculation breaking down old subsidy, new subsidy, ⅓ subsidy, ⅔ subsidy, impost 1692); a tobacco damage certificate for Dennis Dove.
Book-keeping system: the Collector’s sufferance book, land-waiters’ report books, general pocket-books, post-entry books, separate registers for over-entries and damages; the rule against erasures (errors must be struck through and corrected alongside); the Surveyor’s monthly check of all ships cleared, with post-entries standing out six days after clearance.
Goods Inwards — importation laws, prohibited goods, landing hours, navigation acts.
Goods Outwards — export procedures, re-export, drawbacks.
Goods Coastwise — cockets, bonds, certificates.
Fees — tables of lawful and prohibited fees, penalties for extortion.
Fish Laws — herring, pilchard, cod, salmon; packing regulations.
Bounty for the British White-Herring Fishery — the full statutory scheme from 23 Geo. II c. 24.
Iron from American colonies — pig and bar iron import regulations, stamping, certificates.

E
EAST-INDIA COMPANY — a massive legal compendium: the complete statutory framework governing the United Company from William III through George II. Key provisions:

The company’s monopoly of trade “to all places between the Cape of Good Hope and Straits of Magellan for ever,” subject to redemption by Parliament on three years’ notice and repayment of £4,200,000 capital
Ships must post £2,500 security per 100 tons; goods must be sold publicly “by inch of candle”
Persons trading without authorisation forfeit “ship and goods, and double the value thereof”; British subjects found in the East Indies without lawful authority are guilty of “high crime and misdemeanor”
Prohibition on contributing to foreign East India companies (penalty: treble the value or one year’s imprisonment)
Wrought silks, Bengals, and printed calicoes of East Indian, Chinese, or Persian manufacture prohibited to be worn in Great Britain; may be imported only into London and re-exported
A specimen bond for the exportation of prohibited East India goods from the Custom-house of Southampton (1730), listing three pieces of Indian taffety, four Indian damask night-gowns, one piece of cherriderry, nine remnants of chints, seven pieces of pelongs

EXCHANGES (foreign) — the rates of exchange between London and all the principal commercial cities of Europe; the computation of arbitrated exchange; the nature of exchange as compared with the transport of specie.

G
GOODS INWARDS / GOODS OUTWARDS / GOODS COASTWISE — the detailed procedural rules governing the import, export, and coasting trade: landing and lading hours, the navigation acts, the cocket system, drawbacks and bounties.
GREENWICH HOSPITAL — its establishment, maintenance by sixpenny deductions from naval wages, and its provision for wounded and aged seamen.
GRONINGEN — one of the seven United Provinces; its commercial situation, agriculture, and trade.
GUINEA (Africa) — the two great regions of Guinea (Upper and Lower); the kingdoms of Benin, Bonny, Calabar, and the Slave Coast; the commerce in gold, ivory, gum, and enslaved Africans; the European trading forts and factories; the British African Company and the trade to the American plantations.
GUIENNE (France) — the province and its subdivisions: Quercy, Condomois, Armagnac, Gascony, Soules, and Labourd; the commerce in wine (Bordeaux), prunes, and wool.
GUM — a major entry on the several kinds of commercial gums: gum arabic, gum lac, gum olibanum, gum tragacanth, gum anime, gum elemi, and gum guaiac; their sources, uses in manufactures, and trade regulations; the methods for testing their quality by philosophical experiment.
GUNPOWDER — its composition, manufacture, and trade; the regulatory framework.

H
HAMBURGH — a major commercial entry: the city’s situation on the Elbe, its status as a free city, its banking and exchange rules, the Hamburgh Bank and the payment of exchange by bank transfers; the regulations for merchants resident in Hamburg; the treaty rights of English merchants.
HAMPSHIRE — its situation, agriculture, and commerce; its woollen manufactures and the Winchester cloth trade.
HANOVER — the Hanoverian dominions and their commerce; their connection with Great Britain through the Hanoverian succession.
HANSE-TOWNS — the history of the Hanseatic League; its original formation as a league among German trading cities; its treaties with England and other powers; its decline; the continuing privileges of the Hanseatic merchants in England.
HATS — a considerable article of commerce: the manufacture of English beaver and felt hats; the regulations on hat-making and the prohibition on exporting hatters’ materials to the American colonies (creating a colonial grievance); the French hat trade.
HAWKERS AND PEDLARS — persons who carry goods for sale from house to house or from market to market, without a fixed shop; the licensing system and the fees payable; penalties for unlicensed hawking.
HEMP — in the same class with flax; the cultivation and preparation of hemp in Russia and the Baltic; its vital importance for the naval stores supply; the statutory provisions for encouraging the growth of hemp in the American colonies.
HERRING-FISHERY — under the article FISHERIES (given at length): the British white-herring fishery on the Scottish coasts; the bounty system; the French and Dutch competition in the herring trade; the regulations for curing, packing, and exporting herrings; the buss fishery and the seasonal rendezvous.
HOLLAND (the province) — the commerce of North and South Holland; Amsterdam as the great entrepôt of European trade; the system of warehousing and transhipment; the fishing industry of Enkhuizen and other ports; the Bank of Amsterdam; the Dutch East India Company.
HOPS — a plant of the reptile kind whose flower is essential to the brewing of beer; the cultivation of hops in Kent and other counties; the trade in hops between England and the Continent; the statutory regulations on the sale of hops and the stamping of hops sacks.
HUDSON’S BAY — the Bay and Straits; the Hudson’s Bay Company and its exclusive trade in furs; the commerce in beaver, otter, marten, and other peltry; the Company’s posts and the routes of the inland trade with the native nations.
HUNGARY — a kingdom situate between 16 and 23 degrees of longitude; its commerce in cattle, wine, and mineral wealth; the mines of gold, silver, and copper; the fisheries of the Danube and the great lakes; note on the extraordinary cheapness of carp (“1,000 carp have been sold for a crown, and in some places less”).
HYPOTHECATION — of ships and salvage; the hypothecation of a ship before departure for a bottomry loan, giving the lender a lien on ship and cargo; the rules governing salvage of goods from a wreck.

I
ICELAND — an island belonging to Denmark; the fisheries of cod, herring, and halibut that attract English, Dutch, and other fishing vessels; the regulations on the Iceland fishery under English law.
IMPORTATION — the bringing into a kingdom of merchandise from foreign parts; the distinction between prohibited, dutiable, and duty-free imports; the navigation acts as the foundation of the importation system.
IMPOST — a tax or duty laid by the sovereign authority on goods imported or exported; the several kinds of imposts in England (subsidies, tonnage and poundage, additional duties).
INDIA TRADE — See EAST-INDIA TRADE, East-India Company.
INDIA-HOUSE OF SPAIN — the Casa de Contratación at Seville (later Cadiz) for the management of the Spanish colonial trade; its functions in licensing merchants, registering silver, and enforcing the laws of the Indies.
INDIAN ISLANDS — a survey of the East Indian islands including Java, Sumatra, the Moluccas (Ternate, Tidore, Banda), and the government structure of the Dutch East India Company in each.
INDOSTAN / THE EMPIRE OF THE GREAT MOGUL — a comprehensive geographical and commercial survey of the Mughal empire; the principal provinces and their products; the trade routes; the situation of the European trading nations (English, Dutch, French, Portuguese) in the subcontinent; the Mughal court and the conditions of trading at the imperial courts; Bengal, Bombay, and the routes of the coastal trade.
INSURANCE / ASSURANCE — one of the longest entries in the dictionary:
Definition and specimen policy: a complete marine policy for a voyage from St. Petersburgh to London on the ship William and Mary, specifying the full perils clause (seas, men of war, fire, enemies, pirates, rovers, thieves, jettisons, letters of mart, surprisals, arrests, restraints, barratry of the master and mariners, “and all other perils, losses, and misfortunes”), the sue-and-labour clause, the Lombard Street standard clause, the convoy warranty clause, the premium and subscription block, and average clauses (corn and fish free from average unless general or ship stranded; sugar, tobacco, hemp, flax, hides and skins free from average under 5%; other goods free under 3%).
Premiums and abatements: premiums running “very high, sometimes 30 or 40 per cent” when a ship has been long missing; a customary 2% abatement at loss settlement; table showing net receipts at each premium level (at 10% → insured receives 88; at 40% → receives 53).
The incorporation of the insurance companies (1720): the Royal Exchange Assurance and London Assurance companies; their offer of £600,000 toward the civil list debt in exchange for charters; the 6 Geo. I c. 18 creating exclusive corporate rights; shares transferable; forgery of policies made felony without benefit of clergy.
Legal cases (20+): Da Costa v. Scanderet (fraudulent concealment of intelligence), Knight v. Cambridge (barratry), Bond v. Gonfale (1704, Holt CJ on convoy warranty), Green v. Young (embargo conversion to fire-ship), Goddard v. Garrett (no interest → void), Harman v. Vanhatton (bottomry + insurance both recoverable), Newnham, Perkins and Stoakes (1678, the Mayflower-ketch fraud where a master scuttled his own ship).
INVOICE — an account of merchandise shipped or to be shipped, specifying the particulars of each article, its quality, quantity, and price; specimen invoice forms.
IRELAND — a survey of the island’s geography, commerce, and trade with Great Britain; the staple exports (wool, linen, provisions); the restrictions on Irish trade imposed by English statute; the reciprocal benefit of Britain and Ireland.
IRON — the least heavy of all metals except tin; the production of iron in Britain, Sweden, Russia, and the American colonies; the bar iron and pig iron trades; the statutory provisions for encouraging iron imports from the colonies (to discourage smelting in America and preserve the naval stores supply).

J
JAPAN / JAPON — a great country consisting of several large islands; the Dutch East India Company’s exclusive access to Japanese trade (through Nagasaki and the Deshima island factory); the peculiarities of the trade; the commodities exchanged; the prohibition on Christian missionaries and the extraordinary constraints placed on Dutch traders as the price of access.
JERSEY — an island in the English Channel; its particular privileges and their basis in ancient charters; the wool trade.
JETSAM — See Flotsam, and Lagan.

K
KALI — a grey salt brought from Alicant and the Levant; its uses in the manufacture of glass and soap.
KENT — bounded with Sussex on the south-west, Surrey on the north; its hops, wool, and maritime trade; the ports of Dover, Deal, and the Cinque Ports.
KINCARDINSHIRE — a county of Scotland, its situation and trade.

Annuity and Interest Tables
Embedded within the volume are five tables of compound interest, a table of the value of annuities on lives, and conversion tables for the computation of leases and reversions — practical tools for the merchant and financier that Postlethwayt considered essential parts of a complete commercial reference.

Material Articles Index (Letter A)
The volume closes with the beginning of the “Material Articles” index — a condensed digest of the most commercially important entries, arranged alphabetically. The Letter A section of this index lists the key articles under A and directs readers to the relevant full entries.

sources/postlethwayt-universal-dictionar.title: Postlethwayt — Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce, Vol. II (L–Z)
sources/postlethwayt-universal-dictionar.content:
Postlethwayt — Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce, Vol. II (L–Z)
Author: Malachy Postlethwayt (1707–1767)
Title: The Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce, Vol. II
Edition: Fourth edition, London: W. Strahan, J. and F. Rivington, J. Hinton, et al., 1774
Format: Folio, 236,020 lines (~10.7 MB OCR text)
Raw text: Vol. II
Part of: postlethwayt-universal-dictionary (combined entry covering both volumes)

Contents
Volume II contains the alphabetical entries from L through Z, preceded by a dedication to Sir Stephen Theodore Janssen, Baronet, Chamberlain of the City of London, and followed by a comprehensive “Material Articles” index covering both volumes. The alphabetical entries from A through K are in postlethwayt-universal-dictionary-vol1.

Dedication to Sir Stephen Theodore Janssen
Volume II is dedicated to Sir Stephen Theodore Janssen, Baronet, Chamberlain of the City of London, in a substantial essay — approximately 250 lines — that praises Janssen’s public services to trade and the revenue.
The prohibition of French cambrics: Janssen is credited with procuring an Act (around 1744–45) prohibiting the wearing of French cambrics. Before this, Britain paid at least £250,000 a year to France for cambrics; by prohibiting them and replacing them with English-made gauzes, blonds, and other home-made wares, the nation saved and gained a difference of half a million pounds per annum — which, over the twenty years from 1745 to 1765, amounts to ten millions of principal money. The prohibition met with ministerial opposition (the duty on French cambrics had been appropriated) but Janssen’s arguments prevailed. Postlethwayt urges that a similar prohibition on all foreign wrought silks — for which Britain was then paying above a million pounds a year including all smuggled goods — would save the nation twenty millions in ten years and give full employment to the Spitalfields manufacturers.
The reduction of tea duties: Janssen demonstrated that lowering the excise duty on tea would increase the revenue, against ministerial scepticism. Before the Act he procured, the combined excise and customs on tea had not exceeded £170,000 per annum, and the East India Company had imported not above 1,200,000 lbs weight of tea communibus annis. Since the Act, the Exchequer has received yearly from £400,000 to £700,000, and the Company has sold from three to four millions of pounds weight annually — importing and selling no less than sixty millions of pounds weight more than it would otherwise have done. The Company’s extraordinary clear profit from this, at one shilling per pound weight, amounts to three millions; the public revenue has been advantaged by Janssen above seven millions of money.
Intelligence before the Seven Years’ War: When Janssen was Lord Mayor of London in 1755, he wrote to the Duke of Newcastle (then Secretary of State) and Lord Anson (First Lord of the Admiralty) reporting that French ships bound for America were “doubly manned” — which he judged an indubitable proof that France intended war before those ships returned. He proposed seizing the homeward-bound French West India ships without formal declaration of war, “whereby we could not have at once less than eight thousand French sailors prisoners in England, which would be crippling the French navy during that whole war.” The Duke of Newcastle acknowledged in Council that he received this information and suggestion from the Lord Mayor of London; the measure was adopted, and Britain had the prophesied eight thousand French sailors prisoners before the close of the year 1755.

Alphabetical Entries: L through Z
L
LABOUR — opens Volume II immediately after the dedication. A substantial economic analysis — approximately 500 lines — drawn from French economic sources (the passage from Cantillon’s Essai is closely followed throughout):
On the natural price of labour: a labourer’s son from age 7 to 12 becomes an assistant to his father at tasks requiring no art or skill; if the father puts him to a trade, he loses his assistance during apprenticeship, and since the life of a man is commonly calculated at 10 or 12 years only, a tradesman’s wages must exceed a labourer’s in proportion to the expense and risk of his servitude. Those trades attended with danger (sailors, bell-founders, silver miners) earn proportionately more; where capacity, danger, and confidence all combine (pilots, skippers), wages are higher still.
On competition and equilibrium of labour supply: if two tailors in a village make all its clothes and one dies, the survivor may raise his price until a tradesman comes from another village; the number of tradesmen in a village “always proportions itself to the demand, or the work there is for them.” The same holds in market-towns and cities.
On the intrinsic price of commodities: the price of any thing intrinsically “seems to take in the quantity of land with regard to the goodness of the land, and the quantity of labour, with regard to the dearness of the labour.” A pound of flax wrought into Brussels lace employs the labour of one person for near 14 years; the steel spring regulating a good watch may sell at a price making the proportion of steel to workmanship as 1 to 1,000,000; the price of a bucket of water at the river is nothing, but carried into the street sells for one penny — “the measure of the labour of the water-carrier.”
On land and labour as the dual foundations of price: a sustained argument that “the price of any thing intrinsically is the measure of the land, and the labour that enters into its production.” Land, which produces all commodities, must necessarily maintain those who give those commodities their form by labour.
On property in land: it does not appear that Providence gave any man preferential right to the possession of land; “some of the most ancient titles we have any knowledge of, came by violence and conquest.” In Mexico, property in land is vested in Spaniards; in Jerusalem, in Turks. The Roman republic’s original two-acre allotment “soon after fell into few hands.” In all social arrangements, land naturally falls into the hands of a few; the role of the labourer, the slave, and the tradesman is to maintain themselves and their children from what the landlord’s estate can be made to yield.
LADING — See Bills of Lading, Charter-Parties.
LANCASHIRE — the county’s situation, its cotton and woollen manufactures, the ports of Liverpool and Lancaster, and the inland trade routes.
LANGUEDOC (France) — the province and its subdivisions, including Lauragais, Gevaudan, and Vivarais; the Canal du Midi (the Canal of Languedoc) as a commercial artery; the silk, wool, and grain trades; the commerce of Montpellier and Nîmes.
LAPLAND — divided into Danish, Swedish, and Russian Lapland; the commerce in reindeer, furs, fish, and whale oil; the routes of the Lapland trade.
LEAKAGE — an allowance of 12 per cent in the customs on the importation of wine, oil, and other liquids, to compensate for loss in transit.
LEGHORN (Livorno) — an extended commercial and accounting entry, including a specimen double-entry merchant’s ledger for a Leghorn trading account. The accounts shown include:

Cash account — recording receipts from Thomas Dale of Leghorn for three several draughts, received freight from the Anne Galley (Captain Barnby) made from Genoa and Leghorn, and Geminiani’s freight per manifesto
Provision account for Corman of Lisbon (a salt account at Lisbon)
Commission account for a factor in Leghorn
Profit and Loss accounts for the several Leghorn ventures
Wheat Account of Messrs. Dale and Corman

The ledger also contains specimen accounts for John Kelly of London, John King of London, Peter Winberton of Smyrna, David Burrows, and other correspondents — constituting a practical guide to merchant accounting in the Mediterranean trade.
LEVANT TRADE — the trade to Turkey, Syria, and the eastern Mediterranean; the Levant Company and its privileges; the terms on which British merchants reside and trade in the Ottoman empire (liberty of religion guaranteed); the articles of commerce: raw silk, cotton, drugs, and dyestuffs.
LINEN — a major entry — approximately 700 lines — covering the linen trade and its statutory regulation. The trade in Irish linen and its statutory framework; the rules governing imported linens from Germany, Flanders, Holland, and France; the comprehensive legislative history from William III through George II:
Statutory framework: the Anne statutes on linens, silks, and printed calicoes; § 70 of 7 Ann. c. 7 (duties on European linens, gilters, and lawns); the series of Acts from 12 Ann. stat. 2 through 4 Geo. II c. 16 regulating chequered linens, printed goods, and Irish linen importation into Great Britain. The regulations for the linen manufacture in France: all cloths manufactured for export must pass before sworn examiners; thin, ill-woven, or ill-bleached goods are condemned; candidates who wish to export must mark their goods in the weaving and produce authentic certificates of exportation; partnerships of manufacturers joined in fair partnership may export jointly.
LINCOLNSHIRE — its fens and marshes, its wool and grain trade; Lindsey, the third and largest division of the county.

M
MARITIME AFFAIRS — an extended compendium of international maritime law, drawing on the most celebrated French, Dutch, Spanish, and Hanseatic sources. Covers: the laws governing masters and pilots; French ordinances on maritime conduct; the rules of the Dutch sea-law; Spanish ordinances; the Hanseatic statutes; rights and duties of pilots; liabilities of masters in relation to owners and cargo; the law of salvage; regulations for ports and harbours.
MERCHANTS — various entries on the constitution and practice of merchant trading, including the rules for merchant factors in foreign ports and the regulation of the commodity brokers.

N
NAVIGATION — Of the practical art of navigation in relation to ship-sailing. Postlethwayt sets out what a complete treatise of the art ought to contain, according to Sir William Petty’s 28-point programme:

Arithmetic in whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and logarithms
Vulgar, practical, mechanical geometry performable by scale and compass
Trigonometry, right-lined and spherical
The stars to be known
Instruments for use at sea, their construction and use
The whole skill of the magnet and its directive virtues
The hydrography of the globe, the perspective of coasts, the description of the under-water-bottom of the sea
The knowledge of winds and meteors
The history and skill of all sorts of fishings
The art of medicine and surgery peculiar to the sea
The common laws of the Admiralty and jurisdiction of the sea
The several victuallings and clothings fit for seamen
The whole science of ebbing and flowing, and of currents and eddies
Dromometry, and the measures of a ship’s motions at sea
The building of ships of all sorts, with the several riggings and sails
Naval economy according to the several voyages and countries
The art of conning, rowing, and sailing all sorts of vessels
The gunnery, fireworks, and other armatures peculiar to sea and sea fights
The art of loading and unloading the chief commodities to best advantage
The art of weighing up sunken ships and goods, and of diving for sunken goods in deep water
The general philosophy of the motion and figures of the air, the sea, and seasons; of timber, iron, hemp, brimstone, tallow, and their uses in naval affairs
An account of five or six of the best navies of Europe, with their arsenals, magazines, yards, and docks
23–28. An account of all shipping, of all chief commercial parts of the world, of the chief sea-fights and naval expeditions of the last century, of the use of telescopes, the depths of the sea, and the art of making sea-water fresh and potable

Postlethwayt notes he is not acquainted with any book written upon navigation “according to this extensive plan proposed by Sir William Petty,” and recommends the work of Mr J. Robertson, F.R.S., mathematical master at Christ’s Hospital, London — from which he extracts the section on a ship’s reckoning: the account whereby, at any time, it may be known where the ship is and on what course to steer to gain her port.
NETHERLANDS (Austrian) — the Austrian Netherlands and their commerce; the port of Ostend.

O
OSTEND — a city and port town in the Austrian Netherlands in the province of Flanders, situated 12 miles from Bruges.
OSTEND EAST-INDIA COMPANY — Emperor Charles VI attempted to establish an East India company at Ostend in 1718 but was compelled to desist by the English and Dutch. Postlethwayt reproduces the full Memorial presented by the Dutch resident at Brussels (M. Peeters, on behalf of the States-General) to the Marquis de Prie, minister plenipotentiary for the Austrian Netherlands, remonstrating against the Ostend voyages and their interference with the exclusive grants of the Dutch East India and West India companies confirmed by the Treaty of Münster. The company was eventually suspended by the Emperor following the Treaty of Vienna (1731) as the price of the Pragmatic Sanction — “it was the ruin of the late Ostend East-India Company that gave birth to the establishment of the Swedish East-India Company.”

P
PILOTAGE / PILOTS — a comprehensive legal entry on the office of pilot, drawn from French ordinances and English law: a pilot coming aboard a ship where there is already a pilot must not interfere; a pilot undertaking to conduct a vessel while under a compulsory pilotage requirement is liable if he runs the ship aground through ignorance; no master or mariner shall exact greater sums from merchants than those fixed by the ordinances; if they discover any alteration in the channel they are required to give notice; it shall be free for masters of French ships to take pilots from any nation.
PORTUGAL — the kingdom of Portugal, its northern border with Galicia; its geography, products, and commerce; the trade in wine (Oporto and Lisbon), cork, salt, olive oil, and fruits; the trade with Brazil; the Methuen Treaty and its consequences for the English cloth trade; the Lisbon merchants and the English factory there; the salt trade from Setúbal and its importance to the Newfoundland fishery.
PRUSSIA — the kingdom of Prussia, divided into Royal Prussia and Ducal Prussia; the commerce of Danzig; the Baltic grain and timber trade; the export of rye, wheat, hemp, flax, and pot-ash.

R
RUSSIA / MUSCOVY — Russia bounded on the north by the Arctic Ocean; its vast extent; the commerce of Moscow, St Petersburg, Archangel, Narva, and Riga; the staple exports: hemp, flax, iron, tar, pitch, potash, tallow, furs, and leather; the White Sea route and the Baltic routes; the economic transformation under Peter the Great.
RUSSIA COMPANY — the company first projected towards the end of Edward VI’s reign, executed in the first and second years of Philip and Mary, and confirmed by Act of Parliament under Elizabeth in 1566. Its origin in three vessels sent to discover a north-east passage to China, which fell into the White Sea and made up to the port of Archangel; the warm reception by the Muscovites and the resulting petition for letters patent. The charter of 1555 (under Mary) declared the association a body politic under the name “Company of Merchant-Adventurers of England for the Discovery of Lands, Territories, Islands unknown or unfrequented”; confirmed by Elizabeth in 1566 as “the Company of English Merchants for Discovering New Trades.” Its exclusive privilege of trading to Archangel and other ports of Muscovy; the requirement to use only English ships and to export cloths only after they have been dyed and dressed. The company subsisted with reputation for almost a century until the Civil Wars, when the Czar, hearing of the execution of Charles I, expelled all English subjects from his states; the Dutch seized the opportunity and settled in their place. After the Restoration, the company partially re-established its Archangel trade but never with its former vigour.

S
SALT — a commodity of general utility in commerce; the production of salt in England (Cheshire, the sea-salt trade), France, Spain, and Portugal; its vital importance for the preservation of fish and provisions; the regulatory framework governing salt duties and the allowance of duty-free salt to fishing vessels.
SALT-PETRE — a salt, though extracted out of earth; the sources and manufacture of salt-petre; its indispensable role in the manufacture of gunpowder; the East India Company’s supply from Bengal.
SHIPPING — the dimensions, tonnage, and number of guns of men-of-war built in Spain, the Indies, France, England, and Genoa, drawn from Don Geronimo Uztáriz’s Theórica y Práctica de Comercio y de Marina (1724). The building regulations prescribed by Lieutenant-General Don Antonio Gastaneta and approved by the Spanish Crown in 1713 and 1720. The crew complements of Spanish men-of-war: 26 sailors and 26 marines per 100 tons for common ships, 28 of each for the admiral’s ship, plus 100 additional hands for the flagships. The rules of the French, English, and Dutch navies for the manning of their respective fleets are given separately and compared.
SIBERIA / ASIATIC RUSSIA — formerly denominated Scythia; the extent and commerce of Siberia; the fur trade; the overland routes to China.
SILK / SILK-WORMS — two substantial entries:
Silk manufacture of China: a survey of Chinese silk production and its extraordinary cheapness; the reasons all European nations are attracted to the Chinese trade; the methods of silk cultivation in China and how they might be imitated in Europe.
Silk-worms: a memoir upon the breeding of silk-worms in France and all other climates where mulberry trees can be cultivated, by M. de Goyon de la Plombanie. Based on observations made in Languedoc, the memoir argues that the methods commonly followed do not answer the end proposed: in the Indies and eastern climates where worms breed on trees in the open air, the silk is very fine, very strong, and in great abundance; with us, art must correspond with nature. The memo details the causes of failure in French silk breeding: cold mornings that benumb the worms, impure air from confined chambers, variety of food from different soils, leaves gathered wet or faded, the pernicious effect of “people of stinking breaths” and “women at certain times” on these delicate animals. Instructions for a correct method are provided.
SPAIN — a major geographical and commercial entry: Spain situated on the most western part of the European continent; its provinces and their products; the commerce of Cadiz, Seville, Barcelona, and Bilbao; the colonial trade and the Casa de Contratación; the annual fleet to the Indies (the Tierra Firme and New Spain fleets); Spanish wool, wine, oil, and silk; the trade with the American colonies; the Treaties of Commerce with Great Britain; the post-1763 commercial situation.
SWEDEN — the kingdom bounded by the Baltic Sea, the Sound, and the Categat on the south, Norway on the west, Russian and Norwegian Lapland on the north, and Muscovy on the east. The soil, where capable of cultivation, is tolerably fruitful; Sweden imports many sorts of grain from Livonia for want of home supply. The cattle are small in size; sheep bear a coarse wool fit only for peasants’ clothing; forests of pine, fir, beech, birch, alder, and some oak overspread great part of the country. Iron mines and forges are in great number towards the mountainous parts: iron to the value of near £300,000 is exported yearly. The iron industry’s recent difficulties are noted: as the number of forges increased to the point where each undersold the others, and as the prohibition of foreign manufactures reduced the exchange market for iron, prices fell so low that “many thousands of poor people, whose livelihood depends upon these forges and mines, will be reduced to a starving condition.” Finland (part of the Swedish crown) produces pitch, tar, wooden ware, cattle, dried fish, and train-oil.
SWEDISH EAST-INDIA COMPANY — “It was the ruin of the late Ostend East-India Company that gave birth to the establishment of the Swedish East-India Company.” A succinct history of the Swedish company, treating it as a direct consequence of the closing of the Ostend route.

T
TOBACCO — the manner of planting and ordering tobacco in Virginia: the seed is sown in beds of fine mould in the twelve days of January; when plants have grown to the breadth of a shilling they are transplanted into hills about four feet apart, “somewhat after the manner of our hop-yards”; they are kept with diligent weedings; when the plant has put out as many leaves as the ground will nourish “to a substance and largeness that will render them merchantable,” the top is taken off (at 12–16 leaves in very rich ground, 9–10 in mean ground); the plant then puts out suckers which are plucked away once a week until the plant comes to perfection in August. In dry weather with a little breeze the ripe tobacco is cut down, let lie on the ground four hours until the leaves fall to the stalk, then carried to the tobacco-houses where it is hung on tobacco-stalks — “much after the manner they hang herrings in Yarmouth” — for five or six weeks until the stem in the middle of the leaf will snap. The tobacco is then stripped, bundled, and packed in hogsheads. The 1667 storm in Virginia that destroyed above half the standing tobacco crop and blew trees up by their roots throughout the country is recounted as a notable disaster to the trade. The entry continues with the statutory framework governing the tobacco trade: the import regulations, the customs duties, the rules for damaged and unmerchantable tobacco removed by water, and the drawback system.
TREATIES OF COMMERCE AND NAVIGATION — an extensive compendium of commercial treaties, supplementing the treatment given under the article MARITIME AFFAIRS. It opens with the full text of the Treaty of Navigation and Commerce between Great Britain (Queen Anne) and France (Louis XIV), concluded at Utrecht, 31 March 1713:

Article I: reciprocal and entirely perfect liberty of navigation and commerce through all kingdoms, states, dominions, and provinces of both parties in Europe
Article II: in case of rupture, subjects of each party residing in the other’s dominions shall have six months to retire with their families, goods, and effects, and shall enjoy good and speedy justice during that period; their persons and merchandise shall not be detained or troubled by arrest or seizure
Article III: no subject of either party shall exercise acts of hostility and violence against the other, by sea or land or in rivers, ports, or havens, under any colour or pretence whatsoever; no privateering commissions or letters of reprisal shall be issued against the other party’s subjects

Further treaties and commercial articles follow, covering the other major commercial agreements of the 18th century.

U
UNITED PROVINCES / STATES GENERAL — the seven United Provinces of the Netherlands and their commerce; the constitution of the States General; the pre-eminence of Holland and Zeeland in the Atlantic and Baltic trades; the Dutch East India Company and the West India Company; the Bank of Amsterdam.

W
WINE — the regulation and trade in wines; the customs and import duties; the statutory table of measure (the ton must contain 252 gallons for wine, oil, and honey); the Portuguese wine trade under the Methuen Treaty.
WOOL AND WOOLLEN MANUFACTORY — a major entry tracing the progress of woollen manufactures in France and Spain and showing how both nations have made “extraordinary progress” that “must necessarily tend to the greater and greater injury of” British woollen exports. The entry surveys the state of French wool-raising and woollen manufacturing in each of the French provinces; the Spanish wool trade (merino wool and its fine quality); the Biscayan, Castilian, and Catalonian weaving industries. The entry cross-references Biscay, Castille, Catalonia, Factors, and India-House of Spain.
WORCESTERSHIRE — has Herefordshire and Shropshire to the west; its commerce in gloves and metal wares.
WRECK — where a ship is broke to pieces or lost on the sea; the law of wreck; the rules governing goods cast ashore; the statutory provisions for preventing the plundering of wrecks; the rights of the lord of the manor versus the rights of the original owner.

Y
YARN, LINEN — See the end of letter I and the end of the article LINEN; the regulations on the importation of linen yarn from Ireland and the American colonies.
YORKSHIRE — by far the largest county in England; its woollen manufactures in the West Riding (Leeds, Halifax, Bradford); the commerce of Hull; the cloth market at Leeds and the system of clothiers bringing their undressed cloth to the open market on “Cloth Hall” days.
YEAST — a method of curing it; the flowers of wine and beer and their fermentative properties; a practical note for the brewer.

Z
ZAFFRE / SAFREE — a mineral of a bluish colour; its use in painting porcelain and glass blue; where obtained and in what quantities.
ZINCK / ZINCTHUM / MARCASITA PALLIDA — a metallic, sulphurous mineral; its properties and commercial uses in the manufacture of brass and other alloys.

Material Articles Index
Volume II closes with a comprehensive “Material Articles” index covering both volumes of the dictionary, organized by letter (Letter L through Letter Z, with letters for the first volume — A through K — given at the end). Each section provides condensed summaries of the most commercially important entries, directing the reader to the relevant full articles. The index sections include:

Letter L: LABOUR (remarks political thereon in relation to the natural price); LEAKAGE of liquors (allowance at the customs on importation)
Letter M: MERCHANTS and their various employments
Letter N: NOVOGOROD (its commerce)
Letter O: OAK (its nature, growth, and commercial uses)
Letter P: PACKERS (the nature of their employment)
Letter Q: QUACK, in medicine — “a short antidote against general deception”
Letter R: extensive entries on Russian commerce
Letter S: SABLE (curious skins of an animal, where had)
Letter T and beyond: VENICE (its situation, produce, and trade; the sovereign fund of the state revenues of Venice)
Letter W, X, Y, Z: condensed cross-references to the main entries

The index also includes the sections covering the first volume (Letters A through K), appended at the end, making the index in Vol. II a complete reference tool for the entire work.

sources/postlethwayt-universal-dictionar.content:
Postlethwayt — The Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce (4th ed., 1774)
Author: Malachy Postlethwayt (1707–1767)
Title: The Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce: With Large Additions and Improvements, Adapting the Same to the Present State of British Affairs in America, Since the Last Treaty of Peace Made in the Year 1763. With Great Variety of New Remarks and Illustrations Incorporated Throughout the Whole: Together with Everything Essential that is Contained in Savary’s Dictionary; Also, All the Material Laws of Trade and Navigation Relating to these Kingdoms, and the Customs and Usages to which all Traders are Subject
Edition: Fourth edition, printed for W. Strahan, J. and F. Rivington, J. Hinton, et al. (London), 1774
Format: Two folio volumes
OCLC: (multiple editions; 4th ed. OCLC varies)
Raw text:

Vol. I (A–K) (273,340 lines, ~12 MB)
Vol. II (L–Z) (236,020 lines, ~10.7 MB)


Summary
Postlethwayt’s Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce was the first comprehensive English commercial dictionary, published originally in 1751–1755 and modelled in part on Savary’s Dictionnaire universel de commerce (1723–1730). This fourth edition, published seven years after Postlethwayt’s death, represents the culmination of his life’s work — a massive reference work covering every aspect of British and international trade, manufacturing, commercial law, navigation, colonial administration, and economic policy. The list of 22 London booksellers who published this edition attests to its commercial importance, and Adam Smith cited the work in The Wealth of Nations.
The dictionary is far more than an alphabetical reference. It opens with an extensive “A General Idea of the Contents” — a ~100-section prospectus covering the entire scope of commercial knowledge, functioning almost as an independent treatise. Throughout the text, Postlethwayt weaves policy analysis, historical data, comparative commercial law (especially French edicts and arrêts), and practical guidance for merchants and manufacturers. The introduction also contains a remarkable philosophical essay on the relationship between commerce, civilisation, and national character.
The fourth edition is particularly valuable because it was updated to reflect the territorial changes of the Treaty of Paris (1763). Postlethwayt’s method was to retain his pre-war observations and add post-war remarks alongside them, enabling the reader “to judge from plain facts, the natural deductions drawn therefrom, of the different state and condition of the commerce and territories of the diverse powers concerned in the last war."

"A General Idea of the Contents” (Vol. I, front matter)
An extended analytical table of contents covering approximately 100 numbered sections that functions as an independent economic treatise. The full sequence, with Postlethwayt’s original numbering:
Purpose of the work (nos. 1–12): The dictionary is compiled to answer the following purposes — the peculiar benefit and advantage of British traders in general, from the supreme merchant to every subordinate class; for persons of distinction desirous of a political knowledge of trade; for those who would master the nature and constitution of the finances; for those who would acquire a knowledge of the political systems of commerce throughout the world; for those who would be acquainted with commercial and marine treaties between nations.
Commercial policy and imperial relations (nos. 13–25): Concerning the commercial policy of states relative to the mechanical and manufactural arts; the mutual advantage of Great Britain and her American plantations in diverse lights; the reciprocal benefit of Great Britain and Ireland; the landed and trading interests harmonized; the monied interest considered in various important views as compared with the landed and trading, including “reductions of interest, of stockjobbing, bubbling, and gaming, the destruction of trade and traders.”
Public finance and taxation (nos. 26–39): The constitution of trading and monied corporations, their use and abuse; the immensity of the national debts and tax-incumbrances, and “their destructive consequences to the trade of the kingdom, if not speedily prevented”; the qualifications of the British senator; the commercial constitution of parliament; the pernicious consequence of taxes on native commodities; the revenue from the Conquest to the reign of George III.
Trade theory and practice (nos. 40–57): Of importation and exportation in a practical and political light; the balance of trade; augmentation and diminution of coin; the several societies for the discovery of new arts, trades, and manufactures and their progress; the utility of the Royal Society to trade; the jurisdiction of the admiralty relative to commercial concerns; the office of ambassadors, residents, and consuls in foreign states; the computation of annuities on lives, leases, and reversions; commercial arithmetic and the foreign exchanges and their arbitration.
Banking, coinage, and credit (nos. 58–62): The new Mercantile College for training of young British merchants, and a new institution for the education of young persons of distinction for parliamentary business; the constitution of the several banks throughout Europe with illustrations; the standard of gold and silver throughout Europe with the intrinsic value of foreign coins; of trading in bullion, gold, and silver to advantage.
Marine affairs and insurance (nos. 63–73): Of insurances of shipping and merchandise, with “great variety of curious cases” and “the political discussion of the point of injuring the ships and merchandise of enemies in time of war”; foreign weights and measures; the laws, customs, and usages of merchants regarding foreign and inland bills of exchange; of freight, bills of lading, masters and owners of ships, charter parties, averages, barratries, bottomry, shipwrecks, demurrage, and the laws relating thereto; an ample representation of the business of the custom-house and its several departments; the Act of Navigation; an account of the foreign shipping frequenting the ports of England.
London and the commercial metropolis (nos. 74–81): The superior importance of the city of London as the trading metropolis; its commercial connections over the whole kingdom and its mercantile interest over the world; the supreme dignity of London as a corporation, showing “that the greatest families in the kingdom originally sprang from our trading citizens”; concerning the bad policy of want of harmony between the court and the city; anecdotes of the distinguishing services to the state of eminent citizens of London.
Comparative French commercial regulation (nos. 82–92): All the various material French edicts, arrêts, and laws extracted from Savary; the peculiar regulations of the French trading corporations; the strictness of their corporations in requiring proof of qualification by performance of a “masterpiece of workmanship”; their vigilance to manufacture goods of the best quality for foreign markets; Colbert’s wise and political measures while superintendent of the commerce and navigation of France.
Circulation and credit (nos. 93–94): On the circulating cash requisite to carry on the trade of a nation; the nature and effect of paper credit in commercial states and empires.
Coinage and metallurgy (nos. 95–102): The par and equation between gold and silver; Sir Isaac Newton’s representation upon the necessity of lowering the price of guineas from 31s 6d to 21s; the state of the coin and coinage of England from the Revolution to George III; the practical arts of assaying gold and silver; the art of assaying gold and silver from their ores, together with “the knowledge of all metallurgical operations to judge of mines and minerals of every kind”; of subterranean treasures and the art of mineralogy.
Natural productions and philosophy (nos. 103–113): Concerning the vegetable productions of nature as the great objects of traffic throughout the world, geographically and commercially described; variety of philosophical experiments to judge of the quality of natural productions; the productions of art reflecting great variety of capital commodities and manufactures, to whet the invention of British artists; the judges, inspectors, and overseers of the manufactures of France and the woollen manufactories of Great Britain, “which are shamefully neglected.”
World commerce (nos. 114–125): Colbert’s system; public fairs and caravans throughout Europe, Asia, and Africa; the commerce of the Chinese and the East-Indies in general; “the excessive cheapness of their arts, manufactures, and produce” and how all European nations are attracted to trade with them; the peculiarities of the Turkey, Arabian, and Persian trades; the African trade and the inland trade; monopolies in general.
Political arithmetic and public debt (nos. 126–140): Political arithmetic and its application to commercial affairs and finances; the funds of Great Britain; the consequences of “the destructive practice of funding and borrowing in times of war”; the injurious effects of becoming tributaries to foreigners by reason of the magnitude of the national debt; the excessive dearness of all English commodities and manufactures occasioned by taxes — “the principal cause of this nation being undersold at all the markets in Europe, by the French and Dutch”; the connection between dear English commodities and universal smuggling.
The great ends of the work (nos. 141–148): That the commercial grievances of England daily increase and the chief causes seem unattended to; that the performance is intended to suggest variety of ways and means whereby the commercial grievances may be relieved; that one great end is to promote “a happy and lasting Commercial Union between Great Britain and her American colonies at this critical juncture” (1774 — on the eve of the American Revolution); that the author conceives the nation cannot be of more service than “starting a design to save it the future expense of engaging in the Continental Wars of Europe, since they have hitherto contributed so greatly to the enhancement of taxes upon our trade in general.”

The Introduction: Commerce, Civilisation, and National Character
The introduction that follows the “General Idea” is a remarkable philosophical essay in its own right — running over 100 lines and covering the relationship between trade, industry, and national greatness through the lens of world history:
The moral foundations of commerce: Postlethwayt argues that “the exercise of trade and commerce is the soul of the whole British empire” and that “the arduous industry of traders [is] productive of the prosperity of the kingdom.” He draws a direct line from the diligence of commercial citizens to the greatness of the state — “commercial vigilance, activity, and industry, cannot be too much encouraged and inculcated.”
Historical warnings against luxury: A sweeping historical survey traces the fall of great empires to idleness and luxury: the Assyrian monarchy degenerating “into a libidinous and intemperate course of life” until conquered by Cyrus; the Persian monarchy “over-run with ease, luxury, and riot”; Alexander the Great who “no sooner devoted himself to pleasures, and to softer himself in idleness and immoderate excess” than he became “the scorn and contempt of his own soldiers”; the Roman monarchy, where the Turks “who had been constantly inured to hardships and perpetual toil, found the others a people uneasy with their plenty”; and even the Ottoman empire, where Mahomet himself “enjoined it as a law, which even their very emperors were not to be exempted from — namely, to eat no more than the labour of his hands could purchase every day.”
Commerce as the measure of civilisation: Postlethwayt asks pointedly: “What would our gentry, our nobility, or our sovereign be better than those of Barbary, was it not for our superiority of traffic and navigation?” He argues that commerce civilises — the Africans themselves could be “gradually nurtured in all the arts of humanity” through trade rather than slavery, and the failure to develop the African interior trade is one of Britain’s great missed opportunities: “What avails the insignificant advantage we have received by driving the French out of the river Senegal, in comparison to the great and important designs that have been proposed by the author, to enlarge and extend the whole of that commerce in times of peace?”
The nobility, gentry, and the ruling class: A substantial section of the introduction is devoted to the role of the landed aristocracy in commercial society. Postlethwayt relates the remarkable true story of a young German nobleman who, when asked by his prospective father-in-law what trade he had to support his daughter, was told “never to marry his daughter, though his heir, and would have two such great estates, but to a man that had a Manual Trade, by which he might subsist, if drove from his own country.” The young lord learned basket-making in six months and later, when the wars of the Palatinate drove both families from their estates, maintained both his father-in-law and his own family in Holland by making “white twig baskets” of such excellence that they became a general fashion. Postlethwayt uses this story to contrast German and English practices: “amongst their nobility, the younger of whole families are employed in their armies, there is rarely found one of them destitute of some manual art.”
The English gentry and experimental philosophy: Postlethwayt quotes extensively from Bishop Spratt’s History of the Royal Society to argue that the English nobility and gentry should devote themselves to practical and experimental philosophy. Their country seats, “being removed from the tumult of cities, give them the best opportunity and freedom of observation.” Their hospitality and “familiar way of conversing with their neighbourhood will always supply them with intelligence.” He urges: “When a general turn for the useful inventions, in regard to trade, has once taken root among our nobility and gentry, let them go on to the other kinds, which purpose the striking out of new mechanics.” This is a direct appeal to the landed class to become active participants in the commercial and technological improvement of the nation, not rentiers living off their estates.
The introduction concludes with a passage from Spratt about English naval power: “the English greatness will never be supported or increased in this age by any other wars but those by sea.” This maritime destiny places a special burden on the gentry and nobility to “enlighten and adorn” while “the other defend it.”

The City of London: Trading Metropolis, Corporation, and Livery Companies
The dictionary treats the City of London as a subject of extraordinary importance — no other English city or institution receives comparable treatment. The “General Idea of the Contents” devotes seven numbered sections (73–81) to the City, covering every dimension of its commercial and political power.
London as the Trading Metropolis
Postlethwayt describes “the superior importance of the city of London, as the trading metropolis” and its “commercial connections of its tradesmen and citizens over the whole kingdom, as well as its mercantile interest over the world.” The City’s significance is not merely economic — it exercises “the great influence of the trading citizens over the nation, on all state emergencies.” This is a political argument: the commercial classes of London are a national force whose weight is felt in war, finance, and the making of policy.
The Supreme Dignity of London as a Corporation
Postlethwayt asserts “the supreme dignity of London, as a corporation,” showing “that the greatest families in the kingdom originally sprang from our trading citizens, who have distinguished themselves as its chief magistrates.” This is a pointed argument about the social prestige of commerce: the greatest aristocratic families of England trace their origins to London merchants who served as Lord Mayor. Trade is not a demeaning occupation but the very source of the nation’s elite.
The Court and the City
A distinctive political argument appears in the warning against “the bad policy of want of harmony between the court and the city.” Postlethwayt emphasises “the weight the city has given, and ever will give, to the conduct of government, both at home and abroad, in support of the national power and dignity.” This reflects the concrete political reality of 18th-century London: the City’s financial power (controlling the national debt, the Bank of England, and the East India Company) gave it leverage over the Crown and ministry that no other interest could match. The dictionary includes “anecdotes of the distinguishing services to the state of many eminent citizens of London in commercial affairs.”
The Livery Companies: The Great Twelve
The COMPANIES entry in Vol. I provides a complete historical catalogue of the livery companies of the City of London, beginning with the principal twelve — their incorporation dates, founding monarchs, and the trades they represent:

The Mercers (1393, Richard II) — “though then trading for the most part in stuffs of the native growth,” permitted to purchase £20 per annum in lands
The Grocers (1345, Edward III) — “called pepperers before,” greatly inferior to what they now are at the time of incorporation
The Drapers (1630, Henry VI) — “for the most part woollen,” a fraternity from Edward III’s time when he promoted the woollen manufacture by admitting Flemings and other nations “the free use of manual operation within his dominions, that so his subjects might learn the craft”
The Fishmongers (united 1536, Henry VIII) — formerly two companies (stock-fishmongers and salt-fishmongers), “a vocation no less advantageous to this kingdom by their encouragement of the fishing trade”
The Goldsmiths (Richard III) — “an ancient craft, for formerly those that sold worked likewise their own plate”
The Skinners (1327, Edward III) — “first year of the reign,” made a brotherhood in Richard III’s reign
The Merchant Taylors (1501, Henry VII) — formerly called “taylors and linnen-armourers,” first patent of arms 1480
The Haberdashers (1447, Henry VI) — “formerly so called,” incorporated a brotherhood of St Catherine
The Salters (1530, Henry VIII) — “a company of good esteem”
The Ironmongers (1462, Edward IV) — incorporated when “the mines of our nation much improved”
The Vintners (Edward III) — “formerly called wine tunners,” incorporated after Edward III conquered Normandy and “by that means engrossed most of the French vintage”
The Clothworkers (Henry VIII) — incorporation time uncertain

The Remaining City Companies
